Section 9 of 93

Route 53 and DNS in AWS

5 concepts · about 50 minutes

DNS is the control plane of traffic. In AWS, Route 53 provides authoritative zones, health-based routing and the resolver that every VPC uses.

Goals
  • Create public and private hosted zones and choose the right record type
  • Pick a routing policy for failover, latency, weighted or geographic needs
  • Use Route 53 Resolver endpoints to join AWS and on-premises DNS
9.1

Hosted zones and records

In plain words

A hosted zone holds the DNS records for a domain. A public zone answers anyone on the internet; a private zone answers only inside the VPCs you associate.

The problem it solves

You need names for your services that you control, with an API, and the ability to give internal services names that never leak outside.

What it does

  • Common records: A, AAAA, CNAME, MX, TXT, NS, SRV, CAA.
  • Alias records point at AWS resources (ALB, NLB, CloudFront, S3 website, API Gateway, another record) and work at the zone apex, which a CNAME cannot. Queries to alias records for AWS targets are free; check pricing.
  • After registering or delegating, point the registrar's NS records at the four name servers of the hosted zone.
  • Hosted zones are charged monthly plus per query; check the current pricing.

Create a zone and alias

hcldns.tf
resource "aws_route53_zone" "public" {
  name = "example.com"
}

resource "aws_route53_record" "app" {
  zone_id = aws_route53_zone.public.zone_id
  name    = "app.example.com"
  type    = "A"
  alias {
    name                   = aws_lb.web.dns_name
    zone_id                = aws_lb.web.zone_id
    evaluate_target_health = true
  }
}
bashInspect
aws route53 list-hosted-zones --query 'HostedZones[].[Name,Id,Config.PrivateZone]' --output table
aws route53 list-resource-record-sets --hosted-zone-id Z0123456789ABC --query 'ResourceRecordSets[?Type==`A`].[Name,AliasTarget.DNSName]'
dig +short NS example.com
Check yourself
Why use an alias instead of a CNAME at the zone apex?

A CNAME cannot coexist with the other apex records (SOA, NS); an alias is answered as an A or AAAA record and can sit at the apex.

9.2

Routing policies

In plain words

A routing policy decides which answer Route 53 gives when several records share a name.

The problem it solves

A single static answer cannot shift traffic during a failure, a rollout, or between Regions.

What it does

  • Simple: one or more values, returned together.
  • Weighted: split traffic by weight, for gradual rollouts and testing.
  • Latency: answer with the Region giving the lowest latency to the user.
  • Failover: primary and secondary, driven by a health check.
  • Geolocation and Geoproximity: by user location (country, continent) or with a bias; useful for data residency.
  • IP-based: by client CIDR. Multivalue answer: up to eight healthy records.

Weighted canary

hclweighted.tf
resource "aws_route53_record" "blue" {
  zone_id        = aws_route53_zone.public.zone_id
  name           = "api.example.com"
  type           = "CNAME"
  ttl            = 60
  set_identifier = "blue"
  records        = ["blue.example.com"]
  weighted_routing_policy {
    weight = 95
  }
}

resource "aws_route53_record" "green" {
  zone_id        = aws_route53_zone.public.zone_id
  name           = "api.example.com"
  type           = "CNAME"
  ttl            = 60
  set_identifier = "green"
  records        = ["green.example.com"]
  weighted_routing_policy {
    weight = 5
  }
}
9.3

Health checks and failover

In plain words

Route 53 health checks probe an endpoint from several locations and mark it healthy or not. Records tied to a failing check are removed from answers.

The problem it solves

DNS would keep sending users to a dead endpoint without a signal about its state.

What it does

  • Types: endpoint (HTTP, HTTPS, TCP), calculated (combine others) and CloudWatch alarm based (for private resources that Route 53 cannot reach directly).
  • Evaluate target health on alias records to inherit the health of the ALB/NLB targets.
  • Clients cache by TTL, so keep TTLs short (for example 60 seconds) on failover records. Some resolvers ignore low TTLs.
  • Failover is only as good as the check: test a meaningful path such as /healthz that exercises dependencies, but avoid making it so strict that a minor dependency outage drops the whole site.

Failover records

bashCreate a health check
aws route53 create-health-check --caller-reference "api-primary-$(date +%s)" \
  --health-check-config Type=HTTPS,FullyQualifiedDomainName=api-primary.example.com,Port=443,ResourcePath=/healthz,RequestInterval=30,FailureThreshold=3
aws route53 get-health-check-status --health-check-id 11111111-2222-3333-4444-555555555555
Check yourself
Why keep a low TTL on failover records?

Resolvers cache answers for the TTL, so a long TTL delays clients moving to the secondary.

9.4

Private hosted zones

In plain words

A private hosted zone serves DNS names only to the VPCs associated with it, such as db.internal.example.com.

The problem it solves

Internal services need stable names, and you do not want to publish them or their IPs on the internet.

What it does

  • VPC must have enableDnsSupport and enableDnsHostnames turned on.
  • Can be associated with VPCs in other accounts and Regions (authorise first, then associate).
  • Split-horizon: the same name can exist in a public and a private zone with different answers; inside associated VPCs the private zone wins.
  • Interface endpoint private DNS and EKS private cluster endpoints use private zones under the hood.

Create and associate

bashPrivate zone across accounts
aws route53 create-hosted-zone --name internal.example.com --caller-reference "internal-$(date +%s)" \
  --vpc VPCRegion=eu-west-1,VPCId=vpc-0123456789abcdef0
# in the zone-owning account, authorise another account's VPC
aws route53 create-vpc-association-authorization --hosted-zone-id Z0123456789ABC --vpc VPCRegion=eu-west-1,VPCId=vpc-0bbb
# in the other account, accept
aws route53 associate-vpc-with-hosted-zone --hosted-zone-id Z0123456789ABC --vpc VPCRegion=eu-west-1,VPCId=vpc-0bbb
9.5

Route 53 Resolver

In plain words

The Route 53 Resolver is the DNS server every VPC already has at the VPC base address plus two (for example 10.20.0.2) and at 169.254.169.253. Resolver endpoints connect it with on-premises DNS.

The problem it solves

On-premises servers must resolve AWS private names, and VPC workloads must resolve corporate names.

What it does

  • Inbound endpoint: ENIs in your VPC that on-premises DNS can forward to.
  • Outbound endpoint plus forwarding rules: send queries for chosen domains (for example corp.example.com) to on-premises servers. Share rules with AWS RAM to many accounts.
  • Resolver DNS Firewall filters outbound queries by domain lists.
  • Per-ENI query limit exists (check the current quota); heavy DNS from pods can hit it, so run CoreDNS caching and consider NodeLocal DNSCache.

Forwarding rule

hclresolver.tf
resource "aws_route53_resolver_rule" "corp" {
  domain_name          = "corp.example.com"
  rule_type            = "FORWARD"
  resolver_endpoint_id = aws_route53_resolver_endpoint.out.id
  target_ip {
    ip = "192.168.10.10"
  }
}
Tip

Debug from a pod with kubectl exec -it dnsutils -- dig +short db.internal.example.com and compare against dig @169.254.169.253 from a node.

DNS for Kubernetes on AWS
OptionExternalDNS with Route 53
Choose whenIngress and Service hostnames managed from the cluster
Avoid whennames must be created by a separate process
OptionManual records
Choose whena handful of stable names
Avoid whenfrequent app changes
OptionPrivate zone plus Resolver rules
Choose whenhybrid internal naming
Avoid whenpublic-only services

Section 10 of 93

IPv6 and reference VPC designs

4 concepts · about 40 minutes

IPv4 addresses are scarce and billed. IPv6 solves the scale problem, and a reference design ties together everything in this section.

Goals
  • Enable IPv6 and dual-stack subnets and understand egress-only gateways
  • Explain why EKS IPv6 clusters avoid pod IP exhaustion
  • Apply a reference VPC design with a checklist for production
10.1

IPv6 in a VPC

In plain words

IPv6 addresses are 128 bits long and globally unique. AWS gives a VPC a /56 block, and each subnet gets a /64.

The problem it solves

Large container platforms run out of private IPv4 addresses, overlap between networks, and pay for public IPv4 addresses.

What it does

  • Add an Amazon-provided IPv6 CIDR (or bring your own via IPAM) to the VPC and subnets. Every IPv6 address is public by routing design; privacy comes from security groups and routes.
  • Dual-stack subnets support IPv4 and IPv6; IPv6-only subnets exist for some workloads.
  • Outbound-only IPv6 from private subnets uses an egress-only internet gateway; no NAT is needed.
  • DNS64 and NAT64 let IPv6-only workloads reach IPv4-only services through a NAT gateway.

Enable on a VPC

bashDual stack
aws ec2 associate-vpc-cidr-block --vpc-id vpc-0123456789abcdef0 --amazon-provided-ipv6-cidr-block
aws ec2 create-egress-only-internet-gateway --vpc-id vpc-0123456789abcdef0
aws ec2 create-route --route-table-id rtb-0123456789abcdef0 --destination-ipv6-cidr-block ::/0 \
  --egress-only-internet-gateway-id eigw-0123456789abcdef0
Check yourself
How do private subnets get IPv6 outbound access without inbound?

Route ::/0 to an egress-only internet gateway.

10.2

IPv6 and EKS

In plain words

An EKS cluster can be created in IPv6 mode, where pods receive IPv6 addresses and nodes keep IPv4 for the control plane path.

The problem it solves

IPv4 pod addressing runs out of IPs in busy clusters, and secondary CIDR tricks add complexity.

What it does

  • Choose the IP family at cluster creation (ipFamily: ipv6); it cannot be changed later.
  • Each node gets a prefix of IPv6 addresses for its pods; there is no per-ENI IP limit on pods.
  • Pods reach IPv4 services through host-local IPv4 addresses via NAT-like behaviour of the VPC CNI.
  • Requires dual-stack subnets and a supported set of add-ons; confirm the current constraints in the EKS user guide before committing.

Create an IPv6 cluster

yamleksctl-ipv6.yaml
apiVersion: eksctl.io/v1alpha5
kind: ClusterConfig
metadata:
  name: prod-ipv6
  region: eu-west-1
  version: "1.37"
kubernetesNetworkConfig:
  ipFamily: IPv6
addons:
  - name: vpc-cni
  - name: coredns
  - name: kube-proxy
iam:
  withOIDC: true
managedNodeGroups:
  - name: ng-1
    instanceType: m6i.large
    desiredCapacity: 3
Note

Check the supported Kubernetes versions in EKS before using a version number from an example.

10.3

Reference three-tier VPC

In plain words

A common production layout uses three AZs, with public, private and isolated subnets in each, one NAT gateway per AZ and endpoints for AWS services.

The problem it solves

Teams reinvent the same layout with small variations that later hinder peering, inspection and audits.

What it does

  • /16 per VPC from IPAM; /24 public subnets; large private subnets for nodes and pods; /26 or /24 isolated subnets for databases; small subnets for TGW attachments.
  • Gateway endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB, interface endpoints for ECR, STS, logs and others.
  • Flow logs to S3, DNS query logging, default security group stripped of rules.
  • Spoke to TGW; inspection and egress in shared network account.

Community module usage

hclvpc-module.tf
module "vpc" {
  source  = "terraform-aws-modules/vpc/aws"
  version = "~> 5.0"

  name = "prod"
  cidr = "10.20.0.0/16"
  azs  = ["eu-west-1a", "eu-west-1b", "eu-west-1c"]

  public_subnets   = ["10.20.0.0/24", "10.20.1.0/24", "10.20.2.0/24"]
  private_subnets  = ["10.20.32.0/19", "10.20.64.0/19", "10.20.96.0/19"]
  database_subnets = ["10.20.10.0/26", "10.20.10.64/26", "10.20.10.128/26"]

  enable_nat_gateway     = true
  one_nat_gateway_per_az = true
  enable_dns_hostnames   = true

  public_subnet_tags  = { "kubernetes.io/role/elb" = "1" }
  private_subnet_tags = { "kubernetes.io/role/internal-elb" = "1" }
}
Check yourself
Where should databases live in this design?

In isolated subnets with no route to an internet or NAT gateway.

10.4

Production VPC checklist

In plain words

A short list to review before an environment goes live.

The problem it solves

Network mistakes are slow and risky to fix after workloads depend on them.

What it does

  • CIDR unique and registered; room for growth; pod IP strategy decided.
  • At least two AZs (three for quorum systems); NAT per AZ; route tables explicit.
  • Endpoints for S3 and heavy AWS services; endpoint policies where data perimeters matter.
  • Flow logs, Route 53 Resolver query logs and a plan for Reachability Analyzer.
  • Security groups reference groups; no 0.0.0.0/0 on admin ports; Session Manager instead of SSH.
  • IaC for everything, with drift detection.

Guardrail script

bashSpot-check open admin ports
aws ec2 describe-security-groups \
  --filters Name=ip-permission.from-port,Values=22,3389 Name=ip-permission.cidr,Values=0.0.0.0/0 \
  --query 'SecurityGroups[].[GroupId,GroupName,VpcId]' --output table
aws ec2 describe-vpc-endpoints --query 'length(VpcEndpoints)'
aws ec2 describe-flow-logs --query 'FlowLogs[].[ResourceId,LogDestinationType,FlowLogStatus]' --output table

Section 11 of 93

EC2 instance families and the Nitro system

6 concepts · about 40 minutes

EC2 gives you virtual machines. Every EKS node, many databases and most build agents are EC2 instances, so choosing and sizing them well affects both cost and reliability.

Goals
  • Read an instance type name and pick a family for a workload
  • Explain what Nitro changes for performance and security
  • Choose between x86, Graviton and accelerated instances
11.1

Reading an instance type

In plain words

A name like m7g.2xlarge encodes the family (m), generation (7), extra attributes (g) and size (2xlarge).

The problem it solves

There are hundreds of types. Without the naming scheme you cannot compare them or search quickly.

What it does

  • Family letter: t burstable, m general purpose, c compute, r memory, x large memory, i storage, p/g GPU, inf/trn ML accelerators.
  • Attribute letters: g Graviton (Arm), a AMD, i Intel, d local NVMe disk, n enhanced networking, e extra memory or storage, flex flexible price/performance.
  • Size doubles resources at each step: large, xlarge, 2xlarge, 4xlarge and so on, then metal for bare metal.
  • Use describe-instance-types for vCPU, memory, network and EBS limits instead of memorising them.

Query types

bashFind candidates
aws ec2 describe-instance-types --filters Name=vcpu-info.default-vcpus,Values=4 Name=memory-info.size-in-mib,Values=16384 \
  --query 'InstanceTypes[].[InstanceType,NetworkInfo.NetworkPerformance,ProcessorInfo.SupportedArchitectures[0]]' --output table | head -20
aws ec2 describe-instance-types --instance-types m7g.2xlarge \
  --query 'InstanceTypes[0].[VCpuInfo.DefaultVCpus,MemoryInfo.SizeInMiB,EbsInfo.EbsOptimizedInfo.MaximumBandwidthInMbps,NetworkInfo.MaximumNetworkInterfaces,NetworkInfo.Ipv4AddressesPerInterface]'
Check yourself
What does the g in m7g mean?

The instance uses an AWS Graviton (Arm) processor.

11.2

Choosing a family

In plain words

Match the bottleneck of your workload to the family: CPU, memory, storage speed or GPU.

The problem it solves

Oversizing wastes money; undersizing causes throttling and latency.

What it does

  • General purpose (m): balanced; default for many web and Kubernetes nodes.
  • Compute (c): CPU-bound services, batch, encoding, high request rates.
  • Memory (r, x): caches, in-memory databases, JVM-heavy services.
  • Storage (i, d): local NVMe for databases and search with high IOPS.
  • Accelerated (p, g, inf, trn): ML training, inference, graphics.
  • Burstable (t): low baseline with credits; good for dev and idle services. With unlimited mode extra CPU is billed.

Measure first

bashSee what you use
aws cloudwatch get-metric-statistics --namespace AWS/EC2 --metric-name CPUUtilization \
  --dimensions Name=InstanceId,Value=i-0123456789abcdef0 --statistics Average Maximum \
  --start-time "$(date -u -v-7d +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)" --end-time "$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)" --period 3600 | head -30
aws compute-optimizer get-ec2-instance-recommendations --query 'instanceRecommendations[].[instanceArn,finding]' --output table | head
Tip

Compute Optimizer (opt in) gives right-sizing recommendations from CloudWatch data.

11.3

The Nitro system

In plain words

Nitro is the AWS hypervisor and hardware platform. Dedicated Nitro cards handle networking, storage and management, leaving almost all of the host CPU to your instance.

The problem it solves

Older virtualisation shared host CPU with the hypervisor and I/O emulation, causing overhead and jitter, and giving the hypervisor access to your memory.

What it does

  • Nitro cards offload VPC networking, EBS and instance storage encryption, and monitoring.
  • Nitro Security Chip locks down firmware; AWS operators have no technical means to access instance memory.
  • Enables bare metal (.metal) instances and consistent performance.
  • Nitro Enclaves carve out an isolated VM with no network, storage or admin access for processing secrets.
  • Most current generations are Nitro based; some older types are not.

Check hypervisor

bashOn an instance
curl -s -H "X-aws-ec2-metadata-token: $(curl -s -X PUT http://169.254.169.254/latest/api/token -H 'X-aws-ec2-metadata-token-ttl-seconds: 60')" \
  http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/instance-type
ls /sys/devices/virtual/dmi/id/ && cat /sys/devices/virtual/dmi/id/sys_vendor
aws ec2 describe-instance-types --instance-types c7i.large --query 'InstanceTypes[0].Hypervisor'
Check yourself
What does Nitro give besides speed?

Hardware-enforced isolation, no operator access to instance memory, bare metal options and Enclaves.

11.4

Graviton and processor choices

In plain words

Graviton instances use Arm processors designed by AWS. They usually offer better price per performance, but need Arm-compatible binaries and images.

The problem it solves

x86 instances are the default but cost more for the same throughput in many workloads.

What it does

  • Containers must be built for linux/arm64; use multi-arch images (docker buildx --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64).
  • Interpreted languages and Java usually run unchanged; native dependencies need arm64 builds.
  • Mixed node groups can run both architectures; schedule with kubernetes.io/arch node selectors.
  • Test and measure with your own workload; the saving varies.

Multi-arch build and scheduling

bashBuild both architectures
docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 -t 111122223333.dkr.ecr.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/shop:1.0 --push .
kubectl get nodes -L kubernetes.io/arch,node.kubernetes.io/instance-type
yamlPin to Graviton nodes
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: shop
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels: {app: shop}
  template:
    metadata:
      labels: {app: shop}
    spec:
      nodeSelector:
        kubernetes.io/arch: arm64
      containers:
        - name: shop
          image: 111122223333.dkr.ecr.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/shop:1.0
11.5

CPU, vCPU and burstable credits

In plain words

A vCPU is a hardware thread (usually half a core on x86 with hyperthreading; a full core on Graviton). Burstable t instances earn credits when idle and spend them when busy.

The problem it solves

Credit exhaustion silently throttles a t instance to its baseline, appearing as unexplained slowness.

What it does

  • CPUCreditBalance and CPUSurplusCreditBalance metrics show the state; CPUUtilization can mislead because it is relative to the credited share.
  • unlimited mode lets the instance burn beyond credits for a charge; standard throttles.
  • For steady workloads use m or c families rather than a large t.
  • Dedicated Hosts and Instances exist for licensing or compliance; check the pricing and use cases.

Watch credits

bashCredit metric
aws cloudwatch get-metric-statistics --namespace AWS/EC2 --metric-name CPUCreditBalance \
  --dimensions Name=InstanceId,Value=i-0123456789abcdef0 --statistics Minimum \
  --start-time "$(date -u -v-1d +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)" --end-time "$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)" --period 3600
aws ec2 describe-instance-credit-specifications --instance-ids i-0123456789abcdef0
Check yourself
Why can a t3 instance suddenly become slow?

Its CPU credit balance reached zero, so it is held at baseline performance.

11.6

Instance lifecycle and metadata

In plain words

An instance moves through pending, running, stopping, stopped, and terminated states. The instance metadata service describes it from the inside.

The problem it solves

Stop, hibernate, reboot and terminate behave differently regarding data, IP addresses and billing, and surprises cause data loss.

What it does

  • Stop: instance store data is lost, EBS volumes persist, public IPv4 changes unless an Elastic IP is attached; no instance-hour charge but EBS still billed.
  • Terminate: root volume deleted by default (DeleteOnTermination). Enable termination protection on critical hosts.
  • Hibernate saves RAM to an encrypted root volume (supported types only).
  • Metadata paths: instance-id, placement/availability-zone, iam/security-credentials/, spot/instance-action; user data at /latest/user-data.

Operate

bashLifecycle commands
aws ec2 stop-instances --instance-ids i-0123456789abcdef0
aws ec2 start-instances --instance-ids i-0123456789abcdef0
aws ec2 modify-instance-attribute --instance-id i-0123456789abcdef0 --disable-api-termination
aws ec2 describe-instances --instance-ids i-0123456789abcdef0 --query 'Reservations[].Instances[].[State.Name,PrivateIpAddress,PublicIpAddress]'
Careful

Instance store data is lost on stop and terminate, and when the underlying host fails. Never keep the only copy of data there.

← PreviousNext →
Section 12 of 93

EBS, instance store and instance networking

5 concepts · about 50 minutes

Storage and network limits decide how an instance really performs. They also explain many Kubernetes surprises, such as pod-per-node limits and slow volume attach.

Goals
  • Choose an EBS volume type and set size, IOPS and throughput correctly
  • Take and manage snapshots, encryption and fast restore
  • Explain ENIs, ENA, EFA and the limits that bound a node's pods and bandwidth
12.1

EBS volume types

In plain words

Amazon EBS is network-attached block storage that persists independently of the instance. You pick a volume type by the performance profile you need.

The problem it solves

Using the wrong type either wastes money (provisioned IOPS for a log disk) or throttles a database.

What it does

  • gp3 (SSD, general purpose): baseline 3,000 IOPS and 125 MiB/s regardless of size, and you can raise IOPS and throughput independently. Default choice. Check current maximums.
  • gp2: older, IOPS tied to size with burst credits; migrate to gp3.
  • io2 / io2 Block Express: provisioned IOPS, high durability, for latency-sensitive databases.
  • st1 / sc1 (HDD): throughput-oriented, cheap sequential workloads; cannot be boot volumes.
  • Volume is in one AZ and attaches to instances in that AZ only (Multi-Attach only on io1/io2 with restrictions).

gp3 in Terraform and resizing

hclebs.tf
resource "aws_ebs_volume" "data" {
  availability_zone = "eu-west-1a"
  size              = 200
  type              = "gp3"
  iops              = 6000
  throughput        = 250
  encrypted         = true
  kms_key_id        = aws_kms_key.ebs.arn
}
bashModify live
aws ec2 modify-volume --volume-id vol-0123456789abcdef0 --size 300 --iops 8000 --throughput 300
aws ec2 describe-volumes-modifications --volume-ids vol-0123456789abcdef0 --query 'VolumesModifications[].[ModificationState,Progress]'
sudo growpart /dev/nvme1n1 1 && sudo xfs_growfs -d /mnt/data   # extend partition and filesystem
Check yourself
How does gp3 differ from gp2 for performance?

gp3 has a fixed baseline and lets you provision IOPS and throughput independently of size; gp2 ties IOPS to size.

12.2

Instance limits on storage throughput

In plain words

Each instance type has its own maximum EBS bandwidth and IOPS. A fast volume on a small instance is capped by the instance.

The problem it solves

Teams buy io2 volumes and get no improvement because the instance limit is lower than the volume.

What it does

  • Effective IOPS = min(volume limit, instance limit). Check EbsInfo from describe-instance-types.
  • Some smaller types have burst bandwidth for limited time; sustained numbers are lower.
  • CloudWatch VolumeQueueLength, VolumeThroughputPercentage, and the instance-level EBSReadOps and EBSIOBalance% show saturation.
  • On Linux, iostat -x 1 shows await and %util.

Check limits

bashCompare
aws ec2 describe-instance-types --instance-types m7g.large m7g.4xlarge \
  --query 'InstanceTypes[].[InstanceType,EbsInfo.EbsOptimizedInfo.BaselineIops,EbsInfo.EbsOptimizedInfo.MaximumIops,EbsInfo.EbsOptimizedInfo.BaselineBandwidthInMbps]' --output table
iostat -x 1 3
12.3

Snapshots, encryption and fast restore

In plain words

A snapshot is a point-in-time copy of a volume stored in S3-managed storage. Only changed blocks are saved after the first one.

The problem it solves

You need backups, a way to copy data between AZs and Regions, and a template for new volumes.

What it does

  • Snapshots are incremental, crash-consistent. For databases quiesce first or use application-level backups.
  • Automate with Data Lifecycle Manager or AWS Backup; copy to another account or Region for disaster recovery.
  • Encryption uses KMS; turn on EBS encryption by default per Region in each account. Encrypted snapshots can be shared only with a customer managed key.
  • New volumes load data lazily from snapshots; fast snapshot restore removes the first-read latency (extra cost).
  • Recycle Bin can recover accidentally deleted snapshots.

Policies

bashDefault encryption and snapshots
aws ec2 enable-ebs-encryption-by-default
aws ec2 get-ebs-encryption-by-default
aws ec2 create-snapshot --volume-id vol-0123456789abcdef0 --description "pre-upgrade" \
  --tag-specifications 'ResourceType=snapshot,Tags=[{Key=retain,Value=7d}]'
aws ec2 copy-snapshot --source-region eu-west-1 --source-snapshot-id snap-0123456789abcdef0 --region eu-central-1 --encrypted
Check yourself
Why use EBS encryption by default?

Any new volume is encrypted automatically, so nobody can forget to enable it.

12.4

Instance store

In plain words

Instance store is local NVMe or SSD storage physically attached to the host. It is very fast and included in the instance price, but temporary.

The problem it solves

Some workloads need very high IOPS or low latency that networked EBS cannot match, for scratch data, caches, or replicated databases.

What it does

  • Available only on types with d or i/g4ad style storage; size fixed by type.
  • Data survives reboot but not stop, hibernate, terminate or host failure.
  • Encrypted at the hardware level on Nitro.
  • On Kubernetes use the local static provisioner, or mount as emptyDir for scratch, and let the application replicate data.

Format on boot

bashMount instance store at first boot
lsblk -o NAME,SIZE,MODEL | grep -i "Instance Storage"
sudo mkfs.xfs /dev/nvme1n1 && sudo mkdir -p /scratch && sudo mount -o noatime /dev/nvme1n1 /scratch
Danger

Do not put the only copy of a database on instance store without replication across hosts and AZs.

12.5

ENIs, ENA and EFA

In plain words

An elastic network interface (ENI) is a virtual network card with private IPs, a MAC and security groups. ENA is the high-performance driver on Nitro. EFA adds OS-bypass networking for HPC and ML.

The problem it solves

Network throughput, packets per second and the number of IPs you can attach are all bounded by instance type.

What it does

  • Each type allows a maximum number of ENIs and IPv4 addresses per ENI. This bounds pods per node with the default VPC CNI: roughly ENIs * (IPs per ENI - 1) + 2. Verify with the EKS max-pods calculator for your type.
  • Prefix delegation gives ENIs /28 prefixes so a node can host many more pods.
  • Network bandwidth is shown per type; flows to a single destination are limited, and instances have a burst baseline pattern. Check NetworkInfo for numbers.
  • Security groups can be attached to pods in EKS (security groups for pods) using trunk ENIs.

Check limits and drivers

bashENI limits
aws ec2 describe-instance-types --instance-types m7g.large \
  --query 'InstanceTypes[0].NetworkInfo.[MaximumNetworkInterfaces,Ipv4AddressesPerInterface,NetworkPerformance]'
ethtool -i eth0 | head -3      # driver: ena
ethtool -S eth0 | grep -i exceeded   # bw_in_allowance_exceeded and similar counters
kubectl -n kube-system set env daemonset aws-node ENABLE_PREFIX_DELEGATION=true
Check yourself
What does the ENA exceeded counter tell you?

The instance hit a network allowance (bandwidth, packets per second, connection tracking), so packets were dropped or queued.

Section 13 of 93

Placement groups, Spot and purchasing options

5 concepts · about 50 minutes

Where instances sit and how you pay for them both change cost and resilience. Spot and commitments together can cut compute spend considerably, but only with careful design.

Goals
  • Choose between cluster, spread and partition placement groups
  • Run fault-tolerant workloads on Spot safely and handle interruptions
  • Combine On-Demand, Savings Plans and Reserved Instances to cut cost
13.1

Placement groups

In plain words

A placement group influences how EC2 places instances on the underlying hardware.

The problem it solves

Tightly coupled workloads need low latency between nodes; critical replicas need to avoid sharing hardware.

What it does

  • Cluster: instances packed close in one AZ for low latency and high throughput between them. Best for HPC; increases correlated failure risk.
  • Spread: each instance on distinct hardware; limited number per AZ (check current quota). Good for a few critical instances.
  • Partition: instances split into partitions that do not share hardware; fits Kafka, Cassandra, HDFS.
  • Launch all cluster members together and use the same instance type to reduce capacity errors.

Create

bashPlacement groups
aws ec2 create-placement-group --group-name hpc --strategy cluster
aws ec2 create-placement-group --group-name kafka --strategy partition --partition-count 3
aws ec2 run-instances --image-id ami-0123456789abcdef0 --instance-type c7i.8xlarge --count 4 --placement GroupName=hpc
Note

In Kubernetes, topology spread constraints on topology.kubernetes.io/zone and kubernetes.io/hostname achieve spread at the pod level.

13.2

On-Demand and capacity reservations

In plain words

On-Demand is pay-per-second with no commitment. Capacity Reservations guarantee that capacity exists in an AZ, whether or not you run instances.

The problem it solves

In rare capacity shortages, a launch can fail with InsufficientInstanceCapacity, which is unacceptable for disaster-recovery or event-day scaling.

What it does

  • On-Demand is the baseline price against which discounts are calculated.
  • Capacity Reservations are billed at On-Demand rate while active, and are matched by instance attributes. Savings Plans and Regional Reserved Instances discount their price.
  • On-Demand Capacity Reservations for ML (Capacity Blocks) exist for scheduled GPU capacity; check availability.
  • For resilience, diversify instance types and AZs rather than relying on one type.

Create a reservation

bashReserve capacity
aws ec2 create-capacity-reservation --instance-type m7g.large --instance-platform Linux/UNIX \
  --availability-zone eu-west-1a --instance-count 3 --instance-match-criteria open
aws ec2 describe-capacity-reservations --query 'CapacityReservations[].[CapacityReservationId,AvailableInstanceCount,State]'
Check yourself
What does a Capacity Reservation guarantee that a Savings Plan does not?

That the capacity is available in a given AZ; a Savings Plan is only a billing discount.

13.3

Spot Instances

In plain words

Spot uses spare EC2 capacity at a large discount, with the catch that AWS can take it back with a two-minute warning.

The problem it solves

Steady On-Demand pricing is expensive for stateless, batch and CI workloads that could tolerate interruption.

What it does

  • Price is set by AWS (no bidding); you can set a maximum price but usually leave it at the On-Demand price.
  • Interruption notice appears at spot/instance-action in the metadata and as an EventBridge event, about two minutes before reclaim. Rebalance recommendations may arrive earlier.
  • Diversify across many instance types and AZs, and use the price-capacity-optimized allocation strategy.
  • Good fits: stateless web tiers behind a load balancer, workers, CI runners, batch, stream processors with checkpoints. Poor fits: single-instance databases, long non-checkpointed jobs.

ASG with mixed instances

hclspot-asg.tf
resource "aws_autoscaling_group" "workers" {
  name                = "workers"
  min_size            = 2
  max_size            = 20
  vpc_zone_identifier = var.private_subnet_ids

  mixed_instances_policy {
    instances_distribution {
      on_demand_base_capacity                  = 2
      on_demand_percentage_above_base_capacity = 0
      spot_allocation_strategy                 = "price-capacity-optimized"
    }
    launch_template {
      launch_template_specification {
        launch_template_id = aws_launch_template.worker.id
        version            = "$Latest"
      }
      override { instance_type = "m6i.large" }
      override { instance_type = "m6a.large" }
      override { instance_type = "m7g.large" }
      override { instance_type = "c6i.xlarge" }
    }
  }
}
bashWatch for interruption
curl -s -H "X-aws-ec2-metadata-token: $TOKEN" http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/spot/instance-action
aws ec2 describe-spot-price-history --instance-types m7g.large --product-descriptions "Linux/UNIX" --max-items 5
13.4

Savings Plans and Reserved Instances

In plain words

Savings Plans are a commitment to spend a fixed amount per hour for one or three years in return for a lower rate. Reserved Instances commit to specific instance attributes.

The problem it solves

Always-on baseline capacity paid at On-Demand price is the largest avoidable cost.

What it does

  • Compute Savings Plans: apply to EC2 any family, Region, OS, tenancy, plus Fargate and Lambda. Most flexible.
  • EC2 Instance Savings Plans: tied to a family in a Region, deeper discount.
  • Payment options: all upfront, partial, no upfront. Terms: one or three years. Check the current discount ranges.
  • Reserved Instances: Standard (can be sold on a marketplace) and Convertible; also needed for RDS and other services where Savings Plans do not apply.
  • Commit to the stable floor of usage, not the peak; the commitment is owed even if you use less.
  • Plans are purchased in the management account and shared across the organization by default.

Explore

bashCost Explorer recommendations
aws ce get-savings-plans-purchase-recommendation --savings-plans-type COMPUTE_SP \
  --term-in-years ONE_YEAR --payment-option NO_UPFRONT --lookback-period-in-days THIRTY_DAYS \
  --query 'SavingsPlansPurchaseRecommendation.SavingsPlansPurchaseRecommendationSummary'
aws ce get-savings-plans-coverage --time-period Start=2026-10-01,End=2026-10-31
Purchasing option
OptionOn-Demand
Choose whenunknown or short-lived load
Avoid whensteady 24/7 baseline
OptionSpot
Choose whenstateless, interruptible work
Avoid whensingle stateful instance
OptionCompute Savings Plan
Choose whensteady baseline with changing instance types
Avoid whenusage you may stop within the term
OptionEC2 Instance Savings Plan
Choose whenlong-lived known family
Avoid whenyou plan to move to another family soon
OptionCapacity Reservation
Choose whenmust-have capacity in an AZ
Avoid whenflexible workloads that can retry elsewhere
Check yourself
Should you buy a Savings Plan for your peak hourly spend?

No. Commit to the steady minimum; cover peaks with On-Demand or Spot.

13.5

Tenancy, Dedicated Hosts and licences

In plain words

By default instances share physical hosts with other customers (shared tenancy). Dedicated options give you hardware not shared.

The problem it solves

Some software licences are per socket or per core, and some compliance regimes demand single-tenant hardware.

What it does

  • Dedicated Instances: run on hardware dedicated to your account; AWS manages placement.
  • Dedicated Hosts: a whole physical server you control, giving visibility of sockets and cores for BYOL.
  • License Manager tracks licence counts across accounts.
  • Shared tenancy on Nitro is strongly isolated; dedicated tenancy is rarely needed otherwise.

Section 14 of 93

User data, metadata and Systems Manager

5 concepts · about 45 minutes

How an instance configures itself on boot and how you reach it afterwards decide whether your fleet is reproducible and secure.

Goals
  • Bootstrap instances with user data and cloud-init safely
  • Replace SSH with Session Manager and port forwarding
  • Use Run Command, Patch Manager and Parameter Store for fleet operations
14.1

User data and cloud-init

In plain words

User data is a script or cloud-config you pass at launch. The instance runs it once at first boot through cloud-init.

The problem it solves

Manually logging in to configure each server is slow and cannot scale or be reviewed.

What it does

  • Maximum size is 16 KB; keep it tiny and fetch the rest from S3 or a package repository.
  • Scripts start with a shebang; #cloud-config YAML configures packages, users and files.
  • Runs as root, once by default. Output logs in /var/log/cloud-init-output.log.
  • User data is not secret; anyone with ec2:DescribeInstanceAttribute or access to the metadata can read it. Never place passwords in it; use Secrets Manager or Parameter Store.
  • Prefer baking an AMI for anything slow or critical, and use user data for the last mile (cluster join, environment-specific config).

cloud-config example

yamluser-data.yaml
#cloud-config
package_update: true
packages:
  - amazon-cloudwatch-agent
write_files:
  - path: /etc/motd
    content: |
      managed by platform team
runcmd:
  - systemctl enable --now amazon-ssm-agent
  - systemctl enable --now amazon-cloudwatch-agent
bashDebug
sudo cat /var/log/cloud-init-output.log | tail -30
sudo cloud-init status --long
curl -s -H "X-aws-ec2-metadata-token: $TOKEN" http://169.254.169.254/latest/user-data | head
Check yourself
Where can you read what user data ran?

In /var/log/cloud-init-output.log and `cloud-init status --long`.

14.2

Launch templates

In plain words

A launch template is a versioned recipe for an instance: AMI, type, key, roles, network, storage, tags and user data.

The problem it solves

Repeating the same long parameter list everywhere leads to inconsistency. Templates are required by Auto Scaling groups and recommended everywhere.

What it does

  • Versions are immutable; reference $Latest, $Default or a number.
  • Enforce IMDSv2, EBS encryption and detailed tags centrally.
  • Parameters can come from SSM, such as resolve:ssm:/aws/service/ami-amazon-linux-latest/al2023-ami-kernel-default-x86_64.

Terraform

hcllaunch-template.tf
resource "aws_launch_template" "worker" {
  name_prefix   = "worker-"
  image_id      = "resolve:ssm:/aws/service/ami-amazon-linux-latest/al2023-ami-kernel-default-arm64"
  instance_type = "m7g.large"

  iam_instance_profile {
    name = aws_iam_instance_profile.worker.name
  }

  metadata_options {
    http_tokens                 = "required"
    http_put_response_hop_limit = 1
  }

  block_device_mappings {
    device_name = "/dev/xvda"
    ebs {
      volume_size = 50
      volume_type = "gp3"
      encrypted   = true
    }
  }

  user_data = base64encode(file("${path.module}/user-data.yaml"))
}
14.3

SSM Session Manager

In plain words

Session Manager gives you a shell on an instance through the SSM agent, with no inbound ports, bastion hosts or SSH keys.

The problem it solves

SSH needs open port 22, key distribution, bastions and gives weak auditing.

What it does

  • Needs the SSM agent (preinstalled on Amazon Linux and many AMIs), an instance profile with AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore, and outbound HTTPS to SSM endpoints (via NAT or ssm, ssmmessages, ec2messages interface endpoints).
  • Access controlled by IAM, including conditions on tags; sessions logged to CloudWatch Logs or S3 and recorded in CloudTrail.
  • Port forwarding reaches private databases and remote hosts via the instance. Works as an SSH proxy as well.
  • Works for EKS nodes as well; for pods use kubectl exec instead.

Use it

bashShell and port forward
aws ssm start-session --target i-0123456789abcdef0
aws ssm start-session --target i-0123456789abcdef0 \
  --document-name AWS-StartPortForwardingSessionToRemoteHost \
  --parameters '{"host":["db.internal.example.com"],"portNumber":["5432"],"localPortNumber":["15432"]}'
aws ssm describe-instance-information --query 'InstanceInformationList[].[InstanceId,PingStatus,PlatformName]' --output table
jsonssm-tag-scoped.json
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": "ssm:StartSession",
      "Resource": "arn:aws:ec2:*:*:instance/*",
      "Condition": {"StringEquals": {"ssm:resourceTag/env": "dev"}}
    }
  ]
}
Tip

Close port 22 in security groups, then enforce it with an AWS Config rule. Session Manager covers the use case.

Check yourself
What must an instance have to be reachable with Session Manager?

The SSM agent, an instance profile permitting SSM, and outbound HTTPS to the SSM endpoints.

14.4

Run Command, State Manager and Patch Manager

In plain words

Systems Manager can run commands on many instances, keep them in a desired state, and patch them on a schedule.

The problem it solves

Fleet-wide changes through individual logins are slow and unaudited.

What it does

  • Run Command: run a document (script) on instances chosen by tag, with rate control and logging.
  • State Manager: associate a document with targets on a schedule to keep configuration applied.
  • Patch Manager: baselines define which patches are approved; maintenance windows apply them. Report compliance.
  • For immutable fleets (ASG with baked AMIs) prefer replacing instances to patching in place.

Run on a tag

bashRun Command
aws ssm send-command --document-name AWS-RunShellScript \
  --targets Key=tag:env,Values=dev --parameters 'commands=["uptime","df -h /"]' \
  --max-concurrency 10% --max-errors 1 --comment "health snapshot"
aws ssm list-command-invocations --details --query 'CommandInvocations[].[InstanceId,Status]' --output table | head
14.5

Parameter Store and Secrets Manager

In plain words

Parameter Store holds configuration values and optionally encrypted secrets. Secrets Manager adds automatic rotation for credentials.

The problem it solves

Configuration and credentials copied into AMIs, user data or Git are hard to change and leak.

What it does

  • Parameters are hierarchical (/prod/shop/db_host) with IAM permissions per path; SecureString uses KMS.
  • Standard parameters are free; advanced tier adds size and policies (check pricing).
  • Secrets Manager rotates secrets (for example RDS passwords) with Lambda functions, and supports cross-Region replication. Charged per secret and per API calls.
  • Public SSM parameters list the latest AMI IDs.
  • On Kubernetes, the Secrets Store CSI driver with the AWS provider mounts these as files or syncs to Secrets.

Use

bashParameters
aws ssm put-parameter --name /prod/shop/db_host --type String --value db.internal.example.com
aws ssm put-parameter --name /prod/shop/api_key --type SecureString --value "change-me"
aws ssm get-parameters-by-path --path /prod/shop --with-decryption --query 'Parameters[].Name'
aws secretsmanager get-secret-value --secret-id prod/shop/db --query SecretString --output text
Where to keep values
OptionParameter Store
Choose whenconfiguration and simple secrets
Avoid whenautomatic rotation required
OptionSecrets Manager
Choose whendatabase credentials with rotation
Avoid whenplain config values
OptionKubernetes Secret
Choose whenin-cluster consumption
Avoid whenlong-term source of truth without encryption at rest

Section 15 of 93

AMIs and image pipelines

5 concepts · about 40 minutes

An AMI is the template an instance boots from. A reproducible image pipeline means every node in your fleet starts from a known, patched and tested base.

Goals
  • Explain what an AMI contains and how to share and copy it
  • Build hardened images with Packer or EC2 Image Builder
  • Manage AMI lifecycle, deprecation and EKS-optimized images
15.1

What an AMI is

In plain words

An Amazon Machine Image bundles a root volume snapshot, launch permissions and a block device mapping. You launch instances from it in the same Region.

The problem it solves

Installing and configuring software on each new instance is slow and drifts; a golden image makes a boot predictable.

What it does

  • AMIs are Regional; copy them to other Regions or accounts. Backed by EBS snapshots.
  • Choose architecture (x86_64 or arm64), virtualization, boot mode (UEFI or legacy) and IMDS defaults when you register.
  • AWS-published AMIs: Amazon Linux 2023, Bottlerocket (container optimised), Ubuntu, Windows and others; SSM public parameters list the current ID.
  • Launch permissions: private, specific accounts, organization units, or public. Block public AMI sharing in the account settings.

Look up and share

bashAMI commands
aws ssm get-parameter --name /aws/service/ami-amazon-linux-latest/al2023-ami-kernel-default-arm64 --query Parameter.Value --output text
aws ec2 describe-images --owners self --query 'Images[].[ImageId,Name,CreationDate]' --output table
aws ec2 modify-image-attribute --image-id ami-0123456789abcdef0 --launch-permission 'Add=[{OrganizationArn=arn:aws:organizations::111122223333:organization/o-exampleorgid}]'
aws ec2 enable-image-block-public-access --image-block-public-access-state block-new-sharing
Check yourself
Can you launch an AMI in another Region directly?

No. Copy it to that Region first.

15.2

Packer

In plain words

Packer builds machine images from code. It launches a temporary instance, runs provisioners, snapshots it as an AMI and cleans up.

The problem it solves

Hand-built images cannot be reviewed or reproduced.

What it does

  • HCL2 configuration with an amazon-ebs source and provisioners (shell, Ansible).
  • Run in CI; tag the AMI with commit, base AMI and build date.
  • Use a temporary security group and IAM role; keep secrets out of the image.

Template

hclimage.pkr.hcl
packer {
  required_plugins {
    amazon = {
      source  = "github.com/hashicorp/amazon"
      version = ">= 1.3.0"
    }
  }
}

source "amazon-ebs" "base" {
  region        = "eu-west-1"
  instance_type = "m7g.large"
  ssh_username  = "ec2-user"
  ami_name      = "platform-base-{{timestamp}}"
  source_ami_filter {
    filters = {
      name                = "al2023-ami-2023*-arm64"
      root-device-type    = "ebs"
      virtualization-type = "hvm"
    }
    owners      = ["amazon"]
    most_recent = true
  }
  encrypt_boot = true
  tags = {
    built_by = "packer"
  }
}

build {
  sources = ["source.amazon-ebs.base"]
  provisioner "shell" {
    inline = ["sudo dnf -y update", "sudo dnf -y install amazon-cloudwatch-agent"]
  }
}
15.3

EC2 Image Builder

In plain words

EC2 Image Builder is the managed AWS pipeline for images: recipes, components, tests, distribution and scheduled rebuilds.

The problem it solves

You want automatic rebuilds when the base image gets patched, with tests and distribution, without running build servers.

What it does

  • A recipe has a parent image and ordered components (build and test steps, YAML documents).
  • Pipeline schedule or event triggers a build; infrastructure configuration sets the build instance profile and subnet.
  • Distribution copies AMIs to Regions and shares with accounts, and publishes the AMI ID to an SSM parameter for launch templates to read.
  • Integrates with Inspector for vulnerability scanning.

Component document

yamlharden-component.yaml
name: harden
description: Basic hardening
schemaVersion: 1.0
phases:
  - name: build
    steps:
      - name: DisableRootSsh
        action: ExecuteBash
        inputs:
          commands:
            - sed -i 's/^#\?PermitRootLogin.*/PermitRootLogin no/' /etc/ssh/sshd_config
  - name: test
    steps:
      - name: CheckSshd
        action: ExecuteBash
        inputs:
          commands:
            - grep -q '^PermitRootLogin no' /etc/ssh/sshd_config
Image tooling
OptionEC2 Image Builder
Choose whenmanaged, scheduled, AWS-native
Avoid whenmulti-cloud images from one tool
OptionPacker
Choose whenone tool for many clouds and local testing
Avoid whenyou want no build code to maintain
OptionBottlerocket
Choose whencontainer hosts, immutable
Avoid whenyou need general-purpose package management
Check yourself
How does a launch template learn about a new AMI?

From an SSM parameter updated by the pipeline, resolved with resolve:ssm in the template.

15.4

EKS-optimized AMIs and Bottlerocket

In plain words

EKS provides AMIs with kubelet and container runtime preinstalled. Bottlerocket is a minimal, immutable, container-focused OS.

The problem it solves

General-purpose OS images contain much that a node never needs, increasing patch burden and attack surface.

What it does

  • Amazon Linux 2023 and Bottlerocket variants of the EKS-optimized AMI exist per Kubernetes version and architecture; look up the current ID via an SSM parameter under /aws/service/eks/optimized-ami/. Check supported OS families as they change.
  • Bottlerocket updates as a whole image; configuration via TOML user data, no SSH by default (use the admin container through SSM).
  • Managed node groups use these automatically and can roll to a new AMI version through an update.
  • Custom AMIs for EKS must keep the bootstrap contract (nodeadm for AL2023).

Look up the recommended AMI

bashFind the current EKS AMI
aws ssm get-parameter --name /aws/service/eks/optimized-ami/1.37/amazon-linux-2023/arm64/standard/recommended/image_id \
  --query Parameter.Value --output text
aws ssm get-parameter --name /aws/service/bottlerocket/aws-k8s-1.37/arm64/latest/image_id --query Parameter.Value --output text
Note

Replace 1.37 with a Kubernetes version that EKS currently supports. Parameter names and available OS flavours change over time.

15.5

AMI lifecycle and deprecation

In plain words

Old AMIs accumulate snapshots, cost money, and may contain vulnerabilities. A lifecycle policy removes them.

The problem it solves

Hundreds of forgotten images and snapshots cost storage and confuse people about which one is current.

What it does

  • Set a deprecation time so old AMIs are hidden from searches and warn users.
  • Data Lifecycle Manager can create, copy, deprecate and delete AMIs on a schedule.
  • Deregistering an AMI does not delete its snapshots; remove those as well.
  • Tag by pipeline and date; keep the last few known-good versions for rollback.

Clean up

bashDeprecate and deregister
aws ec2 enable-image-deprecation --image-id ami-0123456789abcdef0 --deprecate-at 2026-12-31T00:00:00Z
aws ec2 deregister-image --image-id ami-0aaa
aws ec2 describe-snapshots --owner-ids self --filters Name=description,Values="*ami-0aaa*" --query 'Snapshots[].SnapshotId'

Section 16 of 93

Elastic Load Balancing and the Application Load Balancer

6 concepts · about 50 minutes

A load balancer is the front door of most AWS applications. Choosing the right type and configuring it properly determines latency, cost and how safely you can deploy.

Goals
  • Choose between ALB, NLB and GWLB for a given traffic type
  • Configure ALB listeners, rules and target groups with path and host routing
  • Explain cross-zone behaviour, scaling and the load balancer security group pattern
16.1

The three load balancer types

In plain words

Elastic Load Balancing offers three main types, each working at a different network layer: ALB for HTTP, NLB for TCP, UDP and TLS, GWLB for network appliances.

The problem it solves

One tool cannot suit web routing, ultra-low-latency TCP and transparent firewall insertion at once.

What it does

  • Application Load Balancer (ALB): layer 7. Routes on host, path, headers, query string and method; supports HTTP/2, gRPC, WebSockets, authentication actions, WAF and redirects.
  • Network Load Balancer (NLB): layer 4. Very high throughput, static IPs per AZ, optional Elastic IPs, preserves client IP, TLS termination, PrivateLink source.
  • Gateway Load Balancer (GWLB): layer 3 transparent. Sends all traffic through a fleet of appliances (firewalls, IDS) using GENEVE encapsulation.
  • Classic Load Balancer is legacy; migrate off it.

List them

bashInventory
aws elbv2 describe-load-balancers --query 'LoadBalancers[].[LoadBalancerName,Type,Scheme,State.Code]' --output table
aws elbv2 describe-target-groups --query 'TargetGroups[].[TargetGroupName,Protocol,Port,TargetType]' --output table
Check yourself
Which load balancer keeps the client source IP and gives you a static IP?

The NLB.

16.2

ALB architecture

In plain words

An ALB is a set of managed nodes spread across the subnets you choose. DNS resolves its name to the IP addresses of those nodes, which scale up and down with load.

The problem it solves

You need a single, highly available HTTP endpoint that survives the loss of an AZ and grows with traffic.

What it does

  • Needs at least two subnets in different AZs; public (internet-facing) or private (internal) scheme.
  • IPs change as it scales, so always use the DNS name or a Route 53 alias, never the IPs.
  • Cross-zone load balancing is always on for ALB, so each node can send to targets in any AZ; cross-AZ data between ALB and targets is not charged separately in the same way as other traffic, but check current pricing.
  • Billed per hour plus LCUs (a blend of new connections, active connections, bytes and rule evaluations).
  • Idle timeout defaults to 60 seconds; tune for long requests and keep application keep-alive higher.

Create with Terraform

hclalb.tf
resource "aws_lb" "web" {
  name               = "web"
  load_balancer_type = "application"
  subnets            = var.public_subnet_ids
  security_groups    = [aws_security_group.alb.id]
  idle_timeout       = 60
  drop_invalid_header_fields = true
}
Tip

Turn on access logs to S3 and deletion protection for production load balancers.

16.3

Listeners and rules

In plain words

A listener checks for connections on a port and protocol. Its rules pick an action based on conditions, evaluated in priority order.

The problem it solves

One hostname often fronts many services. You need to send /api to one set of servers and /static to another, redirect HTTP to HTTPS, or return a fixed answer.

What it does

  • Conditions: host header, path pattern, HTTP header, query string, source IP, HTTP method.
  • Actions: forward (one or several weighted target groups), redirect, fixed-response, authenticate-oidc, authenticate-cognito.
  • The default rule catches everything unmatched. Priorities are unique numbers; lowest wins.
  • Check the current quota for rules per listener.

Redirect and route

hcllisteners.tf
resource "aws_lb_listener" "http" {
  load_balancer_arn = aws_lb.web.arn
  port              = 80
  protocol          = "HTTP"
  default_action {
    type = "redirect"
    redirect {
      port        = "443"
      protocol    = "HTTPS"
      status_code = "HTTP_301"
    }
  }
}

resource "aws_lb_listener" "https" {
  load_balancer_arn = aws_lb.web.arn
  port              = 443
  protocol          = "HTTPS"
  ssl_policy        = "ELBSecurityPolicy-TLS13-1-2-2021-06"
  certificate_arn   = aws_acm_certificate.web.arn
  default_action {
    type = "fixed-response"
    fixed_response {
      content_type = "text/plain"
      message_body = "not found"
      status_code  = "404"
    }
  }
}

resource "aws_lb_listener_rule" "api" {
  listener_arn = aws_lb_listener.https.arn
  priority     = 10
  action {
    type             = "forward"
    target_group_arn = aws_lb_target_group.api.arn
  }
  condition {
    path_pattern {
      values = ["/api/*"]
    }
  }
}
Check yourself
Which rule wins when two match?

The one with the lower priority number.

16.4

Target groups

In plain words

A target group is the set of backends a rule forwards to, with its own protocol, port, health check and attributes.

The problem it solves

Backends come and go. The load balancer needs a dynamic, health-aware list.

What it does

  • Target types: instance (by ID), ip (any routable address including pods, on-premises via TGW), lambda, and alb (for NLB in front of ALB).
  • Registered by hand, by an Auto Scaling group, or by a controller (AWS Load Balancer Controller for Kubernetes).
  • Attributes: deregistration_delay (connection draining, default 300 seconds), slow_start, stickiness (cookie), load_balancing.algorithm.type (round robin or least outstanding requests), and anomaly mitigation.
  • A target group can be attached to one ALB or NLB; one load balancer can use many groups.

Weighted forward for canary

hclcanary.tf
resource "aws_lb_listener_rule" "canary" {
  listener_arn = aws_lb_listener.https.arn
  priority     = 20
  action {
    type = "forward"
    forward {
      target_group {
        arn    = aws_lb_target_group.api_v1.arn
        weight = 95
      }
      target_group {
        arn    = aws_lb_target_group.api_v2.arn
        weight = 5
      }
    }
  }
  condition {
    host_header {
      values = ["api.example.com"]
    }
  }
}
bashInspect target health
aws elbv2 describe-target-health --target-group-arn arn:aws:elasticloadbalancing:eu-west-1:111122223333:targetgroup/api/0123456789abcdef \
  --query 'TargetHealthDescriptions[].[Target.Id,TargetHealth.State,TargetHealth.Reason]' --output table
16.5

Security groups and client IP

In plain words

The load balancer and its targets each have security groups. The target should accept traffic only from the load balancer's group.

The problem it solves

Targets in private subnets are still exposed if their security group accepts the whole VPC or the internet.

What it does

  • ALB group: allow 80/443 from the internet (or a prefix list for internal use).
  • Target group: allow the app port from the ALB group by reference, not by CIDR.
  • The ALB terminates the client connection, so the target sees the ALB's IP. The real client IP arrives in the X-Forwarded-For header; also X-Forwarded-Proto and X-Forwarded-Port. Configure the application to trust it only from the ALB.
  • drop_invalid_header_fields and desync_mitigation_mode improve protection against request smuggling.

Reference rule

hclsg-alb-app.tf
resource "aws_vpc_security_group_ingress_rule" "app_from_alb" {
  security_group_id            = aws_security_group.app.id
  referenced_security_group_id = aws_security_group.alb.id
  ip_protocol                  = "tcp"
  from_port                    = 8080
  to_port                      = 8080
}
Careful

Never trust X-Forwarded-For from direct clients. Only accept it when the request came from your load balancer.

Check yourself
How does an app behind an ALB learn the real client IP?

From the X-Forwarded-For header that the ALB adds.

16.6

Authentication and special actions

In plain words

An ALB can authenticate users with OIDC or Cognito before forwarding, and can answer requests itself.

The problem it solves

Internal tools often need SSO in front of them but have no login code.

What it does

  • authenticate-oidc redirects to your identity provider, then passes claims to the target in signed headers x-amzn-oidc-data and x-amzn-oidc-accesstoken. Verify the signature in the application.
  • Needs HTTPS listener and outbound access from the ALB to the IdP.
  • Redirect and fixed-response actions avoid needing a server for maintenance pages and HTTP to HTTPS redirects.
  • Mutual TLS (client certificate verification) is available on ALB listeners; check the current documentation for modes.

Rule with OIDC

hcloidc-rule.tf
resource "aws_lb_listener_rule" "admin" {
  listener_arn = aws_lb_listener.https.arn
  priority     = 5
  action {
    type = "authenticate-oidc"
    authenticate_oidc {
      authorization_endpoint = "https://idp.example.com/oauth2/authorize"
      token_endpoint         = "https://idp.example.com/oauth2/token"
      user_info_endpoint     = "https://idp.example.com/oauth2/userinfo"
      issuer                 = "https://idp.example.com"
      client_id              = var.oidc_client_id
      client_secret          = var.oidc_client_secret
    }
    order = 1
  }
  action {
    type             = "forward"
    target_group_arn = aws_lb_target_group.admin.arn
    order            = 2
  }
  condition {
    path_pattern {
      values = ["/admin/*"]
    }
  }
}

Section 17 of 93

Network Load Balancer and Gateway Load Balancer

5 concepts · about 45 minutes

When you need raw TCP or UDP, static addresses, extreme throughput, or transparent security appliances, the Network and Gateway Load Balancers take over from the ALB.

Goals
  • Configure an NLB with static IPs, TLS listeners and client IP preservation
  • Explain NLB security groups, cross-zone and health check behaviour
  • Build a transparent inspection path with GWLB and GENEVE
17.1

NLB basics

In plain words

The Network Load Balancer forwards TCP, UDP and TLS connections at layer 4 with very low latency. It does not look inside HTTP.

The problem it solves

Non-HTTP protocols (databases, MQTT, gRPC with passthrough, game traffic), fixed IPs for firewall allow-lists and PrivateLink all need layer 4.

What it does

  • One subnet per AZ; each gets a static private IP, or an Elastic IP for internet-facing NLBs.
  • Listener protocols: TCP, UDP, TCP_UDP, TLS, QUIC passthrough options (check current support).
  • Preserves the client source IP for instance targets by default; for IP targets it can be configured. Enable proxy protocol v2 to pass the client IP to targets that cannot see it.
  • Can have security groups attached (a more recent option); if you create without one you cannot add it later in some cases, so check the current documentation before design.
  • Cross-zone load balancing is off by default and billed for inter-AZ data when enabled.

Terraform

hclnlb.tf
resource "aws_lb" "tcp" {
  name               = "tcp-front"
  load_balancer_type = "network"
  internal           = false

  subnet_mapping {
    subnet_id     = var.public_subnet_ids[0]
    allocation_id = aws_eip.nlb_a.id
  }
  subnet_mapping {
    subnet_id     = var.public_subnet_ids[1]
    allocation_id = aws_eip.nlb_b.id
  }
  enable_cross_zone_load_balancing = false
}

resource "aws_lb_target_group" "mqtt" {
  name        = "mqtt"
  port        = 1883
  protocol    = "TCP"
  target_type = "ip"
  vpc_id      = var.vpc_id
  proxy_protocol_v2 = false
  preserve_client_ip = "true"
  health_check {
    protocol = "TCP"
  }
}
Check yourself
Why use an NLB when firewalls on the partner side need fixed IPs?

NLB gives one static IP per AZ, and Elastic IPs for internet-facing ones, so allow-lists stay stable.

17.2

NLB TLS, health checks and draining

In plain words

An NLB can terminate TLS, run TCP or HTTP health checks, and hold existing connections during deregistration.

The problem it solves

Terminating TLS in each backend means certificate rotation everywhere; a hung backend still accepting TCP should leave rotation.

What it does

  • TLS listeners use ACM certificates and a security policy; ALPN policies support HTTP/2 passthrough.
  • Health checks: TCP, HTTP, HTTPS. Targets in an AZ with no healthy target: with cross-zone off, that AZ fails open to all targets (fail-open behaviour when all targets are unhealthy; check current docs).
  • Connection termination on deregistration is off by default; connections remain until idle timeout (350 seconds for TCP flows). Tune with deregistration_delay.connection_termination.enabled.
  • Idle timeout for TCP is 350 seconds; use TCP keepalive on long-lived connections.

Listener

hclnlb-tls.tf
resource "aws_lb_listener" "tls" {
  load_balancer_arn = aws_lb.tcp.arn
  port              = 8883
  protocol          = "TLS"
  ssl_policy        = "ELBSecurityPolicy-TLS13-1-2-2021-06"
  certificate_arn   = aws_acm_certificate.mqtt.arn
  default_action {
    type             = "forward"
    target_group_arn = aws_lb_target_group.mqtt.arn
  }
}
Note

Idle timeout and keepalive values are documented per load balancer type and can change. Check the current limits for your design.

17.3

NLB with PrivateLink and ALB-type targets

In plain words

An NLB is the entry point for PrivateLink endpoint services, and an NLB can forward to an ALB to combine static IPs with layer 7 routing.

The problem it solves

Customers want a stable IP for a layer 7 service, or want to consume your service privately from other VPCs.

What it does

  • target_type = alb registers an ALB as an NLB target: clients connect to the NLB's static IPs, which forward to the ALB.
  • PrivateLink: attach the NLB to an endpoint service; consumers create interface endpoints.
  • Client IP is not preserved across PrivateLink unless proxy protocol is enabled.
Fronting a web service
OptionALB only
Choose whenHTTP routing, WAF and no IP allow-list needed
Avoid whenclients need fixed IPs
OptionNLB then ALB
Choose whenfixed IPs plus path routing
Avoid whenthe extra hop and cost are unacceptable
OptionNLB only
Choose whenpure TCP or UDP
Avoid whenyou need header based routing
17.4

Gateway Load Balancer

In plain words

GWLB puts a fleet of virtual appliances (firewalls, intrusion prevention) transparently in the path of traffic, and scales them as one.

The problem it solves

Inserting an appliance by hand means asymmetric routing, no scaling, and failover scripts.

What it does

  • Operates at layer 3; wraps packets in GENEVE (UDP 6081) and sends them to appliances, which return them unchanged.
  • Preserves the 5-tuple flow stickiness so both directions of a flow reach the same appliance.
  • Exposed to other VPCs through a GWLB endpoint (a PrivateLink type) that appears as a route target.
  • Appliances register in a target group with GENEVE protocol and health checks (TCP, HTTP or HTTPS).

Setup outline

hclgwlb.tf
resource "aws_lb" "gwlb" {
  name               = "inspection"
  load_balancer_type = "gateway"
  subnets            = var.inspection_subnet_ids
}

resource "aws_lb_target_group" "appliances" {
  name     = "appliances"
  port     = 6081
  protocol = "GENEVE"
  vpc_id   = var.inspection_vpc_id
  health_check {
    protocol = "TCP"
    port     = 443
  }
}

resource "aws_vpc_endpoint_service" "gwlb" {
  acceptance_required        = false
  gateway_load_balancer_arns = [aws_lb.gwlb.arn]
}
Check yourself
Which port and protocol does GWLB use to talk to appliances?

GENEVE over UDP 6081.

17.5

Choosing and costing

In plain words

Each type has a different pricing metric and failure behaviour, so decide with both technical and cost data.

The problem it solves

A wrongly chosen load balancer leads to avoidable monthly charges or functional limits.

What it does

  • ALB: LCU billed by the highest of new connections, active connections, processed bytes, rule evaluations.
  • NLB: NLCU on bytes, new and active flows. GWLB: GLCU on similar metrics. Check current pricing for each.
  • Many Kubernetes Services of type LoadBalancer each create their own NLB; consolidate behind a shared ingress ALB to reduce count.
  • Public IPv4 addresses on internet-facing load balancers are billed; consider dual-stack or IPv6-only clients where possible.

Find idle load balancers

bashRequests per load balancer
for lb in $(aws elbv2 describe-load-balancers --query 'LoadBalancers[].LoadBalancerArn' --output text); do
  name=$(echo "$lb" | sed 's#.*:loadbalancer/##')
  echo "$name"
done
aws cloudwatch get-metric-statistics --namespace AWS/ApplicationELB --metric-name RequestCount \
  --dimensions Name=LoadBalancer,Value=app/web/0123456789abcdef --statistics Sum --period 86400 \
  --start-time "$(date -u -v-7d +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)" --end-time "$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)"

Section 18 of 93

TLS certificates, WAF and CloudFront

5 concepts · about 50 minutes

Edge security and delivery sit in front of the load balancer. Together TLS, WAF and a CDN reduce attack surface and origin load.

Goals
  • Issue and attach ACM certificates and choose security policies
  • Protect an ALB with AWS WAF rules and rate limits
  • Put CloudFront in front of an origin with caching, OAC and private origins
18.1

AWS Certificate Manager

In plain words

ACM issues and renews public TLS certificates for free when used with integrated services (ALB, NLB, CloudFront, API Gateway).

The problem it solves

Manual certificate purchases and renewals cause outages when they expire.

What it does

  • DNS validation via a CNAME record in Route 53 (or elsewhere) renews automatically as long as the record stays.
  • Certificates are Regional; CloudFront requires the certificate in us-east-1.
  • Private keys of public ACM certificates cannot be exported; use ACM Private CA or exportable certificates (a newer paid option) if you need them on your own servers.
  • Multiple certificates can be attached to one listener; SNI selects among them.

Terraform

hclacm.tf
resource "aws_acm_certificate" "web" {
  domain_name               = "example.com"
  subject_alternative_names = ["*.example.com"]
  validation_method         = "DNS"
  lifecycle {
    create_before_destroy = true
  }
}

resource "aws_route53_record" "validation" {
  for_each = {
    for o in aws_acm_certificate.web.domain_validation_options : o.domain_name => o
  }
  zone_id = aws_route53_zone.public.zone_id
  name    = each.value.resource_record_name
  type    = each.value.resource_record_type
  records = [each.value.resource_record_value]
  ttl     = 60
}

resource "aws_acm_certificate_validation" "web" {
  certificate_arn         = aws_acm_certificate.web.arn
  validation_record_fqdns = [for r in aws_route53_record.validation : r.fqdn]
}
Check yourself
In which Region must a CloudFront certificate live?

us-east-1.

18.2

TLS policies and end-to-end encryption

In plain words

A security policy on a listener sets the TLS versions and ciphers it accepts. For sensitive data you can also encrypt between the load balancer and the targets.

The problem it solves

Old protocol versions are vulnerable, and plaintext inside the VPC may violate compliance.

What it does

  • Choose a TLS 1.2 plus 1.3 or TLS 1.3-only policy (names like ELBSecurityPolicy-TLS13-1-2-2021-06); check the current list of policy names.
  • ALB can re-encrypt to HTTPS targets; it does not validate the target certificate, so a self-signed one is acceptable.
  • NLB can either terminate TLS or pass it through.
  • For service-to-service encryption in Kubernetes consider a service mesh or Kyma's Istio mTLS.

Test a listener

bashCheck protocol and certificate
openssl s_client -connect app.example.com:443 -servername app.example.com -tls1_3 </dev/null 2>/dev/null | grep -E "Protocol|Cipher|Verify"
aws elbv2 describe-ssl-policies --names ELBSecurityPolicy-TLS13-1-2-2021-06 --query 'SslPolicies[0].SslProtocols'
18.3

AWS WAF

In plain words

AWS WAF inspects HTTP requests on an ALB, CloudFront, API Gateway or AppSync and allows, blocks, counts or challenges them.

The problem it solves

Applications face injection attempts, bots and floods that the application code should not need to filter.

What it does

  • A web ACL holds ordered rules; each rule has an action. The default action applies when nothing matches.
  • Managed rule groups from AWS and vendors (core rule set, known bad inputs, SQL injection, IP reputation, bot control).
  • Rate-based rules limit requests per IP (or other key) in a window.
  • Start new rules in count mode and review logs before switching to block.
  • Web ACL capacity units (WCU) limit rule complexity; check the current quota. Logs go to S3, CloudWatch Logs or Firehose.

Web ACL

hclwaf.tf
resource "aws_wafv2_web_acl" "web" {
  name  = "web"
  scope = "REGIONAL"
  default_action {
    allow {}
  }
  rule {
    name     = "rate"
    priority = 1
    action {
      block {}
    }
    statement {
      rate_based_statement {
        limit              = 1000
        aggregate_key_type = "IP"
      }
    }
    visibility_config {
      cloudwatch_metrics_enabled = true
      metric_name                = "rate"
      sampled_requests_enabled   = true
    }
  }
  rule {
    name     = "core"
    priority = 2
    override_action {
      count {}
    }
    statement {
      managed_rule_group_statement {
        name        = "AWSManagedRulesCommonRuleSet"
        vendor_name = "AWS"
      }
    }
    visibility_config {
      cloudwatch_metrics_enabled = true
      metric_name                = "core"
      sampled_requests_enabled   = true
    }
  }
  visibility_config {
    cloudwatch_metrics_enabled = true
    metric_name                = "web"
    sampled_requests_enabled   = true
  }
}

resource "aws_wafv2_web_acl_association" "alb" {
  resource_arn = aws_lb.web.arn
  web_acl_arn  = aws_wafv2_web_acl.web.arn
}
Tip

The core rule set runs in count mode here so you can review false positives first. Switch override_action to none {} when you are confident.

Check yourself
Why start with count mode?

It shows what would be blocked without affecting real users, so you can tune false positives.

18.4

CloudFront basics

In plain words

CloudFront is a global CDN. Edge locations cache content close to users and speed up dynamic traffic via the AWS backbone.

The problem it solves

Serving everything from one Region is slow for distant users, expensive in egress, and exposes the origin to floods.

What it does

  • A distribution has origins (S3, ALB, custom HTTP), behaviors (path patterns with cache and origin settings) and a viewer protocol policy.
  • Cache policy defines cache key (headers, query strings, cookies) and TTLs; origin request policy defines what is forwarded; keep the cache key minimal for a high hit ratio.
  • Origin Access Control (OAC) lets only CloudFront read a private S3 bucket. For ALB origins use a custom header secret or the managed prefix list for CloudFront origin-facing IPs in the ALB security group, plus VPC origins (a newer option for private ALBs).
  • Edge compute: CloudFront Functions (light) and Lambda@Edge.
  • Invalidations are available but cost beyond a free monthly allotment; prefer versioned file names.

S3 origin with OAC

hclcloudfront.tf
resource "aws_cloudfront_origin_access_control" "site" {
  name                              = "site"
  origin_access_control_origin_type = "s3"
  signing_behavior                  = "always"
  signing_protocol                  = "sigv4"
}

resource "aws_cloudfront_distribution" "site" {
  enabled             = true
  default_root_object = "index.html"
  aliases             = ["www.example.com"]

  origin {
    domain_name              = aws_s3_bucket.site.bucket_regional_domain_name
    origin_id                = "s3-site"
    origin_access_control_id = aws_cloudfront_origin_access_control.site.id
  }

  default_cache_behavior {
    target_origin_id       = "s3-site"
    viewer_protocol_policy = "redirect-to-https"
    allowed_methods        = ["GET", "HEAD"]
    cached_methods         = ["GET", "HEAD"]
    cache_policy_id        = "658327ea-f89d-4fab-a63d-7e88639e58f6"
  }

  restrictions {
    geo_restriction {
      restriction_type = "none"
    }
  }

  viewer_certificate {
    acm_certificate_arn = aws_acm_certificate.cf.arn
    ssl_support_method  = "sni-only"
  }
}
Note

The cache policy ID above is the AWS managed CachingOptimized policy. Confirm the ID with aws cloudfront list-cache-policies --type managed.

18.5

Securing the origin and combining edge services

In plain words

If CloudFront and WAF protect you, attackers must not be able to bypass them by calling the origin directly.

The problem it solves

A public ALB reachable by anyone makes edge protections optional.

What it does

  • Restrict the ALB security group to the CloudFront managed prefix list (com.amazonaws.global.cloudfront.origin-facing).
  • Add a secret header injected by CloudFront and checked by an ALB rule or WAF rule.
  • Attach WAF to CloudFront (global scope, us-east-1) for edge filtering; use another web ACL on the ALB if you also serve direct traffic.
  • Shield Standard is automatic; Shield Advanced adds support and cost protection for critical apps.

Lock the ALB

bashPrefix list in the ALB security group
PL=$(aws ec2 describe-managed-prefix-lists --filters Name=prefix-list-name,Values=com.amazonaws.global.cloudfront.origin-facing \
  --query 'PrefixLists[0].PrefixListId' --output text)
aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress --group-id sg-0123456789abcdef0 \
  --ip-permissions "IpProtocol=tcp,FromPort=443,ToPort=443,PrefixListIds=[{PrefixListId=$PL}]"
Public web entry
OptionCloudFront plus ALB
Choose whenglobal users and cacheable content
Avoid whenpurely internal services
OptionALB with WAF only
Choose whenone Region, mostly dynamic
Avoid whenheavy static assets
OptionAPI Gateway
Choose whenmanaged API features such as keys and throttling
Avoid whenyou already have an ALB doing routing
Check yourself
How do you make sure traffic cannot skip CloudFront?

Allow only the CloudFront origin-facing prefix list (and a secret header) on the origin.
