Section 19 of 93

Load balancing for Kubernetes and operations

5 concepts · about 45 minutes

On EKS the AWS Load Balancer Controller turns Ingress and Service objects into real ALBs and NLBs. Understanding target modes and draining avoids dropped requests during rollouts.

Goals
  • Provision ALBs and NLBs from Kubernetes with the AWS Load Balancer Controller
  • Use IP target mode, readiness gates and pod draining for zero downtime
  • Monitor and troubleshoot load balancers with metrics, logs and health states
19.1

AWS Load Balancer Controller

In plain words

The AWS Load Balancer Controller runs in your cluster, watches Ingress and Service objects and creates ALBs, NLBs, listeners and target groups.

The problem it solves

The in-tree cloud provider only creates Classic or basic NLBs. The controller adds ALB Ingress support, IP targets and fine control through annotations.

What it does

  • Install with Helm; give it a role through IRSA or Pod Identity with the published IAM policy.
  • Ingress with ingressClassName: alb creates an ALB. Service of type LoadBalancer with loadBalancerClass: service.k8s.aws/nlb creates an NLB.
  • Subnets are discovered through kubernetes.io/role/elb and kubernetes.io/role/internal-elb tags.
  • IngressGroup (alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/group.name) merges many Ingresses into one ALB to save cost.

Ingress example

yamlingress.yaml
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: shop
  namespace: shop
  annotations:
    alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/scheme: internet-facing
    alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/target-type: ip
    alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/group.name: public
    alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/listen-ports: '[{"HTTPS":443}]'
    alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/certificate-arn: arn:aws:acm:eu-west-1:111122223333:certificate/example
    alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/healthcheck-path: /healthz
    alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/wafv2-acl-arn: arn:aws:wafv2:eu-west-1:111122223333:regional/webacl/web/example
spec:
  ingressClassName: alb
  rules:
    - host: shop.example.com
      http:
        paths:
          - path: /
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: shop
                port:
                  number: 80
bashInstall
helm repo add eks https://aws.github.io/eks-charts && helm repo update
helm install aws-load-balancer-controller eks/aws-load-balancer-controller -n kube-system \
  --set clusterName=prod --set serviceAccount.create=false --set serviceAccount.name=aws-load-balancer-controller
kubectl -n kube-system rollout status deploy/aws-load-balancer-controller
Check yourself
How can many Ingresses share one ALB?

Give them the same alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/group.name annotation.

19.2

Instance mode versus IP mode

In plain words

The target group can register nodes (instance mode, via NodePort) or pod IPs directly (IP mode).

The problem it solves

Instance mode adds a hop through kube-proxy and node port, and traffic may be forwarded to a pod on another node, hiding client IPs and losing balance.

What it does

  • IP mode: ALB or NLB sends straight to pod IPs from the VPC CNI. Fewer hops, accurate health per pod, works with pod readiness gates. Needs VPC-routable pod IPs.
  • Instance mode: works with any CNI; relies on NodePort and externalTrafficPolicy.
  • With externalTrafficPolicy: Local health checks target only nodes with ready pods, which preserves the client IP for NLB instance mode.

NLB service

yamlnlb-service.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: mqtt
  namespace: shop
  annotations:
    service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-nlb-target-type: ip
    service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-scheme: internal
spec:
  type: LoadBalancer
  loadBalancerClass: service.k8s.aws/nlb
  selector:
    app: mqtt
  ports:
    - port: 1883
      targetPort: 1883
Note

service.k8s.aws/nlb is the controller's default class (verified against the controller documentation on 2026-10-31). If the class on a Service is one the controller does not recognise, the controller ignores that Service, even when the older aws-load-balancer-type annotation is present. The class can be changed with the controller flag --load-balancer-class.

19.3

Zero-downtime deployments

In plain words

Pods must leave the load balancer before they stop, and join it only when ready. Several timers make this work.

The problem it solves

Without coordination, a terminating pod keeps receiving requests for seconds because the load balancer has not yet deregistered it, causing 502 and 504 errors.

What it does

  • Enable the pod readiness gate (label the namespace elbv2.k8s.aws/pod-readiness-gate-inject=enabled) so a rollout waits until the pod is healthy in the target group.
  • On termination: Kubernetes sends SIGTERM; the controller starts deregistration; the load balancer drains for deregistration_delay. Add a preStop sleep of about 10 to 20 seconds so the app keeps serving while deregistration propagates.
  • Make terminationGracePeriodSeconds greater than preStop plus shutdown time.
  • Set the target group deregistration delay lower than default 300 seconds for short requests, via the annotation alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/target-group-attributes.

Deployment snippet

yamlgraceful-deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: shop
  namespace: shop
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels: {app: shop}
  template:
    metadata:
      labels: {app: shop}
    spec:
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 60
      containers:
        - name: shop
          image: 111122223333.dkr.ecr.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/shop:1.0
          lifecycle:
            preStop:
              exec:
                command: ["sleep", "15"]
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet: {path: /healthz, port: 8080}
bashEnable readiness gate
kubectl label namespace shop elbv2.k8s.aws/pod-readiness-gate-inject=enabled
kubectl -n shop get pods -o wide
Check yourself
Why a preStop sleep?

The load balancer needs seconds to stop sending new requests, so the pod must keep serving until deregistration takes effect.

19.4

Health checks in depth

In plain words

A target is healthy when it passes a configured number of consecutive probes, unhealthy after a number of failures. Settings control how quickly the load balancer reacts.

The problem it solves

Too sensitive and healthy targets flap; too slow and failures reach users.

What it does

  • ALB: protocol, path, port, interval (5 to 300 seconds), timeout, healthy and unhealthy thresholds, matcher for success codes.
  • Use a lightweight /healthz that checks the process and critical dependencies lightly; do not run expensive queries every few seconds across all targets.
  • If all targets in a target group are unhealthy the ALB fails open and routes to all of them (check the current documentation for details per type).
  • Target group health and application load balancer health at the DNS level (minimum healthy targets) can influence DNS failover through Route 53 integration.

Inspect and tune

bashHealth check tuning
aws elbv2 modify-target-group --target-group-arn arn:aws:elasticloadbalancing:eu-west-1:111122223333:targetgroup/api/0123456789abcdef \
  --health-check-path /healthz --health-check-interval-seconds 10 --healthy-threshold-count 2 --unhealthy-threshold-count 3
aws elbv2 describe-target-health --target-group-arn arn:aws:elasticloadbalancing:eu-west-1:111122223333:targetgroup/api/0123456789abcdef
19.5

Monitoring and troubleshooting

In plain words

Metrics, access logs and a few common error codes quickly show whether a problem is the client, the load balancer or the target.

The problem it solves

A 5xx at the edge could come from many layers; knowing which one produced it saves hours.

What it does

  • ELB-generated: HTTPCode_ELB_5XX_Count (502 bad gateway, 503 no healthy targets, 504 timeout). Target-generated: HTTPCode_Target_5XX_Count. 460 means the client closed the connection early.
  • Latency: TargetResponseTime. Capacity: ActiveConnectionCount, ConsumedLCUs. Health: HealthyHostCount, UnHealthyHostCount.
  • Access logs to S3 (also connection logs) include elb_status_code, target_status_code and target_processing_time; query with Athena.
  • 502 often means the target closed a connection (keep-alive timeout shorter than the ALB idle timeout); set the app keep-alive above 60 seconds.

Alarm

bashAlarm on ELB 5xx
aws cloudwatch put-metric-alarm --alarm-name web-elb-5xx --namespace AWS/ApplicationELB \
  --metric-name HTTPCode_ELB_5XX_Count --dimensions Name=LoadBalancer,Value=app/web/0123456789abcdef \
  --statistic Sum --period 60 --evaluation-periods 3 --threshold 10 --comparison-operator GreaterThanThreshold \
  --treat-missing-data notBreaching --alarm-actions arn:aws:sns:eu-west-1:111122223333:oncall
Tip

For 502s that appear at random after idle periods, compare the application keep-alive timeout with the ALB idle timeout first.

Check yourself
What is the first thing to check for a 503 from an ALB?

Whether the target group has any healthy targets.

← PreviousNext →
Section 20 of 93

Auto Scaling groups and launch templates

5 concepts · about 45 minutes

An Auto Scaling group (ASG) keeps a fleet of EC2 instances at the size you ask for, replaces failed ones and spreads them across AZs. EKS managed node groups are ASGs underneath.

Goals
  • Create an Auto Scaling group from a launch template across several AZs
  • Explain health checks, capacity limits and AZ rebalancing
  • Use mixed instances and attribute-based selection for resilient capacity
20.1

What an ASG does

In plain words

An ASG is a controller. You say minimum, desired and maximum instance counts and which template to use; it launches and terminates instances to match.

The problem it solves

Manually replacing a failed instance or adding capacity at peak is slow and error prone, and nobody is awake at 3 a.m.

What it does

  • Holds MinSize, MaxSize and DesiredCapacity; scaling policies change desired capacity within the bounds.
  • Spreads instances across the subnets (AZs) you give it and rebalances if an AZ becomes uneven.
  • Replaces instances that fail EC2 status checks, and optionally ELB health checks.
  • Registers instances with load balancer target groups automatically.

Create one

hclasg.tf
resource "aws_autoscaling_group" "web" {
  name                      = "web"
  min_size                  = 2
  max_size                  = 12
  desired_capacity          = 3
  vpc_zone_identifier       = var.private_subnet_ids
  health_check_type         = "ELB"
  health_check_grace_period = 120
  target_group_arns         = [aws_lb_target_group.web.arn]

  launch_template {
    id      = aws_launch_template.web.id
    version = "$Latest"
  }

  tag {
    key                 = "Name"
    value               = "web"
    propagate_at_launch = true
  }
}
bashInspect
aws autoscaling describe-auto-scaling-groups --auto-scaling-group-names web \
  --query 'AutoScalingGroups[].[DesiredCapacity,MinSize,MaxSize,Instances[].[InstanceId,AvailabilityZone,LifecycleState,HealthStatus]]'
aws autoscaling describe-scaling-activities --auto-scaling-group-name web --max-items 5 \
  --query 'Activities[].[StartTime,StatusCode,Description]' --output table
Check yourself
Which values bound what a scaling policy can do?

MinSize and MaxSize; policies only change DesiredCapacity inside them.

20.2

Launch templates in an ASG

In plain words

The ASG reads the launch template at each launch. Which version it uses is a setting on the group.

The problem it solves

Using $Latest means any template edit changes future launches silently; pinning a version makes changes explicit.

What it does

  • Template versions are immutable. Reference a number, $Default or $Latest.
  • Changing the version affects only new instances; existing instances keep their old configuration until replaced via instance refresh.
  • Launch configurations are deprecated; use templates.
  • Put IMDSv2, encrypted volumes, tags and the instance profile in the template.

Update the template

bashVersion and point the ASG
aws ec2 create-launch-template-version --launch-template-id lt-0123456789abcdef0 \
  --source-version 3 --launch-template-data '{"ImageId":"ami-0123456789abcdef0"}'
aws autoscaling update-auto-scaling-group --auto-scaling-group-name web \
  --launch-template LaunchTemplateId=lt-0123456789abcdef0,Version='4'
20.3

Health checks and grace period

In plain words

An ASG decides an instance is unhealthy from EC2 status checks, and optionally from the load balancer's view.

The problem it solves

If only EC2 checks are used, an instance with a crashed application still looks healthy. If the grace period is too short, new instances are killed before they finish booting.

What it does

  • Set health_check_type = ELB to also use target group health.
  • Health check grace period is the time after launch before checks count. Set it longer than your slowest bootstrap.
  • Manually mark an instance unhealthy with set-instance-health, or protect from scale-in with instance protection.
  • Pair with a lifecycle hook for cleaner bootstraps.

Mark and protect

bashHealth operations
aws autoscaling set-instance-health --instance-id i-0123456789abcdef0 --health-status Unhealthy
aws autoscaling set-instance-protection --auto-scaling-group-name web --instance-ids i-0123456789abcdef0 --protected-from-scale-in
Careful

A grace period of 0 with ELB checks and a slow bootstrap causes a launch and kill loop. Watch scaling activities for repeated replacements.

Check yourself
What problem does the grace period solve?

It stops the ASG from replacing instances that are still booting and not yet able to pass health checks.

20.4

Availability Zones and rebalancing

In plain words

An ASG tries to keep an equal number of instances per AZ. If an AZ fails or lacks capacity, it launches elsewhere.

The problem it solves

A single-AZ fleet fails with its AZ. Unbalanced fleets lose more capacity in an outage.

What it does

  • Provide subnets in at least two AZs (three is common).
  • AZ rebalancing terminates and relaunches instances to restore balance, after launching new ones first. Disable it with the AZRebalance suspend process if your workload cannot tolerate it, though that reduces resilience.
  • Capacity rebalancing (for Spot) launches a replacement when AWS signals a rebalance recommendation.
  • For EKS, size per-AZ node groups when using EBS volumes because volumes are AZ bound.

Suspend a process

bashProcess control
aws autoscaling suspend-processes --auto-scaling-group-name web --scaling-processes AZRebalance
aws autoscaling resume-processes  --auto-scaling-group-name web --scaling-processes AZRebalance
aws autoscaling describe-auto-scaling-groups --auto-scaling-group-names web --query 'AutoScalingGroups[].SuspendedProcesses'
20.5

Mixed instances and attribute-based selection

In plain words

A single instance type can run out of capacity or Spot supply. A mixed instances policy lets one ASG use several types and purchase options.

The problem it solves

Hard-coding one type causes InsufficientInstanceCapacity and expensive, interrupted Spot fleets.

What it does

  • instances_distribution sets On-Demand base, percentage above the base, and the Spot allocation strategy.
  • Attribute-based instance type selection lets you state requirements (vCPU, memory range, architecture) instead of listing types.
  • Use weights (weighted_capacity) when types differ in size, so desired capacity is measured in units such as vCPUs.
  • Keep all types comparable in performance; otherwise load balancing becomes uneven.

Attribute-based override

hclabis.tf
resource "aws_autoscaling_group" "flex" {
  name                = "flex"
  min_size            = 2
  max_size            = 30
  vpc_zone_identifier = var.private_subnet_ids

  mixed_instances_policy {
    instances_distribution {
      on_demand_base_capacity                  = 1
      on_demand_percentage_above_base_capacity = 20
      spot_allocation_strategy                 = "price-capacity-optimized"
    }
    launch_template {
      launch_template_specification {
        launch_template_id = aws_launch_template.worker.id
        version            = "$Latest"
      }
      override {
        instance_requirements {
          vcpu_count {
            min = 4
            max = 8
          }
          memory_mib {
            min = 8192
            max = 32768
          }
          cpu_manufacturers     = ["intel", "amd"]
          burstable_performance = "excluded"
        }
      }
    }
  }
}
Check yourself
What does an On-Demand base capacity of 2 mean?

The first two instances are always On-Demand; the rest follow the Spot/On-Demand percentage.

← PreviousNext →
Section 21 of 93

Scaling policies and scheduled scaling

5 concepts · about 45 minutes

Policies decide when the ASG changes size. Picking the right metric matters more than the policy type.

Goals
  • Choose between target tracking, step, simple, scheduled and predictive scaling
  • Configure target tracking on CPU and on load balancer requests per target
  • Tune cooldowns, warm-up and scale-in protection to avoid flapping
21.1

Target tracking

In plain words

You choose a metric and a target value, such as 50 percent average CPU. AWS creates the alarms and adjusts capacity to hold the metric near the target.

The problem it solves

Hand-built alarms and step sizes are hard to tune and often under- or over-react.

What it does

  • Predefined metrics: average CPU, network in and out, and ALBRequestCountPerTarget.
  • Custom metrics are allowed, including metrics that fall as capacity rises (queue depth per instance).
  • Scales out quickly and in conservatively; it will not scale in below what keeps the metric at target.
  • Use several target tracking policies together; the ASG follows the one that gives the largest capacity.

Policies

hcltracking.tf
resource "aws_autoscaling_policy" "cpu" {
  name                   = "cpu-50"
  autoscaling_group_name = aws_autoscaling_group.web.name
  policy_type            = "TargetTrackingScaling"
  target_tracking_configuration {
    predefined_metric_specification {
      predefined_metric_type = "ASGAverageCPUUtilization"
    }
    target_value = 50
  }
}

resource "aws_autoscaling_policy" "requests" {
  name                   = "requests-per-target"
  autoscaling_group_name = aws_autoscaling_group.web.name
  policy_type            = "TargetTrackingScaling"
  target_tracking_configuration {
    predefined_metric_specification {
      predefined_metric_type = "ALBRequestCountPerTarget"
      resource_label         = "${aws_lb.web.arn_suffix}/${aws_lb_target_group.web.arn_suffix}"
    }
    target_value = 500
  }
}
Check yourself
Why prefer requests per target over CPU for web services?

It measures load directly, so scaling reacts before CPU saturates and works for IO-bound apps.

21.2

Step and simple scaling

In plain words

Step scaling adds or removes a different amount depending on how far a CloudWatch alarm is breached. Simple scaling does one fixed action per alarm with a cooldown.

The problem it solves

Some metrics, such as queue depth, need an action proportional to the breach.

What it does

  • Step: define steps like "queue 100 to 500: add 2; above 500: add 5". Alarms you write yourself.
  • Simple scaling waits for the cooldown before acting again; step scaling uses instance warm-up instead and can respond continuously.
  • Prefer target tracking; use step policies for custom, non-proportional metrics.

Queue-based step scaling

bashStep policy
aws autoscaling put-scaling-policy --auto-scaling-group-name workers --policy-name queue-steps \
  --policy-type StepScaling --adjustment-type ChangeInCapacity --metric-aggregation-type Average \
  --estimated-instance-warmup 120 \
  --step-adjustments MetricIntervalLowerBound=0,MetricIntervalUpperBound=400,ScalingAdjustment=2 MetricIntervalLowerBound=400,ScalingAdjustment=5
21.3

Scaling on queue depth

In plain words

For workers that read from SQS, the useful signal is backlog per instance, not CPU.

The problem it solves

Workers may sit idle on CPU while a large queue builds, or be CPU-heavy with an empty queue.

What it does

  • Compute backlog per instance = ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible divided by running instances, and publish as a custom metric (or use metric math in the policy).
  • Set a target such as acceptable backlog per instance (messages that one instance processes within the allowed latency).
  • Combine with scale-in protection so a busy worker is not terminated mid-job, or handle SIGTERM and finish the message.
  • In Kubernetes, KEDA does the equivalent for pods.

Metric math target tracking

jsonqueue-target-tracking.json
{
  "TargetValue": 20.0,
  "CustomizedMetricSpecification": {
    "Metrics": [
      {"Id": "m1", "Label": "visible", "ReturnData": false, "MetricStat": {"Metric": {"Namespace": "AWS/SQS", "MetricName": "ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible", "Dimensions": [{"Name": "QueueName", "Value": "jobs"}]}, "Stat": "Average"}},
      {"Id": "m2", "Label": "instances", "ReturnData": false, "MetricStat": {"Metric": {"Namespace": "AWS/AutoScaling", "MetricName": "GroupInServiceInstances", "Dimensions": [{"Name": "AutoScalingGroupName", "Value": "workers"}]}, "Stat": "Average"}},
      {"Id": "e1", "Label": "backlog per instance", "ReturnData": true, "Expression": "m1 / m2"}
    ]
  }
}
bashApply
aws autoscaling put-scaling-policy --auto-scaling-group-name workers --policy-name backlog \
  --policy-type TargetTrackingScaling --target-tracking-configuration file://queue-target-tracking.json
Note

GroupInServiceInstances requires group metrics collection to be enabled with enable-metrics-collection.

Check yourself
Which metric would you scale SQS workers on?

Backlog per instance (queue depth divided by instances), not CPU.

21.4

Scheduled and predictive scaling

In plain words

Scheduled actions change capacity at set times. Predictive scaling learns daily and weekly patterns and scales ahead of load.

The problem it solves

Reactive scaling lags behind a sudden known peak, such as a nine o'clock login surge.

What it does

  • Scheduled actions set min, max or desired using cron (UTC unless a time zone is given); use for known events and for turning off dev at night.
  • Predictive scaling forecasts from at least a day of history (best with two weeks), and can run in forecast-only mode first.
  • Combine: predictive sets a floor, target tracking handles surprises.

Examples

bashScheduled actions
aws autoscaling put-scheduled-update-group-action --auto-scaling-group-name web --scheduled-action-name weekday-up \
  --recurrence "0 7 * * 1-5" --time-zone "Europe/Dublin" --min-size 4 --desired-capacity 6
aws autoscaling put-scheduled-update-group-action --auto-scaling-group-name web --scheduled-action-name night-down \
  --recurrence "0 20 * * *" --time-zone "Europe/Dublin" --min-size 1 --desired-capacity 1
aws autoscaling describe-scheduled-actions --auto-scaling-group-name web --query 'ScheduledUpdateGroupActions[].[ScheduledActionName,Recurrence]'
21.5

Warm-up, cooldown and scale-in

In plain words

Scaling decisions need time to take effect. Warm-up and cooldown stop the ASG from reacting twice to the same load.

The problem it solves

New instances take minutes to boot. If the policy keeps counting their idle CPU, it concludes there is spare capacity and scales in too early (flapping).

What it does

  • Default instance warmup excludes new instances from metrics for a period; set it to your real time-to-serve.
  • Cooldown pauses simple scaling after an action.
  • Scale-in protection on instances and termination policies (OldestLaunchTemplate, OldestInstance, Default) shape who is removed.
  • Scale in slowly, scale out fast. Alarm on GroupInServiceInstances and on scaling failures.

Settings

bashWarm-up and termination policy
aws autoscaling update-auto-scaling-group --auto-scaling-group-name web \
  --default-instance-warmup 180 --termination-policies OldestLaunchTemplate Default
aws autoscaling enable-metrics-collection --auto-scaling-group-name web --granularity 1Minute
Check yourself
What happens if warm-up is shorter than boot time?

New instances report low load too early, so the ASG thinks it has surplus capacity and may scale in again.

← PreviousNext →
Section 22 of 93

Lifecycle hooks, instance refresh and warm pools

4 concepts · about 45 minutes

Production fleets need controlled starts, graceful shutdowns and safe rollouts. These three features provide them.

Goals
  • Use lifecycle hooks to run work on launch and terminate with correct timeouts
  • Roll out a new AMI using instance refresh with checkpoints and rollback
  • Reduce scale-out latency with warm pools and understand when they pay off
22.1

Lifecycle hooks

In plain words

A lifecycle hook pauses an instance in a wait state when it launches or before it terminates, so your automation can finish its work first.

The problem it solves

Without a hook, an instance enters service the moment it boots (before config is ready) and is removed instantly on scale-in, cutting off in-flight jobs and skipping log upload.

What it does

  • States: Pending:Wait on launch and Terminating:Wait on terminate.
  • The ASG publishes a notification to EventBridge, SNS or SQS. Your automation does the work, then calls complete-lifecycle-action with CONTINUE or ABANDON.
  • HeartbeatTimeout is how long to wait (default one hour); record-lifecycle-action-heartbeat extends it. DefaultResult applies on timeout.
  • On Kubernetes, the node termination handler or Karpenter handles this role for you.

Hook and completion

hclhook.tf
resource "aws_autoscaling_lifecycle_hook" "drain" {
  name                   = "drain"
  autoscaling_group_name = aws_autoscaling_group.web.name
  lifecycle_transition   = "autoscaling:EC2_INSTANCE_TERMINATING"
  heartbeat_timeout      = 300
  default_result         = "CONTINUE"
}
bashComplete from automation
aws autoscaling complete-lifecycle-action --lifecycle-hook-name drain --auto-scaling-group-name web \
  --lifecycle-action-result CONTINUE --instance-id i-0123456789abcdef0
aws autoscaling describe-lifecycle-hooks --auto-scaling-group-name web
Careful

If your automation fails and the default result is CONTINUE, the instance terminates without cleanup. Choose the default deliberately and alarm on hook timeouts.

Check yourself
What happens when a hook times out?

The ASG applies the DefaultResult (CONTINUE or ABANDON).

22.2

Instance refresh

In plain words

Instance refresh replaces instances in an ASG gradually so they pick up a new template version, while keeping a minimum healthy percentage.

The problem it solves

Changing a template does nothing to running instances. Terminating all at once causes an outage.

What it does

  • MinHealthyPercentage sets how much capacity must stay healthy; InstanceWarmup sets the wait before counting a new instance healthy.
  • Checkpoints pause the refresh at percentages (for example 20 and 50) so you can verify before continuing.
  • Auto rollback returns to the previous configuration if alarms fire or the refresh fails (check the current documentation for supported triggers).
  • Skip-matching skips instances already on the target configuration.

Start and monitor

bashRefresh
aws autoscaling start-instance-refresh --auto-scaling-group-name web \
  --preferences '{"MinHealthyPercentage":90,"InstanceWarmup":120,"CheckpointPercentages":[20,50],"CheckpointDelay":600,"AutoRollback":true,"SkipMatching":true}'
aws autoscaling describe-instance-refreshes --auto-scaling-group-name web \
  --query 'InstanceRefreshes[0].[Status,PercentageComplete,StatusReason]'
aws autoscaling cancel-instance-refresh --auto-scaling-group-name web
hclrefresh-in-terraform.tf
resource "aws_autoscaling_group" "web_refresh" {
  name                = "web-refresh"
  min_size            = 3
  max_size            = 9
  vpc_zone_identifier = var.private_subnet_ids

  launch_template {
    id      = aws_launch_template.web.id
    version = aws_launch_template.web.latest_version
  }

  instance_refresh {
    strategy = "Rolling"
    preferences {
      min_healthy_percentage = 90
      instance_warmup        = 120
    }
  }
}
Check yourself
Does updating the launch template version replace running instances?

No. You need an instance refresh (or manual replacement) to roll it out.

22.3

Warm pools

In plain words

A warm pool keeps pre-initialised instances stopped (or hibernated or running) next to the ASG, so scale-out takes seconds instead of the full boot time.

The problem it solves

Applications with long initialisation (large images, big caches, JVM warm-up) cannot respond to sudden spikes if each instance takes several minutes.

What it does

  • Pool states: Stopped (pay only for EBS), Hibernated, or Running.
  • On scale-out the ASG takes instances from the pool first, then launches from scratch if the pool is empty.
  • Lifecycle hooks run when instances enter the pool, so pre-initialisation work is done once.
  • Costs: EBS and, for running, full instance cost. Savings: lower over-provisioning. Check current pricing and support for your instance types; EKS support has specific requirements.

Add a pool

bashWarm pool
aws autoscaling put-warm-pool --auto-scaling-group-name web --pool-state Stopped \
  --min-size 2 --max-group-prepared-capacity 6 --instance-reuse-policy ReuseOnScaleIn=true
aws autoscaling describe-warm-pool --auto-scaling-group-name web --query 'Instances[].[InstanceId,LifecycleState]'
Reducing scale-out time
OptionSmaller, faster image (baked AMI)
Choose whenany fleet; always first
Avoid whenimage is already minimal
OptionWarm pool
Choose whenboot plus init takes minutes and spikes are sharp
Avoid whenscale events are slow and predictable
OptionPredictive scaling
Choose whenrepeating daily pattern
Avoid whentraffic is random
OptionOver-provision
Choose whencannot tolerate any delay
Avoid whencost is tight
22.4

Auto Scaling for EKS and Karpenter

In plain words

EKS managed node groups use ASGs. Karpenter and Cluster Autoscaler decide when nodes are needed from pending pods.

The problem it solves

Pod autoscaling alone cannot create capacity; something must add nodes when pods are unschedulable.

What it does

  • Cluster Autoscaler changes ASG desired capacity based on pending pods and node utilisation; needs ASG tags k8s.io/cluster-autoscaler/enabled.
  • Karpenter launches instances directly (no ASG) matching pod requirements, consolidating and replacing nodes, and handles Spot interruptions.
  • Order of scaling: HPA or KEDA scales pods, then the node autoscaler adds nodes.
  • Do not put manual scaling policies on an ASG managed by Cluster Autoscaler.

Cluster Autoscaler tags

hclca-tags.tf
resource "aws_autoscaling_group" "ng" {
  name                = "eks-ng"
  min_size            = 2
  max_size            = 10
  vpc_zone_identifier = var.private_subnet_ids
  launch_template {
    id      = aws_launch_template.worker.id
    version = "$Latest"
  }
  tag {
    key                 = "k8s.io/cluster-autoscaler/enabled"
    value               = "true"
    propagate_at_launch = false
  }
  tag {
    key                 = "k8s.io/cluster-autoscaler/prod"
    value               = "owned"
    propagate_at_launch = false
  }
}
Note

Item 9 of this track covers Karpenter in depth. Here the key point is that the ASG remains a building block for managed node groups.

Check yourself
What triggers node scale-out in Kubernetes?

Pods that cannot be scheduled (Pending), which Cluster Autoscaler or Karpenter react to.

Section 23 of 93

S3 fundamentals and storage classes

5 concepts · about 45 minutes

Amazon S3 is object storage with effectively unlimited capacity. It holds logs, backups, static sites, ML data, Terraform state and container registry layers, so it is part of nearly every design.

Goals
  • Describe the S3 data model, consistency and durability
  • Choose a storage class by access pattern and retrieval needs
  • Create buckets safely with Block Public Access and ownership controls
23.1

Buckets, objects and keys

In plain words

A bucket is a named container in one Region. An object is a blob of data with a key (its full name), metadata and optional tags. There are no real folders; slashes in keys are only a naming convention.

The problem it solves

Traditional file systems struggle with billions of files and need servers. S3 offers an HTTP API with no servers to run.

What it does

  • Bucket names are globally unique within a partition. Create them in the Region closest to the workload.
  • Objects can be up to 5 TB; a single PUT up to 5 GB, so use multipart upload for larger objects (recommended from about 100 MB).
  • S3 provides strong read-after-write consistency for all operations.
  • Designed for 99.999999999 percent (11 nines) durability by storing data redundantly across multiple AZs for most classes.
  • Prefixes (logs/2026/10/) group keys for listing, permissions and lifecycle rules.

Everyday commands

bashaws s3 and s3api
aws s3 mb s3://acme-data-eu --region eu-west-1
aws s3 cp ./report.csv s3://acme-data-eu/reports/2026/10/report.csv
aws s3 sync ./site s3://acme-data-eu/site --delete --exclude ".git/*"
aws s3 ls s3://acme-data-eu/reports/ --recursive --human-readable --summarize
aws s3api head-object --bucket acme-data-eu --key reports/2026/10/report.csv
Check yourself
Does S3 have real folders?

No. Keys are flat strings; the console shows prefixes as folders.

23.2

Secure bucket defaults

In plain words

New buckets should block public access, enforce ownership by the bucket owner, encrypt data and require TLS.

The problem it solves

Publicly exposed buckets are a repeated cause of data leaks, often through an old ACL or an overly broad policy.

What it does

  • Block Public Access (four settings) overrides ACLs and policies that would make data public. Enable at the account level, and in each bucket.
  • Object Ownership = BucketOwnerEnforced disables ACLs entirely; control access with policies only. This is the default for new buckets.
  • Default encryption with SSE-S3 is applied to all new objects automatically.
  • Bucket policy denying aws:SecureTransport = false forces HTTPS.

Terraform baseline

hclbucket.tf
resource "aws_s3_bucket" "data" {
  bucket = "acme-data-eu"
}

resource "aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block" "data" {
  bucket                  = aws_s3_bucket.data.id
  block_public_acls       = true
  block_public_policy     = true
  ignore_public_acls      = true
  restrict_public_buckets = true
}

resource "aws_s3_bucket_ownership_controls" "data" {
  bucket = aws_s3_bucket.data.id
  rule {
    object_ownership = "BucketOwnerEnforced"
  }
}

data "aws_iam_policy_document" "tls_only" {
  statement {
    effect    = "Deny"
    actions   = ["s3:*"]
    resources = [aws_s3_bucket.data.arn, "${aws_s3_bucket.data.arn}/*"]
    principals {
      type        = "*"
      identifiers = ["*"]
    }
    condition {
      test     = "Bool"
      variable = "aws:SecureTransport"
      values   = ["false"]
    }
  }
}

resource "aws_s3_bucket_policy" "data" {
  bucket = aws_s3_bucket.data.id
  policy = data.aws_iam_policy_document.tls_only.json
}
bashAccount-wide block
aws s3control put-public-access-block --account-id 111122223333 \
  --public-access-block-configuration BlockPublicAcls=true,IgnorePublicAcls=true,BlockPublicPolicy=true,RestrictPublicBuckets=true
Check yourself
What does BucketOwnerEnforced do?

Disables ACLs, so the bucket owner owns every object and policies are the only access control.

23.3

Storage classes

In plain words

A storage class trades storage price against retrieval cost, retrieval time and minimum duration.

The problem it solves

Keeping rarely used data in the standard class overpays, while moving hot data to a cold class makes reads slow or costly.

What it does

  • S3 Standard: frequent access, no retrieval fee, lowest latency.
  • S3 Intelligent-Tiering: moves objects between access tiers automatically for a small monitoring fee per object; best when patterns are unknown. Small objects (under 128 KB) are not auto-tiered.
  • Standard-IA and One Zone-IA: infrequent access, retrieval fee, 30-day minimum, 128 KB minimum billable size. One Zone-IA keeps data in a single AZ.
  • Glacier Instant Retrieval: archive with millisecond access, 90-day minimum.
  • Glacier Flexible Retrieval: minutes to hours, 90-day minimum. Glacier Deep Archive: lowest price, hours (about 12 or more), 180-day minimum.
  • S3 Express One Zone: single-digit millisecond directory buckets for hot, latency-sensitive data. Check current pricing and Regions.
  • Minimum durations, sizes and prices change; verify them on the current pricing page.

Set a class on upload

bashChoose at write time
aws s3 cp backup.tar.gz s3://acme-data-eu/backups/ --storage-class GLACIER_IR
aws s3 cp scratch.bin s3://acme-data-eu/tmp/ --storage-class INTELLIGENT_TIERING
aws s3api list-objects-v2 --bucket acme-data-eu --prefix backups/ --query 'Contents[].[Key,StorageClass,Size]' --output table
Tip

For Kubernetes logs and backups, write directly into Intelligent-Tiering or add a lifecycle rule, rather than leaving everything in Standard.

23.4

Restoring archived objects

In plain words

Objects in Glacier Flexible Retrieval and Deep Archive are not readable until you request a restore, which creates a temporary copy.

The problem it solves

An application that reads archived keys directly fails with InvalidObjectState.

What it does

  • restore-object with a tier: Expedited (minutes, Flexible only), Standard, Bulk (cheapest, slowest). Days setting controls how long the copy stays.
  • Poll head-object for the Restore header, or enable event notifications for s3:ObjectRestore:Completed.
  • Glacier Instant Retrieval objects are readable immediately.
  • Use S3 Batch Operations to restore many objects.

Restore

bashRequest and check
aws s3api restore-object --bucket acme-data-eu --key archive/2024.tar \
  --restore-request '{"Days":7,"GlacierJobParameters":{"Tier":"Standard"}}'
aws s3api head-object --bucket acme-data-eu --key archive/2024.tar --query Restore
Check yourself
Can you GET a Deep Archive object directly?

No. Restore it first and read the temporary copy.

23.5

Consistency, durability and availability

In plain words

S3 reads see the latest write immediately. Durability is about not losing data; availability is about reaching it.

The problem it solves

Engineers confuse durability with protection from deletion and corruption. S3 will faithfully store a deletion you ask for.

What it does

  • Strong consistency removes old workarounds such as listing delays.
  • 11 nines is the designed durability; availability differs per class (for example 99.99 percent for Standard; check the current SLA table).
  • Protect against human error with versioning, MFA delete, Object Lock and replication, not by relying on durability.
  • Regional endpoints: reach them via a gateway endpoint from a VPC; use the same Region as compute to avoid transfer fees.

Checks

bashCheck protection state
aws s3api get-bucket-versioning --bucket acme-data-eu
aws s3api get-public-access-block --bucket acme-data-eu
aws s3api get-bucket-encryption --bucket acme-data-eu
← PreviousNext →
Section 24 of 93

S3 versioning, lifecycle and inventory

5 concepts · about 45 minutes

Time is the main cost driver in S3. Versioning protects data, lifecycle rules control its cost, and inventory tools tell you what you have.

Goals
  • Enable versioning and recover deleted or overwritten objects
  • Write lifecycle rules that transition, expire and clean up safely
  • Use Inventory, Storage Lens and Batch Operations to manage large buckets
24.1

Versioning

In plain words

With versioning on, every write creates a new version and a delete adds a delete marker instead of removing data.

The problem it solves

Overwrites and deletes are permanent by default, so a script bug can destroy data.

What it does

  • Each version has a version ID. A plain GET returns the latest non-deleted version.
  • Deleting with a version ID permanently removes that version; deleting without one adds a delete marker.
  • Versioning can be suspended but never fully turned off once enabled.
  • Noncurrent versions cost storage, so pair versioning with lifecycle rules.
  • MFA Delete requires MFA to permanently delete versions or change versioning state (root user only to enable).

Recover

bashVersions and restore
aws s3api put-bucket-versioning --bucket acme-data-eu --versioning-configuration Status=Enabled
aws s3api list-object-versions --bucket acme-data-eu --prefix reports/a.csv \
  --query '{Versions:Versions[].[VersionId,IsLatest,LastModified],Markers:DeleteMarkers[].[VersionId,IsLatest]}'
# undo a delete by removing the delete marker
aws s3api delete-object --bucket acme-data-eu --key reports/a.csv --version-id EXAMPLEMARKERVERSIONID
# restore an older version by copying it onto the key
aws s3api copy-object --bucket acme-data-eu --key reports/a.csv --copy-source "acme-data-eu/reports/a.csv?versionId=EXAMPLEOLDVERSIONID"
Check yourself
What does deleting an object in a versioned bucket do?

It adds a delete marker; earlier versions remain and can be restored.

24.2

Lifecycle rules

In plain words

A lifecycle configuration is a set of rules that move objects to cheaper classes or delete them after a number of days, optionally filtered by prefix, tag or size.

The problem it solves

Manual cleanup of logs, backups and old versions never happens, so cost grows forever.

What it does

  • Transition actions move current or noncurrent versions between classes (respecting minimum days between transitions, check the current rules).
  • Expiration deletes current objects (or adds a delete marker in versioned buckets) and, for noncurrent versions, permanently removes them after N days.
  • Abort incomplete multipart uploads after some days; leftovers are billed invisibly.
  • Expired object delete markers cleanup; filter by prefix, tags, ObjectSizeGreaterThan / LessThan.
  • Rules run asynchronously, typically at midnight UTC; changes take time to apply.

A typical rule set

jsonlifecycle.json
{
  "Rules": [
    {
      "ID": "logs-tiering",
      "Status": "Enabled",
      "Filter": {"Prefix": "logs/"},
      "Transitions": [
        {"Days": 30, "StorageClass": "STANDARD_IA"},
        {"Days": 90, "StorageClass": "GLACIER"}
      ],
      "Expiration": {"Days": 365},
      "NoncurrentVersionExpiration": {"NoncurrentDays": 30},
      "AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload": {"DaysAfterInitiation": 7}
    },
    {
      "ID": "clean-delete-markers",
      "Status": "Enabled",
      "Filter": {"Prefix": ""},
      "Expiration": {"ExpiredObjectDeleteMarker": true}
    }
  ]
}
bashApply
aws s3api put-bucket-lifecycle-configuration --bucket acme-data-eu --lifecycle-configuration file://lifecycle.json
aws s3api get-bucket-lifecycle-configuration --bucket acme-data-eu --query 'Rules[].ID'
Careful

Transitioning many tiny objects to IA or Glacier can cost more than it saves because of per-object fees and the 128 KB minimum billable size. Filter by size and test with a small prefix.

Check yourself
Why add AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload?

Failed multipart uploads leave hidden parts that you pay for until they are aborted.

24.3

Versioning plus lifecycle in Terraform

In plain words

Treat bucket configuration as code so that versioning and retention are consistent and reviewed.

The problem it solves

Console changes drift and nobody knows why a bucket keeps data forever.

What it does

  • Provider v4 and later split settings into separate resources (aws_s3_bucket_versioning, aws_s3_bucket_lifecycle_configuration).
  • Lifecycle rules depend on versioning when they use noncurrent actions.
  • Use modules for standard buckets: logs, backups, data lake, static site.

Resources

hcllifecycle.tf
resource "aws_s3_bucket_versioning" "data" {
  bucket = aws_s3_bucket.data.id
  versioning_configuration {
    status = "Enabled"
  }
}

resource "aws_s3_bucket_lifecycle_configuration" "data" {
  bucket     = aws_s3_bucket.data.id
  depends_on = [aws_s3_bucket_versioning.data]

  rule {
    id     = "logs"
    status = "Enabled"
    filter {
      prefix = "logs/"
    }
    transition {
      days          = 30
      storage_class = "STANDARD_IA"
    }
    expiration {
      days = 365
    }
    noncurrent_version_expiration {
      noncurrent_days = 30
    }
    abort_incomplete_multipart_upload {
      days_after_initiation = 7
    }
  }
}
24.4

S3 Inventory and Storage Lens

In plain words

Listing a billion objects through the API is slow and expensive. Inventory delivers a scheduled report file; Storage Lens shows usage and activity trends across accounts.

The problem it solves

You cannot optimise or audit what you cannot see: which prefixes are huge, which objects are unencrypted or cold.

What it does

  • S3 Inventory: daily or weekly CSV, ORC or Parquet listing with size, class, encryption, replication state and more, delivered to another bucket. Query with Athena.
  • S3 Storage Lens: dashboards for the organization with metrics on bytes, request rates, incomplete multipart uploads, noncurrent versions, and recommendations; advanced metrics are paid.
  • Storage Class Analysis suggests when to move data to IA.
  • CloudWatch request metrics (opt in per prefix) give 4xx, 5xx and latency.

Enable inventory

bashInventory configuration
aws s3api put-bucket-inventory-configuration --bucket acme-data-eu --id weekly --inventory-configuration '{
  "Id":"weekly","IsEnabled":true,"IncludedObjectVersions":"Current","Schedule":{"Frequency":"Weekly"},
  "Destination":{"S3BucketDestination":{"Bucket":"arn:aws:s3:::acme-inventory","Format":"Parquet","Prefix":"acme-data-eu"}},
  "OptionalFields":["Size","StorageClass","EncryptionStatus","LastModifiedDate"]}'
aws s3api list-bucket-inventory-configurations --bucket acme-data-eu
Check yourself
Why use Inventory instead of list-objects for huge buckets?

It produces a scheduled bulk report cheaply, avoiding millions of slow, billed LIST calls.

24.5

Batch Operations and cost review

In plain words

S3 Batch Operations runs one action (copy, tag, restore, invoke a Lambda function, replace ACLs, set Object Lock) across a manifest of objects.

The problem it solves

One-off fleet changes such as re-encrypting existing objects or restoring archives need a reliable bulk mechanism.

What it does

  • Manifest from an Inventory report or a CSV of keys. Job produces a completion report.
  • Typical uses: copy in place to apply new encryption keys, add tags, restore archived data, replicate existing objects.
  • Check costs: requests, transfers across Regions, retrieval fees, minimum duration penalties for early deletion in IA and Glacier classes.
  • Cost levers: lifecycle, Intelligent-Tiering, fewer small objects (compact logs), same-Region access, gateway endpoint.

Job outline

bashCreate a tagging job
aws s3control create-job --account-id 111122223333 --no-confirmation-required --priority 10 \
  --role-arn arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/s3-batch \
  --operation '{"S3PutObjectTagging":{"TagSet":[{"Key":"reviewed","Value":"2026"}]}}' \
  --manifest '{"Spec":{"Format":"S3BatchOperations_CSV_20180820","Fields":["Bucket","Key"]},"Location":{"ObjectArn":"arn:aws:s3:::acme-inventory/manifest.csv","ETag":"example"}}' \
  --report '{"Bucket":"arn:aws:s3:::acme-inventory","Format":"Report_CSV_20180820","Enabled":true,"Prefix":"reports","ReportScope":"AllTasks"}'

Section 25 of 93

S3 replication and encryption

5 concepts · about 50 minutes

Data protection in S3 has two halves: where copies live (replication) and who can decrypt them (encryption).

Goals
  • Configure same-Region and cross-Region replication and know what it does not copy
  • Choose between SSE-S3, SSE-KMS, DSSE-KMS and client-side encryption
  • Use bucket keys and KMS key policies to control cost and access
25.1

Replication

In plain words

S3 Replication copies new objects asynchronously from a source bucket to one or more destination buckets, in the same Region (SRR) or another (CRR), in the same or another account.

The problem it solves

You need disaster recovery in another Region, data residency copies, log aggregation across accounts, or lower latency for remote readers.

What it does

  • Requires versioning on both buckets and an IAM role that S3 assumes to read from the source and write to the destination.
  • Rules filter by prefix or tag. Replicates new objects only; existing objects need Batch Replication.
  • Can change owner, storage class and KMS key on the destination. Delete markers replication is optional; permanent version deletes are not replicated, which protects against malicious deletes.
  • Replication Time Control (RTC) gives a 15-minute SLA with metrics, for an extra fee.
  • Bidirectional replication is possible with replica modification sync; avoid loops.

Configuration

jsonreplication.json
{
  "Role": "arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/s3-replication",
  "Rules": [
    {
      "ID": "backups-to-dr",
      "Status": "Enabled",
      "Priority": 1,
      "Filter": {"Prefix": "backups/"},
      "DeleteMarkerReplication": {"Status": "Disabled"},
      "Destination": {
        "Bucket": "arn:aws:s3:::acme-data-dr",
        "StorageClass": "STANDARD_IA"
      }
    }
  ]
}
bashApply and monitor
aws s3api put-bucket-replication --bucket acme-data-eu --replication-configuration file://replication.json
aws s3api head-object --bucket acme-data-eu --key backups/a.tar --query ReplicationStatus
aws s3api head-object --bucket acme-data-dr --key backups/a.tar --query ReplicationStatus   # REPLICA
Check yourself
Are objects that existed before the rule replicated?

No. Use S3 Batch Replication for existing objects.

25.2

Encryption at rest

In plain words

Every S3 object is encrypted at rest. You choose who manages the key.

The problem it solves

Compliance and key-ownership rules differ; some data must be decryptable only by specific principals, with an audit trail.

What it does

  • SSE-S3 (AES-256, keys managed by S3): default for all new objects since 2023, no cost, no extra audit.
  • SSE-KMS: keys in AWS KMS (AWS managed aws/s3 or your customer managed key). Every use is logged in CloudTrail; access needs both S3 and KMS permissions. KMS request quotas and cost apply.
  • DSSE-KMS: two layers of encryption for special compliance cases.
  • SSE-C: you supply the key per request; S3 does not store it. Uncommon. Check the current status of SSE-C defaults as they have changed.
  • Client-side: encrypt before upload with your own tooling or the AWS Encryption SDK.

SSE-KMS with bucket keys

hclkms-bucket.tf
resource "aws_kms_key" "s3" {
  description         = "S3 data key"
  enable_key_rotation = true
}

resource "aws_s3_bucket_server_side_encryption_configuration" "data" {
  bucket = aws_s3_bucket.data.id
  rule {
    apply_server_side_encryption_by_default {
      sse_algorithm     = "aws:kms"
      kms_master_key_id = aws_kms_key.s3.arn
    }
    bucket_key_enabled = true
  }
}
Tip

Enable S3 Bucket Keys with SSE-KMS. They cut KMS requests substantially, lowering cost and the chance of KMS throttling.

25.3

KMS permissions for S3

In plain words

With SSE-KMS a caller needs permission on the bucket and on the key. A missing key permission looks like an S3 access denied.

The problem it solves

Cross-account reads and replication fail with confusing errors when the key policy does not name the other principal.

What it does

  • Reader needs s3:GetObject and kms:Decrypt; writer needs s3:PutObject and kms:GenerateDataKey (and kms:Encrypt for some paths).
  • The key policy must allow the account (via the root statement enabling IAM) or the principal explicitly; cross-account needs both key policy and IAM policy.
  • Replication role needs kms:Decrypt on the source key and kms:Encrypt/GenerateDataKey on the destination key.
  • Use kms:ViaService and kms:CallerAccount conditions to restrict key use to S3.
  • Enforce encryption with a bucket policy condition on s3:x-amz-server-side-encryption.

Reader policy and key conditions

jsonreader-kms.json
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {"Effect": "Allow", "Action": "s3:GetObject", "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::acme-data-eu/reports/*"},
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": "kms:Decrypt",
      "Resource": "arn:aws:kms:eu-west-1:111122223333:key/11111111-2222-3333-4444-555555555555",
      "Condition": {"StringEquals": {"kms:ViaService": "s3.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com"}}
    }
  ]
}
bashDebug an access denied
aws kms describe-key --key-id alias/s3-data --query 'KeyMetadata.[KeyState,KeyManager]'
aws kms get-key-policy --key-id alias/s3-data --policy-name default --query Policy --output text | python3 -m json.tool | head -30
Check yourself
A read fails only for SSE-KMS objects. What do you check first?

The caller's kms:Decrypt permission and the key policy, in addition to the S3 policy.

25.4

Enforcing encryption and transit security

In plain words

Policies can reject uploads that do not meet your encryption and TLS standards.

The problem it solves

Defaults help but a developer may request another algorithm or key.

What it does

  • Deny PutObject unless s3:x-amz-server-side-encryption equals aws:kms and the key ARN matches (s3:x-amz-server-side-encryption-aws-kms-key-id).
  • Deny non-TLS requests, and require a minimum TLS version with s3:TlsVersion.
  • Default bucket encryption applies when no header is sent, so such a policy must permit requests without headers if you rely on defaults; test before enforcing.
  • Use Access Analyzer and AWS Config rules (s3-bucket-server-side-encryption-enabled) to report drift.

Policy

jsonenforce-kms.json
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Sid": "DenyWrongKey",
      "Effect": "Deny",
      "Principal": "*",
      "Action": "s3:PutObject",
      "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::acme-data-eu/*",
      "Condition": {
        "StringNotEqualsIfExists": {
          "s3:x-amz-server-side-encryption-aws-kms-key-id": "arn:aws:kms:eu-west-1:111122223333:key/11111111-2222-3333-4444-555555555555"
        },
        "Null": {"s3:x-amz-server-side-encryption-aws-kms-key-id": "false"}
      }
    },
    {
      "Sid": "MinimumTls",
      "Effect": "Deny",
      "Principal": "*",
      "Action": "s3:*",
      "Resource": ["arn:aws:s3:::acme-data-eu", "arn:aws:s3:::acme-data-eu/*"],
      "Condition": {"NumericLessThan": {"s3:TlsVersion": "1.2"}}
    }
  ]
}
25.5

Multi-Region Access Points and replication patterns

In plain words

A Multi-Region Access Point gives one global endpoint that routes requests to the closest replicated bucket.

The problem it solves

Multi-Region applications want one name, low latency reads and failover without client logic.

What it does

  • Create the access point over buckets in different Regions that are already linked by replication.
  • Requests are routed over the AWS network to the lowest-latency bucket; failover controls shift traffic between active and passive buckets.
  • Use with two-way replication for active-active. Reads are eventually consistent across Regions.
  • Requests are signed with SigV4A (multi-Region signing); use a recent SDK or CLI.
  • Extra data routing and request costs apply; check current pricing.
Multi-Region data
OptionCross-Region replication
Choose whenDR copy, residency
Avoid whenyou need one global endpoint for clients
OptionMulti-Region Access Point
Choose whenactive-active reads and failover
Avoid whensingle Region applications
OptionBackups with AWS Backup
Choose whenscheduled, vault-locked copies
Avoid whenlow RPO sync is required
Check yourself
Why must versioning be enabled before replication?

Replication tracks object versions, so both source and destination need versioning.

Section 26 of 93

S3 access control, access points and presigned URLs

5 concepts · about 50 minutes

S3 has several overlapping ways to grant access. A clear mental model, and one place where rules live, avoids both leaks and mystery denials.

Goals
  • Combine IAM, bucket policies and access points without conflicting rules
  • Generate and constrain presigned URLs and presigned POST for uploads
  • Use Object Lock and MFA delete to make data tamper resistant
26.1

How S3 authorises requests

In plain words

S3 combines the caller's IAM policies, the bucket policy, access point policies, Block Public Access, ACLs (if enabled) and any organization SCPs/RCPs. Evaluation follows the IAM logic: explicit deny wins, otherwise some allow is needed.

The problem it solves

People add a policy in one place and wonder why another still denies, or leave an ACL allowing public read.

What it does

  • Same-account access: an allow in either the identity policy or the bucket policy is enough (unless the bucket policy only names the account root, in which case identity policies must allow).
  • Cross-account: both sides must allow.
  • Keep ACLs disabled with BucketOwnerEnforced.
  • Prefer prefix-scoped bucket policies or access points over one huge bucket policy.

Bucket policy for a prefix

jsonprefix-policy.json
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Sid": "TeamRead",
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Principal": {"AWS": "arn:aws:iam::444455556666:role/analytics"},
      "Action": ["s3:GetObject"],
      "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::acme-data-eu/shared/analytics/*"
    },
    {
      "Sid": "TeamList",
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Principal": {"AWS": "arn:aws:iam::444455556666:role/analytics"},
      "Action": "s3:ListBucket",
      "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::acme-data-eu",
      "Condition": {"StringLike": {"s3:prefix": ["shared/analytics/*"]}}
    }
  ]
}
Check yourself
Can an object ACL still expose data in a BucketOwnerEnforced bucket?

No. ACLs are disabled, so only policies apply.

26.2

S3 Access Points

In plain words

An access point is a named endpoint attached to a bucket with its own policy and optional VPC restriction.

The problem it solves

A shared bucket used by dozens of teams ends up with an unreadable bucket policy near the size limit.

What it does

  • Each access point has its own DNS name and ARN (arn:aws:s3:region:account:accesspoint/name) and its own policy; the bucket policy simply delegates to access points in the same account.
  • VPC-restricted access points accept requests only from the specified VPC.
  • Object Lambda access points transform data on read (redact, convert) with a Lambda function.
  • Multi-Region access points route across buckets (see replication).
  • Applications use the access point ARN in place of the bucket name.

Create

bashAccess point with a VPC restriction
aws s3control create-access-point --account-id 111122223333 --bucket acme-data-eu --name ingest-ap \
  --vpc-configuration VpcId=vpc-0123456789abcdef0
aws s3control put-access-point-policy --account-id 111122223333 --name ingest-ap --policy file://ap-policy.json
aws s3 cp ./file s3://arn:aws:s3:eu-west-1:111122223333:accesspoint/ingest-ap/incoming/file
jsondelegate-to-access-points.json
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Principal": {"AWS": "*"},
      "Action": "*",
      "Resource": ["arn:aws:s3:::acme-data-eu", "arn:aws:s3:::acme-data-eu/*"],
      "Condition": {"StringEquals": {"s3:DataAccessPointAccount": "111122223333"}}
    }
  ]
}
26.3

Presigned URLs

In plain words

A presigned URL carries a signature that lets anyone who holds it perform one specific S3 operation until it expires, without AWS credentials.

The problem it solves

Browsers and partners need to upload or download a single object, and you do not want to proxy the bytes through your servers or share credentials.

What it does

  • The URL is signed with the credentials of the signer, so it can do only what the signer's permissions allow, and stops working if those credentials expire or are revoked.
  • Expiry up to seven days with IAM user keys; shorter limited by the session lifetime for temporary credentials.
  • Generate from the SDK or CLI. PUT URLs for uploads; GET for downloads. Presigned POST adds form conditions such as size limits and content type.
  • Treat URLs as bearer secrets; keep expiry short, avoid logging them.

Create them

bashCLI
aws s3 presign s3://acme-data-eu/reports/a.csv --expires-in 600
pythonPython (boto3) PUT and POST
import boto3

s3 = boto3.client("s3", region_name="eu-west-1")

put_url = s3.generate_presigned_url(
    "put_object",
    Params={"Bucket": "acme-data-eu", "Key": "uploads/photo.jpg", "ContentType": "image/jpeg"},
    ExpiresIn=300,
)

post = s3.generate_presigned_post(
    Bucket="acme-data-eu",
    Key="uploads/${filename}",
    Fields={"Content-Type": "image/jpeg"},
    Conditions=[["content-length-range", 1, 10_000_000], {"Content-Type": "image/jpeg"}],
    ExpiresIn=300,
)
print(put_url[:60], post["url"])
Careful

A presigned URL made with an assumed role dies when that role session ends, even if the expiry is longer. Sign with a suitably long-lived identity for long links.

Check yourself
Why use presigned POST instead of PUT for browser uploads?

POST lets you enforce conditions such as maximum size and content type.

26.4

Object Lock and MFA delete

In plain words

Object Lock makes object versions write-once-read-many (WORM) for a retention period or indefinitely.

The problem it solves

Ransomware, insider threats and regulations (financial records, audit logs) require data that nobody can delete or alter, including administrators.

What it does

  • Must be enabled when a bucket is created (it can be enabled on existing buckets with support involvement; check the current rules). Requires versioning.
  • Governance mode: users with special permission (s3:BypassGovernanceRetention) can override. Compliance mode: nobody, including root, can delete or shorten retention until it expires.
  • Legal hold: indefinite lock independent of retention, toggled with a permission.
  • A default retention can apply to every new object. Lifecycle expiration respects locks.
  • MFA Delete: needs MFA for permanent version deletion; different from Object Lock and managed only by the root user.

Create a locked bucket

bashObject Lock setup
aws s3api create-bucket --bucket acme-audit-logs --region eu-west-1 --create-bucket-configuration LocationConstraint=eu-west-1 \
  --object-lock-enabled-for-bucket
aws s3api put-object-lock-configuration --bucket acme-audit-logs \
  --object-lock-configuration '{"ObjectLockEnabled":"Enabled","Rule":{"DefaultRetention":{"Mode":"GOVERNANCE","Days":30}}}'
aws s3api get-object-retention --bucket acme-audit-logs --key log.gz --version-id EXAMPLEVERSIONID
Danger

Compliance mode retention cannot be shortened or removed, and you pay for the storage until it ends. Test in governance mode with short periods first.

26.5

Event notifications and access logging

In plain words

S3 can announce changes and record access, giving you hooks for automation and audit trails.

The problem it solves

You need to react to uploads and prove who accessed sensitive data.

What it does

  • Event notifications (and EventBridge integration) fire on object created, removed, restored, replication and lifecycle events; targets include Lambda, SQS, SNS and EventBridge.
  • Server access logs are best-effort deliveries of request records to another bucket; CloudTrail data events give reliable object-level API logging at extra cost.
  • Use the same Region log bucket, no logging loop, and lifecycle on the logs.
  • Enable EventBridge for fan-out, filtering and archive.

Enable EventBridge

bashNotifications
aws s3api put-bucket-notification-configuration --bucket acme-data-eu --notification-configuration '{"EventBridgeConfiguration":{}}'
aws s3api get-bucket-notification-configuration --bucket acme-data-eu
Check yourself
Which logging gives reliable object level auditing?

CloudTrail data events; server access logs are best effort.

Section 27 of 93

S3 performance, transfer and use from Kubernetes

5 concepts · about 45 minutes

S3 scales to very high request rates per prefix, but only if your clients are built to take advantage of that.

Goals
  • Design key layouts and clients for high request rates and throughput
  • Use multipart upload, byte-range fetches and Transfer Acceleration appropriately
  • Access S3 from pods through Pod Identity, the Mountpoint CSI driver and endpoints
27.1

Request rates and prefixes

In plain words

S3 scales automatically per prefix. Each prefix supports thousands of requests per second, and you can use many prefixes in parallel.

The problem it solves

A single hot key or a single client thread becomes the bottleneck and S3 returns 503 Slow Down errors during a spike.

What it does

  • Documented baseline per prefix is at least 3,500 PUT/COPY/POST/DELETE and 5,500 GET/HEAD requests per second; check the current performance guidelines.
  • Spread load across prefixes when you need more. Random hash prefixes are no longer required for performance but help spread very heavy workloads.
  • Retry with exponential backoff and jitter; the AWS SDKs do this for you.
  • Parallelise requests and reuse HTTP connections.

Tune the CLI

bashAWS CLI transfer settings
aws configure set default.s3.max_concurrent_requests 32
aws configure set default.s3.multipart_threshold 64MB
aws configure set default.s3.multipart_chunksize 32MB
aws s3 cp s3://acme-data-eu/big/dataset.tar ./dataset.tar
Check yourself
What should clients do on a 503 Slow Down?

Retry with exponential backoff and jitter and spread keys across prefixes.

27.2

Multipart upload and byte-range fetches

In plain words

Large objects are uploaded in parts in parallel, and downloaded in ranges in parallel.

The problem it solves

A single stream is limited by one connection's throughput and a failure restarts the whole transfer.

What it does

  • Multipart: parts of 5 MiB to 5 GiB, up to 10,000 parts; the final object up to 5 TB. Failed parts retry individually.
  • Always add a lifecycle rule to abort stale multipart uploads.
  • Byte-range GETs fetch pieces in parallel (8 to 16 MiB chunks are typical) and let you read just the footer of a Parquet file.
  • Use additional checksums (CRC32, CRC32C, SHA-1, SHA-256) for end-to-end integrity; the SDK computes CRC by default in recent versions.

Python transfer config

pythonParallel upload with boto3
import boto3
from boto3.s3.transfer import TransferConfig

cfg = TransferConfig(multipart_threshold=64 * 1024 * 1024,
                     multipart_chunksize=64 * 1024 * 1024,
                     max_concurrency=16, use_threads=True)
s3 = boto3.client("s3")
s3.upload_file("backup.tar.gz", "acme-data-eu", "backups/backup.tar.gz", Config=cfg)

# read only the last 1 MiB of an object
tail = s3.get_object(Bucket="acme-data-eu", Key="backups/backup.tar.gz", Range="bytes=-1048576")["Body"].read()
print(len(tail))
bashClean up stale uploads
aws s3api list-multipart-uploads --bucket acme-data-eu --query 'Uploads[].[Key,Initiated,UploadId]' --output table
aws s3api abort-multipart-upload --bucket acme-data-eu --key backups/old.tar --upload-id EXAMPLEUPLOADID
27.3

Network path and Transfer Acceleration

In plain words

Where your client sits relative to the bucket decides latency and cost. Transfer Acceleration routes uploads through the nearest CloudFront edge.

The problem it solves

Long-distance uploads over the public internet are slow and inconsistent; traffic from private subnets through NAT is expensive.

What it does

  • Same-Region access from EC2 or EKS is free of data transfer charges; cross-Region and internet egress are billed.
  • Use the S3 gateway endpoint for private subnets and an endpoint policy to restrict buckets.
  • Transfer Acceleration (bucketname.s3-accelerate.amazonaws.com) helps for far-away clients uploading to a central bucket; extra per GB fee; test with the speed comparison tool.
  • Requester Pays shifts transfer cost to the downloader for shared datasets.
  • Consider CloudFront in front of S3 for repeated public reads.

Enable acceleration

bashAcceleration
aws s3api put-bucket-accelerate-configuration --bucket acme-data-eu --accelerate-configuration Status=Enabled
aws configure set default.s3.use_accelerate_endpoint true
aws s3 cp ./large.bin s3://acme-data-eu/uploads/large.bin
Check yourself
How do you avoid NAT cost for S3 traffic from private subnets?

Add an S3 gateway VPC endpoint and route the subnets to it.

27.4

S3 from pods

In plain words

Pods access S3 using IAM roles through Pod Identity or IRSA. The Mountpoint for Amazon S3 CSI driver can mount a bucket as a file system for read-heavy workloads.

The problem it solves

Applications built for POSIX files cannot call the S3 API directly, and baked-in keys are unsafe.

What it does

  • Give the service account a role scoped to the bucket and prefix it needs.
  • Mountpoint supports sequential writes of new objects and fast reads, but not random writes, renames or file locking. Good for ML data loading and batch reads; not a general NFS replacement.
  • The CSI driver is installed as an EKS add-on (aws-mountpoint-s3-csi-driver) and uses static provisioning of a PersistentVolume pointing to a bucket.
  • Cache reads on local disk if the same data is read repeatedly.

Static volume

yamls3-pv.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolume
metadata:
  name: s3-datasets
spec:
  capacity:
    storage: 1200Gi
  accessModes:
    - ReadWriteMany
  mountOptions:
    - allow-delete
    - region eu-west-1
    - prefix datasets/
  csi:
    driver: s3.csi.aws.com
    volumeHandle: s3-datasets
    volumeAttributes:
      bucketName: acme-data-eu
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: s3-datasets
  namespace: ml
spec:
  accessModes:
    - ReadWriteMany
  storageClassName: ""
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 1200Gi
  volumeName: s3-datasets
Note

The capacity field is required by Kubernetes but ignored by the driver. Check the add-on documentation for the mount options your version supports.

27.5

Choosing an S3 design

In plain words

Pulling the section together: a short decision flow for a new bucket.

The problem it solves

Each setting is easy alone, but the combination decides cost, safety and speed.

What it does

  • Purpose and sensitivity decide encryption and access pattern (SSE-KMS with a customer key for regulated data; SSE-S3 otherwise).
  • Data lifetime decides lifecycle and class (Intelligent-Tiering for unknown patterns).
  • Recovery goals decide versioning, replication and Object Lock.
  • Consumers decide the access path (access points, presigned URLs, CloudFront, gateway endpoint).
  • Codify all of it in a module.
Backup bucket
OptionVersioning plus lifecycle
Choose whenany important data
Avoid whenyou need immutability against admins
OptionAdd Object Lock
Choose whencompliance or ransomware protection
Avoid whendata must be deletable at will
OptionAdd cross-Region replication
Choose whenregional disaster recovery
Avoid whendata residency forbids copies
Check yourself
Which feature protects against an administrator deleting audit logs?

Object Lock in compliance mode (with retention).
