Section 28 of 93

Lambda execution model and scaling

7 concepts · about 55 minutes

Lambda runs your function code on demand without servers to manage. Understanding the execution environment lifecycle explains almost every performance and cost surprise.

Goals
  • Explain how Lambda runs code in execution environments and what a cold start is
  • Size memory and timeout and calculate the cost of an invocation pattern
  • Control concurrency with reserved and provisioned concurrency
28.1

The execution environment lifecycle

In plain words

Lambda creates an isolated execution environment (a Firecracker micro VM) for your function, runs your code in it, and reuses it for later requests until it is retired.

The problem it solves

You want code to run only when needed, but starting a fresh runtime for every request would be slow and expensive.

What it does

  • Init phase: download code, start the runtime, run code outside the handler. Happens once per environment.
  • Invoke phase: your handler runs. A warm environment skips init.
  • Shutdown phase: the environment is frozen or retired at an unpredictable time. Never rely on it staying alive.
  • One environment handles one request at a time. Parallel requests need parallel environments.

Reuse state outside the handler

pythonhandler.py
import json
import boto3

# runs once per environment (init phase)
s3 = boto3.client("s3")

def handler(event, context):
    # runs on every invoke
    return {"statusCode": 200, "body": json.dumps({"request": context.aws_request_id})}
Check yourself
Where should you create SDK clients?

Outside the handler so warm invocations reuse them.

28.2

Cold starts

In plain words

A cold start is the extra latency of the init phase when no warm environment is available.

The problem it solves

Users notice a slow first request after idle time or during a traffic burst that needs new environments.

What it does

  • Affected by runtime (compiled or lightweight runtimes start faster than a JVM), package size, memory (more memory means more CPU), VPC is no longer a major cost, and heavy imports.
  • Only a small share of invocations are cold in steady traffic; bursts and deployments create more.
  • Mitigate with smaller packages, lazy imports, SnapStart for supported runtimes, or provisioned concurrency.
  • Measure it: the Init Duration field in the REPORT log line appears only on cold starts.

Find cold starts in Logs Insights

bashCount cold starts
aws logs start-query --log-group-name /aws/lambda/orders \
  --start-time $(date -d '-1 hour' +%s) --end-time $(date +%s) \
  --query-string 'filter @type="REPORT" | stats count(*) as total, count(@initDuration) as cold, avg(@initDuration) as avgInitMs'
Tip

Optimise the p99 first. Average latency hides cold starts.

28.3

Memory, CPU and timeout

In plain words

You pick memory from 128 MB up to 10,240 MB. CPU and network scale in proportion to memory. The timeout can be up to 15 minutes.

The problem it solves

Too little memory makes a function slow and sometimes more expensive. Too much wastes money.

What it does

  • Billing is GB-seconds: memory in GB times billed duration in seconds, plus a per-request charge. Duration is billed in 1 ms increments.
  • A CPU-bound function often costs the same or less at higher memory because it finishes faster.
  • Find the best setting by testing several memory sizes, or use AWS Compute Optimizer recommendations or the open source Lambda Power Tuning tool.
  • Set the timeout just above realistic maximum runtime so runaway calls stop early.

Worked cost example

Example using illustrative prices of $0.0000166667 per GB-second and $0.20 per million requests (check current regional pricing and the free tier). A function at 512 MB runs 200 ms and is called 5 million times a month.

  • GB-seconds = 5,000,000 x 0.5 GB x 0.2 s = 500,000
  • Compute = 500,000 x 0.0000166667 = about $8.33
  • Requests = 5 x $0.20 = $1.00
  • Total = about $9.33 per month before free tier.
Check yourself
What two numbers multiply to give GB-seconds?

Memory in GB and billed duration in seconds, per invocation, summed over all invocations.

28.4

Concurrency and throttling

In plain words

Concurrency is the number of environments serving requests at the same moment. It is roughly requests per second multiplied by average duration in seconds.

The problem it solves

Without limits, one noisy function can use all the account concurrency and starve others, or overwhelm a database.

What it does

  • Account quota per Region (check the current quota; it starts at a default and can be raised).
  • Reserved concurrency guarantees capacity for a function and also caps it. Use it to protect downstream systems.
  • Over the limit, synchronous callers get a 429 TooManyRequestsException; asynchronous events retry for a while; stream and queue pollers slow down.
  • Scaling rate is limited per function; check the current quota for burst behaviour.

Reserve and cap

bashSet reserved concurrency
aws lambda put-function-concurrency --function-name orders --reserved-concurrent-executions 50
aws lambda get-function-concurrency --function-name orders

Example: 100 requests per second at 0.3 s average needs about 100 x 0.3 = 30 concurrent environments.

Check yourself
How do you estimate required concurrency?

Requests per second times average duration in seconds.

28.5

Provisioned concurrency

In plain words

Provisioned concurrency keeps a chosen number of environments initialised and ready, so those requests avoid cold starts.

The problem it solves

Latency-sensitive APIs cannot accept occasional multi-second first requests.

What it does

  • Attached to a published version or alias, not to $LATEST.
  • You pay for the provisioned capacity while it is configured, plus a lower duration rate while serving.
  • Requests above the provisioned number spill to normal on-demand environments, which can be cold.
  • Can be scaled with Application Auto Scaling on a schedule or on utilisation.

Configure with Terraform

hclprovisioned.tf
resource "aws_lambda_alias" "live" {
  name             = "live"
  function_name    = aws_lambda_function.orders.function_name
  function_version = aws_lambda_function.orders.version
}

resource "aws_lambda_provisioned_concurrency_config" "orders" {
  function_name                     = aws_lambda_function.orders.function_name
  qualifier                         = aws_lambda_alias.live.name
  provisioned_concurrent_executions = 10
}
Careful

Provisioned concurrency costs money while idle. Use a schedule if the traffic is only in office hours.

28.6

Versions and aliases

In plain words

Publishing creates an immutable version of code and configuration. An alias is a named pointer to a version, and can split traffic between two versions.

The problem it solves

Deploying to $LATEST changes live behaviour instantly and gives no safe rollback.

What it does

  • Versions are numbered and cannot be changed.
  • Aliases such as live are what event sources and API Gateway call.
  • An alias can send a weight such as 10 percent to a new version for a canary release. CodeDeploy automates the shift and rollback.
  • Rolling back is moving the alias to the previous version.

Weighted alias

bashCanary
aws lambda publish-version --function-name orders
aws lambda update-alias --function-name orders --name live \
  --function-version 12 --routing-config 'AdditionalVersionWeights={"13"=0.1}'
Check yourself
What does a function URL or API call normally target, `$LATEST` or an alias?

An alias, so deployments are controlled and reversible.

28.7

Execution role and resource policy

In plain words

Two different policies apply. The execution role says what the function may call. The resource-based policy says who may invoke the function.

The problem it solves

People confuse the two and either grant too much or get access denied for the wrong reason.

What it does

  • The execution role has a trust policy for lambda.amazonaws.com and permissions for logs and your data sources.
  • The resource policy grants principals such as apigateway.amazonaws.com or events.amazonaws.com permission to invoke, restricted with SourceArn.
  • Without SourceArn, a service principal permission could be used by any account's resource of that type (confused deputy).

Invoke permission

jsonRole permissions
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": ["dynamodb:GetItem", "dynamodb:PutItem"],
      "Resource": "arn:aws:dynamodb:eu-west-1:111122223333:table/orders"
    }
  ]
}
bashAllow API Gateway to invoke
aws lambda add-permission --function-name orders --statement-id apigw \
  --action lambda:InvokeFunction --principal apigateway.amazonaws.com \
  --source-arn arn:aws:execute-api:eu-west-1:111122223333:abc123/*/GET/orders

Section 29 of 93

Lambda packaging, event sources and operations

7 concepts · about 55 minutes

Once a function runs, the next questions are how to package it, what triggers it, and how to operate it safely.

Goals
  • Package functions as zip, layers or container images and choose between them
  • Match event sources to synchronous, asynchronous and polling invocation
  • Observe and cost-control Lambda in production including SnapStart
29.1

Zip packages and layers

In plain words

A zip package holds your code and dependencies. A layer is a separate zip that is mounted under /opt and shared between functions.

The problem it solves

Copying the same large library into every function makes deployments slow and hard to patch.

What it does

  • Zip limit is 50 MB zipped direct upload and 250 MB unzipped including layers (check the current quota).
  • Up to five layers per function. Layers are versioned and immutable.
  • Good for shared SDKs, extensions and binaries. Poor for fast-changing business code.
  • A layer update does not change existing functions until they are updated to the new layer version.

Publish a layer

bashPublish and attach
aws lambda publish-layer-version --layer-name common-utils \
  --zip-file fileb://layer.zip --compatible-runtimes python3.12
aws lambda update-function-configuration --function-name orders \
  --layers arn:aws:lambda:eu-west-1:111122223333:layer:common-utils:4
Check yourself
Does publishing a new layer version update the functions that use it?

No. Each function must be updated to reference the new version.

29.2

Container image functions

In plain words

Lambda can run a container image up to 10 GB stored in Amazon ECR instead of a zip.

The problem it solves

Large machine learning libraries, custom OS packages or existing container build pipelines do not fit the zip limits or workflow.

What it does

  • Base on an AWS provided Lambda base image or add the Runtime Interface Client to your own image.
  • Same execution model as zip: still one request at a time, still a cold start, but images are cached lazily so large images start reasonably.
  • Scan in ECR and sign images like any other container.
  • Not the same as running a long-lived container. Use ECS or Fargate for that.

Example Dockerfile

dockerfileDockerfile
FROM public.ecr.aws/lambda/python:3.12
COPY requirements.txt ${LAMBDA_TASK_ROOT}
RUN pip install -r requirements.txt
COPY app.py ${LAMBDA_TASK_ROOT}
CMD ["app.handler"]
29.3

Synchronous, asynchronous and polling invocation

In plain words

There are three ways Lambda is invoked, and each has different retry behaviour.

The problem it solves

Wrong assumptions about retries cause duplicate processing or lost events.

What it does

  • Synchronous (API Gateway, ALB, function URL, SDK RequestResponse): caller waits and handles errors itself.
  • Asynchronous (S3, SNS, EventBridge): Lambda queues the event, retries failed runs twice by default, and can send failures to a destination or DLQ.
  • Polling (SQS, Kinesis, DynamoDB Streams, Kafka): the Lambda service polls and invokes with batches; retries follow the source semantics.
  • Assume at-least-once delivery. Make handlers idempotent.

Async failure destination

bashSend failures to SQS
aws lambda put-function-event-invoke-config --function-name orders \
  --maximum-retry-attempts 1 --maximum-event-age-in-seconds 3600 \
  --destination-config '{"OnFailure":{"Destination":"arn:aws:sqs:eu-west-1:111122223333:orders-failed"}}'
Check yourself
Which invocation types retry automatically inside the Lambda service?

Asynchronous and polling. Synchronous callers must retry themselves.

29.4

SQS and stream event source mappings

In plain words

An event source mapping is a Lambda-managed poller that reads a queue or stream and invokes your function with batches.

The problem it solves

Writing your own consumer loop needs scaling, checkpointing and retry code.

What it does

  • SQS: configure BatchSize, MaximumBatchingWindowInSeconds and partial batch response so one bad message does not retry the whole batch.
  • Set the queue visibility timeout to at least six times the function timeout, as AWS recommends.
  • Kinesis and DynamoDB Streams: ordered per shard, with BisectBatchOnFunctionError, retry limits and an on-failure destination.
  • Use ScalingConfig.MaximumConcurrency for SQS to protect a database.

Mapping with partial batch

hclmapping.tf
resource "aws_lambda_event_source_mapping" "orders" {
  event_source_arn        = aws_sqs_queue.orders.arn
  function_name           = aws_lambda_function.orders.arn
  batch_size              = 10
  function_response_types = ["ReportBatchItemFailures"]
  scaling_config {
    maximum_concurrency = 20
  }
}
29.5

Function URLs and Lambda in a VPC

In plain words

A function URL is a built-in HTTPS endpoint. A function can also attach to your VPC to reach private resources.

The problem it solves

Simple webhooks do not need API Gateway, and some functions must reach a private database.

What it does

  • Function URL auth: AWS_IAM (SigV4) or NONE (public). It has no throttling, WAF or custom domain features of API Gateway; front with CloudFront if needed.
  • VPC attachment creates network interfaces in your subnets using shared Hyperplane ENIs. Give at least two subnets in different AZs.
  • A VPC function has no internet unless the subnet routes to a NAT gateway; use VPC endpoints for AWS services.
  • Use RDS Proxy for relational databases to avoid connection storms.

Create a URL

bashFunction URL
aws lambda create-function-url-config --function-name hook --auth-type AWS_IAM
29.6

SnapStart and runtime choices

In plain words

SnapStart takes a snapshot of an initialised environment after the init phase and restores it for new environments, cutting cold start time.

The problem it solves

Java and similar runtimes with long init are too slow on cold start for interactive APIs.

What it does

  • Enabled on published versions, for supported runtimes (check the current supported runtimes and regions).
  • Code must be snapshot safe: do not cache unique values, network connections or random seeds created during init. Use runtime hooks to refresh.
  • Alternative: provisioned concurrency, or a faster-starting runtime.
  • Arm64 (Graviton) functions are usually cheaper per GB-second; check the current price and test your dependencies.

Enable

bashSnapStart
aws lambda update-function-configuration --function-name orders-java \
  --snap-start ApplyOn=PublishedVersions
aws lambda publish-version --function-name orders-java
Check yourself
Why must uniqueness-sensitive values be created after restore?

The snapshot is copied to many environments, so values made during init would be shared.

29.7

Observability and cost control

In plain words

Lambda writes logs to CloudWatch Logs automatically, emits metrics, and supports X-Ray and OpenTelemetry tracing.

The problem it solves

Short-lived functions leave nothing to log into after they are gone, and costs grow silently with invocations.

What it does

  • Key metrics: Invocations, Errors, Throttles, Duration, ConcurrentExecutions, IteratorAge for streams.
  • Use structured JSON logging and set log retention; log groups never expire by default.
  • Active tracing gives a service map through downstream calls.
  • Cost levers: right-size memory, Arm64, shorter timeouts, batching, filter events at the source, avoid polling loops, and set log retention.
  • Alarm on Errors, Throttles and p99 Duration.

Log retention and alarm

hclobservability.tf
resource "aws_cloudwatch_log_group" "orders" {
  name              = "/aws/lambda/orders"
  retention_in_days = 30
}

resource "aws_cloudwatch_metric_alarm" "errors" {
  alarm_name          = "orders-errors"
  namespace           = "AWS/Lambda"
  metric_name         = "Errors"
  dimensions          = { FunctionName = "orders" }
  statistic           = "Sum"
  period              = 60
  evaluation_periods  = 5
  threshold           = 5
  comparison_operator = "GreaterThanOrEqualToThreshold"
}
Check yourself
What two default behaviours of Lambda logs can quietly raise cost?

Log groups keep data forever and verbose logging per invocation adds ingestion charges.

Section 30 of 93

API Gateway and AppSync

8 concepts · about 55 minutes

API Gateway and AppSync put a managed, scalable front door on Lambda, containers and other backends. This section covers choosing the right product and operating it.

Goals
  • Choose between REST API, HTTP API, WebSocket API and AppSync
  • Secure and throttle an API with authorizers, usage plans and WAF
  • Deploy stages safely and troubleshoot common integration errors
30.1

The API products compared

In plain words

API Gateway offers REST APIs, HTTP APIs and WebSocket APIs. AppSync offers managed GraphQL.

The problem it solves

Teams pick a product by habit and then find a needed feature missing, or pay for features they never use.

What it does

  • HTTP API: lower cost and latency, JWT authorizers, Lambda and HTTP integrations, simple routes. The default for most new work.
  • REST API: more features such as usage plans with API keys, request validation, WAF integration, resource policies, caching, private endpoints and per-method settings.
  • WebSocket API: persistent two-way connections with route selection by message content.
  • AppSync: GraphQL with resolvers to DynamoDB, Lambda, HTTP, OpenSearch and RDS, plus real-time subscriptions.
  • Feature sets change, so check the current feature comparison before deciding.
Which API front door
OptionHTTP API
Choose whensimple proxy to Lambda or a service and JWT auth
Avoid whenyou need API keys, usage plans or WAF directly on the API
OptionREST API
Choose whenyou need usage plans, WAF, caching or private APIs
Avoid whenyou only need a cheap proxy
OptionAppSync
Choose whenclients need flexible queries and live subscriptions
Avoid whena simple fixed REST contract is enough
Check yourself
Which product gives usage plans with API keys?

The REST API type.

30.2

Integrations and request flow

In plain words

An integration connects a route to a backend. The gateway receives the request, authorises it, applies throttling, calls the backend and returns the answer.

The problem it solves

Backends should not each implement authentication, throttling and TLS themselves.

What it does

  • Lambda proxy integration passes the whole request as an event and expects a response object with statusCode, headers and body.
  • HTTP proxy integration forwards to a public URL. Private integrations reach an ALB, NLB or Cloud Map service through a VPC link.
  • AWS service integrations call services such as SQS or Step Functions directly without Lambda.
  • Maximum integration timeout is limited (about 29 seconds by default for REST; check the current quota). Long work should be asynchronous.

HTTP API in Terraform

hclhttp-api.tf
resource "aws_apigatewayv2_api" "orders" {
  name          = "orders"
  protocol_type = "HTTP"
}

resource "aws_apigatewayv2_integration" "lambda" {
  api_id                 = aws_apigatewayv2_api.orders.id
  integration_type       = "AWS_PROXY"
  integration_uri        = aws_lambda_function.orders.invoke_arn
  payload_format_version = "2.0"
}

resource "aws_apigatewayv2_route" "get_orders" {
  api_id    = aws_apigatewayv2_api.orders.id
  route_key = "GET /orders"
  target    = "integrations/${aws_apigatewayv2_integration.lambda.id}"
}

resource "aws_apigatewayv2_stage" "default" {
  api_id      = aws_apigatewayv2_api.orders.id
  name        = "$default"
  auto_deploy = true
}
Check yourself
Why do long jobs not belong behind a synchronous API integration?

The integration timeout is short, so return 202 and process asynchronously.

30.3

Authentication and authorisation

In plain words

API Gateway can verify callers with IAM, Cognito or JWT tokens, or call your own Lambda authorizer.

The problem it solves

An open API invites abuse. You need identity checked before the backend runs.

What it does

  • IAM auth: callers sign with SigV4. Good for service to service.
  • JWT authorizer (HTTP API): validates issuer, audience and signature of tokens from Cognito, IAM Identity Center or any OIDC provider, no code needed.
  • Lambda authorizer: your function returns an IAM policy; results can be cached for a TTL.
  • Mutual TLS is available for custom domains where clients present certificates.
  • Pass the verified claims to the backend; do not trust client-provided identity headers.

Add a JWT authorizer

hcljwt.tf
resource "aws_apigatewayv2_authorizer" "jwt" {
  api_id           = aws_apigatewayv2_api.orders.id
  authorizer_type  = "JWT"
  name             = "oidc"
  identity_sources = ["$request.header.Authorization"]
  jwt_configuration {
    audience = ["orders-api"]
    issuer   = "https://idp.example.com/"
  }
}
30.4

Throttling, usage plans and WAF

In plain words

Throttling limits request rates. On REST APIs, usage plans attach rate and quota limits to API keys. WAF blocks malicious traffic.

The problem it solves

One client or attacker can exhaust backend capacity or run up cost.

What it does

  • Account-level and stage-level throttling use a token bucket of rate and burst (check the current default quotas).
  • Per-route throttling is available for HTTP APIs and per-method for REST APIs.
  • API keys identify clients for metering; they are not a security mechanism on their own.
  • Attach AWS WAF to a REST API stage, or put CloudFront with WAF in front of any API.
  • Clients should retry 429 with exponential backoff and jitter.

Stage throttling

bashSet default route throttling
aws apigatewayv2 update-stage --api-id abc123 --stage-name '$default' \
  --default-route-settings ThrottlingBurstLimit=200,ThrottlingRateLimit=100
Check yourself
Is an API key a good way to authenticate users?

No. It identifies a client for metering. Use IAM or JWT for authentication.

30.5

Stages, deployments and custom domains

In plain words

A stage is a named, deployed version of an API such as prod. A custom domain with an ACM certificate maps your own hostname to stages.

The problem it solves

You need different environments and a stable URL that does not change when the API is redeployed.

What it does

  • REST APIs need an explicit deployment to a stage; HTTP APIs can auto-deploy.
  • Stage variables and Lambda aliases support canary releases; REST stages have canary settings with a traffic percentage.
  • Custom domains use a certificate in the same Region (regional) or in us-east-1 (edge optimised), then a Route 53 alias record. Base path mappings pick API and stage.
  • Enable access logs with a JSON format and set retention.

Access logs

hclstage-logs.tf
resource "aws_apigatewayv2_stage" "prod" {
  api_id      = aws_apigatewayv2_api.orders.id
  name        = "prod"
  auto_deploy = true
  access_log_settings {
    destination_arn = aws_cloudwatch_log_group.api.arn
    format          = jsonencode({ requestId = "$context.requestId", status = "$context.status", ip = "$context.identity.sourceIp", latency = "$context.responseLatency" })
  }
}
30.6

Private APIs and VPC links

In plain words

A private REST API is reachable only through an interface VPC endpoint. A VPC link lets any API call private backends.

The problem it solves

Internal services must not be exposed to the internet, but you still want one managed gateway.

What it does

  • Private REST API: resource policy limits access to specific VPC endpoints.
  • HTTP API VPC link to a private ALB, NLB or Cloud Map namespace; the link runs ENIs in your subnets.
  • Backends need security groups that allow traffic from the VPC link group.
  • For internal east-west traffic between many services, also consider VPC Lattice.

Create a link

bashVPC link
aws apigatewayv2 create-vpc-link --name internal \
  --subnet-ids subnet-0aaa subnet-0bbb --security-group-ids sg-0123456789abcdef0
Check yourself
What does a VPC link need to reach a private ALB?

ENIs in your subnets and a security group allowed by the ALB or targets.

30.7

AppSync and GraphQL

In plain words

AppSync is managed GraphQL. Clients ask for exactly the fields they need in one call, and can subscribe to changes.

The problem it solves

Mobile and web clients make many REST calls and receive too much or too little data.

What it does

  • A schema defines types, queries, mutations and subscriptions.
  • Resolvers map fields to data sources. JavaScript resolvers run in AppSync without a Lambda for DynamoDB and HTTP sources.
  • Auth modes: API key, IAM, Cognito, OIDC, Lambda. You can mix modes per field.
  • Subscriptions push updates over WebSockets. Merged APIs combine schemas from several teams.

Minimal schema

graphqlschema.graphql
type Order { id: ID! status: String! total: Float }
type Query { getOrder(id: ID!): Order }
type Mutation { setStatus(id: ID!, status: String!): Order }
type Subscription { onStatus(id: ID!): Order @aws_subscribe(mutations: ["setStatus"]) }
30.8

Troubleshooting API errors

In plain words

Most API Gateway failures come from a short list: permissions, timeouts, malformed responses and throttling.

The problem it solves

The client sees a vague 500, 502, 503 or 504 and it is not obvious which hop failed.

What it does

  • 403: authorizer denied, WAF blocked, missing resource policy, or wrong host.
  • 429: throttled by API Gateway or the backend.
  • 500 Internal server error with Lambda proxy: Lambda response was not in the expected shape, or the invoke permission is missing.
  • 502: backend returned an invalid response or connection failed. 504: integration timeout.
  • Turn on access logs and execution logs for the stage, and use X-Ray. Compare gateway latency with integrationLatency.

Query the logs

bashErrors in the last hour
aws logs start-query --log-group-name /aws/apigw/orders \
  --start-time $(date -d '-1 hour' +%s) --end-time $(date +%s) \
  --query-string 'fields @timestamp, status, routeKey, integrationLatency | filter status >= 500 | sort @timestamp desc | limit 20'
Check yourself
A Lambda proxy returns a plain string and API Gateway gives 500. Why?

The proxy integration expects a structured response with statusCode and body.

Section 31 of 93

AWS Step Functions

7 concepts · about 50 minutes

Step Functions coordinates work across services with a visual state machine, built in retries and a durable execution history.

Goals
  • Model a workflow as a state machine in Amazon States Language
  • Choose between Standard and Express workflows
  • Add retries, catches, parallel and map states for reliable orchestration
31.1

What a state machine is

In plain words

A state machine is a JSON definition of steps (states), the order between them and the data passed along. Each run is an execution.

The problem it solves

Long processes with many steps, retries and branches become tangled in application code and are hard to see when they fail.

What it does

  • Written in Amazon States Language (ASL), a JSON format.
  • State types: Task, Choice, Parallel, Map, Wait, Pass, Succeed, Fail.
  • The state input and output are JSON. InputPath, Parameters, ResultSelector, ResultPath and OutputPath shape data; JSONata is also supported (check the current docs).
  • The console shows each execution graphically with inputs and outputs.

A small definition

jsonorder.asl.json
{
  "Comment": "Order flow",
  "StartAt": "Validate",
  "States": {
    "Validate": {
      "Type": "Task",
      "Resource": "arn:aws:states:::lambda:invoke",
      "Parameters": {"FunctionName": "validate-order", "Payload.$": "$"},
      "OutputPath": "$.Payload",
      "Next": "Charge"
    },
    "Charge": {
      "Type": "Task",
      "Resource": "arn:aws:states:::lambda:invoke",
      "Parameters": {"FunctionName": "charge", "Payload.$": "$"},
      "OutputPath": "$.Payload",
      "End": true
    }
  }
}
Check yourself
What language defines a Step Functions workflow?

Amazon States Language, a JSON format.

31.2

Standard versus Express workflows

In plain words

Standard workflows run up to a year with exactly-once step semantics. Express workflows run up to five minutes at very high rates with at-least-once semantics.

The problem it solves

Human approval flows and high-volume event processing have opposite needs.

What it does

  • Standard: billed per state transition; full execution history stored; supports .waitForTaskToken and long waits.
  • Express: billed by requests and duration; history goes to CloudWatch Logs; good for streaming data transformation and microservice orchestration; asynchronous or synchronous start.
  • Make Express steps idempotent because they may run more than once.
  • Check the current duration limits and pricing.
Which workflow type
OptionStandard
Choose whenlong running, human approval, audit needs
Avoid whenmillions of short events per hour with tight cost
OptionExpress
Choose whenhigh volume short processing, API backends
Avoid whenyou need to wait days or need exactly-once
Check yourself
Which type needs idempotent steps because they may repeat?

Express.

31.3

Service integrations and patterns

In plain words

Step Functions can call over 200 AWS services directly (SDK integrations) without Lambda glue code.

The problem it solves

Lambda functions that only call another API add cost, latency and code to maintain.

What it does

  • Request Response: call and move on.
  • Run a Job (.sync): wait until the job finishes, for ECS tasks, Glue jobs, CodeBuild, Batch and others.
  • Wait for callback (.waitForTaskToken): pause until an external system returns the token. Use for human approval.
  • Direct integrations include DynamoDB, SQS, SNS, EventBridge, ECS, Bedrock and more; check the current list.

Run an ECS task and wait

jsonecs-sync.json
{
  "StartAt": "RunBatch",
  "States": {
    "RunBatch": {
      "Type": "Task",
      "Resource": "arn:aws:states:::ecs:runTask.sync",
      "Parameters": {
        "LaunchType": "FARGATE",
        "Cluster": "arn:aws:ecs:eu-west-1:111122223333:cluster/batch",
        "TaskDefinition": "arn:aws:ecs:eu-west-1:111122223333:task-definition/etl:7"
      },
      "End": true
    }
  }
}
31.4

Errors, retries and catch

In plain words

Each Task can declare how to Retry on named errors and where to go on failure with Catch.

The problem it solves

Transient failures are normal in distributed systems. Without declared handling, one blip fails the whole process.

What it does

  • Retry: ErrorEquals, IntervalSeconds, MaxAttempts, BackoffRate, optional JitterStrategy.
  • Catch: route to a compensation or notification state, saving the error in ResultPath.
  • Built-in error names such as States.ALL, States.Timeout, States.TaskFailed.
  • TimeoutSeconds and HeartbeatSeconds stop stuck tasks.
  • Backoff example: interval 2 s, rate 2 and MaxAttempts 3 gives waits of 2, 4 and 8 seconds, total 14 seconds.

Retry and catch

jsonretry.json
{
  "Type": "Task",
  "Resource": "arn:aws:states:::lambda:invoke",
  "Parameters": {"FunctionName": "charge", "Payload.$": "$"},
  "Retry": [
    {"ErrorEquals": ["Lambda.ServiceException", "Lambda.TooManyRequestsException"], "IntervalSeconds": 2, "MaxAttempts": 4, "BackoffRate": 2.0}
  ],
  "Catch": [
    {"ErrorEquals": ["States.ALL"], "ResultPath": "$.error", "Next": "Refund"}
  ],
  "TimeoutSeconds": 30,
  "Next": "Done"
}
Check yourself
Sum the waits for interval 2 s, rate 2.0, 4 retries.

2 + 4 + 8 + 16 = 30 seconds if all four retries occur.

31.5

Parallel, Map and Distributed Map

In plain words

Parallel runs different branches at once. Map runs the same steps for each item of a list. Distributed Map processes huge datasets such as S3 objects in parallel child executions.

The problem it solves

Sequential loops are slow, and a Lambda loop over a million files hits time limits.

What it does

  • Parallel waits for all branches; a failure fails the state unless caught.
  • Map has MaxConcurrency to protect downstream systems.
  • Distributed Map reads items from S3 (CSV, JSON, object lists) and starts many child workflow executions; check the current concurrency limits.
  • Tolerated failure percentage lets a batch finish despite a few bad items.

Map state

jsonmap.json
{
  "Type": "Map",
  "ItemsPath": "$.items",
  "MaxConcurrency": 5,
  "ItemProcessor": {
    "ProcessorConfig": {"Mode": "INLINE"},
    "StartAt": "One",
    "States": {"One": {"Type": "Pass", "End": true}}
  },
  "End": true
}
31.6

Saga pattern and human approval

In plain words

A saga undoes completed steps when a later step fails. Step Functions expresses this with Catch states that run compensation tasks.

The problem it solves

Distributed transactions across services cannot use a database rollback.

What it does

  • Each forward step has a matching compensation (refund, release stock).
  • Catch routes to compensations in reverse order.
  • For approvals, a .waitForTaskToken task sends the token in an email or ticket; the approver calls SendTaskSuccess or SendTaskFailure.
  • Add a task timeout so approvals do not wait forever.

Send approval

bashApprove
aws stepfunctions send-task-success --task-token "$TOKEN" --task-output '{"approved":true}'
Check yourself
How does a human approval step pause a workflow?

A waitForTaskToken task hands out a token and resumes when SendTaskSuccess or SendTaskFailure is called with it.

31.7

Operating Step Functions

In plain words

Operate workflows with logging, alarms, tracing and infrastructure as code.

The problem it solves

A workflow that silently fails or loops costs money and loses business events.

What it does

  • Metrics: ExecutionsFailed, ExecutionsTimedOut, ExecutionThrottled, ExecutionTime.
  • Turn on logging to CloudWatch Logs (always for Express) and X-Ray tracing.
  • Use the Workflow Studio for design and redrive to resume a failed Standard execution from the failure point.
  • The state machine role needs only the actions it calls.
  • Cost: Standard billed per state transition. For example 1,000,000 executions of 10 transitions each is 10,000,000 transitions; check the current price per 1,000 transitions to price it.

Terraform

hclsfn.tf
resource "aws_sfn_state_machine" "orders" {
  name       = "orders"
  role_arn   = aws_iam_role.sfn.arn
  definition = file("${path.module}/order.asl.json")
  logging_configuration {
    log_destination        = "${aws_cloudwatch_log_group.sfn.arn}:*"
    include_execution_data = false
    level                  = "ERROR"
  }
}
Check yourself
Which action restarts a failed Standard execution from its failed step?

Redrive.

Section 32 of 93

Amazon EventBridge

8 concepts · about 50 minutes

EventBridge is the serverless event router of AWS. Producers emit events, rules match them, and targets react, without producers knowing who listens.

Goals
  • Route events with buses and rules using event patterns
  • Use Pipes and Scheduler for point to point integration and timed jobs
  • Add archive, replay, retries and dead letter queues for reliable delivery
32.1

Events, buses and rules

In plain words

An event is a JSON record of something that happened. An event bus receives events. A rule matches events by pattern and sends them to targets.

The problem it solves

Direct calls between services couple them tightly; adding a new consumer means changing the producer.

What it does

  • The default bus receives events from AWS services. Custom buses carry your application events. Partner buses receive SaaS events.
  • A rule has an event pattern (or a schedule) and up to five targets (check the current quota).
  • Targets include Lambda, SQS, SNS, Step Functions, ECS tasks, API destinations, another bus, Kinesis and many more.
  • Delivery is at least once; consumers must be idempotent.

A custom bus and rule

hclbus.tf
resource "aws_cloudwatch_event_bus" "shop" {
  name = "shop"
}

resource "aws_cloudwatch_event_rule" "order_created" {
  name           = "order-created"
  event_bus_name = aws_cloudwatch_event_bus.shop.name
  event_pattern = jsonencode({
    source        = ["shop.orders"]
    "detail-type" = ["OrderCreated"]
  })
}

resource "aws_cloudwatch_event_target" "to_queue" {
  rule           = aws_cloudwatch_event_rule.order_created.name
  event_bus_name = aws_cloudwatch_event_bus.shop.name
  arn            = aws_sqs_queue.fulfilment.arn
}
Check yourself
Does the producer need to know the consumers?

No. It only publishes to the bus.

32.2

Event patterns

In plain words

An event pattern is a JSON document that lists the fields and values an event must have to match.

The problem it solves

Targets should receive only the events they care about, filtered before invocation so you do not pay to discard them.

What it does

  • Match on exact values, arrays (any of), prefix, suffix, anything-but, numeric, exists, cidr and wildcard.
  • All named fields must match (AND); values inside an array are OR.
  • Test patterns with the console sandbox or aws events test-event-pattern.
  • Content filtering at the rule saves downstream cost compared with filtering in code.

Pattern with numeric filter

jsonpattern.json
{
  "source": ["shop.orders"],
  "detail-type": ["OrderCreated"],
  "detail": {
    "total": [{"numeric": [">=", 100]}],
    "country": [{"anything-but": ["XX"]}]
  }
}
bashTest a pattern
aws events test-event-pattern --event-pattern file://pattern.json --event file://event.json
Check yourself
Within one field, are listed values AND or OR?

OR. Different fields are combined with AND.

32.3

Targets, input transformation and retries

In plain words

Each target can reshape the event with an input transformer, and EventBridge retries failed deliveries before giving up.

The problem it solves

Targets need a specific payload, and temporary failures should not lose events.

What it does

  • Input transformer picks fields with JSON paths and builds a template.
  • Retry policy: maximum event age (up to 24 hours) and attempts (up to 185). Check the current limits.
  • Attach a dead letter queue (SQS) per target to capture undeliverable events.
  • Targets need an IAM role (for Step Functions, ECS, Kinesis) or a resource policy (Lambda, SQS, SNS).

Target with DLQ

hcltarget-dlq.tf
resource "aws_cloudwatch_event_target" "fn" {
  rule           = aws_cloudwatch_event_rule.order_created.name
  event_bus_name = aws_cloudwatch_event_bus.shop.name
  arn            = aws_lambda_function.fulfil.arn
  retry_policy {
    maximum_event_age_in_seconds = 3600
    maximum_retry_attempts       = 5
  }
  dead_letter_config {
    arn = aws_sqs_queue.eventbridge_dlq.arn
  }
}
Careful

The DLQ queue policy must allow events.amazonaws.com to send messages or failures are lost silently.

32.4

Cross-account and cross-Region buses

In plain words

A bus can receive events from other accounts and Regions and forward events to another bus.

The problem it solves

Central teams want a single place for audit or integration events, and multi-account organisations need controlled sharing.

What it does

  • A resource policy on the receiving bus allows specific accounts or an Organization (aws:PrincipalOrgID).
  • A rule with a bus target forwards matching events; the sender needs a role to put events.
  • Global endpoints with Route 53 health checks provide failover of event ingestion between two Regions.
  • Keep the pattern narrow at the sender to limit cross-account volume.

Bus policy by organization

jsonbus-policy.json
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [{
    "Sid": "AllowOrg",
    "Effect": "Allow",
    "Principal": "*",
    "Action": "events:PutEvents",
    "Resource": "arn:aws:events:eu-west-1:111122223333:event-bus/central",
    "Condition": {"StringEquals": {"aws:PrincipalOrgID": "o-exampleorgid"}}
  }]
}
Check yourself
How do you let every account in your organization send to a bus?

A bus resource policy with an aws:PrincipalOrgID condition.

32.5

Archive and replay, schema registry

In plain words

An archive stores events from a bus so you can replay them later. The schema registry discovers and stores event shapes.

The problem it solves

After a bug or when adding a new consumer, you need to reprocess past events, and developers need to know the event structure.

What it does

  • Archives filter by pattern and have a retention period.
  • Replay sends archived events in a time window to chosen rules; replayed events carry a replay marker, so make consumers idempotent.
  • Schema discovery records event schemas and can generate code bindings.
  • Use versioned detail-type values such as OrderCreated.v2 for evolution.

Create an archive

bashArchive
aws events create-archive --archive-name shop-all --event-source-arn arn:aws:events:eu-west-1:111122223333:event-bus/shop --retention-days 30
32.6

EventBridge Pipes

In plain words

A pipe connects one source to one target, with optional filtering, enrichment and transformation in between.

The problem it solves

Gluing a queue or stream to a target with a Lambda function adds code to maintain.

What it does

  • Sources: SQS, Kinesis, DynamoDB Streams, MSK, self-managed Kafka, MQ.
  • Optional filter, then optional enrichment (Lambda, API Gateway, Step Functions or API destination), then the target.
  • Handles batching, polling and partial failures for you.
  • Use Pipes for point to point and buses for many to many.

Pipe from SQS to Step Functions

hclpipe.tf
resource "aws_pipes_pipe" "orders" {
  name     = "orders-to-workflow"
  role_arn = aws_iam_role.pipe.arn
  source   = aws_sqs_queue.orders.arn
  target   = aws_sfn_state_machine.orders.arn
  source_parameters {
    sqs_queue_parameters {
      batch_size = 1
    }
  }
}
Check yourself
Bus or pipe for one queue feeding one workflow?

A pipe.

32.7

EventBridge Scheduler

In plain words

Scheduler runs one-time or recurring schedules using cron, rate or at() expressions and calls over 270 services directly.

The problem it solves

Cron on a server is a single point of failure and old EventBridge scheduled rules do not scale to millions of per-customer timers.

What it does

  • Time zones and flexible time windows are supported.
  • Schedules live in schedule groups. Each has a target, role, retry policy and optional DLQ.
  • One-time schedules can auto-delete after running.
  • Replaces ad-hoc scheduled rules for new work; check the current quota on schedules per account.

Nightly Lambda

hclschedule.tf
resource "aws_scheduler_schedule" "nightly" {
  name                         = "nightly-report"
  schedule_expression          = "cron(0 2 * * ? *)"
  schedule_expression_timezone = "Europe/London"
  flexible_time_window {
    mode = "OFF"
  }
  target {
    arn      = aws_lambda_function.report.arn
    role_arn = aws_iam_role.scheduler.arn
  }
}
32.8

API destinations and operations

In plain words

API destinations let a rule call any HTTPS endpoint with managed authentication and rate limiting.

The problem it solves

You want to push events to a SaaS webhook without writing and hosting a forwarding function.

What it does

  • A connection stores credentials (basic, API key, OAuth) in Secrets Manager managed by EventBridge.
  • The destination sets the endpoint, method and an invocation rate limit.
  • Monitor FailedInvocations, ThrottledRules, InvocationsFailedToBeSentToDlq and target DLQ depth.
  • CloudTrail data events can audit PutEvents if needed.

Alarm on failures

hclalarm.tf
resource "aws_cloudwatch_metric_alarm" "eb_failed" {
  alarm_name          = "eventbridge-failed-invocations"
  namespace           = "AWS/Events"
  metric_name         = "FailedInvocations"
  statistic           = "Sum"
  period              = 300
  evaluation_periods  = 1
  threshold           = 1
  comparison_operator = "GreaterThanOrEqualToThreshold"
}
Check yourself
Where are OAuth secrets for an API destination kept?

In a connection, stored by EventBridge in Secrets Manager.

Section 33 of 93

SQS and SNS messaging

7 concepts · about 55 minutes

Queues decouple speed and failure between producers and consumers. Topics broadcast one message to many subscribers. Together they form the classic fan-out.

Goals
  • Choose between standard and FIFO queues and topics
  • Tune visibility timeout, long polling and dead letter queues
  • Build SNS to SQS fan-out with filtering and correct policies
33.1

SQS basics

In plain words

SQS is a managed queue. Producers send messages, consumers poll and delete them after processing.

The problem it solves

If a consumer is slow or down, a direct call loses work or blocks the caller.

What it does

  • Messages up to 1 MiB (check the current quota), retained 60 seconds to 14 days (default 4 days).
  • Pay per request, with batching of up to 10 messages.
  • Long polling (ReceiveMessageWaitTimeSeconds up to 20) cuts empty responses and cost.
  • No servers, scales automatically, encrypted at rest with SSE-SQS by default or a KMS key.

Create a queue

hclqueue.tf
resource "aws_sqs_queue" "orders" {
  name                       = "orders"
  receive_wait_time_seconds  = 20
  visibility_timeout_seconds = 60
  message_retention_seconds  = 345600
  sqs_managed_sse_enabled    = true
}
Check yourself
Why use long polling?

It reduces empty receives, lowering cost and latency.

33.2

Visibility timeout

In plain words

When a consumer receives a message it becomes invisible for the visibility timeout. If it is not deleted in time, it becomes visible again and another consumer may get it.

The problem it solves

Without it two consumers would process the same message at once; with a value too short you get duplicates.

What it does

  • Default 30 seconds, maximum 12 hours.
  • Set it longer than your worst case processing time. For Lambda consumers, AWS recommends at least six times the function timeout.
  • A consumer can extend it with ChangeMessageVisibility for long jobs.
  • Delivery is at least once for standard queues, so processing must be idempotent.

Extend while working

bashExtend visibility
aws sqs change-message-visibility --queue-url https://sqs.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/111122223333/orders \
  --receipt-handle "$HANDLE" --visibility-timeout 300
Check yourself
Lambda timeout is 30 s. What visibility timeout does AWS recommend at least?

180 seconds, six times 30.

33.3

Standard versus FIFO queues

In plain words

Standard queues give very high throughput with at-least-once delivery and best-effort ordering. FIFO queues keep order per message group and support deduplication.

The problem it solves

Some workloads, such as ledger updates, need strict order and no duplicates; others only need speed.

What it does

  • FIFO name must end in .fifo.
  • MessageGroupId defines the ordering lane. Messages in one group are processed one at a time, in order. Different groups run in parallel.
  • Deduplication by MessageDeduplicationId or content hash within a five minute window.
  • FIFO throughput is lower by default; high throughput mode raises it per group count (check the current quotas).
Queue type
OptionStandard
Choose whenthroughput matters and handlers are idempotent
Avoid whenorder is a hard requirement
OptionFIFO
Choose whenorder per entity such as an account
Avoid whenyou need huge parallelism in one group

FIFO queue

hclfifo.tf
resource "aws_sqs_queue" "ledger" {
  name                        = "ledger.fifo"
  fifo_queue                  = true
  content_based_deduplication = true
}
33.4

Dead letter queues and redrive

In plain words

A dead letter queue (DLQ) is another queue that receives messages that failed too many times.

The problem it solves

A poison message can loop forever, wasting compute and blocking the rest of a FIFO group.

What it does

  • Redrive policy: maxReceiveCount and the DLQ ARN. A DLQ for a FIFO queue must be FIFO.
  • DLQ retention should be longer than the source queue because the original enqueue time is kept.
  • Alarm on ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible of the DLQ.
  • Redrive to source moves messages back after you fix the bug.

Redrive policy

hcldlq.tf
resource "aws_sqs_queue" "orders_dlq" {
  name                      = "orders-dlq"
  message_retention_seconds = 1209600
}

resource "aws_sqs_queue_redrive_policy" "orders" {
  queue_url = aws_sqs_queue.orders.id
  redrive_policy = jsonencode({
    deadLetterTargetArn = aws_sqs_queue.orders_dlq.arn
    maxReceiveCount     = 5
  })
}
bashRedrive
aws sqs start-message-move-task --source-arn arn:aws:sqs:eu-west-1:111122223333:orders-dlq
Check yourself
Why give the DLQ longer retention?

The message age counts from first enqueue, so a short DLQ retention could expire messages immediately.

33.5

SNS topics and subscriptions

In plain words

SNS publishes a message to a topic, and every subscriber receives a copy.

The problem it solves

One event often needs several reactions, such as email, queue and function, and the publisher should not loop over them.

What it does

  • Subscribers: SQS, Lambda, HTTPS, email, SMS, mobile push, Firehose.
  • FIFO topics pair with FIFO queues for ordered fan-out.
  • Filter policies on subscriptions send only matching messages, on attributes or body.
  • Delivery retries and a subscription DLQ handle failures.

Topic with filtered subscription

hclsns.tf
resource "aws_sns_topic" "orders" {
  name = "orders"
}

resource "aws_sns_topic_subscription" "billing" {
  topic_arn            = aws_sns_topic.orders.arn
  protocol             = "sqs"
  endpoint             = aws_sqs_queue.billing.arn
  raw_message_delivery = true
  filter_policy        = jsonencode({ type = ["paid"] })
}
Check yourself
Which feature stops a subscriber receiving irrelevant messages?

A subscription filter policy.

33.6

Fan-out policy and permissions

In plain words

SNS needs permission to send to a queue, and the queue policy is where most fan-out setups fail.

The problem it solves

Messages published but never arriving is almost always a missing or too broad queue policy.

What it does

  • The queue policy allows sns.amazonaws.com to sqs:SendMessage with condition aws:SourceArn equal to the topic.
  • Encrypted topics and queues need KMS key policy access for the service.
  • Cross-account subscriptions need permission on both sides.
  • Use raw message delivery to skip the SNS JSON envelope.

Queue policy

jsonqueue-policy.json
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [{
    "Effect": "Allow",
    "Principal": {"Service": "sns.amazonaws.com"},
    "Action": "sqs:SendMessage",
    "Resource": "arn:aws:sqs:eu-west-1:111122223333:billing",
    "Condition": {"ArnEquals": {"aws:SourceArn": "arn:aws:sns:eu-west-1:111122223333:orders"}}
  }]
}
33.7

Choosing SQS, SNS, EventBridge and Kinesis

In plain words

All four move data between components, but with different delivery models.

The problem it solves

Picking the wrong one leads to lost ordering, missed replays or unnecessary cost.

What it does

  • SQS: one consumer group pulls work; buffering and retries.
  • SNS: push fan-out to many subscribers, simple filtering.
  • EventBridge: rich pattern routing, SaaS and AWS service events, schedules, archive and replay.
  • Kinesis or MSK: ordered replayable streams read by many consumers at their own pace.
  • Common combo: EventBridge or SNS to SQS per consumer, then Lambda.
Pick one
OptionSQS
Choose whenyou need a buffer and retries for one worker pool
Avoid whenmany independent subscribers need copies
OptionSNS
Choose whensimple push to several endpoints
Avoid whenyou need replay or complex routing
OptionEventBridge
Choose whenrouting across services and accounts
Avoid whenyou need very high throughput of ordered records
OptionKinesis
Choose whenordered high volume records and several readers
Avoid whena simple task queue is enough
Check yourself
Which service retains a stream so a new consumer can read from the past?

Kinesis (or MSK). EventBridge offers archive and replay of events.

Section 34 of 93

ECS and Fargate tasks

6 concepts · about 55 minutes

Amazon ECS is AWS's own container orchestrator. It is simpler than Kubernetes and deeply integrated with IAM, load balancers and CloudWatch.

Goals
  • Describe clusters, task definitions, tasks and services
  • Write a Fargate task definition with correct roles and logging
  • Choose between Fargate and EC2 launch types
34.1

ECS building blocks

In plain words

A cluster groups capacity. A task definition describes containers. A task is a running instance of it. A service keeps a desired number of tasks running.

The problem it solves

You need to run containers reliably without managing a control plane.

What it does

  • The ECS control plane is free and fully managed. You pay for the compute (Fargate or EC2).
  • Task definitions are versioned as family:revision.
  • Run once with RunTask (batch) or continuously with a service (web).
  • Compute: Fargate (serverless), EC2 (your instances) or ECS Anywhere (your hardware).

List

bashInspect
aws ecs list-clusters
aws ecs describe-services --cluster shop --services web --query 'services[].[serviceName,desiredCount,runningCount]'
Check yourself
What keeps a number of tasks running and replaces failed ones?

An ECS service.

34.2

Task definition anatomy

In plain words

The task definition lists containers, images, CPU and memory, ports, environment, secrets, logging and roles.

The problem it solves

The same image needs different resources and settings in each environment, and secrets must not be baked in.

What it does

  • Fargate requires networkMode: awsvpc, and task-level cpu and memory from supported combinations (check the current table).
  • essential: true containers stop the whole task if they exit.
  • secrets inject values from Secrets Manager or Parameter Store at start.
  • Logging with the awslogs driver sends stdout to CloudWatch Logs.
  • Fargate platform includes ephemeral storage (20 GiB default, configurable up to a higher maximum; check the current quota).

Fargate task definition

jsontaskdef.json
{
  "family": "web",
  "requiresCompatibilities": ["FARGATE"],
  "networkMode": "awsvpc",
  "cpu": "512",
  "memory": "1024",
  "runtimePlatform": {"cpuArchitecture": "ARM64", "operatingSystemFamily": "LINUX"},
  "executionRoleArn": "arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/ecsExecution",
  "taskRoleArn": "arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/webTask",
  "containerDefinitions": [{
    "name": "web",
    "image": "111122223333.dkr.ecr.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/web:1.4.2",
    "essential": true,
    "portMappings": [{"containerPort": 8080}],
    "secrets": [{"name": "DB_PASSWORD", "valueFrom": "arn:aws:secretsmanager:eu-west-1:111122223333:secret:db-AbCdEf"}],
    "logConfiguration": {
      "logDriver": "awslogs",
      "options": {"awslogs-group": "/ecs/web", "awslogs-region": "eu-west-1", "awslogs-stream-prefix": "web"}
    }
  }]
}
34.3

Task role versus execution role

In plain words

Two roles apply. The execution role lets ECS pull the image, write logs and fetch secrets. The task role is what your application code uses to call AWS.

The problem it solves

Mixing them gives the app permissions it should not have, or leaves ECS unable to start the task.

What it does

  • Execution role: ECR pull, logs:CreateLogStream, logs:PutLogEvents, secret read for injected values. Use the managed policy AmazonECSTaskExecutionRolePolicy plus secret access.
  • Task role: trusts ecs-tasks.amazonaws.com, holds only the application permissions.
  • Credentials reach the container through the task metadata credential endpoint, so the SDK works with no keys.
  • Each service should have its own task role.

Trust policy

jsontask-role-trust.json
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [{
    "Effect": "Allow",
    "Principal": {"Service": "ecs-tasks.amazonaws.com"},
    "Action": "sts:AssumeRole"
  }]
}
Check yourself
The task cannot pull the image from ECR. Which role is missing a permission?

The execution role.

34.4

Fargate networking and sizing

In plain words

Each Fargate task gets its own ENI and private IP in your subnet (awsvpc), with its own security group.

The problem it solves

Tasks must reach registries and AWS APIs, and be reachable only by the right sources.

What it does

  • Tasks in private subnets need NAT or VPC endpoints for ECR (api and dkr), S3 (gateway), CloudWatch Logs and Secrets Manager.
  • Every task consumes one IP, so size subnets for peak tasks plus deployments.
  • Security group per service: allow the app port from the load balancer security group only.
  • Sizing example: 4 tasks at 0.5 vCPU and 1 GB. Total 2 vCPU and 4 GB. Use measured utilisation to right size.

Security group reference

hclecs-sg.tf
resource "aws_vpc_security_group_ingress_rule" "web_from_alb" {
  security_group_id            = aws_security_group.web.id
  referenced_security_group_id = aws_security_group.alb.id
  ip_protocol                  = "tcp"
  from_port                    = 8080
  to_port                      = 8080
}
34.5

Fargate versus EC2 launch type

In plain words

Fargate runs tasks without you managing servers. The EC2 launch type runs tasks on your own instances.

The problem it solves

Choosing wrongly means paying for idle servers or lacking features such as GPUs.

What it does

  • Fargate: per second billing for vCPU and memory, strong task isolation, no patching, Spot and ARM supported.
  • EC2: lower unit cost at high steady utilisation with Savings Plans, GPUs, large sizes, daemon tasks, host access.
  • Mixed with capacity providers in one cluster.
  • Fargate does not support privileged containers or host networking.
Compute choice
OptionFargate
Choose whensmall team and variable load
Avoid whenyou need GPUs or privileged mode
OptionEC2
Choose whensteady high utilisation or special hardware
Avoid whennobody can patch and scale instances
Check yourself
Which launch type supports privileged containers?

EC2, not Fargate.

34.6

Logging, metrics and ECS Exec

In plain words

ECS sends container output to CloudWatch Logs and metrics to CloudWatch; ECS Exec opens a shell in a running container using SSM.

The problem it solves

Containers are ephemeral; you cannot SSH in, yet you must debug.

What it does

  • awslogs or FireLens (Fluent Bit) route logs to CloudWatch, S3 or third parties.
  • Container Insights adds task level CPU, memory and network metrics.
  • ECS Exec needs enableExecuteCommand, the Session Manager plugin and task role SSM messages permissions. Commands are logged via CloudTrail and can be logged to S3 or CloudWatch.
  • Task stopped reasons appear in describe-tasks (for example CannotPullContainerError).

Open a shell

bashECS Exec
aws ecs execute-command --cluster shop --task "$TASK_ID" --container web --interactive --command "/bin/sh"
aws ecs describe-tasks --cluster shop --tasks "$TASK_ID" --query 'tasks[].stoppedReason'
Check yourself
What does a CannotPullContainerError usually point to?

Missing network path to the registry or missing execution role permission.

Section 35 of 93

ECS services, discovery and App Runner

7 concepts · about 50 minutes

After tasks run, services need traffic, scaling, safe deployments and a way to find each other. This section also compares ECS with EKS and App Runner.

Goals
  • Run ECS services with load balancers, deployments and autoscaling
  • Use capacity providers and service discovery
  • Decide between ECS, EKS and App Runner for a workload
35.1

ECS services and deployments

In plain words

A service keeps the desired number of tasks running and replaces failed ones. It also performs rolling or blue/green deployments of new task definition revisions.

The problem it solves

Manually starting and replacing containers does not give zero downtime updates.

What it does

  • Rolling update (ECS controller) uses minimumHealthyPercent and maximumPercent. With desired 4, min 100 and max 200, ECS starts up to 4 new tasks before stopping old ones.
  • The deployment circuit breaker stops a failing rollout and can roll back automatically.
  • Blue/green through CodeDeploy, or the native ECS blue/green strategy where available (check the current documentation).
  • Health: ALB target health plus container health checks.

Service with circuit breaker

hclservice.tf
resource "aws_ecs_service" "web" {
  name            = "web"
  cluster         = aws_ecs_cluster.shop.id
  task_definition = aws_ecs_task_definition.web.arn
  desired_count   = 4
  launch_type     = "FARGATE"

  deployment_minimum_healthy_percent = 100
  deployment_maximum_percent         = 200

  deployment_circuit_breaker {
    enable   = true
    rollback = true
  }

  network_configuration {
    subnets         = var.private_subnet_ids
    security_groups = [aws_security_group.web.id]
  }

  load_balancer {
    target_group_arn = aws_lb_target_group.web.arn
    container_name   = "web"
    container_port   = 8080
  }
}
Check yourself
Desired 4, min healthy 100, max 200. How many tasks can run at once during deploy?

Up to 8.

35.2

Service auto scaling

In plain words

Application Auto Scaling changes a service's desired count based on metrics.

The problem it solves

Fixed task counts waste money at night and fail under peak load.

What it does

  • Target tracking on ECSServiceAverageCPUUtilization, memory, or ALB RequestCountPerTarget.
  • Step and scheduled scaling are also available.
  • Set min and max capacity and sensible cooldowns.
  • Scale-in protects against dropped requests through ALB deregistration delay.

Policy

hclautoscale.tf
resource "aws_appautoscaling_target" "web" {
  service_namespace  = "ecs"
  resource_id        = "service/shop/web"
  scalable_dimension = "ecs:service:DesiredCount"
  min_capacity       = 2
  max_capacity       = 20
}

resource "aws_appautoscaling_policy" "cpu" {
  name               = "cpu70"
  policy_type        = "TargetTrackingScaling"
  service_namespace  = aws_appautoscaling_target.web.service_namespace
  resource_id        = aws_appautoscaling_target.web.resource_id
  scalable_dimension = aws_appautoscaling_target.web.scalable_dimension
  target_tracking_scaling_policy_configuration {
    target_value = 70
    predefined_metric_specification {
      predefined_metric_type = "ECSServiceAverageCPUUtilization"
    }
  }
}
Check yourself
Which metric scales on traffic share per task behind an ALB?

ALBRequestCountPerTarget.

35.3

Capacity providers

In plain words

A capacity provider tells a cluster where tasks may run: Fargate, Fargate Spot or an Auto Scaling group of EC2 instances.

The problem it solves

You want a cheap Spot share with an on-demand baseline, or automatic EC2 scaling to fit tasks.

What it does

  • Strategy: base guarantees a minimum on one provider; weight splits the rest.
  • Example: base 2 on FARGATE, then weight 1 FARGATE and weight 3 FARGATE_SPOT. For 10 tasks, 2 base plus 8 split 1:3 gives 2 + 2 = 4 on FARGATE and 6 on Spot.
  • EC2 providers use managed scaling to add instances when tasks are pending.
  • Fargate Spot tasks may be interrupted with a two minute warning (SIGTERM); handle it.

Strategy

hclcapacity.tf
resource "aws_ecs_cluster_capacity_providers" "shop" {
  cluster_name       = aws_ecs_cluster.shop.name
  capacity_providers = ["FARGATE", "FARGATE_SPOT"]
  default_capacity_provider_strategy {
    capacity_provider = "FARGATE"
    base              = 2
    weight            = 1
  }
  default_capacity_provider_strategy {
    capacity_provider = "FARGATE_SPOT"
    weight            = 3
  }
}
35.4

Service discovery and Service Connect

In plain words

Services find each other by name. Cloud Map gives DNS names; ECS Service Connect adds a managed proxy with retries, metrics and short names.

The problem it solves

Task IPs change on every deployment, so hard coded addresses break.

What it does

  • Cloud Map service discovery registers task IPs in a private DNS namespace.
  • Service Connect defines a namespace and port aliases; a sidecar proxy handles load balancing, outlier detection and per-request metrics.
  • Alternative: an internal ALB per service, simple but costs per ALB.
  • For cross-cluster or cross-VPC, consider VPC Lattice.

Namespace

bashCreate namespace
aws servicediscovery create-private-dns-namespace --name shop.local --vpc vpc-0abc123
aws ecs update-service --cluster shop --service web --service-connect-configuration enabled=true,namespace=shop.local
Check yourself
Why not use task IPs directly?

They change on every task replacement.

35.5

ECS versus EKS

In plain words

ECS is simple and AWS specific. EKS is Kubernetes, portable, with a large ecosystem and more to operate.

The problem it solves

Teams adopt Kubernetes for fashion and then carry its operational weight without needing it.

What it does

  • ECS: no cluster upgrades, no control plane fee, IAM native, fewer concepts. Best for AWS-only teams with modest scale and few platform engineers.
  • EKS: Helm, operators, CRDs, service mesh, portability, hiring pool; control plane billed per cluster per hour (check current pricing) plus upgrade work.
  • Both run on Fargate or EC2; both integrate with ALB, IAM and CloudWatch.
  • Switching later is a rewrite of manifests and deployment tooling, not of the containers.
Orchestrator
OptionECS on Fargate
Choose whensmall team and plain web services
Avoid whenyou need CRDs, operators or Helm charts
OptionEKS
Choose whenyou already use Kubernetes tooling and need portability
Avoid whennobody owns cluster upgrades
OptionApp Runner
Choose whena single web service from image or source
Avoid whenyou need sidecars or private non-HTTP services
Check yourself
Name two reasons to choose EKS over ECS.

Kubernetes ecosystem and portability (Helm, operators, CRDs); existing Kubernetes skills.

35.6

AWS App Runner

In plain words

App Runner builds or pulls your web app and runs it with HTTPS, scaling and a load balancer, with almost no configuration.

The problem it solves

Small teams want to deploy a container web app without learning VPCs, ALBs and task definitions.

What it does

  • Source: ECR image or a code repository (supported runtimes).
  • Auto scaling on concurrency, with a configurable minimum so there is no cold start. Billed for provisioned memory while idle and vCPU while active.
  • Optional VPC connector for outbound private access, and private ingress via a VPC endpoint.
  • Limits: HTTP-only services, no sidecars, fewer controls. Check the current service availability notes before starting new projects.

Terraform

hclapprunner.tf
resource "aws_apprunner_service" "web" {
  service_name = "web"
  source_configuration {
    authentication_configuration {
      access_role_arn = aws_iam_role.apprunner_ecr.arn
    }
    image_repository {
      image_identifier      = "111122223333.dkr.ecr.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/web:1.4.2"
      image_repository_type = "ECR"
      image_configuration {
        port = "8080"
      }
    }
  }
}
35.7

ECS troubleshooting

In plain words

Most ECS issues sit in a few places: image pull, health checks, memory limits and permissions.

The problem it solves

Tasks flap between running and stopped and the service never becomes stable.

What it does

  • CannotPullContainerError: no route to ECR or missing execution role permission.
  • Task failed ELB health checks: wrong health check path or port, or the app is slow to start; use a health check grace period.
  • Exit code 137: killed for out of memory or SIGKILL; raise memory.
  • ResourceInitializationError: secrets or ENI setup failed, often missing endpoints.
  • Use service events: aws ecs describe-services shows recent messages.

Read recent events

bashService events
aws ecs describe-services --cluster shop --services web --query 'services[0].events[:5].[createdAt,message]' --output table
Check yourself
A task exits with code 137. What is the first suspect?

Out of memory kill; check memory limits and usage.

← PreviousNext →
Section 36 of 93

EFS and FSx file storage

7 concepts · about 45 minutes

When many servers or containers need the same files, block storage is not enough. AWS offers managed file systems for each protocol and performance profile.

Goals
  • Choose between EBS, EFS, S3 and the FSx family
  • Configure EFS mount targets, access points and throughput modes
  • Pick the right FSx variant for Windows, Lustre, NetApp ONTAP or OpenZFS
36.1

Storage types compared

In plain words

Block (EBS) attaches to one instance. File (EFS, FSx) is shared over NFS or SMB. Object (S3) is accessed over HTTP API.

The problem it solves

Choosing the wrong type leads to poor performance or code rewrites.

What it does

  • EBS: single instance (Multi-Attach only for some volume types), low latency.
  • EFS: elastic shared NFS for Linux, many clients across AZs.
  • FSx: managed specialised file systems.
  • S3: cheapest for large objects, no POSIX semantics.
Shared storage
OptionEFS
Choose whenmany Linux clients need a growing shared POSIX filesystem
Avoid whenyou need SMB or extreme parallel throughput
OptionFSx for Windows
Choose whenWindows apps need SMB and Active Directory
Avoid whenworkloads are Linux only
OptionFSx for Lustre
Choose whenHPC or ML needs very high throughput with S3 linkage
Avoid whenyou need long term durable general storage
OptionS3
Choose whenfiles are written once and read as objects
Avoid whenapplications require file locking and POSIX
Check yourself
Which service gives shared NFS across AZs with elastic size?

EFS.

36.2

EFS architecture and storage classes

In plain words

EFS is a regional NFS 4.x file system with mount targets in each AZ subnet. Capacity grows and shrinks automatically.

The problem it solves

Provisioning and resizing shared file servers is manual and a single server is a single point of failure.

What it does

  • Create one mount target per AZ; clients mount via DNS name or the EFS mount helper.
  • Storage classes: Standard (Multi-AZ), One Zone, plus Infrequent Access and Archive tiers via lifecycle policies (check the current class list and prices).
  • Encryption at rest with KMS and in transit with TLS through the mount helper.
  • Security groups on mount targets must allow TCP 2049 from clients.

Terraform

hclefs.tf
resource "aws_efs_file_system" "shared" {
  encrypted = true
  lifecycle_policy {
    transition_to_ia = "AFTER_30_DAYS"
  }
}

resource "aws_efs_mount_target" "az" {
  for_each        = toset(var.private_subnet_ids)
  file_system_id  = aws_efs_file_system.shared.id
  subnet_id       = each.value
  security_groups = [aws_security_group.efs.id]
}
bashMount with the helper
sudo mount -t efs -o tls fs-0123456789abcdef0:/ /mnt/shared
Check yourself
Which port must the mount target security group allow?

TCP 2049 (NFS).

36.3

EFS performance and throughput modes

In plain words

EFS has performance behaviour set by its throughput mode: Elastic, Provisioned or Bursting.

The problem it solves

Throughput needs differ between a quiet web content share and a busy analytics job.

What it does

  • Elastic scales throughput up and down with the workload and bills per data transferred; recommended default for spiky or unknown workloads.
  • Provisioned fixes throughput regardless of stored size and bills for it.
  • Bursting ties baseline to stored size, with burst credits.
  • Latency is higher than EBS (network file system); small file metadata heavy workloads suffer.
  • Check the current throughput limits per file system.

Change mode

bashSet elastic throughput
aws efs update-file-system --file-system-id fs-0123456789abcdef0 --throughput-mode elastic
36.4

Access points and permissions

In plain words

An access point is an application entry into an EFS file system that enforces a root directory and POSIX identity.

The problem it solves

Many apps share one filesystem but must not see each other's data or run as root.

What it does

  • Each access point fixes a path, UID and GID and creates the directory with given permissions.
  • IAM authorisation: the file system policy and elasticfilesystem:ClientMount / ClientWrite permissions control who may mount.
  • Lambda and Fargate attach through access points.
  • Use a resource policy to require TLS (aws:SecureTransport).

Policy requiring TLS

jsonefs-policy.json
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [{
    "Effect": "Deny",
    "Principal": {"AWS": "*"},
    "Action": "*",
    "Condition": {"Bool": {"aws:SecureTransport": "false"}}
  }]
}
Check yourself
How can two apps share one EFS yet stay isolated?

Give each its own access point with a distinct path and POSIX identity.

36.5

FSx for Windows and NetApp ONTAP

In plain words

FSx for Windows File Server offers SMB shares with Active Directory. FSx for NetApp ONTAP offers NFS, SMB and iSCSI with NetApp features.

The problem it solves

Windows applications and enterprise NAS users need native protocols and features that EFS lacks.

What it does

  • Windows: integrates with AWS Managed Microsoft AD or self-managed AD, DFS namespaces, shadow copies, Multi-AZ option.
  • ONTAP: snapshots, clones, SnapMirror replication, tiering to a capacity pool, multi-protocol. Good for migrating NetApp users.
  • Backups through AWS Backup or built-in daily backups.
  • Check each variant's current Region availability and throughput capacities.

Create (CLI shape)

bashFSx Windows
aws fsx create-file-system --file-system-type WINDOWS --storage-capacity 1024 \
  --subnet-ids subnet-0aaa subnet-0bbb --storage-type SSD \
  --windows-configuration DeploymentType=MULTI_AZ_1,PreferredSubnetId=subnet-0aaa,ThroughputCapacity=64,ActiveDirectoryId=d-1234567890
36.6

FSx for Lustre and OpenZFS

In plain words

FSx for Lustre is a high performance parallel file system for HPC and machine learning. FSx for OpenZFS gives NFS with ZFS snapshots and clones.

The problem it solves

Training jobs and simulations read data at rates that standard network file systems cannot sustain.

What it does

  • Lustre scratch deployments: fastest and cheapest, not replicated. Persistent deployments: replicated within an AZ for longer-term data.
  • Data repository association links a path to an S3 bucket: lazy load on first read and export changes back.
  • OpenZFS: low latency NFS, instant snapshots and clones, for migrating ZFS or Linux NAS.
  • Both are single-AZ options in many configurations; check current deployment types.

Link to S3

bashLustre with S3
aws fsx create-file-system --file-system-type LUSTRE --storage-capacity 1200 \
  --subnet-ids subnet-0aaa --lustre-configuration DeploymentType=SCRATCH_2
aws fsx create-data-repository-association --file-system-id fs-0abc --file-system-path /data --data-repository-path s3://ml-datasets/train
Check yourself
Which FSx variant is meant for HPC and ML with S3 integration?

FSx for Lustre.

36.7

Backups, cost and operating file systems

In plain words

Protect shared files with backups, watch growth and pick storage tiers to control cost.

The problem it solves

A shared filesystem tends to accumulate data nobody owns, and one deletion can affect many servers.

What it does

  • AWS Backup protects EFS and FSx with schedules, retention and cross-account copies.
  • EFS lifecycle moves cold files to Infrequent Access; example: 10 TB with 70 percent untouched for 30 days leaves 3 TB in Standard and 7 TB in IA. Compute the monthly cost with the current per-GB prices.
  • Monitor PercentIOLimit, BurstCreditBalance, ClientConnections for EFS.
  • Replication copies EFS to another Region (read-only target).

Enable backup policy

bashEFS automatic backups
aws efs put-backup-policy --file-system-id fs-0123456789abcdef0 --backup-policy Status=ENABLED
