Section 37 of 93

Streaming with Kinesis and MSK

6 concepts · about 55 minutes

Streams hold ordered records for a time so many consumers can read them, replay them and process in near real time.

Goals
  • Compare Kinesis Data Streams, Firehose and Amazon MSK
  • Size a stream by shards and choose capacity modes
  • Build reliable consumers and deliver streams to S3
37.1

Streaming fundamentals

In plain words

A stream is an append-only log of records split into partitions. Producers write, consumers read from their own position.

The problem it solves

Queues delete messages after one consumer. Analytics, audit and several downstream systems need the same data, in order, replayable.

What it does

  • Records with the same partition key go to the same shard or partition and keep their order.
  • Retention lets late or new consumers read history.
  • Throughput scales by adding shards or partitions.
  • Consumers track a position (checkpoint) so they can resume.

Choose

Kinesis Data Streams is native and serverless. MSK runs Apache Kafka. Firehose is for delivery without code.

Check yourself
What guarantees order for related records?

Writing them with the same partition key so they land in one shard or partition.

37.2

Kinesis Data Streams shards and capacity

In plain words

A shard accepts up to 1 MB per second or 1,000 records per second of writes and delivers up to 2 MB per second of reads (check the current quotas).

The problem it solves

Undersized streams throttle producers; oversized streams waste money.

What it does

  • Provisioned mode: you choose shard count. On-demand mode: capacity scales automatically within documented limits.
  • Hot partition keys overload a single shard even when others are idle.
  • Sizing example: 6 MB per second peak ingest needs at least 6 shards, so provision 7 for headroom.
  • Retention defaults to 24 hours and can be extended (check the current maximum).
  • ProvisionedThroughputExceededException means slow down and retry with backoff.

Create and write

bashStream commands
aws kinesis create-stream --stream-name clicks --shard-count 7
aws kinesis put-record --stream-name clicks --partition-key user-42 --data "$(echo -n '{"page":"/"}' | base64)"
Check yourself
Peak is 6 MB per second at 1 MB per shard. How many shards at minimum?

6.

37.3

Consumers and enhanced fan-out

In plain words

Consumers read with the shared 2 MB per second per shard limit, or get a dedicated 2 MB per second each with enhanced fan-out.

The problem it solves

Several consumers on one shard compete for read throughput and add latency.

What it does

  • Standard consumers poll with GetRecords.
  • Enhanced fan-out uses HTTP/2 push to a registered consumer, typically around 70 ms latency.
  • The Kinesis Client Library (KCL) manages leases, checkpoints and resharding.
  • Lambda reads through an event source mapping with batch size, parallelization factor and on-failure destination.

Lambda mapping

hclkinesis-mapping.tf
resource "aws_lambda_event_source_mapping" "clicks" {
  event_source_arn                   = aws_kinesis_stream.clicks.arn
  function_name                      = aws_lambda_function.process.arn
  starting_position                  = "LATEST"
  batch_size                         = 100
  parallelization_factor             = 2
  bisect_batch_on_function_error     = true
  maximum_retry_attempts             = 3
}
37.4

Firehose delivery

In plain words

Amazon Data Firehose loads streaming data into S3, Redshift, OpenSearch, Splunk and HTTP endpoints, with buffering and optional transformation.

The problem it solves

Writing, batching and retrying delivery code for data lakes is repetitive.

What it does

  • Buffer by size or time, then write files to S3 with prefix partitions like year=!{timestamp:yyyy}/.
  • Convert JSON to Parquet or ORC using a Glue schema.
  • Optional Lambda transformation and dynamic partitioning.
  • Source can be direct PUT, a Kinesis stream, MSK or CloudWatch Logs subscriptions.

Delivery stream

hclfirehose.tf
resource "aws_kinesis_firehose_delivery_stream" "to_s3" {
  name        = "clicks-to-s3"
  destination = "extended_s3"
  kinesis_source_configuration {
    kinesis_stream_arn = aws_kinesis_stream.clicks.arn
    role_arn           = aws_iam_role.firehose.arn
  }
  extended_s3_configuration {
    role_arn            = aws_iam_role.firehose.arn
    bucket_arn          = aws_s3_bucket.lake.arn
    buffering_size      = 64
    buffering_interval  = 300
    prefix              = "clicks/dt=!{timestamp:yyyy-MM-dd}/"
    error_output_prefix = "errors/!{firehose:error-output-type}/"
  }
}
Check yourself
What two triggers flush a Firehose buffer?

Buffer size and buffer interval, whichever comes first.

37.5

Amazon MSK

In plain words

Amazon MSK runs Apache Kafka brokers for you, in your VPC, with Kafka protocol compatibility.

The problem it solves

You already have Kafka clients, connectors and skills, but running brokers and ZooKeeper-free controllers yourself is heavy.

What it does

  • Provisioned clusters across three AZs (broker sizes) or MSK Serverless for variable workloads.
  • Auth: IAM access control, SASL/SCRAM, mutual TLS; encryption in transit and at rest.
  • MSK Connect runs Kafka Connect connectors. Tiered storage keeps old data cheaply.
  • Replication factor 3 with min.insync.replicas 2 tolerates one AZ failure without write loss using acks=all.

Cluster outline

hclmsk.tf
resource "aws_msk_cluster" "events" {
  cluster_name           = "events"
  kafka_version          = "3.6.0"
  number_of_broker_nodes = 3
  broker_node_group_info {
    instance_type   = "kafka.m5.large"
    client_subnets  = var.private_subnet_ids
    security_groups = [aws_security_group.msk.id]
    storage_info {
      ebs_storage_info {
        volume_size = 500
      }
    }
  }
  client_authentication {
    sasl {
      iam = true
    }
  }
  encryption_info {
    encryption_in_transit {
      client_broker = "TLS"
    }
  }
}
Note

Check the currently supported Kafka versions before choosing one.

37.6

Choosing Kinesis, MSK, SQS and EventBridge

In plain words

Pick by the access pattern, the ecosystem you already use and the operations you accept.

The problem it solves

Teams over-build with Kafka when a queue suffices, or force queue semantics onto an analytics pipeline.

What it does

  • Kinesis: AWS native, easy Lambda integration, fewer knobs.
  • MSK: Kafka ecosystem, Connect, Streams, larger records and retention flexibility.
  • SQS: independent tasks, no ordering across messages, delete on success.
  • EventBridge: event routing with rules, not high-volume analytics streams.
  • Estimating monthly shard cost: shards x hours x price per shard-hour plus PUT payload units. For 7 shards over 730 hours that is 5,110 shard-hours; multiply by the current price.
Streaming service

Choose whenAWS native producers and Lambda consumers
Avoid whenyou must reuse Kafka clients and connectors
OptionMSK

Avoid whenthe team cannot operate Kafka concepts

Avoid whenyou need custom consumers and replay

Which option is best to just land logs in S3 as Parquet?

Section 38 of 93

Athena, Glue and Lake Formation

7 concepts · about 55 minutes

A data lake keeps raw and curated data in S3. Glue catalogs and transforms it, Athena queries it, and Lake Formation controls who sees what.

Goals
  • Query S3 data with Athena and reduce scan cost with partitioning and Parquet
  • Catalog and transform data with Glue crawlers and jobs
  • Govern a data lake with Lake Formation permissions
38.1

Athena serverless SQL

In plain words

Athena runs SQL directly on files in S3 with no servers, and bills by data scanned.

The problem it solves

Loading everything into a warehouse first is slow and costly for ad-hoc questions on logs and raw files.

What it does

  • Uses the Trino and Presto engine for SQL, and supports CSV, JSON, Parquet, ORC, Avro and Iceberg tables.
  • Needs a table definition in the Glue Data Catalog and an S3 location for query results.
  • Workgroups separate teams, enforce result locations and set per-query scan limits.
  • Cost example: scanning 2 TB at a price of 5 dollars per TB is 10 dollars. Check the current price per TB.

Run a query

bashStart a query
aws athena start-query-execution --work-group analytics \
  --query-string "SELECT status, count(*) FROM weblogs WHERE dt = '2026-10-30' GROUP BY status" \
  --query-execution-context Database=lake
Check yourself
What does Athena bill on?

The amount of data scanned by each query.

38.2

Cutting scan cost with partitions and Parquet

In plain words

Store data in a columnar format (Parquet) and in partitioned folders so a query reads only the columns and days it needs.

The problem it solves

CSV scans every byte of every file, so cost and time grow with total data size.

What it does

  • Partition folders such as dt=2026-10-30/ allow partition pruning when you filter on dt.
  • Parquet reads only referenced columns and compresses well, often reducing scanned bytes by an order of magnitude.
  • Avoid many tiny files; target files of about 128 MB or more.
  • Partition projection computes partitions in the table definition, avoiding crawler runs.
  • Example: 365 daily partitions of 10 GB is 3,650 GB. A one-day query scans 10 GB, which is 1/365 of the total.

Convert with CTAS

bashCreate a Parquet table
aws athena start-query-execution --work-group analytics --query-string \
 "CREATE TABLE weblogs_pq WITH (format='PARQUET', partitioned_by=ARRAY['dt'], external_location='s3://lake/curated/weblogs/') AS SELECT * FROM weblogs"
Check yourself
Daily partitions of 10 GB for a year: scan for one day?

10 GB, versus 3,650 GB without pruning.

38.3

Glue Data Catalog and crawlers

In plain words

The Glue Data Catalog is a central metadata store of databases and tables. Crawlers scan data and create or update table definitions.

The problem it solves

Every tool needs to know where data lives and what its schema is.

What it does

  • Used by Athena, EMR, Redshift Spectrum and Glue jobs.
  • Crawlers infer schema and partitions on a schedule; for known layouts define tables in IaC instead.
  • Schema changes can break queries; use a schema evolution policy.
  • Iceberg tables in the catalog add ACID updates and time travel.

Database and table in Terraform

hclglue.tf
resource "aws_glue_catalog_database" "lake" {
  name = "lake"
}

resource "aws_glue_crawler" "weblogs" {
  name          = "weblogs"
  database_name = aws_glue_catalog_database.lake.name
  role          = aws_iam_role.glue.arn
  schedule      = "cron(0 3 * * ? *)"
  s3_target {
    path = "s3://lake/raw/weblogs/"
  }
}
38.4

Glue ETL jobs

In plain words

Glue jobs run Apache Spark or Python scripts on managed workers to clean and convert data.

The problem it solves

Raw data is messy; you need repeatable transformation without running a cluster.

What it does

  • Types: Spark, Spark streaming, Python shell, Ray; Glue Studio for visual design.
  • Billed per DPU-hour (check current price) with per-second billing and a minimum duration; right-size workers and use auto scaling.
  • Job bookmarks track processed data for incremental runs.
  • Triggers and workflows chain jobs, or orchestrate from Step Functions or MWAA.

Job definition

hclglue-job.tf
resource "aws_glue_job" "curate" {
  name              = "curate-weblogs"
  role_arn          = aws_iam_role.glue.arn
  glue_version      = "4.0"
  worker_type       = "G.1X"
  number_of_workers = 5
  command {
    name            = "glueetl"
    script_location = "s3://lake/scripts/curate.py"
  }
  default_arguments = {
    "--job-bookmark-option" = "job-bookmark-enable"
  }
}
Check yourself
What does a job bookmark do?

Remembers what was processed so reruns handle only new data.

38.5

Lake Formation permissions

In plain words

Lake Formation adds database-style grants (table, column, row) on top of the Glue catalog, instead of writing S3 bucket policies per user.

The problem it solves

S3 policies cannot express column or row restrictions, and every team ends up with ad-hoc bucket access.

What it does

  • Register S3 locations; Lake Formation vends temporary credentials to integrated engines such as Athena.
  • Grant to IAM principals with SELECT on specific columns; data filters give row-level security.
  • LF-tags apply grants by classification such as sensitivity=pii.
  • Cross-account sharing uses AWS RAM style grants to catalog resources.

Grant columns

bashColumn grant
aws lakeformation grant-permissions \
  --principal DataLakePrincipalIdentifier=arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/Analyst \
  --permissions SELECT \
  --resource '{"TableWithColumns":{"DatabaseName":"lake","Name":"customers","ColumnNames":["id","country"]}}'
Check yourself
How would you hide a PII column from analysts?

Grant SELECT on only the allowed columns, or use LF-tags with a sensitivity classification.

38.6

Iceberg tables and the lakehouse

In plain words

Apache Iceberg is an open table format giving a data lake ACID updates, schema evolution and time travel.

The problem it solves

Plain Parquet folders cannot update or delete rows safely or handle concurrent writers.

What it does

  • Athena supports Iceberg with MERGE, UPDATE, DELETE and OPTIMIZE.
  • S3 Tables is an AWS managed Iceberg table offering; check current availability.
  • Compaction keeps small files in check; snapshots expire with VACUUM.
  • Open format means Spark, Trino, Redshift and others can read the same table.

Create an Iceberg table

bashAthena DDL
aws athena start-query-execution --work-group analytics --query-string \
 "CREATE TABLE orders_ice (id bigint, status string, ts timestamp) PARTITIONED BY (day(ts)) LOCATION 's3://lake/iceberg/orders/' TBLPROPERTIES ('table_type'='ICEBERG')"
38.7

Data lake zones and cost governance

In plain words

Organise the lake into raw, cleaned and curated zones with clear ownership, lifecycle and access rules.

The problem it solves

An ungoverned lake turns into a swamp of unknown, duplicated and risky data.

What it does

  • Separate buckets or prefixes per zone; raw is immutable and kept for reprocessing.
  • S3 lifecycle moves old raw data to colder classes; Intelligent-Tiering for unknown access.
  • Workgroup scan limits and budgets stop runaway queries.
  • Tag datasets with owner and classification; CloudTrail and Lake Formation logs give audit trails.

Workgroup scan limit

hclworkgroup.tf
resource "aws_athena_workgroup" "analytics" {
  name = "analytics"
  configuration {
    enforce_workgroup_configuration    = true
    bytes_scanned_cutoff_per_query     = 107374182400
    result_configuration {
      output_location = "s3://lake/athena-results/"
    }
  }
}

Here 107374182400 bytes is 100 GiB (100 x 1024 x 1024 x 1024).

Check yourself
What stops a single query scanning terabytes by mistake?

A workgroup scan cutoff per query.

Section 39 of 93

Amazon OpenSearch Service

6 concepts · about 45 minutes

OpenSearch Service runs search and log analytics clusters. It is powerful but needs careful sizing and index management.

Goals
  • Describe domains, nodes, shards and replicas
  • Size a domain and secure it inside a VPC
  • Manage index lifecycle, snapshots and the serverless option
39.1

When to use OpenSearch

In plain words

OpenSearch indexes JSON documents so you can run full-text search, filters, aggregations and vector search quickly.

The problem it solves

Databases are poor at free-text search, relevance ranking and fast aggregations over logs.

What it does

  • Use cases: application search, log analytics, observability, security analytics, vector search for AI retrieval.
  • It is not a primary database; keep the source of truth elsewhere and index copies.
  • Ingest from Firehose, Logstash, Fluent Bit, DynamoDB streams or OpenSearch Ingestion.
  • Managed domains or OpenSearch Serverless collections.

Check cluster health

bashHealth
curl -s -u "$USER:$PASS" "https://$DOMAIN/_cluster/health?pretty"
Check yourself
Is OpenSearch a good system of record?

No. Keep the source of truth in a database and treat the index as a derived copy.

39.2

Domains, nodes, shards and replicas

In plain words

A domain is a cluster. Indexes are split into primary shards, each with replica copies on other nodes.

The problem it solves

One node is a single point of failure, and one huge shard cannot be spread out for speed.

What it does

  • Production: three dedicated master nodes and data nodes across three AZs (Multi-AZ with standby is an option; check the current options).
  • Primary shard count is fixed at index creation; replicas can change at any time.
  • Aim for shard sizes of roughly 10 to 50 GB (guideline, depending on use) and avoid thousands of tiny shards.
  • Example: 300 GB of data per day index with 30 GB shards needs 10 primaries; with 1 replica that is 20 shards total and 600 GB of storage before overhead.

Index settings

jsonindex-settings.json
{
  "settings": {
    "index": {
      "number_of_shards": 10,
      "number_of_replicas": 1
    }
  }
}
Check yourself
Can you change primary shard count of an existing index freely?

No. It is fixed at creation; reindex, split or shrink to change it.

39.3

Sizing storage and instances

In plain words

Size by raw data per day, retention, replicas and overhead, then choose instance types for memory and IOPS.

The problem it solves

Undersized domains go red under load; oversized ones are very expensive.

What it does

  • Storage estimate = source data x (1 + replicas) x indexing overhead (often around 1.1 to 1.45 depending on mappings, check by testing) x days retained.
  • Example: 100 GB per day, 1 replica, overhead 1.25, 14 days gives 100 x 2 x 1.25 x 14 = 3,500 GB, plus free space headroom of about 25 percent so provision about 4,375 GB.
  • Memory-optimised (R family) or Graviton nodes for search; UltraWarm and cold tiers store older data cheaply.
  • Keep JVM heap pressure under control; alarm on it.

Sizing in Python

pythonsize.py
daily_gb, replicas, overhead, days = 100, 1, 1.25, 14
data = daily_gb * (1 + replicas) * overhead * days
print(data, data / 0.8)
39.4

Network and access security

In plain words

Put the domain in a VPC, use fine-grained access control and a resource policy, and encrypt everything.

The problem it solves

Public domains with weak policies are a common source of data leaks.

What it does

  • VPC domains have no public endpoint; reach them through the VPC, VPN or a proxy.
  • Fine-grained access control maps IAM or internal users to roles for index, document and field level security.
  • Enable node-to-node encryption, encryption at rest with KMS, enforce HTTPS and TLS 1.2 or later.
  • Sign requests with SigV4 for IAM access.

Domain policy

jsondomain-policy.json
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [{
    "Effect": "Allow",
    "Principal": {"AWS": "arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/search-app"},
    "Action": "es:ESHttp*",
    "Resource": "arn:aws:es:eu-west-1:111122223333:domain/logs/*"
  }]
}
Check yourself
Why prefer a VPC domain?

It has no public endpoint, reducing exposure.

39.5

Index lifecycle and snapshots

In plain words

Use Index State Management policies to roll over, move, and delete indexes on a schedule. Snapshots protect against loss.

The problem it solves

Time-series indexes grow forever and a failed cluster can lose data.

What it does

  • Rollover by size or age; transition to UltraWarm; delete after retention.
  • Automated hourly snapshots are kept by the service for a limited time; for long-term backups register a manual snapshot repository in S3.
  • Rebuild from the source of truth when possible; snapshots speed recovery.
  • Use index templates so every new index gets the right mappings and settings.

ISM policy

jsonism-policy.json
{
  "policy": {
    "description": "hot to delete",
    "default_state": "hot",
    "states": [
      {"name": "hot", "actions": [{"rollover": {"min_size": "50gb", "min_index_age": "1d"}}],
       "transitions": [{"state_name": "delete", "conditions": {"min_index_age": "30d"}}]},
      {"name": "delete", "actions": [{"delete": {}}], "transitions": []}
    ]
  }
}
39.6

OpenSearch Serverless and operations

In plain words

OpenSearch Serverless removes node and shard management: you create a collection and pay for compute (OCUs) and storage.

The problem it solves

Capacity planning and cluster upgrades consume time for teams with variable search needs.

What it does

  • Collection types: search, time series, vector search.
  • Security through encryption, network and data access policies instead of node roles.
  • Billed in OpenSearch Compute Units with a minimum; for small steady workloads a managed domain can be cheaper. Check the current minimums and price.
  • For managed domains monitor ClusterStatus.red, FreeStorageSpace, JVMMemoryPressure, CPUUtilization.
Pick
OptionManaged domain
Choose whensteady load and you need tuning control
Avoid whennobody can size and patch clusters
OptionServerless
Choose whenvariable load and a small team
Avoid whenyou need features not yet supported there

Alarm

resource "aws_cloudwatch_metric_alarm" "red" {
  alarm_name          = "opensearch-red"
  namespace           = "AWS/ES"
  metric_name         = "ClusterStatus.red"
  statistic           = "Maximum"
  period              = 60
  evaluation_periods  = 1
  threshold           = 1
  comparison_operator = "GreaterThanOrEqualToThreshold"
}

Section 40 of 93

RDS high availability and replicas

6 concepts · about 50 minutes

Amazon RDS runs MySQL, PostgreSQL, MariaDB, Oracle, SQL Server and Db2 as a managed service. AWS patches the host, takes backups and replaces failed hardware; you still own schema, queries, sizing and the recovery plan.

Goals
  • Choose between Single-AZ, Multi-AZ instance and Multi-AZ DB cluster deployments
  • Use read replicas for scale and cross-Region copies and know what they do not protect
  • Tune engines safely with parameter groups and subnet groups
40.1

What RDS manages and what you still own

In plain words

RDS gives you a database endpoint without giving you the operating system. You choose the engine, version, instance class and storage; AWS runs the host, the install, backups and failover automation.

The problem it solves

Running your own database on EC2 means you patch the OS, script backups, build replication and rehearse failover. Most teams do this badly under pressure.

What it does

  • RDS handles provisioning, minor-version patching in a maintenance window, automated backups, monitoring hooks and Multi-AZ failover.
  • You cannot SSH to the host. You tune through parameter groups and observe with CloudWatch, Enhanced Monitoring and Performance Insights.
  • You remain responsible for schema design, indexes, connection handling in the app, security groups, encryption choices and tested restores.
  • RDS Custom (Oracle, SQL Server) is a variant that allows OS access when a packaged application demands it.

Create a small instance

bashCreate a PostgreSQL instance
aws rds create-db-instance \
  --db-instance-identifier shop-db \
  --engine postgres --engine-version 16.4 \
  --db-instance-class db.m6g.large \
  --allocated-storage 100 --storage-type gp3 \
  --master-username shopadmin --manage-master-user-password \
  --db-subnet-group-name shop-private \
  --vpc-security-group-ids sg-0123456789abcdef0 \
  --multi-az --storage-encrypted \
  --backup-retention-period 7 \
  --no-publicly-accessible
aws rds describe-db-instances --db-instance-identifier shop-db \
  --query 'DBInstances[0].[DBInstanceStatus,Endpoint.Address]'
Tip

--manage-master-user-password makes RDS keep the master password in Secrets Manager and rotate it, so no password ever appears in your shell history or Terraform state. Check the engine versions currently offered with aws rds describe-db-engine-versions.

Check yourself
Which part of the database can you not reach on RDS?

The operating system of the host; you use parameter groups and the service APIs instead.

40.2

Multi-AZ instance deployment

In plain words

RDS keeps a second, hidden copy of your database in another Availability Zone. Every write is copied to it synchronously. If the primary fails, RDS points the same DNS name at the copy.

The problem it solves

A single instance dies with its host or its AZ. You want an automatic recovery with no data loss and no application change.

What it does

  • The standby is not readable; it exists only for failover and for taking backups without load on the primary.
  • Storage is replicated synchronously at the storage level (or via engine mirroring for SQL Server), so committed data is not lost.
  • Failover is triggered by host failure, AZ outage, instance class change, patching or a manual reboot with failover. It usually takes one to two minutes because DNS changes and the engine must recover.
  • Clients keep the same endpoint; they must reconnect, so use short DNS caching and retry logic.

Operate failover

bashTest a failover on a non-production instance
aws rds reboot-db-instance --db-instance-identifier shop-db --force-failover
aws rds describe-events --source-type db-instance --source-identifier shop-db --duration 30
Careful

The standby costs the same as the primary, so Multi-AZ doubles instance cost. It protects against infrastructure failure, not against a bad DELETE; that needs backups and PITR.

Check yourself
Can you send read queries to the standby of a Multi-AZ instance?

No. Use a read replica or a Multi-AZ DB cluster for readable standbys.

40.3

Multi-AZ DB cluster deployment

In plain words

A newer RDS layout for MySQL and PostgreSQL with one writer and two readable standbys in three AZs. Commits are acknowledged when at least one standby has the data.

The problem it solves

The classic Multi-AZ standby sits idle and failover is slow. Teams wanted readable standbys and faster recovery without moving to Aurora.

What it does

  • One writer instance and two reader instances in different AZs, each with local storage; replication is semi-synchronous.
  • A cluster endpoint always points to the writer, a reader endpoint load-balances across readers.
  • Failover is typically much faster than the instance model (the RDS user guide says typically under 35 seconds; it depends on replica lag, so check the guide for your engine).
  • Write latency is lower than the instance model because storage is local NVMe-backed on supported classes.
Which Multi-AZ shape
OptionMulti-AZ instance
Choose whenany engine, simple HA, cost matters
Avoid whenyou need to read from the standby
OptionMulti-AZ DB cluster
Choose whenMySQL or PostgreSQL with read scaling and quick failover
Avoid whenyou need Oracle or SQL Server
OptionAurora
Choose whenstorage-level replication, up to 15 readers, fastest failover
Avoid whenyou need an engine Aurora does not offer

Create a cluster

bashMulti-AZ DB cluster
aws rds create-db-cluster \
  --db-cluster-identifier shop-cluster \
  --engine postgres --engine-version 16.4 \
  --db-cluster-instance-class db.m6gd.large \
  --storage-type io1 --allocated-storage 100 --iops 3000 \
  --master-username shopadmin --manage-master-user-password \
  --db-subnet-group-name shop-private
40.4

Read replicas

In plain words

A read replica is another database instance that continuously receives changes from a source instance asynchronously. You send reporting and read-heavy queries to it.

The problem it solves

One primary cannot serve all reads and writes, and analytics queries slow down the transactional workload.

What it does

  • Replication is asynchronous, so replicas can lag. Always watch the ReplicaLag CloudWatch metric.
  • MySQL, MariaDB and PostgreSQL support up to 15 replicas per source (check the current quota); replicas can live in another Region.
  • A replica can be promoted to a standalone database, which is the basis of a manual cross-Region DR plan.
  • Replicas can be Multi-AZ themselves and can use a different instance class.
  • A read replica is not a backup: a destructive statement on the primary replicates too.

Create and promote

bashReplica lifecycle
aws rds create-db-instance-read-replica \
  --db-instance-identifier shop-db-ro1 \
  --source-db-instance-identifier shop-db \
  --db-instance-class db.m6g.large
aws cloudwatch get-metric-statistics --namespace AWS/RDS --metric-name ReplicaLag \
  --dimensions Name=DBInstanceIdentifier,Value=shop-db-ro1 \
  --start-time "$(date -u -v-30M +%FT%TZ)" --end-time "$(date -u +%FT%TZ)" \
  --period 60 --statistics Maximum
aws rds promote-read-replica --db-instance-identifier shop-db-ro1
Careful

Promotion breaks replication permanently. Plan how applications and DNS move to the promoted database before you need it.

Check yourself
Why is a read replica not a substitute for backups?

Replication is continuous, so a bad write or drop is copied to the replica within seconds.

40.5

Parameter groups and option groups

In plain words

A parameter group is a named set of engine settings such as max_connections or innodb_buffer_pool_size. You attach it to an instance because you cannot edit config files on the host.

The problem it solves

Default engine settings are generic. Production needs tuned memory, logging and connection limits that are repeatable across environments.

What it does

  • Default parameter groups are read-only. Create a custom group, modify it, and attach it.
  • Parameters are dynamic (applied immediately) or static (applied at reboot). The instance shows pending-reboot until you reboot.
  • Aurora has two levels: a DB cluster parameter group for cluster-wide settings and a DB parameter group per instance.
  • Many values use formulas such as {DBInstanceClassMemory/32768}, so they scale with the class.
  • Option groups add engine features (Oracle, SQL Server, MySQL plugins) and are separate from parameters.

Create and attach

bashCustom PostgreSQL parameters
aws rds create-db-parameter-group --db-parameter-group-name shop-pg16 \
  --db-parameter-group-family postgres16 --description "Shop tuning"
aws rds modify-db-parameter-group --db-parameter-group-name shop-pg16 --parameters \
  "ParameterName=log_min_duration_statement,ParameterValue=500,ApplyMethod=immediate" \
  "ParameterName=shared_preload_libraries,ParameterValue=pg_stat_statements,ApplyMethod=pending-reboot"
aws rds modify-db-instance --db-instance-identifier shop-db \
  --db-parameter-group-name shop-pg16 --apply-immediately
aws rds describe-db-instances --db-instance-identifier shop-db \
  --query 'DBInstances[0].DBParameterGroups'
hclThe same in Terraform
resource "aws_db_parameter_group" "shop" {
  name   = "shop-pg16"
  family = "postgres16"

  parameter {
    name  = "log_min_duration_statement"
    value = "500"
  }
  parameter {
    name         = "shared_preload_libraries"
    value        = "pg_stat_statements"
    apply_method = "pending-reboot"
  }
}
Check yourself
What does a status of pending-reboot mean?

A static parameter was changed and takes effect only after the instance reboots.

40.6

Subnet groups, security groups and encryption

In plain words

A DB subnet group tells RDS which private subnets (at least two AZs) it may place instances in. Security groups decide who can connect. Encryption at rest uses KMS and is chosen when you create the database.

The problem it solves

A database reachable from the internet or stored unencrypted fails every audit and widens the blast radius of any mistake.

What it does

  • Put RDS in private subnets and set PubliclyAccessible=false.
  • Allow port 5432 or 3306 only from the application security group, not from CIDR ranges.
  • Encryption at rest cannot be turned on later in place; you copy an unencrypted snapshot to an encrypted one and restore. Replicas and snapshots inherit it.
  • Force TLS with rds.force_ssl=1 (PostgreSQL) or require_secure_transport=ON (MySQL) in the parameter group.

Terraform

hclSubnet group and security group
resource "aws_db_subnet_group" "shop" {
  name       = "shop-private"
  subnet_ids = var.private_subnet_ids
}

resource "aws_security_group" "db" {
  name   = "shop-db"
  vpc_id = var.vpc_id
}

resource "aws_vpc_security_group_ingress_rule" "from_app" {
  security_group_id            = aws_security_group.db.id
  referenced_security_group_id = var.app_sg_id
  ip_protocol                  = "tcp"
  from_port                    = 5432
  to_port                      = 5432
}
Check yourself
How do you encrypt an existing unencrypted RDS database?

Copy a snapshot with a KMS key, then restore a new instance from the encrypted copy and cut over.

Section 41 of 93

RDS backups, PITR, upgrades and RDS Proxy

6 concepts · about 50 minutes

Failover protects you from hardware. Backups protect you from people, bugs and bad deployments. This section covers the recovery tools and the operational features around them.

Goals
  • Configure automated backups and restore to a point in time
  • Manage snapshots across accounts and Regions
  • Upgrade engines with low downtime and pool connections with RDS Proxy
41.1

Automated backups and retention

In plain words

RDS takes a daily storage snapshot during your backup window and continuously uploads transaction logs to S3. Together they allow recovery to any second in the retention period.

The problem it solves

You need recovery without scripting dumps, and without stopping writes while the backup runs.

What it does

  • Retention is 0 to 35 days; 0 disables automated backups (and also disables replicas for some engines). Default is 7 for console creations.
  • The backup is a storage-level snapshot, so there is a brief I/O pause on Single-AZ; on Multi-AZ instances it is taken from the standby.
  • Automated backups are deleted with the instance unless you choose to retain them, so take a final snapshot.
  • Backups live in RDS-managed S3; you cannot browse them, only restore from them.

Settings

bashSet retention and window
aws rds modify-db-instance --db-instance-identifier shop-db \
  --backup-retention-period 14 \
  --preferred-backup-window 02:00-03:00 \
  --copy-tags-to-snapshot --apply-immediately
aws rds describe-db-instance-automated-backups \
  --db-instance-identifier shop-db \
  --query 'DBInstanceAutomatedBackups[].[Status,RestoreWindow]'
Check yourself
What happens to automated backups when you delete the instance?

They are removed after deletion unless you retain them; take a final or manual snapshot first.

41.2

Point-in-time recovery

In plain words

PITR rebuilds your database as it was at a chosen second. It always creates a new instance; it never rewinds the existing one.

The problem it solves

Someone ran an UPDATE without a WHERE clause at 14:07. You need the data as of 14:06 without losing everything since last night.

What it does

  • LatestRestorableTime is usually within the last five minutes.
  • The restored instance has a new endpoint, default parameter and security groups unless you specify them, and cold caches.
  • Standard recovery pattern is restore beside production, copy back the affected rows or switch the application, then delete the extra instance.
  • Restore time depends on the size of the logs to replay, so rehearse and record it for your RTO.

Restore

bashPITR to a new instance
aws rds restore-db-instance-to-point-in-time \
  --source-db-instance-identifier shop-db \
  --target-db-instance-identifier shop-db-restore \
  --restore-time 2026-10-30T08:36:00Z \
  --db-subnet-group-name shop-private \
  --vpc-security-group-ids sg-0123456789abcdef0
aws rds wait db-instance-available --db-instance-identifier shop-db-restore
Danger

A restore does not copy tags, option settings or IAM database authentication in every case; verify the restored instance's security settings before you connect applications to it.

Check yourself
Does PITR overwrite the original instance?

No, it creates a new instance with a new endpoint.

41.3

Manual snapshots, copies and sharing

In plain words

A manual snapshot is a backup you create and keep until you delete it. You can copy it to another Region or share it with another account.

The problem it solves

Automated backups expire and stay in one Region. DR and account-isolation strategies need copies elsewhere that you control.

What it does

  • Take snapshots before risky changes, major upgrades or deletions.
  • copy-db-snapshot --source-region makes a cross-Region copy; encrypted snapshots need a KMS key in the destination Region.
  • Share to another account with modify-db-snapshot-attribute; snapshots encrypted with the default AWS-managed key cannot be shared, use a customer managed key and grant the other account access.
  • AWS Backup can schedule and copy RDS and Aurora snapshots centrally with vault lock for immutability.

Commands

bashSnapshot, copy, share
aws rds create-db-snapshot --db-instance-identifier shop-db --db-snapshot-identifier shop-pre-upgrade
aws rds copy-db-snapshot --region eu-west-1 \
  --source-region us-east-1 \
  --source-db-snapshot-identifier arn:aws:rds:us-east-1:111122223333:snapshot:shop-pre-upgrade \
  --target-db-snapshot-identifier shop-pre-upgrade-eu \
  --kms-key-id alias/shop-eu
aws rds modify-db-snapshot-attribute --db-snapshot-identifier shop-pre-upgrade \
  --attribute-name restore --values-to-add 444455556666
Check yourself
Why can a snapshot encrypted with the default aws/rds key not be shared?

The AWS-managed key policy cannot be edited to grant another account; use a customer managed key.

41.4

Maintenance, minor upgrades and blue/green deployments

In plain words

RDS patches in a weekly maintenance window. For major upgrades or risky changes, a blue/green deployment builds a synchronized copy (green), lets you change and test it, and then switches over.

The problem it solves

In-place major upgrades mean an outage you cannot roll back easily.

What it does

  • Enable auto-minor-version-upgrade for minor patches; schedule the window outside peak hours.
  • A blue/green deployment creates a staging environment with logical replication from production. You upgrade or tune green, test, then switch over, usually in under a minute for supported engines.
  • Switchover renames endpoints so the application needs no change; blue remains until you delete it.
  • Major engine upgrades require a compatible parameter group family and extension compatibility; test on a restored copy first.

CLI

bashBlue/green upgrade
aws rds create-blue-green-deployment \
  --blue-green-deployment-name shop-pg17 \
  --source arn:aws:rds:us-east-1:111122223333:db:shop-db \
  --target-engine-version 17.2 \
  --target-db-parameter-group-name shop-pg17
aws rds switchover-blue-green-deployment \
  --blue-green-deployment-identifier bgd-0123456789abcdef \
  --switchover-timeout 300
Tip

Always take a manual snapshot first and check the current list of engines and versions that support blue/green in the RDS documentation.

Check yourself
How does blue/green avoid application changes?

Switchover swaps the endpoint names so the same hostnames point at the new environment.

41.5

RDS Proxy

In plain words

RDS Proxy is a managed connection pool that sits between your application and the database. Applications connect to the proxy; the proxy keeps a small set of warm connections to the database.

The problem it solves

Hundreds of pods or Lambda functions each opening connections exhaust max_connections, and every failover forces slow reconnect storms.

What it does

  • Multiplexing: many client connections share fewer database connections between transactions.
  • Pinning happens when session state (temporary tables, SET statements, prepared statements on some engines) ties a client to one connection, which reduces pooling. Watch the DatabaseConnectionsCurrentlyBorrowed and pinning metrics.
  • During failover the proxy holds client connections and reconnects to the new writer, cutting visible failover time.
  • Credentials come from Secrets Manager; clients may authenticate to the proxy with IAM.
  • The proxy endpoint is reachable only from inside the VPC. Aurora also gets optional read-only endpoints.

Create with Terraform

hclRDS Proxy for the shop database
resource "aws_db_proxy" "shop" {
  name                   = "shop-proxy"
  engine_family          = "POSTGRESQL"
  role_arn               = aws_iam_role.proxy.arn
  vpc_subnet_ids         = var.private_subnet_ids
  vpc_security_group_ids = [aws_security_group.proxy.id]
  require_tls            = true
  idle_client_timeout    = 1800

  auth {
    auth_scheme = "SECRETS"
    iam_auth    = "REQUIRED"
    secret_arn  = aws_secretsmanager_secret.db.arn
  }
}

resource "aws_db_proxy_default_target_group" "shop" {
  db_proxy_name = aws_db_proxy.shop.name
  connection_pool_config {
    max_connections_percent      = 80
    max_idle_connections_percent = 40
  }
}

resource "aws_db_proxy_target" "shop" {
  db_proxy_name          = aws_db_proxy.shop.name
  target_group_name      = aws_db_proxy_default_target_group.shop.name
  db_instance_identifier = aws_db_instance.shop.identifier
}
Note

RDS Proxy has an hourly cost per vCPU of the database. Use it when connection counts or failover time hurt, not by default.

Check yourself
What is connection pinning?

A client is locked to one database connection because of session state, so the proxy cannot share that connection with others.

41.6

Monitoring RDS

In plain words

Three layers show database health: CloudWatch metrics from the hypervisor, Enhanced Monitoring from an OS agent, and Performance Insights which shows which SQL consumes time.

The problem it solves

"The database is slow" is not actionable. You need to tell CPU saturation from lock waits, storage IOPS limits and bad queries.

What it does

  • CloudWatch: CPUUtilization, FreeableMemory, DatabaseConnections, ReadIOPS/WriteIOPS, DiskQueueDepth, FreeStorageSpace, ReplicaLag.
  • Enhanced Monitoring (1 to 60 second granularity) shows per-process OS metrics.
  • Performance Insights reports DB Load in average active sessions by wait event, SQL, user and host.
  • Export engine logs (error, slow query, postgresql) to CloudWatch Logs with --cloudwatch-logs-export-configuration.
  • Enable storage autoscaling (--max-allocated-storage) to avoid running out of space.

Alarm on storage and CPU

bashFree storage alarm
aws cloudwatch put-metric-alarm --alarm-name shop-db-low-storage \
  --namespace AWS/RDS --metric-name FreeStorageSpace \
  --dimensions Name=DBInstanceIdentifier,Value=shop-db \
  --statistic Minimum --period 300 --evaluation-periods 3 \
  --threshold 10737418240 --comparison-operator LessThanThreshold \
  --alarm-actions arn:aws:sns:us-east-1:111122223333:ops-alerts
Check yourself
What does DB Load in Performance Insights measure?

The average number of active sessions, broken down by wait event, SQL statement, user or host.

Section 42 of 93

Aurora architecture, storage and failover

6 concepts · about 45 minutes

Aurora is AWS's cloud-built MySQL and PostgreSQL compatible engine. The big difference from RDS is not the SQL layer but the storage layer, which changes how replicas, backups and failover behave.

Goals
  • Explain how Aurora separates compute from a shared distributed storage volume
  • Use cluster, reader and custom endpoints correctly
  • Predict failover behaviour and tune it with priorities and RDS Proxy
42.1

Aurora compared with RDS

In plain words

In RDS each instance owns its own EBS volume. In Aurora, all instances in a cluster share one distributed storage volume that spans three AZs. Instances only do compute.

The problem it solves

Classic replication copies data to every replica's own disk, so replicas lag, storage is paid per copy, and promoting a replica takes time.

What it does

  • Compute instances (one writer, up to 15 readers) read and write the same volume.
  • Storage grows automatically in 10 GiB steps up to the documented maximum (check the current quota).
  • Replica lag is typically milliseconds because readers read the shared volume, not a stream of redo.
  • Aurora only replicates redo log records to storage, which cuts write amplification.

Create a cluster

bashAurora PostgreSQL cluster with a writer
aws rds create-db-cluster --db-cluster-identifier shop-aurora \
  --engine aurora-postgresql --engine-version 16.4 \
  --master-username shopadmin --manage-master-user-password \
  --db-subnet-group-name shop-private --storage-encrypted \
  --backup-retention-period 14 --vpc-security-group-ids sg-0123456789abcdef0
aws rds create-db-instance --db-cluster-identifier shop-aurora \
  --db-instance-identifier shop-aurora-1 --engine aurora-postgresql \
  --db-instance-class db.r6g.large
Check yourself
Why is Aurora replica lag small?

Readers read the same shared storage volume instead of applying a replicated log to their own disks.

42.2

Quorum storage and self-healing

In plain words

Every 10 GiB chunk of data is stored six times, two in each of three AZs. A write succeeds when four of six copies confirm; a read needs three.

The problem it solves

Losing a disk or a whole AZ must not lose data or block writes, and repairs must not need a human.

What it does

  • Losing a whole AZ removes two copies, leaving four, so writes (which need four) continue.
  • Reads survive an AZ plus one more copy lost.
  • A failed segment is rebuilt in the background from healthy copies because segments are small, so repair is quick.
  • Backups are continuous to S3 and do not impact the writer; restores create a new cluster.

Observe

bashCluster members and volume use
aws rds describe-db-clusters --db-cluster-identifier shop-aurora \
  --query 'DBClusters[0].DBClusterMembers[].[DBInstanceIdentifier,IsClusterWriter,PromotionTier]'
aws cloudwatch get-metric-statistics --namespace AWS/RDS --metric-name VolumeBytesUsed \
  --dimensions Name=DBClusterIdentifier,Value=shop-aurora \
  --start-time "$(date -u -v-1H +%FT%TZ)" --end-time "$(date -u +%FT%TZ)" \
  --period 300 --statistics Maximum
Check yourself
How many copies of data does Aurora keep and in how many AZs?

Six copies across three AZs.

42.3

Endpoints

In plain words

An Aurora cluster publishes several DNS names. Use the right one so writes reach the writer and reads spread over readers.

The problem it solves

After failover the writer moves to a different instance. Hard-coded instance names break; stable names do not.

What it does

  • Cluster endpoint always points to the current writer. Use it for writes.
  • Reader endpoint load-balances connections across readers (per connection, not per query), so a long-lived pool can become uneven.
  • Custom endpoints group chosen instances, for example big readers for analytics.
  • Instance endpoints point to one instance; use only for diagnostics.

Custom endpoint

bashAnalytics endpoint on selected readers
aws rds create-db-cluster-endpoint --db-cluster-identifier shop-aurora \
  --db-cluster-endpoint-identifier analytics --endpoint-type READER \
  --static-members shop-aurora-3 shop-aurora-4
Tip

JDBC and psycopg pools cache DNS. Set a low DNS TTL in the JVM (networkaddress.cache.ttl) so the pool follows the writer after failover.

Check yourself
Should an application connect to an instance endpoint for writes?

No; the writer role moves on failover, so use the cluster endpoint.

42.4

Failover mechanics

In plain words

If the writer fails, Aurora promotes a reader to be the new writer. No data copy is needed because storage is shared, so it is much faster than RDS.

The problem it solves

Database downtime during an AZ failure directly costs revenue, and slow DNS or pool behaviour can extend it.

What it does

  • Promotion order follows promotion tier (0 to 15, lowest first); within a tier the largest instance wins, then arbitrary.
  • With at least one reader, service is typically restored in less than 60 seconds, and often in less than 30 seconds (AWS Aurora user guide, high availability page). Treat 60 seconds as the planning figure. With no reader, Aurora creates a new instance, which takes longer.
  • The cluster endpoint DNS is updated; applications must reconnect.
  • Aurora PostgreSQL supports cluster cache management, keeping the buffer cache of a priority-0 replica warm.

Practise

bashPlanned failover test
aws rds failover-db-cluster --db-cluster-identifier shop-aurora
aws rds describe-events --source-type db-cluster --source-identifier shop-aurora --duration 15
aws rds modify-db-instance --db-instance-identifier shop-aurora-2 --promotion-tier 0
Check yourself
Which reader is promoted first?

The one with the lowest promotion tier; ties go to the largest instance.

42.5

Aurora features worth knowing

In plain words

Aurora adds operations features that RDS lacks: fast cloning, backtrack (MySQL), parallel query, and the I/O-Optimized storage configuration.

The problem it solves

Creating a test copy of a 2 TB database or undoing a bad deploy should take minutes, not hours.

What it does

  • Cloning uses copy-on-write; a clone is created in minutes and only diverging pages are paid for. Great for test data and migration rehearsals.
  • Backtrack (Aurora MySQL) rewinds the same cluster to a time in place; not available for PostgreSQL.
  • Storage configurations: Standard (pay per I/O) or I/O-Optimized (no per-I/O charge, higher instance and storage price). Compare using Cost Explorer once I/O is above roughly a quarter of your Aurora spend; check current pricing.
  • Data API and aws_s3 import/export extend integration options.

Clone

bashClone via point in time
aws rds restore-db-cluster-to-point-in-time --db-cluster-identifier shop-aurora-clone \
  --source-db-cluster-identifier shop-aurora --restore-type copy-on-write \
  --use-latest-restorable-time
aws rds create-db-instance --db-cluster-identifier shop-aurora-clone \
  --db-instance-identifier shop-aurora-clone-1 --engine aurora-postgresql \
  --db-instance-class db.r6g.large
Check yourself
What does a clone cost initially?

Almost nothing for storage; you pay for changed pages and the clone's instances.

42.6

Aurora with RDS Proxy and connection strategy

In plain words

Aurora failover is fast, but clients are not. Pools must detect the change, reconnect and retry.

The problem it solves

Applications that keep dead TCP connections open turn a failover of under a minute into minutes of errors.

What it does

  • Use RDS Proxy to hold connections while the writer changes.
  • Set connection validation, tcpKeepAlive and short max connection lifetime in the pool.
  • Retry idempotent operations with backoff; transactions in flight at failover are lost and must be retried.
  • The AWS Advanced JDBC Wrapper understands Aurora topology and fails over faster than DNS alone.

Pool settings (HikariCP example)

yamlapplication.yaml
spring:
  datasource:
    url: jdbc:postgresql://shop-aurora.cluster-abc123.us-east-1.rds.amazonaws.com:5432/shop
    hikari:
      maximum-pool-size: 20
      max-lifetime: 600000
      connection-timeout: 5000
      keepalive-time: 60000
Check yourself
Why set a max connection lifetime?

So pooled connections are recycled and eventually follow DNS to the new writer after failover.

← PreviousNext →
Section 43 of 93

Aurora Global Database and Serverless v2

5 concepts · about 45 minutes

Two Aurora features change architecture: Global Database for multi-Region reach and Serverless v2 for elastic compute.

Goals
  • Design a cross-Region Aurora topology and perform switchover or failover
  • Size Aurora Serverless v2 with ACU ranges
  • Pick between provisioned and Serverless v2 on cost and behaviour
43.1

Global Database

In plain words

A Global Database is one primary Aurora cluster in one Region and up to several read-only secondary clusters in other Regions. Storage-level replication copies changes between them.

The problem it solves

Users on another continent need low-latency reads, and a regional outage needs a recovery path measured in a minute, not hours of snapshot restores.

What it does

  • Replication is physical at the storage layer, usually under one second lag, with no impact on writer performance.
  • Secondary clusters serve reads locally; writes can be forwarded to the primary with write forwarding (at higher latency).
  • Typical RPO is seconds and RTO about a minute for unplanned failover (check current AWS figures).
  • Each secondary has its own compute instances, parameter groups and KMS key.

Create

bashAdd a Region to an existing cluster
aws rds create-global-cluster --global-cluster-identifier shop-global \
  --source-db-cluster-identifier arn:aws:rds:us-east-1:111122223333:cluster:shop-aurora \
  --region us-east-1
aws rds create-db-cluster --global-cluster-identifier shop-global \
  --db-cluster-identifier shop-aurora-eu --engine aurora-postgresql \
  --engine-version 16.4 --kms-key-id alias/shop-eu --region eu-west-1 \
  --db-subnet-group-name shop-private-eu
Check yourself
How does Global Database replicate?

At the storage layer, not through the database engine, so the writer is not slowed.

43.2

Switchover versus failover

In plain words

Planned switchover moves the primary role without data loss. Unplanned failover promotes a secondary after an outage and may lose a few seconds of writes.

The problem it solves

You need one operation for maintenance and Region evacuation and another for disasters, and you must know their data guarantees.

What it does

  • Switchover (managed planned) waits for the secondary to catch up, swaps roles and keeps replication; RPO zero.
  • Failover (--allow-data-loss) detaches and promotes the chosen secondary; the old primary must be rebuilt as a secondary later.
  • Applications need a Region-aware endpoint. Use Route 53 failover records or the global writer endpoint for the write path.
  • Rehearse in a game day; record the time from decision to first successful write.

Commands

bashSwitchover and failover
aws rds switchover-global-cluster --global-cluster-identifier shop-global \
  --target-db-cluster-identifier arn:aws:rds:eu-west-1:111122223333:cluster:shop-aurora-eu
aws rds failover-global-cluster --global-cluster-identifier shop-global \
  --target-db-cluster-identifier arn:aws:rds:eu-west-1:111122223333:cluster:shop-aurora-eu \
  --allow-data-loss
Careful

Check AuroraGlobalDBReplicationLag before choosing failover; it tells you roughly how much data may be lost.

Check yourself
What distinguishes switchover from failover?

Switchover is planned with no data loss; failover is for outages and may lose the unreplicated tail.

43.3

Serverless v2 capacity model

In plain words

Serverless v2 instances scale their CPU and memory continuously between a minimum and maximum number of Aurora Capacity Units (ACUs). One ACU is about 2 GiB of memory with matching CPU and networking.

The problem it solves

Provisioned instances are sized for peak and idle the rest of the time; spiky and dev workloads waste money.

What it does

  • You set MinCapacity and MaxCapacity on the cluster, for example 0.5 to 16 ACU. Scaling is in fine steps, within seconds, without dropping connections.
  • Readers and writers can be Serverless v2 or provisioned in the same cluster.
  • Newer versions can scale to zero ACUs and auto-pause (check availability for your engine version).
  • You are billed per ACU-hour used. The minimum sets the floor and the buffer cache size.

Configure

bashSet the ACU range and add a serverless instance
aws rds modify-db-cluster --db-cluster-identifier shop-aurora \
  --serverless-v2-scaling-configuration MinCapacity=0.5,MaxCapacity=16
aws rds create-db-instance --db-cluster-identifier shop-aurora \
  --db-instance-identifier shop-aurora-sv2 --engine aurora-postgresql \
  --db-instance-class db.serverless
hclTerraform
resource "aws_rds_cluster" "shop" {
  cluster_identifier = "shop-aurora"
  engine             = "aurora-postgresql"
  engine_mode        = "provisioned"
  database_name      = "shop"
  master_username    = "shopadmin"
  manage_master_user_password = true

  serverlessv2_scaling_configuration {
    min_capacity = 0.5
    max_capacity = 16
  }
}

resource "aws_rds_cluster_instance" "shop" {
  cluster_identifier = aws_rds_cluster.shop.id
  instance_class     = "db.serverless"
  engine             = aws_rds_cluster.shop.engine
}
Check yourself
What does the minimum ACU influence besides cost?

The buffer cache size and how quickly the database can absorb a sudden burst.

43.4

Choosing capacity and avoiding surprises

In plain words

Serverless v2 is flexible, but a badly chosen range gives either high bills or throttled performance.

The problem it solves

A maximum that is too low causes slow queries; a minimum that is too high removes savings; max_connections is derived from the maximum ACU.

What it does

  • Watch ServerlessDatabaseCapacity and ACUUtilization in CloudWatch.
  • max_connections depends on the maximum capacity, so a tiny max with many pods causes "too many connections". Use RDS Proxy.
  • Mix a provisioned writer with Serverless v2 readers to absorb read spikes, or the reverse for dev stacks.
  • Compare cost using the AWS Pricing Calculator with your measured average ACU, not the maximum.

Alarm

bashAlarm when the max is almost reached
aws cloudwatch put-metric-alarm --alarm-name shop-acu-high \
  --namespace AWS/RDS --metric-name ACUUtilization \
  --dimensions Name=DBClusterIdentifier,Value=shop-aurora \
  --statistic Average --period 300 --evaluation-periods 3 \
  --threshold 90 --comparison-operator GreaterThanThreshold \
  --alarm-actions arn:aws:sns:us-east-1:111122223333:ops-alerts
Check yourself
Why can Serverless v2 produce "too many connections" at a low maximum?

The default connection limit scales with the maximum ACU setting.

43.5

Choosing between RDS, Aurora and the rest

In plain words

Pick the database by access pattern, scale and cost, not by habit.

The problem it solves

Using Aurora where plain RDS suffices doubles cost; using RDS where you need multi-Region or many readers hits a wall.

What it does

  • RDS PostgreSQL or MySQL Multi-AZ: simple, cheaper, any version lag acceptable.
  • Aurora: more readers, fast failover, Global Database, cloning, large storage.
  • Aurora Serverless v2: variable load and many small environments.
  • DynamoDB: key-value and document access at any scale with single-digit millisecond latency.
  • ElastiCache: caching and session data, never the system of record.
Pick a datastore
OptionRDS Multi-AZ
Choose whena standard relational app of moderate size
Avoid whenyou need more than five readers or multi-Region writes
OptionAurora provisioned
Choose whensteady heavy OLTP with many readers
Avoid whenthe workload is tiny and cost-sensitive
OptionAurora Serverless v2
Choose whenspiky, unpredictable, or many dev databases
Avoid whenconstant 24/7 high load where reservations win
OptionDynamoDB
Choose whenkey-based access, huge scale, no joins
Avoid whenyou need ad hoc SQL analytics

Section 44 of 93

DynamoDB and ElastiCache

5 concepts · about 45 minutes

Not everything belongs in a relational database. DynamoDB and ElastiCache cover key-value storage and caching and are common neighbours of EKS workloads.

Goals
  • Model DynamoDB tables with partition and sort keys and choose a capacity mode
  • Use indexes, TTL, streams and global tables appropriately
  • Deploy ElastiCache for Redis or Valkey with replication and failover
44.1

DynamoDB tables and keys

In plain words

DynamoDB is a fully managed key-value and document database. Each item is found by its partition key, and optionally a sort key that orders items sharing the same partition key.

The problem it solves

Relational databases are hard to scale horizontally. DynamoDB gives predictable single-digit millisecond reads and writes at nearly any size if you design around access patterns.

What it does

  • The partition key is hashed to place data across partitions; a poor key (for example a date) makes a hot partition.
  • Query by exact partition key plus an optional sort-key condition. A Scan reads everything and should be avoided.
  • Items are up to 400 KB (check the quota); attributes are schemaless except keys.
  • Design from the questions your application asks, and often put several entity types in one table.

Create and use

bashCreate a table and query it
aws dynamodb create-table --table-name shop-orders \
  --attribute-definitions AttributeName=customer_id,AttributeType=S AttributeName=order_date,AttributeType=S \
  --key-schema AttributeName=customer_id,KeyType=HASH AttributeName=order_date,KeyType=RANGE \
  --billing-mode PAY_PER_REQUEST
aws dynamodb put-item --table-name shop-orders \
  --item '{"customer_id":{"S":"C1"},"order_date":{"S":"2026-10-12"},"total":{"N":"75"}}'
aws dynamodb query --table-name shop-orders \
  --key-condition-expression "customer_id = :c AND order_date >= :d" \
  --expression-attribute-values '{":c":{"S":"C1"},":d":{"S":"2026-10-01"}}'
Check yourself
Why avoid Scan?

It reads every item, consuming capacity proportional to the table size.

44.2

Capacity modes and throttling

In plain words

You pay for reads and writes in one of two modes: on-demand (per request) or provisioned (capacity units per second, optionally with auto scaling).

The problem it solves

Underprovisioned tables throttle with ProvisionedThroughputExceededException; overprovisioned ones waste money.

What it does

  • On-demand needs no planning and handles spikes; per-request price is higher.
  • Provisioned with autoscaling is cheaper for predictable traffic; reserved capacity discounts exist.
  • One RCU is one strongly consistent read per second of up to 4 KB; one WCU is one write of up to 1 KB per second. Eventually consistent reads cost half.
  • Use exponential backoff and jitter; AWS SDKs retry by default.
  • The Standard-IA table class lowers storage cost for rarely read data.

Switch mode

bashProvisioned with autoscaling target
aws dynamodb update-table --table-name shop-orders --billing-mode PROVISIONED \
  --provisioned-throughput ReadCapacityUnits=50,WriteCapacityUnits=25
aws application-autoscaling register-scalable-target --service-namespace dynamodb \
  --resource-id table/shop-orders --scalable-dimension dynamodb:table:ReadCapacityUnits \
  --min-capacity 50 --max-capacity 500
Check yourself
How much does an eventually consistent 4 KB read cost compared with strongly consistent?

Half of one read capacity unit.

44.3

Indexes, TTL and streams

In plain words

Secondary indexes give alternative query keys. TTL deletes expired items for free. Streams emit a change record for each write.

The problem it solves

A key design serves one access pattern; other queries need alternative keys, and applications need to react to changes or expire data without cron jobs.

What it does

  • Global secondary index (GSI): different partition and sort key, its own capacity, eventually consistent.
  • Local secondary index (LSI): same partition key, alternative sort key; must be created with the table.
  • TTL: an attribute holding a Unix epoch time; DynamoDB deletes items some time after expiry (usually within days, so filter in queries).
  • Streams feed Lambda or Kinesis for events, search sync and audit.
  • PITR continuous backups restore to any second in the last 35 days; enable it on every important table.

Enable features

bashTTL, PITR and a GSI
aws dynamodb update-time-to-live --table-name shop-orders \
  --time-to-live-specification Enabled=true,AttributeName=expires_at
aws dynamodb update-continuous-backups --table-name shop-orders \
  --point-in-time-recovery-specification PointInTimeRecoveryEnabled=true
Tip

Choose a GSI key with high cardinality; a status field with three values creates a hot partition.

Check yourself
Can you add an LSI to an existing table?

No; LSIs must be defined at table creation.

44.4

Global tables and access from EKS

In plain words

A global table replicates a DynamoDB table across Regions with multi-writer semantics. Pods access DynamoDB through IAM roles.

The problem it solves

Multi-Region active-active applications need local low-latency writes, and pods must reach the table without static credentials.

What it does

  • Global tables (version 2019.11.21) replicate asynchronously, usually within a second; conflicts resolve last writer wins by timestamp.
  • Use a VPC gateway endpoint for DynamoDB so traffic stays on the AWS network and avoids NAT charges.
  • Grant the pod an IAM role via IRSA or Pod Identity with least privilege on the table ARN.

Least privilege policy

jsonPod role policy for shop-orders
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": ["dynamodb:GetItem", "dynamodb:PutItem", "dynamodb:Query", "dynamodb:UpdateItem"],
      "Resource": [
        "arn:aws:dynamodb:us-east-1:111122223333:table/shop-orders",
        "arn:aws:dynamodb:us-east-1:111122223333:table/shop-orders/index/*"
      ]
    }
  ]
}
bashGateway endpoint to avoid NAT cost
aws ec2 create-vpc-endpoint --vpc-id vpc-0abc --service-name com.amazonaws.us-east-1.dynamodb \
  --route-table-ids rtb-0111 rtb-0222
Check yourself
How are write conflicts resolved in global tables?

Last writer wins, based on timestamps.

44.5

ElastiCache for Redis and Valkey

In plain words

ElastiCache runs in-memory stores (Valkey, Redis OSS, Memcached) as a managed service. Applications use them to hold hot data and sessions with sub-millisecond reads.

The problem it solves

Repeated database reads for the same product or session data waste capacity and add latency.

What it does

  • A replication group has one primary and up to five replicas across AZs; with Multi-AZ and automatic failover, a replica is promoted on failure.
  • Cluster mode enabled shards data over several node groups for more memory and throughput.
  • Use TLS in transit (--transit-encryption-enabled), at-rest encryption and AUTH or IAM authentication.
  • Eviction policy (maxmemory-policy, often allkeys-lru) decides what happens when memory fills.
  • Cache is not the system of record: design for cold starts and use TTLs.
  • ElastiCache Serverless removes node sizing; you pay for data stored and compute used (check current pricing).

Create

hclValkey replication group with Multi-AZ
resource "aws_elasticache_replication_group" "shop" {
  replication_group_id       = "shop-cache"
  description                = "Shop sessions and catalog cache"
  engine                     = "valkey"
  node_type                  = "cache.r7g.large"
  num_cache_clusters         = 3
  automatic_failover_enabled = true
  multi_az_enabled           = true
  at_rest_encryption_enabled = true
  transit_encryption_enabled = true
  subnet_group_name          = aws_elasticache_subnet_group.shop.name
  security_group_ids         = [aws_security_group.cache.id]
  parameter_group_name       = "default.valkey7"
}
Check yourself
What happens to the data if the cache cluster is lost?

Nothing authoritative is lost, since the database is the source of truth; the cache is rebuilt on demand.

Section 45 of 93

EKS control plane and cluster creation

6 concepts · about 45 minutes

Amazon EKS is managed Kubernetes. AWS runs the API server and etcd; you run the nodes and everything on them. If you operate Kyma, you already know the Kubernetes layer; this section shows what is specific to AWS.

Goals
  • Describe what AWS runs in the EKS control plane and what you run
  • Create a cluster with eksctl and Terraform
  • Control endpoint access and enable control plane logging
45.1

What EKS manages

In plain words

EKS runs the Kubernetes control plane (API servers, etcd, controller manager, scheduler) in an AWS-managed account, spread over multiple AZs. You pay a fixed hourly fee per cluster and manage worker capacity separately.

The problem it solves

Running a highly available etcd and API server yourself means certificates, backups, upgrades and 3 AM incidents.

What it does

  • The API server runs as at least two instances across AZs behind a load balancer; etcd runs across three AZs. AWS scales and patches them.
  • Worker nodes join through ENIs that EKS places in your subnets (the cross-account ENIs), which carry kubelet-to-API traffic.
  • You choose the Kubernetes minor version; each version has a standard support period, then paid extended support (check the current EKS version calendar).
  • Provisioned control plane tiers can raise API capacity for very large clusters (check current offerings).

See it

bashDescribe a cluster
aws eks describe-cluster --name shop-prod \
  --query 'cluster.{version:version,endpoint:endpoint,private:resourcesVpcConfig.endpointPrivateAccess,public:resourcesVpcConfig.endpointPublicAccess,platform:platformVersion}'
aws eks update-kubeconfig --name shop-prod --alias shop-prod
kubectl get nodes -o wide
Check yourself
Where do you find etcd on an EKS cluster?

You do not; it runs in the AWS managed account and is not accessible to you.

45.2

Creating a cluster with eksctl

In plain words

eksctl reads a YAML file and creates the cluster, its IAM roles, node groups and optional VPC through CloudFormation.

The problem it solves

A cluster needs a VPC with tagged subnets, IAM roles, security groups, an OIDC provider and node groups. Doing it by hand through the console is slow and not repeatable.

What it does

  • Config files are declarative: eksctl create cluster -f cluster.yaml.
  • It can reuse an existing VPC (vpc.subnets) or create a new one with public and private subnets across AZs.
  • It creates the OIDC provider (iam.withOIDC) required for IRSA.
  • Prefer a Terraform or CloudFormation pipeline for long-lived environments, and eksctl for labs and quick starts.

Cluster file

yamlcluster.yaml
apiVersion: eksctl.io/v1alpha5
kind: ClusterConfig
metadata:
  name: shop-prod
  region: us-east-1
  version: "1.37"
iam:
  withOIDC: true
vpc:
  cidr: 10.20.0.0/16
  nat:
    gateway: HighlyAvailable
availabilityZones: ["us-east-1a", "us-east-1b", "us-east-1c"]
managedNodeGroups:
  - name: system
    instanceType: m6i.large
    minSize: 2
    maxSize: 4
    desiredCapacity: 2
    privateNetworking: true
    labels: {role: system}
cloudWatch:
  clusterLogging:
    enableTypes: ["api", "audit", "authenticator"]
bashCreate and check
eksctl create cluster -f cluster.yaml
eksctl get cluster --region us-east-1
Tip

Pick the Kubernetes version from eksctl version support or aws eks describe-cluster-versions; versions in examples age quickly.

Check yourself
Why does the config enable OIDC?

IRSA needs an IAM OIDC identity provider for the cluster so pods can assume roles.

45.3

Creating a cluster with Terraform

In plain words

The community module terraform-aws-modules/eks/aws creates the cluster, IAM, security groups and node groups from variables.

The problem it solves

Cluster creation must live in version control, be reviewed, and be reproducible for each environment.

What it does

  • The module takes vpc_id, subnet_ids (private subnets for nodes) and control_plane_subnet_ids.
  • Access entries and add-ons are modelled as inputs so the whole platform stays declarative.
  • State holds the cluster; protect it in an S3 bucket with locking.

Module call

hclmain.tf
module "eks" {
  source  = "terraform-aws-modules/eks/aws"
  version = "~> 20.0"

  cluster_name    = "shop-prod"
  cluster_version = "1.37"
  vpc_id          = module.vpc.vpc_id
  subnet_ids      = module.vpc.private_subnets

  cluster_endpoint_public_access  = false
  cluster_endpoint_private_access = true
  enable_irsa                     = true

  cluster_enabled_log_types = ["api", "audit", "authenticator"]

  eks_managed_node_groups = {
    system = {
      instance_types = ["m6i.large"]
      min_size       = 2
      max_size       = 4
      desired_size   = 2
    }
  }
}
Check yourself
Which subnets should nodes use?

Private subnets, with egress through NAT gateways or VPC endpoints.

45.4

API endpoint access

In plain words

The Kubernetes API endpoint can be public, private or both. Private means it resolves to the ENIs in your VPC and is reachable only from the VPC or connected networks.

The problem it solves

A public API endpoint exposed to 0.0.0.0/0 is attack surface. But a fully private one is unreachable from CI runners and laptops unless you plan connectivity.

What it does

  • Public only (default for new clusters): reachable from the internet, restrict with publicAccessCidrs.
  • Public and private: nodes use the private path; admins use the public path from allowed CIDRs.
  • Private only: reach it via VPN, Direct Connect, a bastion, or SSM port forwarding.
  • Authentication still uses IAM; authorisation uses Kubernetes RBAC or access entries.

Restrict it

bashLock down the endpoint
aws eks update-cluster-config --name shop-prod \
  --resources-vpc-config endpointPublicAccess=true,publicAccessCidrs=203.0.113.0/24,endpointPrivateAccess=true
aws eks wait cluster-active --name shop-prod
Check yourself
Do nodes need the public endpoint to join?

No; with private access enabled they reach the API through the VPC.

45.5

Control plane logging and audit

In plain words

EKS can send five log types to CloudWatch Logs: api, audit, authenticator, controllerManager and scheduler.

The problem it solves

When someone deletes a deployment or a role mapping breaks authentication, you need evidence of who did what.

What it does

  • Logs go to /aws/eks/<cluster>/cluster. They cost ingestion and storage, so set retention.
  • audit records every API call with user and verb; authenticator shows IAM identity mapping failures.
  • Query them with CloudWatch Logs Insights.

Enable and query

bashEnable audit logs and set retention
aws eks update-cluster-config --name shop-prod \
  --logging '{"clusterLogging":[{"types":["api","audit","authenticator"],"enabled":true}]}'
aws logs put-retention-policy --log-group-name /aws/eks/shop-prod/cluster --retention-in-days 30
aws logs start-query --log-group-name /aws/eks/shop-prod/cluster \
  --start-time $(date -u -v-1H +%s) --end-time $(date -u +%s) \
  --query-string 'fields @timestamp, user.username, verb, objectRef.resource, objectRef.name | filter verb = "delete" | sort @timestamp desc | limit 20'
Check yourself
Which log type helps debug IAM identity to Kubernetes user mapping?

The authenticator log.

45.6

Cluster tags, networking requirements and sizing

In plain words

EKS and its controllers find subnets through tags, and the cluster needs enough free IP addresses.

The problem it solves

Missing subnet tags make load balancers fail to place, and small subnets run out of IPs when pods get VPC addresses.

What it does

  • Tag public subnets kubernetes.io/role/elb=1 and private subnets kubernetes.io/role/internal-elb=1.
  • Karpenter and the AWS Load Balancer Controller also use karpenter.sh/discovery or kubernetes.io/cluster/<name> tags.
  • Because pods use VPC IPs, size subnets generously (for example /19 or larger for nodes) or add a secondary CIDR for pods.
  • Use at least two AZs, preferably three, with one NAT gateway per AZ for production.

Tag with CLI

bashTag a private subnet
aws ec2 create-tags --resources subnet-0aaa subnet-0bbb subnet-0ccc \
  --tags Key=kubernetes.io/role/internal-elb,Value=1 Key=karpenter.sh/discovery,Value=shop-prod
Check yourself
What happens if subnets lack the elb tags?

The Load Balancer Controller cannot auto-discover subnets and provisioning fails unless you list subnets explicitly.
