Section 46 of 93

EKS compute with node groups and Fargate

5 concepts · about 45 minutes

Pods run on worker capacity. EKS offers three ways to supply it, and most real clusters use more than one.

Goals
  • Create managed node groups with the right AMI type and update strategy
  • Use Fargate profiles where serverless pods fit
  • Choose between node group, Fargate and Karpenter
46.1

Managed node groups

In plain words

A managed node group is an Auto Scaling group of EC2 instances that EKS creates, registers and upgrades for you. Nodes are normal EC2 instances in your account.

The problem it solves

Self-managed nodes need AMI selection, bootstrap scripts, drain logic during upgrades and node-to-cluster auth wiring.

What it does

  • Choose instance types, min, max and desired size, subnets, labels and taints.
  • EKS handles join, health and a rolling update that cordons and drains nodes, honoring PodDisruptionBudgets.
  • Capacity type can be ON_DEMAND or SPOT.
  • Use launch templates for custom user data, disk size or security groups.
  • Cluster Autoscaler can scale the group; Karpenter replaces that approach.

Create one

basheksctl managed node group
eksctl create nodegroup --cluster shop-prod --name general \
  --node-type m6i.xlarge --nodes 3 --nodes-min 3 --nodes-max 9 \
  --node-private-networking --managed
hclTerraform node group with taint
resource "aws_eks_node_group" "batch" {
  cluster_name    = aws_eks_cluster.this.name
  node_group_name = "batch"
  node_role_arn   = aws_iam_role.node.arn
  subnet_ids      = var.private_subnet_ids
  capacity_type   = "SPOT"
  instance_types  = ["m6i.large", "m5.large", "m6a.large"]

  scaling_config {
    desired_size = 2
    min_size     = 0
    max_size     = 10
  }

  taint {
    key    = "workload"
    value  = "batch"
    effect = "NO_SCHEDULE"
  }
}
Check yourself
Who creates the EC2 instances of a managed group?

EKS, through an Auto Scaling group in your account.

46.2

Node AMIs and operating systems

In plain words

EKS provides optimized AMIs: Amazon Linux 2023, Bottlerocket (a minimal container OS), Windows, and GPU/accelerated variants.

The problem it solves

General Linux images carry packages you do not need and require patching; node OS patching is a security routine.

What it does

  • AL2023 is the current default Amazon Linux for new nodes (AL2 is end of life, check the support date).
  • Bottlerocket: read-only root file system, API-driven updates, smaller attack surface.
  • Nodes are replaced, not patched: update the AMI version and roll the group.
  • Access nodes with SSM Session Manager instead of SSH keys.

Find the recommended AMI

bashLatest recommended AMI id from SSM
aws ssm get-parameter --name /aws/service/eks/optimized-ami/1.37/amazon-linux-2023/x86_64/standard/recommended/image_id \
  --query Parameter.Value --output text
Check yourself
Why use SSM Session Manager for node access?

It needs no inbound ports or SSH keys and logs sessions through IAM and CloudTrail.

46.3

Updating node groups

In plain words

Updating a group replaces its nodes with new ones using a newer AMI or Kubernetes version, one batch at a time.

The problem it solves

A node upgrade must not drop traffic. Draining evicts pods, so the cluster needs enough spare capacity and sane budgets.

What it does

  • maxUnavailable (count or percent) in updateConfig controls the batch size.
  • Pods with a PodDisruptionBudget that cannot be satisfied block the drain; the update fails after a timeout unless forced.
  • Order: control plane first, then add-ons, then nodes. Nodes may lag the control plane by a limited number of minor versions (check the version skew policy).

Command

bashRolling update
aws eks update-nodegroup-version --cluster-name shop-prod --nodegroup-name general
aws eks update-nodegroup-config --cluster-name shop-prod --nodegroup-name general \
  --update-config maxUnavailablePercentage=33
aws eks wait nodegroup-active --cluster-name shop-prod --nodegroup-name general
Careful

After Gardener- or controller-driven maintenance, verify no node stays cordoned: kubectl get nodes should not show SchedulingDisabled.

Check yourself
What stops a drain from completing?

A PodDisruptionBudget that cannot be satisfied, or pods without a controller to recreate them.

46.4

Fargate

In plain words

Fargate runs each pod in its own small, AWS-managed micro VM. There are no nodes for you to patch or scale.

The problem it solves

Small teams or bursty jobs may not want node management at all, and some compliance cases want per-pod isolation.

What it does

  • A Fargate profile selects pods by namespace and labels; matching pods go to Fargate automatically.
  • Each pod gets its own ENI and IP in private subnets; billing is per vCPU and memory requested, rounded up to supported sizes.
  • Limits: no DaemonSets, no privileged pods, no hostPath or hostNetwork, no GPUs, EBS volumes unsupported (EFS works). Check current limits.
  • Pods start slower than on warm nodes.
  • Logging is via the built-in Fluent Bit router configured with a ConfigMap aws-logging in aws-observability.

Profile

bashCreate a profile
eksctl create fargateprofile --cluster shop-prod --name batch \
  --namespace batch --labels tier=serverless
Check yourself
Can a DaemonSet run on Fargate?

No; each pod has its own micro VM and DaemonSets are not supported.

46.5

Choosing compute

In plain words

Match compute to the workload, and keep a small stable system node group even if you use Karpenter.

The problem it solves

Using one compute type for everything either wastes money or blocks features.

What it does

  • Run controllers such as Karpenter itself on a managed node group or Fargate, so they never depend on the capacity they create.
  • Use Karpenter or Spot groups for stateless scalable workloads.
  • Use dedicated groups with taints for GPU, high memory or licensed software.
Compute choice
OptionManaged node group
Choose whenstable baseline, system add-ons, predictable pools
Avoid whenyou want per-pod right sizing and fast scale
OptionKarpenter
Choose whenvariable workloads and cost optimisation
Avoid whenyou need only a handful of fixed nodes
OptionFargate
Choose whenisolated jobs, no node ops
Avoid whenyou need DaemonSets, GPUs or EBS
OptionSpot
Choose whenstateless, interruption tolerant
Avoid whendatabases and single replicas

Section 47 of 93

EKS networking with the VPC CNI

5 concepts · about 50 minutes

EKS uses the Amazon VPC CNI plugin. Pods get real VPC IP addresses, which makes networking fast and simple to reason about but ties pod count to ENI limits and subnet size.

Goals
  • Explain how pods receive VPC IP addresses and what limits pod density
  • Enable prefix delegation and custom networking when IPs run short
  • Apply security groups for pods and network policies
47.1

How the VPC CNI assigns IPs

In plain words

Each node has one or more ENIs. Each ENI has secondary private IPs. The CNI daemon (aws-node) hands one of those IPs to every pod on the node.

The problem it solves

Overlay networks add encapsulation and hide pod identity from VPC tools. Using native VPC IPs lets security groups, flow logs and routing treat pods like instances.

What it does

  • Pods on the same node and across nodes communicate with no overlay; the VPC routes pod IPs.
  • The IP warm pool keeps spare IPs ready (WARM_IP_TARGET, WARM_ENI_TARGET, MINIMUM_IP_TARGET).
  • Max pods per node depends on instance type: ENIs x (IPs per ENI - 1) + 2. Use the AWS max-pods-calculator.sh for exact values.
  • Subnets must have enough free IPs; every pod consumes one.

Check settings

bashInspect the CNI
kubectl -n kube-system get ds aws-node -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.containers[0].env}' | tr ',' '\n' | grep -E 'WARM|PREFIX|MINIMUM' || true
kubectl get pods -A -o wide | awk '{print $8}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head
kubectl -n kube-system logs ds/aws-node -c aws-node --tail=20
Check yourself
Why can a pod fail with "failed to assign an IP address"?

The subnet or the node's ENI limits have no free IPs left.

47.2

Prefix delegation

In plain words

Instead of assigning single IPs to an ENI, EKS assigns /28 prefixes (16 addresses each), multiplying how many pods a node can run.

The problem it solves

Small instance types hit pod limits (a t3.medium supports only 17 pods) long before CPU or memory runs out.

What it does

  • Set ENABLE_PREFIX_DELEGATION=true on the aws-node DaemonSet; requires Nitro instances.
  • Max pods rises (the recommended cap is 110 for instances under 30 vCPUs and 250 above, check current guidance).
  • Prefixes need contiguous /28 blocks; fragmented subnets may fail. Use subnet CIDR reservations to reserve prefix space.
  • New nodes must set --max-pods accordingly; managed node groups and Karpenter compute this with the right setting.

Enable

bashTurn on prefix mode
kubectl set env ds/aws-node -n kube-system ENABLE_PREFIX_DELEGATION=true WARM_PREFIX_TARGET=1
aws eks update-addon --cluster-name shop-prod --addon-name vpc-cni \
  --configuration-values '{"env":{"ENABLE_PREFIX_DELEGATION":"true","WARM_PREFIX_TARGET":"1"}}'
Note

Existing nodes keep their old limits. Replace nodes after the change.

Check yourself
What does a /28 prefix provide?

16 IPv4 addresses for pods on one ENI slot.

47.3

Custom networking and IPv6

In plain words

When the main subnets are exhausted, custom networking places pod ENIs in a secondary CIDR (like 100.64.0.0/16). IPv6 clusters avoid the problem entirely.

The problem it solves

Corporate VPC ranges are often small. Running out of IPs blocks scaling although nodes have capacity.

What it does

  • Add a secondary CIDR to the VPC and create subnets per AZ.
  • Define an ENIConfig per AZ and set AWS_VPC_K8S_CNI_CUSTOM_NETWORK_CFG=true, ENI_CONFIG_LABEL_DEF=topology.kubernetes.io/zone.
  • With custom networking the primary ENI is not used for pods, which lowers pod capacity per node; combine with prefix delegation.
  • IPv6 clusters give every pod a unique IPv6 address and avoid exhaustion; outbound IPv4 goes through NAT64/egress-only gateways. Choose at cluster creation; it cannot be changed later.

ENIConfig

yamlENIConfig for us-east-1a
apiVersion: crd.k8s.amazonaws.com/v1alpha1
kind: ENIConfig
metadata:
  name: us-east-1a
spec:
  subnet: subnet-0aaa1111bbb22222c
  securityGroups:
    - sg-0123456789abcdef0
Check yourself
Can an existing IPv4 cluster be converted to IPv6?

No; the IP family is fixed at creation.

47.4

Security groups for pods

In plain words

Normally all pods on a node share the node's security group. This feature lets a pod have its own security group through a dedicated branch ENI.

The problem it solves

Database security groups allow the node group's SG, which means every pod on those nodes can reach the database.

What it does

  • Enable ENABLE_POD_ENI=true on aws-node; supported Nitro instance types provide trunk ENIs.
  • Create a SecurityGroupPolicy that selects pods by label or service account and lists security group IDs.
  • The database SG then allows only the pod SG, giving pod-level segmentation without Kubernetes network policy.
  • Pods with SGs consume trunk/branch ENI capacity and start slower; set POD_SECURITY_GROUP_ENFORCING_MODE per your needs.

Policy

yamlSecurityGroupPolicy
apiVersion: vpcresources.k8s.aws/v1beta1
kind: SecurityGroupPolicy
metadata:
  name: orders-sg
  namespace: shop
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: orders
  securityGroups:
    groupIds:
      - sg-0aaa1111bbb22222c
bashEnable the feature
kubectl set env daemonset aws-node -n kube-system ENABLE_POD_ENI=true
kubectl -n kube-system rollout status ds/aws-node
Check yourself
What problem does SecurityGroupPolicy solve?

It lets individual pods carry their own security group instead of sharing the node's.

47.5

Network policy and service networking

In plain words

The VPC CNI can enforce Kubernetes NetworkPolicy using eBPF on supported versions. Service traffic goes through kube-proxy (iptables or IPVS).

The problem it solves

By default every pod can reach every other pod. In multi-team clusters you need default-deny with explicit allows.

What it does

  • Enable with enableNetworkPolicy: "true" in the VPC CNI add-on configuration (check the minimum version).
  • Start with a default-deny policy per namespace, then allow ingress from known namespaces and egress to DNS and the database.
  • Network policy covers pod to pod; it does not control egress to arbitrary AWS APIs by name. Use SGs or a firewall for that.
  • Alternatively use Cilium as the CNI in chaining mode (support and operation differ, review AWS guidance).

Policy

yamlDeny all, allow from the ingress namespace
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: default-deny
  namespace: shop
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes: ["Ingress"]
---
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-ingress-ns
  namespace: shop
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web
  policyTypes: ["Ingress"]
  ingress:
    - from:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels:
              kubernetes.io/metadata.name: ingress
      ports:
        - port: 8080
Check yourself
What is the first policy to apply in a namespace?

A default-deny policy, followed by explicit allows.

Section 48 of 93

EKS identity and access

7 concepts · about 55 minutes

Two separate questions: who may call the Kubernetes API (people, CI, nodes) and which AWS permissions do pods get. EKS answers the first with access entries and the second with IRSA or Pod Identity.

Goals
  • Grant humans and pipelines cluster access with access entries instead of aws-auth
  • Give pods AWS permissions with IRSA or EKS Pod Identity
  • Choose between IRSA and Pod Identity and troubleshoot both
48.1

How authentication reaches Kubernetes

In plain words

kubectl on EKS signs a request with your IAM credentials (aws eks get-token). The EKS authenticator checks the signature, finds which Kubernetes identity your IAM principal maps to, and Kubernetes RBAC then decides what you can do.

The problem it solves

Kubernetes has no user database. EKS must bridge IAM identities (roles, users, SSO sessions) to Kubernetes users and groups safely.

What it does

  • Authentication: IAM. Authorisation: Kubernetes RBAC (or an EKS access policy that maps to it).
  • The kubeconfig from aws eks update-kubeconfig uses an exec credential plugin calling aws eks get-token.
  • IAM Identity Center roles appear as IAM roles named AWSReservedSSO_<permission-set>_<hash>.
  • Tokens are short-lived (about 15 minutes) and are renewed automatically.

Inspect your identity

bashWho am I
aws sts get-caller-identity
aws eks get-token --cluster-name shop-prod --query status.expirationTimestamp
kubectl auth whoami
kubectl auth can-i --list --namespace shop | head
Check yourself
Where do Kubernetes users come from on EKS?

From IAM principals mapped through access entries or aws-auth; Kubernetes itself has no user store.

48.2

Access entries

In plain words

An access entry is an EKS API object that maps an IAM principal to Kubernetes permissions. Predefined access policies such as AmazonEKSClusterAdminPolicy or AmazonEKSViewPolicy can be scoped to namespaces.

The problem it solves

The older aws-auth ConfigMap was easy to break: a YAML typo could lock out every administrator, and editing it required Kubernetes access to begin with.

What it does

  • Manage entries with the AWS API, CLI, Terraform or CloudFormation, with IAM-level audit in CloudTrail.
  • Authentication mode on the cluster: CONFIG_MAP, API_AND_CONFIG_MAP, or API. New clusters should use API.
  • Attach EKS access policies (AmazonEKSAdminPolicy, AmazonEKSEditPolicy, AmazonEKSViewPolicy, AmazonEKSClusterAdminPolicy) or map the principal to your own RBAC groups with --kubernetes-groups.
  • The cluster creator no longer receives a hidden admin; set bootstrapClusterCreatorAdminPermissions deliberately.

Create entries

bashAdmin and namespace-scoped access
aws eks update-cluster-config --name shop-prod \
  --access-config authenticationMode=API
aws eks create-access-entry --cluster-name shop-prod \
  --principal-arn arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/PlatformAdmin
aws eks associate-access-policy --cluster-name shop-prod \
  --principal-arn arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/PlatformAdmin \
  --policy-arn arn:aws:eks::aws:cluster-access-policy/AmazonEKSClusterAdminPolicy \
  --access-scope type=cluster
aws eks associate-access-policy --cluster-name shop-prod \
  --principal-arn arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/ShopDev \
  --policy-arn arn:aws:eks::aws:cluster-access-policy/AmazonEKSEditPolicy \
  --access-scope type=namespace,namespaces=shop
hclTerraform
resource "aws_eks_access_entry" "dev" {
  cluster_name  = aws_eks_cluster.this.name
  principal_arn = aws_iam_role.shop_dev.arn
}

resource "aws_eks_access_policy_association" "dev" {
  cluster_name  = aws_eks_cluster.this.name
  principal_arn = aws_iam_role.shop_dev.arn
  policy_arn    = "arn:aws:eks::aws:cluster-access-policy/AmazonEKSEditPolicy"

  access_scope {
    type       = "namespace"
    namespaces = ["shop"]
  }
}
Careful

Switching to API mode is one way: you cannot return to CONFIG_MAP. Create entries for every role in aws-auth first (including node roles if you use self-managed nodes).

Check yourself
Which authentication mode is recommended for new clusters?

API, which uses access entries only.

48.3

The aws-auth ConfigMap (legacy)

In plain words

aws-auth in kube-system listed mapRoles and mapUsers entries. It still exists on older clusters and you will meet it while migrating.

The problem it solves

You need to read and migrate it without locking yourself out.

What it does

  • mapRoles maps role ARNs to usernames and groups (for example system:masters).
  • Nodes in self-managed groups needed a system:nodes entry; managed node groups add it automatically.
  • Migration: set mode API_AND_CONFIG_MAP, create equivalent access entries, test, then switch to API.
  • Never edit it live without a backup: kubectl get cm aws-auth -n kube-system -o yaml > aws-auth.bak.

Example

yamlaws-auth ConfigMap (legacy format)
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: aws-auth
  namespace: kube-system
data:
  mapRoles: |
    - rolearn: arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/PlatformAdmin
      username: platform-admin
      groups:
        - system:masters
Check yourself
Why migrate away from aws-auth?

It is error-prone, needs Kubernetes access to edit, and a typo can lock everyone out; access entries are API managed and audited.

48.4

IRSA, IAM Roles for Service Accounts

In plain words

IRSA lets a Kubernetes service account assume an IAM role. The cluster's OIDC issuer signs a projected token; AWS STS trusts that issuer and swaps the token for temporary credentials.

The problem it solves

Giving the node role all permissions means every pod gets them. Static access keys in secrets leak and never rotate.

What it does

  • Requires an IAM OIDC provider for the cluster issuer URL.
  • The role trust policy conditions on the service account: system:serviceaccount:<namespace>:<name> in the sub claim, and sts.amazonaws.com in aud.
  • The service account is annotated with eks.amazonaws.com/role-arn; a mutating webhook injects AWS_ROLE_ARN and AWS_WEB_IDENTITY_TOKEN_FILE into pods.
  • AWS SDKs use the credential chain automatically.

Trust policy and service account

jsonTrust policy for the orders role
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Principal": {
        "Federated": "arn:aws:iam::111122223333:oidc-provider/oidc.eks.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/id/EXAMPLED539D4633E53DE1B71EXAMPLE"
      },
      "Action": "sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity",
      "Condition": {
        "StringEquals": {
          "oidc.eks.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/id/EXAMPLED539D4633E53DE1B71EXAMPLE:sub": "system:serviceaccount:shop:orders",
          "oidc.eks.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/id/EXAMPLED539D4633E53DE1B71EXAMPLE:aud": "sts.amazonaws.com"
        }
      }
    }
  ]
}
yamlServiceAccount
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: orders
  namespace: shop
  annotations:
    eks.amazonaws.com/role-arn: arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/shop-orders
bashCreate it with eksctl
eksctl create iamserviceaccount --cluster shop-prod --namespace shop --name orders \
  --attach-policy-arn arn:aws:iam::111122223333:policy/shop-orders-ddb --approve
Danger

A trust policy without the sub condition lets any service account in the cluster assume the role. Always scope it to namespace and name.

Check yourself
Which claim restricts a role to one service account?

The token `sub` claim, formatted `system:serviceaccount:<ns>:<name>`.

48.5

EKS Pod Identity

In plain words

Pod Identity is the newer, simpler mechanism. An agent on each node serves credentials to pods; you link a role to a service account with an EKS API call, not an OIDC trust policy per cluster.

The problem it solves

IRSA needs an OIDC provider per cluster, a trust policy that embeds the issuer URL, and rewrites when you rebuild a cluster. It also hits IAM OIDC provider quotas across many clusters.

What it does

  • Install the EKS Pod Identity Agent add-on (a DaemonSet).
  • The role trusts the service principal pods.eks.amazonaws.com with actions sts:AssumeRole and sts:TagSession; the same role works for any cluster.
  • Create an association: cluster, namespace, service account, role. No annotation on the service account.
  • Session tags (cluster, namespace, service account) enable ABAC policies.
  • Not available on Fargate or for the cluster's own controllers that require IRSA in some add-ons; check the current support list. Cross-account use works by role chaining.

Set it up

jsonTrust policy for Pod Identity
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Principal": {"Service": "pods.eks.amazonaws.com"},
      "Action": ["sts:AssumeRole", "sts:TagSession"]
    }
  ]
}
bashAgent and association
aws eks create-addon --cluster-name shop-prod --addon-name eks-pod-identity-agent
aws eks create-pod-identity-association --cluster-name shop-prod \
  --namespace shop --service-account orders \
  --role-arn arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/shop-orders
aws eks list-pod-identity-associations --cluster-name shop-prod
Check yourself
What is the trust principal for Pod Identity roles?

The service principal pods.eks.amazonaws.com.

48.6

IRSA versus Pod Identity and troubleshooting

In plain words

Both give pods temporary role credentials. Prefer Pod Identity on new EC2-based clusters, keep IRSA where Pod Identity is not supported (Fargate, some add-ons, other clusters).

The problem it solves

Teams mix both and then cannot tell why a pod gets AccessDenied or uses the node role.

What it does

  • IRSA works on EC2, Fargate and non-EKS clusters via OIDC. Pod Identity works on EC2 nodes only.
  • SDK too old? Credentials fall back to the node role (IMDS). Update the SDK and set hop limit 1 on IMDS so pods cannot use it.
  • Debug checklist: service account name and namespace, annotation or association, trust policy, token mounted, role permissions, permission boundaries, SCPs.
  • Use aws sts get-caller-identity inside the pod to see the effective role.
Which to use
OptionPod Identity
Choose whennew EC2 or Karpenter based clusters, many clusters
Avoid whenthe workload runs on Fargate
OptionIRSA
Choose whenFargate, or a component that documents IRSA only
Avoid whenyou want to avoid per-cluster OIDC trust

Debug in the pod

bashEffective identity
kubectl -n shop exec deploy/orders -- env | grep -E 'AWS_(ROLE|WEB|CONTAINER)'
kubectl -n shop exec deploy/orders -- aws sts get-caller-identity
kubectl -n shop get sa orders -o yaml | grep role-arn
Tip

Block pods from the node's instance profile: launch templates with HttpPutResponseHopLimit=1 and HttpTokens=required for IMDSv2.

Check yourself
How can a pod accidentally use the node role?

By falling back to IMDS when the SDK does not find IRSA or Pod Identity credentials.

48.7

Kubernetes RBAC on top of IAM

In plain words

Access entries map principals to groups; RBAC binds those groups to Roles and ClusterRoles. Keep roles narrow and namespaced.

The problem it solves

Giving system:masters to everyone makes audit logs meaningless and increases blast radius.

What it does

  • Use ClusterRole for reusable rules and RoleBinding to apply them per namespace.
  • Bind to groups, not individual users, so offboarding is an IAM change.
  • Avoid wildcards on verbs and resources; separate read-only, deploy and admin duties.
  • Combine with admission controls (Pod Security Admission, Kyverno or Gatekeeper) to restrict what workloads can do.

Bind a group

yamlRole and binding for the shop-devs group
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata:
  name: deployer
  namespace: shop
rules:
  - apiGroups: ["apps"]
    resources: ["deployments"]
    verbs: ["get", "list", "watch", "patch"]
  - apiGroups: [""]
    resources: ["pods", "pods/log"]
    verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
  name: deployer-shop-devs
  namespace: shop
subjects:
  - kind: Group
    name: shop-devs
    apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
roleRef:
  kind: Role
  name: deployer
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
bashCreate the entry with the group
aws eks create-access-entry --cluster-name shop-prod \
  --principal-arn arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/ShopDev \
  --kubernetes-groups shop-devs
Check yourself
Why bind roles to groups?

Membership then follows the IAM role, so removing access is one change in IAM.

Section 49 of 93

EKS add-ons CoreDNS, kube-proxy and storage CSI

6 concepts · about 50 minutes

A bare EKS cluster needs networking, DNS and storage components before it is useful. EKS manages them as add-ons so AWS tests versions against each Kubernetes release.

Goals
  • Manage EKS add-ons with versions and configuration values
  • Tune CoreDNS and understand kube-proxy modes
  • Provision persistent storage with the EBS and EFS CSI drivers
49.1

What EKS add-ons are

In plain words

An add-on is a packaged operational component (VPC CNI, CoreDNS, kube-proxy, EBS CSI, Pod Identity Agent, metrics-server and more) that EKS installs and can update for you.

The problem it solves

Installing these with raw manifests or Helm leaves you to track version compatibility on every cluster upgrade.

What it does

  • Install and upgrade with aws eks create-addon and update-addon; list versions compatible with your Kubernetes version using describe-addon-versions.
  • --configuration-values accepts a JSON or YAML document validated by a schema (describe-addon-configuration).
  • --resolve-conflicts OVERWRITE|PRESERVE decides what happens to fields you changed manually.
  • Self-managed fields can be adopted by importing an existing install.
  • Some add-ons need an IAM role (IRSA or Pod Identity), supplied with --pod-identity-associations or --service-account-role-arn.

Manage

bashAdd-on commands
aws eks describe-addon-versions --kubernetes-version 1.37 --addon-name coredns \
  --query 'addons[0].addonVersions[0:3].[addonVersion,compatibilities[0].defaultVersion]'
aws eks list-addons --cluster-name shop-prod
aws eks describe-addon --cluster-name shop-prod --addon-name vpc-cni \
  --query 'addon.[addonVersion,status]'
aws eks describe-addon-configuration --addon-name coredns --addon-version v1.11.3-eksbuild.2 \
  --query configurationSchema --output text | head -c 600
Check yourself
What does resolve-conflicts PRESERVE do?

It keeps fields you changed manually rather than overwriting them with the add-on defaults.

49.2

CoreDNS

In plain words

CoreDNS answers every in-cluster DNS lookup, such as orders.shop.svc.cluster.local, and forwards other names to the VPC resolver.

The problem it solves

If DNS is slow or overloaded, every service call becomes slow, and "it's always DNS" outages are common.

What it does

  • Runs as a Deployment with two replicas by default; scale with autoscaling configuration or cluster-proportional-autoscaler.
  • Pods use ndots:5, so a name such as api.example.com triggers several failing searches first; use fully qualified names with a trailing dot or lower ndots in dnsConfig for chatty workloads.
  • The VPC resolver (.2 address) has a per-ENI limit of 1024 packets per second; spread CoreDNS across nodes and consider NodeLocal DNSCache.
  • Customise through the Corefile in the coredns ConfigMap or add-on configuration.

Tune

yamlCoreDNS add-on configuration values
replicaCount: 3
resources:
  limits:
    memory: 170Mi
  requests:
    cpu: 100m
    memory: 70Mi
topologySpreadConstraints:
  - maxSkew: 1
    topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
    whenUnsatisfiable: ScheduleAnyway
    labelSelector:
      matchLabels:
        k8s-app: kube-dns
bashApply and test
aws eks update-addon --cluster-name shop-prod --addon-name coredns \
  --configuration-values file://coredns.yaml --resolve-conflicts OVERWRITE
kubectl run dnstest --rm -it --image=busybox:1.36 --restart=Never -- nslookup kubernetes.default
Check yourself
Why does ndots:5 slow external lookups?

Names with fewer than five dots are tried with each search domain first, creating extra failing queries.

49.3

kube-proxy

In plain words

kube-proxy programs each node so that a Service IP reaches one of its pods, using iptables rules or IPVS.

The problem it solves

Pods need stable virtual IPs for services even though pod IPs change constantly.

What it does

  • Default mode is iptables; rule count grows with services and endpoints, which slows updates in very large clusters.
  • ipvs mode scales better with thousands of services (check the current add-on support).
  • Keep kube-proxy's minor version within the supported skew of the control plane and update it during cluster upgrades.
  • Services use externalTrafficPolicy: Local to preserve client IPs and skip an extra hop.

Inspect

bashSee rules and version
kubectl -n kube-system get ds kube-proxy -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.containers[0].image}{"\n"}'
kubectl -n kube-system get cm kube-proxy-config -o jsonpath='{.data.config}' | grep -E 'mode|iptables'
kubectl get svc,endpointslices -n shop
Check yourself
What changes in kube-proxy when a pod is replaced?

The endpoint list changes and rules on every node are updated to the new pod IP.

49.4

EBS CSI driver

In plain words

The EBS CSI driver creates and attaches EBS volumes for PersistentVolumeClaims. In-tree volume plugins are removed, so every cluster needs this add-on for block storage.

The problem it solves

Stateful apps need disks that survive pod restarts and follow the pod to the right AZ.

What it does

  • An EBS volume lives in one AZ; a pod using it can only run in that AZ. Use volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer so the volume is created where the pod lands.
  • The controller needs IAM permissions (AmazonEBSCSIDriverPolicy) through Pod Identity or IRSA, and the KMS key permission if you encrypt with a CMK.
  • Supports gp3 (set IOPS and throughput), io2, expansion of volumes, and VolumeSnapshot.
  • Reclaim policy Delete removes the EBS volume when the PVC goes; use Retain for important data.

StorageClass

yamlgp3 StorageClass
apiVersion: storage.k8s.io/v1
kind: StorageClass
metadata:
  name: gp3
provisioner: ebs.csi.aws.com
volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer
allowVolumeExpansion: true
reclaimPolicy: Delete
parameters:
  type: gp3
  encrypted: "true"
  iops: "3000"
  throughput: "125"
bashInstall the add-on with Pod Identity
aws eks create-addon --cluster-name shop-prod --addon-name aws-ebs-csi-driver \
  --pod-identity-associations serviceAccount=ebs-csi-controller-sa,roleArn=arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/ebs-csi
Check yourself
Why use WaitForFirstConsumer?

The volume is then created in the AZ where the pod is scheduled instead of an arbitrary AZ.

49.5

EFS CSI driver

In plain words

Amazon EFS is a shared NFS file system that works across AZs. The EFS CSI driver mounts it in pods, including on Fargate.

The problem it solves

Several pods in different AZs need the same files (uploads, shared models), which EBS cannot offer.

What it does

  • Supports ReadWriteMany; storage grows automatically; you pay per GB stored and throughput mode.
  • Use access points to give each application its own root directory and POSIX identity.
  • Mount targets must exist in each AZ, with a security group allowing TCP 2049 from the nodes.
  • Dynamic provisioning creates one access point per PVC; encryption in transit is on by default for the mount helper.

StorageClass

yamlEFS StorageClass with access points
apiVersion: storage.k8s.io/v1
kind: StorageClass
metadata:
  name: efs
provisioner: efs.csi.aws.com
parameters:
  provisioningMode: efs-ap
  fileSystemId: fs-0123456789abcdef0
  directoryPerms: "700"
Check yourself
Which volume type supports ReadWriteMany across AZs?

EFS; an EBS volume attaches to one node in one AZ.

49.6

Other useful add-ons

In plain words

A few more add-ons round out a production cluster: metrics-server, the Pod Identity Agent, the CloudWatch Observability add-on, and the CSI snapshot controller.

The problem it solves

Autoscaling, observability and backups depend on components that a new cluster lacks.

What it does

  • metrics-server feeds kubectl top and the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler.
  • amazon-cloudwatch-observability installs the CloudWatch agent and Fluent Bit for Container Insights.
  • snapshot-controller enables VolumeSnapshot for EBS backups.
  • aws-guardduty-agent provides runtime threat detection if you use GuardDuty EKS Runtime Monitoring.
  • Commit add-ons to Terraform so every cluster has an identical baseline.

Terraform

hclAdd-ons in the EKS module
module "eks" {
  source  = "terraform-aws-modules/eks/aws"
  version = "~> 20.0"
  # cluster arguments omitted

  cluster_addons = {
    coredns                = { most_recent = true }
    kube-proxy             = { most_recent = true }
    vpc-cni                = { most_recent = true, before_compute = true }
    eks-pod-identity-agent = { most_recent = true }
    metrics-server         = { most_recent = true }
  }
}
Check yourself
Which add-on provides data for the HPA?

metrics-server.

Section 50 of 93

AWS Load Balancer Controller and ingress

5 concepts · about 50 minutes

Kubernetes asks for a load balancer; on EKS the AWS Load Balancer Controller (LBC) turns that request into a real ALB or NLB. It replaces the legacy in-tree controller.

Goals
  • Install the AWS Load Balancer Controller with the right IAM permissions
  • Expose services with ALB Ingress and NLB Services
  • Use target types, health checks and certificate annotations correctly
50.1

What the controller does

In plain words

The LBC watches Ingress and Service objects. For an Ingress with the alb class it builds an Application Load Balancer; for a Service of type LoadBalancer with the right annotation it builds a Network Load Balancer.

The problem it solves

Without it, Services create old Classic Load Balancers, and there is no native way to get path routing, WAF, or direct-to-pod targets.

What it does

  • Runs as a Deployment in kube-system, with IAM permissions to manage ELB, security groups and target groups.
  • Discovers subnets by tag: kubernetes.io/role/elb for internet-facing, kubernetes.io/role/internal-elb for internal.
  • Registers pods directly (target-type: ip) or nodes via NodePort (instance).
  • Manages security groups and can share one ALB across many Ingress resources through IngressGroup.

Install

bashInstall with Helm
curl -o iam-policy.json https://raw.githubusercontent.com/kubernetes-sigs/aws-load-balancer-controller/main/docs/install/iam_policy.json
aws iam create-policy --policy-name AWSLoadBalancerControllerIAMPolicy --policy-document file://iam-policy.json
eksctl create iamserviceaccount --cluster shop-prod --namespace kube-system \
  --name aws-load-balancer-controller \
  --attach-policy-arn arn:aws:iam::111122223333:policy/AWSLoadBalancerControllerIAMPolicy --approve
helm repo add eks https://aws.github.io/eks-charts && helm repo update
helm install aws-load-balancer-controller eks/aws-load-balancer-controller -n kube-system \
  --set clusterName=shop-prod --set serviceAccount.create=false \
  --set serviceAccount.name=aws-load-balancer-controller
Check yourself
Which subnet tag selects internet-facing load balancer subnets?

kubernetes.io/role/elb=1.

50.2

ALB Ingress

In plain words

An Ingress with ingressClassName: alb creates an ALB with listeners and rules from the Ingress paths and annotations.

The problem it solves

You want one HTTPS entry point with host and path routing, TLS from ACM, and optional WAF, without running your own proxy.

What it does

  • alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/scheme: internet-facing | internal.
  • target-type: ip sends traffic directly to pod IPs, skipping NodePort hops; requires VPC CNI.
  • listen-ports, certificate-arn, ssl-redirect configure HTTPS; ACM supplies and renews the certificate.
  • healthcheck-path, success-codes control target health.
  • wafv2-acl-arn attaches a WAF web ACL.
  • group.name merges several Ingress objects into one ALB to save cost.

Ingress

yamlShop Ingress
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: shop
  namespace: shop
  annotations:
    alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/scheme: internet-facing
    alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/target-type: ip
    alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/listen-ports: '[{"HTTP":80},{"HTTPS":443}]'
    alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/ssl-redirect: "443"
    alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/certificate-arn: arn:aws:acm:us-east-1:111122223333:certificate/11111111-2222-3333-4444-555555555555
    alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/healthcheck-path: /healthz
    alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/group.name: shop-public
spec:
  ingressClassName: alb
  rules:
    - host: shop.example.com
      http:
        paths:
          - path: /api
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: orders
                port:
                  number: 80
          - path: /
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: web
                port:
                  number: 80
Check yourself
Why prefer target-type ip?

The ALB talks straight to pods, avoiding the extra NodePort hop and giving even load distribution.

50.3

NLB Services

In plain words

A Service of type LoadBalancer with the controller's annotations creates a Network Load Balancer for TCP, UDP or TLS traffic.

The problem it solves

Non-HTTP protocols, static IPs, extremely low latency or PrivateLink exposure need layer 4, not an ALB.

What it does

  • Set service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-type: external and aws-load-balancer-nlb-target-type: ip.
  • aws-load-balancer-scheme: internet-facing or internal.
  • NLB supports Elastic IPs per AZ (aws-load-balancer-eip-allocations) and security groups on the NLB.
  • Preserve client IP with target-type ip by default; mind the proxy protocol option for ip-mode.
  • Use loadBalancerClass: service.k8s.aws/nlb on modern versions.

Service

yamlInternal NLB for a gRPC service
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: payments-grpc
  namespace: shop
  annotations:
    service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-scheme: internal
    service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-nlb-target-type: ip
spec:
  type: LoadBalancer
  loadBalancerClass: service.k8s.aws/nlb
  selector:
    app: payments
  ports:
    - port: 443
      targetPort: 9090
      protocol: TCP
Check yourself
When would you pick an NLB over an ALB?

For non-HTTP protocols, static IPs, or very high throughput with low latency.

50.4

Health checks, graceful shutdown and readiness gates

In plain words

A load balancer sends traffic only to targets marked healthy. Deployments can drop requests if pods leave the target group late or join too early.

The problem it solves

Rolling updates produce brief 502 and 504 errors when a terminating pod is still receiving requests from the ALB.

What it does

  • Add a pod readiness gate by labeling the namespace elbv2.k8s.aws/pod-readiness-gate-inject=enabled; the pod is Ready only once the target group reports it healthy.
  • Add a preStop sleep (about 15 to 30 seconds) so the ALB deregisters the target before the app stops, and set terminationGracePeriodSeconds higher than that.
  • Make the ALB deregistration delay (deregistration_delay.timeout_seconds) comparable to the shutdown time.
  • Health check path must be cheap and not depend on downstream systems.

Config

yamlDeployment fragment
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: web
  namespace: shop
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: web
    spec:
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 45
      containers:
        - name: web
          image: 111122223333.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/shop/web:1.4.2
          lifecycle:
            preStop:
              exec:
                command: ["sleep", "20"]
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /healthz
              port: 8080
bashEnable readiness gates
kubectl label namespace shop elbv2.k8s.aws/pod-readiness-gate-inject=enabled
Check yourself
What causes 502s during rolling updates?

The pod stops before the load balancer has deregistered it, so requests still reach a dead target.

50.5

WAF, Shield, TLS and sharing ALBs

In plain words

Security features attach to the ALB through annotations: AWS WAF for request filtering, ACM for certificates, and Shield for DDoS.

The problem it solves

Public endpoints get scanned, scraped and attacked; terminating TLS and filtering at the edge keeps that away from your pods.

What it does

  • alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/wafv2-acl-arn attaches an existing web ACL.
  • alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/ssl-policy selects a TLS policy (use a TLS 1.2+ policy).
  • Shield Standard is automatic on ALB; Shield Advanced adds response support and cost protection.
  • One ALB per team or per environment is cheaper and easier to manage than one per Ingress; use group.name, but be aware of blast radius and the rule limit per listener (check the current quota).
  • Pair with ExternalDNS to publish the hostnames.

Annotations

yamlWAF and TLS policy annotations
metadata:
  annotations:
    alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/wafv2-acl-arn: arn:aws:wafv2:us-east-1:111122223333:regional/webacl/shop/aaaaaaaa-bbbb-cccc-dddd-eeeeeeeeeeee
    alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/ssl-policy: ELBSecurityPolicy-TLS13-1-2-2021-06
Check yourself
Where does TLS terminate with an ALB?

At the ALB, using an ACM certificate; traffic to pods can be plain or re-encrypted.

Section 51 of 93

EKS upgrades and day-2 operations

5 concepts · about 50 minutes

Kubernetes releases a minor version about three times a year, and each EKS version has a finite support window. Upgrading is a routine task, not an event.

Goals
  • Plan and execute a Kubernetes minor version upgrade end to end
  • Detect deprecated APIs and add-on incompatibilities before upgrading
  • Run PodDisruptionBudgets, topology spread and troubleshooting routines
51.1

Version support and cadence

In plain words

EKS supports each Kubernetes minor version for a standard support period, then offers a paid extended support period, after which the cluster is upgraded automatically.

The problem it solves

Skipping upgrades makes them bigger and riskier, and extended support costs more per cluster hour.

What it does

  • Only upgrade one minor version at a time (1.36 to 1.37, never two minors at once).
  • You cannot downgrade a control plane.
  • Check EKS cluster insights (aws eks list-insights) for deprecated API usage and add-on compatibility.
  • Calendar: look up the current dates on the Amazon EKS Kubernetes versions page.

Insights

bashPre-upgrade checks
aws eks list-insights --cluster-name shop-prod \
  --filter kubernetesVersions=1.37 \
  --query 'insights[].[name,insightStatus.status]' --output table
aws eks describe-cluster --name shop-prod --query cluster.version
kubectl get nodes -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,VER:.status.nodeInfo.kubeletVersion
Check yourself
Can you jump two minor versions at once?

No; upgrade one minor version at a time.

51.2

Upgrade order and procedure

In plain words

Upgrade the control plane first, then add-ons, then nodes. Each step is verified before the next.

The problem it solves

Upgrading in the wrong order can break compatibility: nodes cannot be newer than the control plane, and add-ons may need newer versions.

What it does

  1. Read release notes and check deprecations and insights.
  2. Upgrade non-production first and run smoke tests.
  3. aws eks update-cluster-version (control plane, roughly 10 to 25 minutes, API remains available).
  4. Update add-ons: vpc-cni, kube-proxy, coredns, CSI drivers.
  5. Roll node groups, or let Karpenter drift replace nodes.
  6. Update Helm-managed controllers such as the LB controller, Karpenter and cert-manager.

Commands

bashControl plane then add-ons
aws eks update-cluster-version --name shop-prod --kubernetes-version 1.37
aws eks wait cluster-active --name shop-prod
for a in vpc-cni kube-proxy coredns; do
  aws eks update-addon --cluster-name shop-prod --addon-name $a --resolve-conflicts PRESERVE
done
aws eks update-nodegroup-version --cluster-name shop-prod --nodegroup-name general
bashFind removed APIs in manifests
kubectl get --raw /metrics | grep apiserver_requested_deprecated_apis
# or scan YAML in git
kubent
pluto detect-files -d ./manifests --target-versions k8s=v1.37.0
Check yourself
Why must you not downgrade a control plane?

EKS does not support it; rollback means creating a new cluster, so test before upgrading production.

51.3

Blue/green cluster upgrades

In plain words

Instead of upgrading in place, build a second cluster on the new version, shift traffic to it, and retire the old one.

The problem it solves

An in-place upgrade cannot be rolled back. Some teams need a reversible path for critical systems.

What it does

  • Needs everything as code (Terraform, GitOps) so the new cluster reaches parity quickly.
  • Traffic moves with weighted Route 53 records or a shared ALB/NLB front.
  • Stateful data stays outside the cluster (RDS, DynamoDB, S3) or is replicated.
  • Costs double briefly and operations are more complex; in-place with good staging is enough for most teams.
Upgrade strategy
OptionIn place
Choose whena good staging cluster, GitOps, PDBs in place
Avoid whenyou cannot tolerate any rollback risk
OptionBlue/green cluster
Choose whencritical systems, big API changes
Avoid whenyou lack automation to rebuild quickly
51.4

Disruption control with PDBs and topology spread

In plain words

A PodDisruptionBudget limits how many pods of an app may be voluntarily evicted at once. Topology spread constraints distribute pods across AZs and nodes.

The problem it solves

Drains during upgrades can take all replicas of a service down together, or leave them all in one AZ.

What it does

  • PDB minAvailable: 1 or maxUnavailable: 1 keeps service up while nodes roll. A PDB set to zero allowed disruptions blocks every drain.
  • topologySpreadConstraints with topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone spreads replicas across AZs.
  • Combine with at least two replicas and readiness probes.
  • Single replica Deployments cannot be both HA and drainable; give them two.

Manifests

yamlPDB and spread for the web deployment
apiVersion: policy/v1
kind: PodDisruptionBudget
metadata:
  name: web
  namespace: shop
spec:
  maxUnavailable: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: web
  namespace: shop
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: web
    spec:
      topologySpreadConstraints:
        - maxSkew: 1
          topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
          whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule
          labelSelector:
            matchLabels:
              app: web
      containers:
        - name: web
          image: nginx:1.27
Check yourself
What does a PDB with maxUnavailable 0 do to upgrades?

It blocks node drains, so the node update stalls.

51.5

Troubleshooting routine

In plain words

When nodes do not join, pods stay Pending or traffic fails, work from the control plane outward.

The problem it solves

EKS failures are spread across IAM, networking and Kubernetes, and guessing wastes time.

What it does

  • Node not joining: node role has AmazonEKSWorkerNodePolicy, AmazonEKS_CNI_Policy, AmazonEC2ContainerRegistryReadOnly; security groups allow node to control plane (TCP 443); an access entry of type EC2_LINUX exists; check the node's journalctl -u kubelet.
  • Pod Pending: kubectl describe pod events (insufficient CPU, no IPs, taints, unbound PVC).
  • ImagePullBackOff: ECR permissions, VPC endpoint or NAT, image tag exists.
  • Use the EKS node monitoring agent and aws eks log collector script for node diagnostics.
  • Check CloudTrail and the authenticator logs for IAM errors.

Commands

bashFirst minute commands
kubectl get pods -A --field-selector=status.phase!=Running | head -20
kubectl describe pod <pod> -n shop | tail -20
kubectl get events -A --sort-by=.lastTimestamp | tail -15
kubectl get nodes -o wide
kubectl top nodes
Check yourself
Where do you look first for a pod stuck in Pending?

The Events section of `kubectl describe pod`.

Section 52 of 93

Amazon ECR registries and image supply chain

6 concepts · about 45 minutes

Amazon Elastic Container Registry (ECR) stores your container images and OCI artifacts. For EKS it is the default registry because nodes authenticate with IAM and pulls stay on the AWS network.

Goals
  • Create repositories with immutable tags, encryption and least privilege access
  • Apply lifecycle policies, image scanning and replication
  • Use pull-through cache and VPC endpoints to make pulls fast and private
52.1

Repositories and authentication

In plain words

An ECR registry exists per account and Region (111122223333.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com). Inside it you create one repository per image name.

The problem it solves

Public registries rate-limit pulls and offer no IAM control. You need a private store that your cluster can reach without passwords.

What it does

  • aws ecr get-login-password gives a token valid for 12 hours that docker login or helm registry login uses.
  • EKS nodes pull using their node role (AmazonEC2ContainerRegistryReadOnly or AmazonEC2ContainerRegistryPullOnly); no imagePullSecret is needed in the same account.
  • Cross-account pulls need a repository policy allowing the other account plus an IAM policy on the puller.
  • Immutable tags stop 1.4.2 from being overwritten; use them for release tags.
  • Encryption at rest is automatic (AES-256) or with a KMS key set at creation.

Create and push

bashCreate a repository and push
aws ecr create-repository --repository-name shop/web \
  --image-tag-mutability IMMUTABLE \
  --image-scanning-configuration scanOnPush=true \
  --encryption-configuration encryptionType=KMS
ACCT=$(aws sts get-caller-identity --query Account --output text)
REG=$ACCT.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com
aws ecr get-login-password --region us-east-1 | docker login --username AWS --password-stdin $REG
docker tag shop-web:1.4.2 $REG/shop/web:1.4.2
docker push $REG/shop/web:1.4.2
hclTerraform
resource "aws_ecr_repository" "web" {
  name                 = "shop/web"
  image_tag_mutability = "IMMUTABLE"

  image_scanning_configuration {
    scan_on_push = true
  }
  encryption_configuration {
    encryption_type = "KMS"
  }
}
Check yourself
Why use immutable tags?

A released tag always points at the same image, so deployments and audits are reproducible.

52.2

Lifecycle policies

In plain words

A lifecycle policy deletes images automatically by age or count, based on rules you write.

The problem it solves

CI pushes an image on every commit. Without cleanup you pay for thousands of old layers, and scans get noisy.

What it does

  • Rules have a priority, a tagStatus (tagged, untagged, any), optional tagPrefixList and a countType (imageCountMoreThan, sinceImagePushed).
  • Preview the result with start-lifecycle-policy-preview before applying.
  • Always keep recent release tags: retain by prefix such as v or release-.
  • Images in use by running pods are not protected, so keep enough history to roll back.

Policy

jsonlifecycle.json
{
  "rules": [
    {
      "rulePriority": 1,
      "description": "Keep 20 release images",
      "selection": {"tagStatus": "tagged", "tagPrefixList": ["v"], "countType": "imageCountMoreThan", "countNumber": 20},
      "action": {"type": "expire"}
    },
    {
      "rulePriority": 2,
      "description": "Expire untagged after 7 days",
      "selection": {"tagStatus": "untagged", "countType": "sinceImagePushed", "countUnit": "days", "countNumber": 7},
      "action": {"type": "expire"}
    }
  ]
}
bashApply
aws ecr put-lifecycle-policy --repository-name shop/web --lifecycle-policy-text file://lifecycle.json
Check yourself
Why preview a lifecycle policy?

A wrong rule can delete images that are still deployed or needed for rollback.

52.3

Image scanning

In plain words

ECR checks images for known vulnerabilities (CVEs). Basic scanning uses the open source Clair-based database; enhanced scanning uses Amazon Inspector for continuous scanning of OS and language packages.

The problem it solves

Images age: a clean image today has a known CVE next month, so a one-off scan at build time is not enough.

What it does

  • Basic: scan on push or manually; results per tag.
  • Enhanced: Inspector rescans when new CVEs appear and when the image is pulled recently (configurable duration); findings flow to Security Hub and EventBridge.
  • Gate pipelines: fail the build for critical findings in your own scanner (Trivy, Grype) and use ECR for continuous monitoring.
  • Pair with minimal base images (distroless, Alpine, Chainguard) to reduce findings.

Enable and read

bashEnhanced scanning and findings
aws ecr put-registry-scanning-configuration --scan-type ENHANCED \
  --rules '[{"scanFrequency":"CONTINUOUS_SCAN","repositoryFilters":[{"filter":"shop/*","filterType":"WILDCARD"}]}]'
aws ecr describe-image-scan-findings --repository-name shop/web --image-id imageTag=1.4.2 \
  --query 'imageScanFindings.findingSeverityCounts'
Check yourself
What does enhanced scanning add over basic?

Continuous rescans through Inspector, including language packages, with events and Security Hub integration.

52.4

Replication and cross-Region DR

In plain words

ECR replicates images automatically to other Regions or accounts when they are pushed.

The problem it solves

A regional outage must not stop you from pulling images in the DR Region, and cross-Region pulls are slow and cost data transfer.

What it does

  • Configured at the registry level with rules and optional repository filters.
  • Only images pushed after the rule exists are replicated; use a script to copy older images.
  • Pods in the DR cluster pull from the local replica registry hostname.
  • Replication of repository policies, lifecycle policies and tags is separate: manage those in code in each Region.

Rule

bashCross-Region replication
aws ecr put-replication-configuration --replication-configuration '{
  "rules":[{"destinations":[{"region":"eu-west-1","registryId":"111122223333"}],
            "repositoryFilters":[{"filter":"shop/","filterType":"PREFIX_MATCH"}]}]}'
Check yourself
Are images pushed before the rule existed replicated?

No; only new pushes are replicated.

52.5

Pull-through cache

In plain words

A pull-through cache rule makes ECR fetch and store images from an upstream registry (Docker Hub, Quay, GitHub Container Registry, registry.k8s.io, Amazon ECR Public, and others) on first pull.

The problem it solves

Docker Hub rate limits break node scale-outs, and arbitrary public images carry supply-chain risk.

What it does

  • Create a rule with a repository prefix such as docker-hub and the upstream URL; some upstreams need credentials stored in Secrets Manager.
  • Pull ACCT.dkr.ecr.REGION.amazonaws.com/docker-hub/library/nginx:1.27 and ECR caches it.
  • Cached images are rescanned and periodically refreshed from upstream.
  • Combine with an admission policy that allows only your registry domain.

Create

bashRule for Docker Hub
aws secretsmanager create-secret --name ecr-pullthroughcache/docker-hub \
  --secret-string '{"username":"myuser","accessToken":"REPLACE_ME"}'
aws ecr create-pull-through-cache-rule --ecr-repository-prefix docker-hub \
  --upstream-registry-url registry-1.docker.io \
  --credential-arn arn:aws:secretsmanager:us-east-1:111122223333:secret:ecr-pullthroughcache/docker-hub-AbCdEf
Check yourself
Why use a cache for public images?

It avoids rate limits and outages of the upstream registry and lets you scan the images.

52.6

Private access and permissions

In plain words

Nodes in private subnets reach ECR either through a NAT gateway or through VPC endpoints. Endpoints avoid NAT data processing charges and keep image traffic private.

The problem it solves

Pulling large images through NAT is expensive and sends AWS-internal traffic along an internet-bound path.

What it does

  • Create interface endpoints com.amazonaws.<region>.ecr.api and ecr.dkr, plus an S3 gateway endpoint, because image layers are served from S3.
  • Allow HTTPS (443) from the node security groups to the endpoints.
  • Use repository policies with conditions (aws:PrincipalOrgID) to share images inside an organisation.
  • CI roles need push permissions only on their repositories, never ecr:* on all resources.

Least privilege for CI

jsonCI push policy
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {"Effect": "Allow", "Action": "ecr:GetAuthorizationToken", "Resource": "*"},
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": [
        "ecr:BatchCheckLayerAvailability", "ecr:InitiateLayerUpload", "ecr:UploadLayerPart",
        "ecr:CompleteLayerUpload", "ecr:PutImage", "ecr:BatchGetImage", "ecr:GetDownloadUrlForLayer"
      ],
      "Resource": "arn:aws:ecr:us-east-1:111122223333:repository/shop/*"
    }
  ]
}
Check yourself
Why is an S3 gateway endpoint part of private ECR access?

ECR serves image layers from S3, so layer downloads need an S3 path.

Section 53 of 93

Karpenter provisioning and NodePools

5 concepts · about 55 minutes

Karpenter is a node autoscaler for Kubernetes. Instead of resizing Auto Scaling groups, it looks at unschedulable pods and launches the best-fitting EC2 instances directly through the EC2 Fleet API.

Goals
  • Explain how Karpenter provisions nodes directly from pending pods
  • Write NodePool and EC2NodeClass resources with sane constraints
  • Control Spot usage, limits, taints and disruption budgets
53.1

Karpenter versus Cluster Autoscaler

In plain words

The Cluster Autoscaler changes the size of pre-defined node groups. Karpenter has no node groups: it reads pod requirements and creates nodes of any suitable instance type.

The problem it solves

Node groups force you to guess instance types in advance, scale slowly, and strand capacity when pod shapes change.

What it does

  • Watches pending pods, batches them, and picks instance types that satisfy CPU, memory, GPU, zone, architecture and labels.
  • Launches in about a minute or less, depending on AMI and pod startup.
  • Removes or replaces nodes when they are empty, underused or drifted.
  • Karpenter itself runs on a small managed node group or Fargate, not on nodes it controls.

Install

bashHelm install (check chart version in the docs)
helm upgrade --install karpenter oci://public.ecr.aws/karpenter/karpenter \
  --version "${KARPENTER_VERSION}" --namespace kube-system \
  --set settings.clusterName=shop-prod \
  --set settings.interruptionQueue=shop-prod \
  --set controller.resources.requests.cpu=1 --set controller.resources.requests.memory=1Gi \
  --wait
kubectl get nodepools,ec2nodeclasses
Check yourself
Where should the Karpenter controller itself run?

On a small managed node group or Fargate, outside the capacity it provisions.

53.2

EC2NodeClass

In plain words

An EC2NodeClass describes AWS-specific settings for nodes: AMI, subnets, security groups, IAM role, block devices and metadata options.

The problem it solves

NodePools should stay cloud-neutral, but each node still needs concrete AWS configuration.

What it does

  • amiSelectorTerms pick the AMI by alias such as al2023@latest, or pin a version for production (al2023@v20250101).
  • subnetSelectorTerms and securityGroupSelectorTerms find resources by tag karpenter.sh/discovery.
  • role is the node IAM role name (an access entry of type EC2_LINUX is created for it).
  • metadataOptions enforce IMDSv2 and hop limit 1; blockDeviceMappings size encrypted gp3 root volumes.
  • userData allows extra kubelet configuration.

Example

yamlEC2NodeClass default
apiVersion: karpenter.k8s.aws/v1
kind: EC2NodeClass
metadata:
  name: default
spec:
  role: KarpenterNodeRole-shop-prod
  amiSelectorTerms:
    - alias: al2023@latest
  subnetSelectorTerms:
    - tags:
        karpenter.sh/discovery: shop-prod
  securityGroupSelectorTerms:
    - tags:
        karpenter.sh/discovery: shop-prod
  metadataOptions:
    httpTokens: required
    httpPutResponseHopLimit: 1
  blockDeviceMappings:
    - deviceName: /dev/xvda
      ebs:
        volumeSize: 50Gi
        volumeType: gp3
        encrypted: true
Tip

Pin an AMI version in production and roll it deliberately; @latest means any new AMI triggers drift replacement across the fleet.

Check yourself
How does Karpenter find subnets?

By tag selectors in EC2NodeClass, usually `karpenter.sh/discovery`.

53.3

NodePool requirements and limits

In plain words

A NodePool states which nodes Karpenter may create: instance categories, sizes, architectures, capacity types, zones and a total resource cap.

The problem it solves

Without constraints Karpenter may launch giant or exotic instances, or scale forever on a runaway deployment.

What it does

  • requirements use well-known labels: karpenter.sh/capacity-type (on-demand, spot), kubernetes.io/arch, topology.kubernetes.io/zone, karpenter.k8s.aws/instance-category, instance-generation, instance-size.
  • Widen the instance list (many families and sizes) for better Spot availability and price.
  • limits cap total CPU and memory in the pool; set them to your budget.
  • taints and labels direct specific workloads to specific pools; weight orders pools.
  • expireAfter recycles nodes after a lifetime (for example 720h), keeping AMIs fresh.

NodePool

yamlGeneral purpose NodePool
apiVersion: karpenter.sh/v1
kind: NodePool
metadata:
  name: general
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      nodeClassRef:
        group: karpenter.k8s.aws
        kind: EC2NodeClass
        name: default
      requirements:
        - key: karpenter.sh/capacity-type
          operator: In
          values: ["on-demand", "spot"]
        - key: kubernetes.io/arch
          operator: In
          values: ["amd64", "arm64"]
        - key: karpenter.k8s.aws/instance-category
          operator: In
          values: ["c", "m", "r"]
        - key: karpenter.k8s.aws/instance-generation
          operator: Gt
          values: ["5"]
      expireAfter: 720h
  limits:
    cpu: "200"
    memory: 800Gi
  disruption:
    consolidationPolicy: WhenEmptyOrUnderutilized
    consolidateAfter: 1m
Check yourself
What does the limits field protect against?

A runaway workload or bug creating unbounded nodes and cost.

53.4

Spot capacity and interruptions

In plain words

Spot instances cost much less but can be reclaimed with a two-minute notice. Karpenter listens for interruption events and replaces nodes proactively.

The problem it solves

Spot saves large amounts of money for stateless services, but naive use causes outages.

What it does

  • Set settings.interruptionQueue so Karpenter reads SQS messages from EventBridge (Spot interruption, rebalance recommendation, scheduled change, instance state change).
  • It cordons, drains and launches a replacement as soon as it gets notice.
  • Use many instance types for diversification; Karpenter uses the price-capacity-optimized strategy.
  • Spread replicas across zones and nodes, set PDBs, and keep graceful shutdown under two minutes.
  • Mix: baseline on-demand pool plus Spot pool for burst, selected via node selectors or tolerations.

Spot only pool

yamlSpot pool with taint
apiVersion: karpenter.sh/v1
kind: NodePool
metadata:
  name: spot-batch
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      nodeClassRef:
        group: karpenter.k8s.aws
        kind: EC2NodeClass
        name: default
      taints:
        - key: workload
          value: batch
          effect: NoSchedule
      requirements:
        - key: karpenter.sh/capacity-type
          operator: In
          values: ["spot"]
  limits:
    cpu: "100"
Check yourself
How much warning does a Spot interruption give?

Two minutes.

53.5

Pod specs that help Karpenter

In plain words

Karpenter packs pods based on their requests. Accurate requests, labels and topology rules lead to efficient nodes.

The problem it solves

Pods without requests look free, cause overcommit, and make bin packing unpredictable.

What it does

  • Always set CPU and memory requests (and memory limits).
  • Use nodeSelector or affinity on karpenter.sh/nodepool or capacity type to steer workloads.
  • Use topologySpreadConstraints over zones so Karpenter launches in several zones.
  • Annotate pods that must not be moved with karpenter.sh/do-not-disrupt: "true" (use sparingly; it blocks consolidation and upgrades).
  • Use Vertical Pod Autoscaler recommendations or tooling (Goldilocks, Kubecost) to set requests.

Deployment

yamlWeb on the general pool
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: web
  namespace: shop
spec:
  replicas: 4
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: web
    spec:
      nodeSelector:
        karpenter.sh/nodepool: general
      topologySpreadConstraints:
        - maxSkew: 1
          topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
          whenUnsatisfiable: ScheduleAnyway
          labelSelector:
            matchLabels:
              app: web
      containers:
        - name: web
          image: nginx:1.27
          resources:
            requests: {cpu: 250m, memory: 256Mi}
            limits: {memory: 256Mi}
Check yourself
What does Karpenter use to size nodes?

The resource requests of pending pods.

← PreviousNext →
Section 54 of 93

Karpenter consolidation, drift and operations

5 concepts · about 45 minutes

Launching nodes is half the job. Karpenter also removes and replaces them to keep the fleet cheap and fresh. Done carelessly, that disrupts workloads, so you control it with budgets.

Goals
  • Configure consolidation and disruption budgets to cut cost safely
  • Use drift and expiry to roll AMIs and configuration
  • Debug unschedulable pods and Karpenter decisions
54.1

Consolidation

In plain words

Consolidation deletes empty nodes and replaces underused nodes with fewer or cheaper ones, moving pods in between.

The problem it solves

After a traffic peak the cluster stays large and nearly empty. Manual scale-down is slow and conservative.

What it does

  • consolidationPolicy: WhenEmpty only removes empty nodes; WhenEmptyOrUnderutilized also repacks.
  • consolidateAfter is a delay after a pod change before consolidation is considered.
  • Single-node, multi-node and Spot-to-Spot consolidation exist; Spot-to-Spot is behind a feature gate (check the docs).
  • Karpenter respects PDBs and do-not-disrupt. Pods without a controller are not moved.

Observe

bashDecisions and events
kubectl get nodeclaims
kubectl get events -A --field-selector reason=DisruptionLaunching,reason=DisruptionTerminating
kubectl -n kube-system logs deploy/karpenter | grep -i -E 'consolidat|disrupt' | tail
kubectl describe nodepool general | sed -n '/Disruption/,/Limits/p'
Check yourself
What is the difference between WhenEmpty and WhenEmptyOrUnderutilized?

The second also repacks partly used nodes, not only removes empty ones.

54.2

Disruption budgets

In plain words

A budget limits how many nodes Karpenter may disrupt at once, optionally only in a time window and only for certain reasons.

The problem it solves

A new AMI or a quiet period might make Karpenter replace most nodes together and cause incidents.

What it does

  • budgets list nodes (count or percent), optional reasons (Empty, Drifted, Underutilized) and schedule with duration.
  • Several budgets apply together; the most restrictive wins.
  • Block all voluntary disruption during business hours with nodes: "0" and a cron schedule.
  • Involuntary events (Spot interruption, failures) are not affected by budgets.

Budgets

yamlNodePool disruption section
apiVersion: karpenter.sh/v1
kind: NodePool
metadata:
  name: general
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      nodeClassRef:
        group: karpenter.k8s.aws
        kind: EC2NodeClass
        name: default
      requirements:
        - key: karpenter.sh/capacity-type
          operator: In
          values: ["on-demand"]
  disruption:
    consolidationPolicy: WhenEmptyOrUnderutilized
    consolidateAfter: 5m
    budgets:
      - nodes: "10%"
      - nodes: "0"
        reasons: ["Underutilized"]
        schedule: "0 9 * * mon-fri"
        duration: 8h
Check yourself
Do budgets limit Spot interruptions?

No; involuntary disruptions are outside budgets.

54.3

Drift and expiry

In plain words

Drift means a node no longer matches its NodePool or EC2NodeClass (new AMI, changed subnets, changed requirements). Karpenter replaces drifted nodes. expireAfter replaces nodes at a maximum age.

The problem it solves

Node patching by hand is slow. You want fresh AMIs and consistent config without a maintenance window project.

What it does

  • Changing amiSelectorTerms to a new AMI marks all nodes drifted; they are replaced gradually, within your budgets.
  • Kubernetes upgrade flow: upgrade control plane, then Karpenter drifts nodes to the new AMI for that minor version.
  • expireAfter: 720h bounds node lifetime (about 30 days), a good security hygiene default.
  • Test AMI changes on a canary NodePool first.

Pin and roll

bashRoll by changing the AMI alias
kubectl patch ec2nodeclass default --type merge \
  -p '{"spec":{"amiSelectorTerms":[{"alias":"al2023@v20250115"}]}}'
kubectl get nodeclaims -w
Check yourself
What triggers drift?

A change in NodePool or EC2NodeClass settings, including a new selected AMI, so existing nodes no longer match.

54.4

Debugging provisioning problems

In plain words

When pods stay Pending, Karpenter logs say why no instance could be launched.

The problem it solves

Causes are spread: no capacity, limits reached, impossible requirements, missing IAM permissions, subnet IP exhaustion.

What it does

  • Look at pod events (FailedScheduling), kubectl get nodeclaims, and the controller log.
  • InsufficientInstanceCapacity → widen instance types or zones.
  • NodePool limits exceeded → raise limits or find the leak.
  • UnauthorizedOperation → check the controller's role (Pod Identity or IRSA) and the node role pass-role permission.
  • no subnets found → fix the karpenter.sh/discovery tag.
  • Nodes launch but do not join → node role access entry, security group, AMI/bootstrap.

Commands

bashFind the reason
kubectl get pods -A --field-selector=status.phase=Pending
kubectl describe pod <pod> -n shop | grep -A5 Events
kubectl get nodeclaims -o wide
kubectl -n kube-system logs deploy/karpenter --tail=100 | grep -i -E 'error|failed|insufficient'
Check yourself
Where do you look when no NodeClaim is created?

The Karpenter logs and the pod's scheduling constraints; requirements may be impossible or limits reached.

54.5

Cost and safety checklist

In plain words

Karpenter saves money mostly through right-sizing, Spot and consolidation. Keep a short list of controls.

The problem it solves

Savings disappear when requests are inflated or Spot is unmanaged; risk rises when budgets are missing.

What it does

  • Wide instance requirements, ARM (Graviton) nodes where images are multi-arch.
  • Limits per NodePool tied to a budget; alerts on node count and spend.
  • PDBs and zone spread on every production workload; PreStop hooks for graceful stop.
  • Pinned AMI in production and canary in dev; expireAfter set.
  • Dashboards: karpenter_nodes_total, karpenter_pods_startup_duration_seconds, interruption counts.

Multi-arch check

bashCheck image architectures
docker buildx imagetools inspect 111122223333.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/shop/web:1.4.2 | grep -E 'Platform'
Check yourself
Which setting guards against a runaway scale-out?

NodePool limits.
