Section 55 of 93

ExternalDNS and Route 53 automation

6 concepts · about 40 minutes

Creating an ALB is automatic; pointing shop.example.com at it is usually not. ExternalDNS closes that gap by watching Kubernetes resources and writing DNS records.

Goals
  • Explain how ExternalDNS turns Ingress and Service hostnames into Route 53 records
  • Install it with least privilege IAM and ownership TXT records
  • Use policies, filters and weighted records for safe automation and migrations
55.1

What ExternalDNS does

In plain words

ExternalDNS is a controller that reads hostnames from Ingress, Service and Gateway resources and creates matching records in a DNS provider such as Route 53.

The problem it solves

Manual DNS edits drift from the cluster, get forgotten when services are deleted, and block self-service deployments.

What it does

  • Watches sources (ingress, service, gateway-httproute, crd) and extracts hosts and targets.
  • For an ALB it creates an alias A/AAAA record; for other targets it creates CNAME or A records.
  • Writes a companion TXT record to mark ownership so it never edits records it did not create.
  • Reconciles on an interval and on events; deleting the Ingress removes the record when policy allows deletes.

Check what it manages

bashRecords ExternalDNS created
ZONE=$(aws route53 list-hosted-zones-by-name --dns-name example.com --query 'HostedZones[0].Id' --output text)
aws route53 list-resource-record-sets --hosted-zone-id "$ZONE" \
  --query "ResourceRecordSets[?contains(Name,'shop')].[Name,Type,AliasTarget.DNSName]" --output table
kubectl -n external-dns logs deploy/external-dns --tail=20
Check yourself
Why does ExternalDNS write TXT records?

They mark ownership so it only changes records it created.

55.2

IAM permissions

In plain words

ExternalDNS needs to list hosted zones and change record sets, and nothing else. Scope the permissions to the zones it manages.

The problem it solves

A controller with route53:* on all zones could redirect your whole domain if compromised.

What it does

  • route53:ChangeResourceRecordSets on the specific hosted zone ARN.
  • route53:ListHostedZones, ListHostedZonesByName, ListResourceRecordSets, ListTagsForResource on * (read only).
  • Attach the role with Pod Identity or IRSA to the external-dns service account.
  • For cross-account zones, assume a role in the DNS account with --aws-assume-role.

Policy

jsonExternalDNS IAM policy
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": ["route53:ChangeResourceRecordSets"],
      "Resource": ["arn:aws:route53:::hostedzone/Z0123456789ABCDEFGHIJ"]
    },
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": [
        "route53:ListHostedZones",
        "route53:ListHostedZonesByName",
        "route53:ListResourceRecordSets",
        "route53:ListTagsForResource"
      ],
      "Resource": ["*"]
    }
  ]
}
Check yourself
Which action needs to be restricted to a zone ARN?

ChangeResourceRecordSets, because it modifies records.

55.3

Installing and configuring

In plain words

Install via the official Helm chart and set the provider, domain filters, policy and TXT owner ID.

The problem it solves

Default settings may take over records from other clusters sharing a zone.

What it does

  • provider: aws, domainFilters limit zones, zoneIdFilters pin to a zone ID.
  • txtOwnerId must be unique per cluster so two clusters do not overwrite each other.
  • policy: upsert-only never deletes; sync also deletes. Start with upsert-only until trusted.
  • sources choose what to watch, interval the reconcile period.

Helm values

yamlvalues.yaml for the external-dns chart
provider:
  name: aws
env:
  - name: AWS_DEFAULT_REGION
    value: us-east-1
domainFilters:
  - example.com
policy: upsert-only
registry: txt
txtOwnerId: shop-prod
sources:
  - ingress
  - service
serviceAccount:
  create: true
  name: external-dns
bashInstall
helm repo add external-dns https://kubernetes-sigs.github.io/external-dns/
helm upgrade --install external-dns external-dns/external-dns -n external-dns --create-namespace -f values.yaml
Check yourself
Why must txtOwnerId be unique per cluster?

Otherwise one cluster may overwrite or delete records that another cluster owns.

55.4

Annotations, private zones and split horizon

In plain words

Annotations on a Service or Ingress add hostnames, TTLs and per-record settings. Public and private hosted zones can both exist for the same name.

The problem it solves

Internal clients should resolve internal load balancers while the internet resolves public ones.

What it does

  • external-dns.alpha.kubernetes.io/hostname sets names on a Service (Ingress reads hosts from rules).
  • external-dns.alpha.kubernetes.io/ttl sets the TTL.
  • Run two ExternalDNS instances with --aws-zone-type=public and --aws-zone-type=private, selecting Ingresses by ingressClass or annotation filter.
  • Private zones attach to VPCs; resolution only works from associated VPCs.

Service example

yamlService with hostname and TTL
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: payments
  namespace: shop
  annotations:
    external-dns.alpha.kubernetes.io/hostname: payments.internal.example.com
    external-dns.alpha.kubernetes.io/ttl: "60"
    service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-scheme: internal
    service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-nlb-target-type: ip
spec:
  type: LoadBalancer
  loadBalancerClass: service.k8s.aws/nlb
  selector:
    app: payments
  ports:
    - port: 443
      targetPort: 9090
Check yourself
How can one cluster serve both public and private names?

Run separate ExternalDNS instances filtered to public and private zones.

55.5

Weighted records for migrations

In plain words

ExternalDNS supports Route 53 routing policies through annotations, so you can send 10 percent of traffic to a new cluster.

The problem it solves

Cutting over a whole hostname at once is risky, and DNS TTL makes rollback slow.

What it does

  • Annotations external-dns.alpha.kubernetes.io/aws-weight and set-identifier create weighted records.
  • Each cluster sets its own weight for the same name; Route 53 splits answers proportionally.
  • Lower TTL days before a cutover (for example 60 seconds).
  • Failover and latency policies are also available for DR designs (check the provider docs for annotations).

Annotations

yamlWeighted record on the new cluster
metadata:
  annotations:
    external-dns.alpha.kubernetes.io/aws-weight: "10"
    external-dns.alpha.kubernetes.io/set-identifier: green-cluster
    external-dns.alpha.kubernetes.io/ttl: "60"
Check yourself
What must differ between two weighted records of the same name?

The set identifier.

55.6

Troubleshooting ExternalDNS

In plain words

Most problems are IAM, filters or ownership conflicts, and the controller log shows which.

The problem it solves

Records do not appear, or they flip between clusters.

What it does

  • AccessDenied in the log → fix the role or the zone ARN.
  • No records created → domain filter does not match, wrong ingress class, or the Ingress has no address yet (ALB not provisioned).
  • "Skipping record: owned by another" → another owner ID holds the TXT record; remove it or change the owner.
  • Add --log-level=debug and --dry-run while testing.

Check

bashDiagnose
kubectl get ingress -A
kubectl -n external-dns logs deploy/external-dns | grep -i -E 'error|denied|skip|owner' | tail
dig +short shop.example.com
Check yourself
What first checks apply when a record is missing?

The Ingress must have an address, the domain must match filters, IAM must allow the change, and no other owner must hold the record.

Section 56 of 93

cert-manager and TLS certificates

5 concepts · about 45 minutes

TLS certificates expire. Automating issuance and renewal removes a whole class of outages. On AWS you have two main tools: ACM for load balancers and cert-manager for certificates that live inside the cluster.

Goals
  • Choose between ACM, cert-manager with Let's Encrypt and a private CA
  • Configure issuers with DNS-01 validation through Route 53
  • Rotate and monitor certificates inside the cluster
56.1

ACM versus cert-manager

In plain words

AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) issues free public certificates that attach to ALB, NLB (TLS listener), CloudFront and API Gateway. You cannot export the private key. cert-manager creates certificates as Kubernetes Secrets that pods can mount.

The problem it solves

Some TLS endpoints are pods themselves (mTLS, webhooks, ingress controllers such as NGINX or Istio gateways) and need a key in the cluster.

What it does

  • ACM public certs auto-renew when DNS validation records remain in place.
  • cert-manager supports ACME (Let's Encrypt), a private CA, Vault, and AWS Private CA via a plugin.
  • Use ACM at the edge when an ALB terminates TLS; use cert-manager for in-cluster TLS and mTLS.
  • ACM Private CA issues certificates for internal use at an hourly CA fee.
Pick a certificate source
OptionACM
Choose whenan ALB or CloudFront terminates TLS
Avoid whenthe pod itself needs the private key
Optioncert-manager with Let's Encrypt
Choose whenin-cluster ingress or a webhook needs public trust
Avoid whenyou cannot use DNS-01 or HTTP-01 at all
Optioncert-manager with private CA
Choose wheninternal mTLS between services
Avoid whenclients cannot trust your private root

Request an ACM certificate

bashDNS validated ACM certificate
aws acm request-certificate --domain-name shop.example.com \
  --subject-alternative-names "*.shop.example.com" --validation-method DNS
aws acm describe-certificate --certificate-arn arn:aws:acm:us-east-1:111122223333:certificate/11111111-2222-3333-4444-555555555555 \
  --query 'Certificate.DomainValidationOptions[0].ResourceRecord'
Check yourself
Can you export the private key of an ACM public certificate?

No; it stays inside AWS-integrated services.

56.2

Installing cert-manager

In plain words

cert-manager runs as three deployments (controller, webhook, cainjector) and adds CRDs: Issuer, ClusterIssuer, Certificate, CertificateRequest.

The problem it solves

Without a controller, renewing certificates means cron jobs and manual secret updates.

What it does

  • Install with Helm and crds.enabled=true (older charts use installCRDs).
  • A Certificate resource names the DNS names, issuer and target Secret.
  • The controller renews at two thirds of the lifetime by default (configurable with renewBefore).
  • Ingress annotations (cert-manager.io/cluster-issuer) create certificates automatically from Ingress TLS sections.

Install

bashHelm install
helm repo add jetstack https://charts.jetstack.io && helm repo update
helm upgrade --install cert-manager jetstack/cert-manager -n cert-manager --create-namespace \
  --set crds.enabled=true
kubectl -n cert-manager get pods
Check yourself
When does cert-manager renew by default?

At two thirds of the certificate lifetime.

56.3

ACME DNS-01 with Route 53

In plain words

DNS-01 proves domain ownership by creating a TXT record. It works for wildcard names and for clusters not reachable from the internet.

The problem it solves

HTTP-01 needs a public endpoint on port 80, which many clusters do not have, and it cannot issue wildcard certificates.

What it does

  • A ClusterIssuer with the ACME server URL and a Route 53 solver.
  • cert-manager needs route53:ChangeResourceRecordSets on the zone and route53:GetChange, ListHostedZonesByName; give it a Pod Identity or IRSA role.
  • Use the Let's Encrypt staging endpoint while testing to avoid rate limits.
  • Certificates last 90 days (check current CA policy); renewal is automatic.

ClusterIssuer

yamlLet's Encrypt with Route 53
apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1
kind: ClusterIssuer
metadata:
  name: letsencrypt-prod
spec:
  acme:
    server: https://acme-v02.api.letsencrypt.org/directory
    email: platform@example.com
    privateKeySecretRef:
      name: letsencrypt-prod-key
    solvers:
      - dns01:
          route53:
            region: us-east-1
            hostedZoneID: Z0123456789ABCDEFGHIJ
---
apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1
kind: Certificate
metadata:
  name: shop-tls
  namespace: shop
spec:
  secretName: shop-tls
  dnsNames:
    - shop.example.com
  issuerRef:
    name: letsencrypt-prod
    kind: ClusterIssuer
Check yourself
Why use the staging ACME server first?

It has far higher rate limits, so configuration mistakes do not lock you out.

56.4

Private CA for internal mTLS

In plain words

A private CA issues certificates your own services trust. cert-manager can run a self-signed root in the cluster or call AWS Private CA.

The problem it solves

Service-to-service encryption needs certificates with short lifetimes and automated rotation, which a public CA does not provide for internal names.

What it does

  • A selfSigned issuer creates a root; a ca issuer signs leaf certificates from it.
  • Short lifetimes (24 hours to 90 days) reduce exposure; use duration and renewBefore.
  • aws-privateca-issuer plugin issues from AWS Private CA with IAM controlled access.
  • A service mesh (Istio, Linkerd) usually manages workload mTLS itself; use cert-manager for the mesh root if required.

Manifests

yamlSelf-signed root and CA issuer
apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1
kind: ClusterIssuer
metadata:
  name: selfsigned
spec:
  selfSigned: {}
---
apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1
kind: Certificate
metadata:
  name: internal-root
  namespace: cert-manager
spec:
  isCA: true
  commonName: internal-root
  secretName: internal-root
  privateKey:
    algorithm: ECDSA
    size: 256
  issuerRef:
    name: selfsigned
    kind: ClusterIssuer
---
apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1
kind: ClusterIssuer
metadata:
  name: internal-ca
spec:
  ca:
    secretName: internal-root
Check yourself
Why prefer short certificate lifetimes?

Compromised keys expire quickly and automation makes rotation cheap.

56.5

Monitoring and troubleshooting

In plain words

Certificates fail quietly: a renewal error shows up only on expiry day. Watch cert-manager's status and metrics.

The problem it solves

Expiry outages are common and entirely preventable.

What it does

  • kubectl get certificate -A shows READY state; kubectl describe certificate and certificaterequest, order, challenge show why issuance fails.
  • Prometheus metric certmanager_certificate_expiration_timestamp_seconds supports alerts such as "expires in less than 14 days".
  • Common failures: DNS-01 IAM denied, wrong hosted zone, rate limits, webhook not ready after install.
  • cmctl status certificate and cmctl renew assist operations.

Commands

bashFind the failing step
kubectl get certificate -A
kubectl -n shop describe certificate shop-tls | tail -20
kubectl -n shop get certificaterequest,order,challenge
kubectl -n cert-manager logs deploy/cert-manager --tail=30
yamlPrometheus alert rule
groups:
  - name: certs
    rules:
      - alert: CertificateExpiringSoon
        expr: (certmanager_certificate_expiration_timestamp_seconds - time()) < 14 * 24 * 3600
        for: 1h
        labels:
          severity: warning
        annotations:
          summary: "Certificate {{ $labels.name }} expires in less than 14 days"
Check yourself
Which metric helps alert on expiry?

certmanager_certificate_expiration_timestamp_seconds.

Section 57 of 93

External Secrets with AWS Secrets Manager

6 concepts · about 45 minutes

Kubernetes Secrets are base64, not encryption, and putting values in Git is risky. The External Secrets Operator (ESO) keeps the source of truth in AWS and copies values into the cluster when needed.

Goals
  • Sync secrets from AWS Secrets Manager and Parameter Store into Kubernetes
  • Configure a SecretStore with Pod Identity or IRSA and scoped IAM
  • Handle rotation, refresh intervals and templating safely
57.1

The problem with Kubernetes Secrets

In plain words

A Secret object is stored in etcd, readable by anyone with get secret rights in the namespace, and often committed to Git in some encoded form.

The problem it solves

Rotating a database password means editing manifests and redeploying. Auditing who read what is hard.

What it does

  • EKS encrypts etcd at rest, and you can add envelope encryption with your own KMS key to Secrets.
  • RBAC must restrict get/list on secrets; avoid cluster-wide read.
  • Better pattern: store in Secrets Manager (versioned, audited, rotated) and sync into the cluster, or mount via the Secrets Store CSI driver.
  • Never print secrets in logs or CI output.

Enable envelope encryption

bashEncrypt Kubernetes secrets with a KMS key
aws eks associate-encryption-config --cluster-name shop-prod \
  --encryption-config '[{"resources":["secrets"],"provider":{"keyArn":"arn:aws:kms:us-east-1:111122223333:key/11111111-2222-3333-4444-555555555555"}}]'
Check yourself
Is base64 encryption?

No; it is an encoding anyone can reverse.

57.2

ESO architecture

In plain words

ESO adds custom resources: a SecretStore (or cluster-wide ClusterSecretStore) says how to reach the provider, and an ExternalSecret says which remote keys to pull and what Secret to create.

The problem it solves

Applications want an ordinary Kubernetes Secret or environment variable without knowing about AWS.

What it does

  • The operator reconciles every refreshInterval and updates the target Secret when the remote value changes.
  • Targets can be templated to build config files or connection strings.
  • creationPolicy, deletionPolicy decide ownership and cleanup.
  • Providers: AWS Secrets Manager, Parameter Store, and many others (Vault, GCP, Azure).

Install

bashHelm install
helm repo add external-secrets https://charts.external-secrets.io
helm upgrade --install external-secrets external-secrets/external-secrets \
  -n external-secrets --create-namespace --set installCRDs=true
kubectl -n external-secrets get pods
Check yourself
What is the difference between SecretStore and ExternalSecret?

The store defines how to authenticate to the provider; the ExternalSecret defines which values to fetch and the Secret to create.

57.3

IAM and ClusterSecretStore

In plain words

ESO's service account assumes an IAM role that can read only the secrets it should. The store references that service account.

The problem it solves

Operators with secretsmanager:* on everything can read every secret in the account.

What it does

  • Allow secretsmanager:GetSecretValue and DescribeSecret on specific ARNs or a name prefix such as shop/*.
  • Add kms:Decrypt if secrets use a customer managed key.
  • For Parameter Store allow ssm:GetParameter on /shop/*.
  • Use separate roles per team when multi-tenant, with namespaced SecretStore objects.

Policy and store

jsonESO read policy
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": ["secretsmanager:GetSecretValue", "secretsmanager:DescribeSecret"],
      "Resource": "arn:aws:secretsmanager:us-east-1:111122223333:secret:shop/*"
    },
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": "kms:Decrypt",
      "Resource": "arn:aws:kms:us-east-1:111122223333:key/11111111-2222-3333-4444-555555555555"
    }
  ]
}
yamlClusterSecretStore using a service account (IRSA)
apiVersion: external-secrets.io/v1beta1
kind: ClusterSecretStore
metadata:
  name: aws-secrets
spec:
  provider:
    aws:
      service: SecretsManager
      region: us-east-1
      auth:
        jwt:
          serviceAccountRef:
            name: external-secrets
            namespace: external-secrets
Note

With Pod Identity, omit the auth block so ESO uses the default AWS credential chain; confirm support in your ESO version.

Check yourself
Why scope the policy to a prefix?

A compromised operator then reads only the intended secrets, not the whole account.

57.4

ExternalSecret resources

In plain words

An ExternalSecret names remote keys and the Kubernetes Secret to produce.

The problem it solves

You need specific properties (like username and password from one JSON secret) mapped into specific keys.

What it does

  • data maps single keys: remoteRef.key and optional property for JSON fields.
  • dataFrom with extract imports all keys of a JSON secret.
  • target.template can compose strings, such as a full connection URL.
  • Pods consume the Secret with envFrom or a volume. Volume mounts update on refresh; environment variables need a pod restart (use Reloader or a rollout trigger).

Example

yamlMap a Secrets Manager secret to a Secret
apiVersion: external-secrets.io/v1beta1
kind: ExternalSecret
metadata:
  name: db-credentials
  namespace: shop
spec:
  refreshInterval: 1h
  secretStoreRef:
    kind: ClusterSecretStore
    name: aws-secrets
  target:
    name: db-credentials
    creationPolicy: Owner
    template:
      data:
        DATABASE_URL: "postgres://{{ .username }}:{{ .password }}@shop-db.example.internal:5432/shop"
  dataFrom:
    - extract:
        key: shop/db
bashCreate the source secret
aws secretsmanager create-secret --name shop/db \
  --secret-string '{"username":"shop","password":"CHANGE_ME"}'
kubectl -n shop get externalsecret db-credentials
Check yourself
Why do environment variables not follow secret rotation automatically?

Environment values are set at container start; only mounted files update in place.

57.5

Rotation and reload

In plain words

Secrets Manager can rotate credentials automatically with a Lambda. ESO then copies the new value, and applications must pick it up.

The problem it solves

Rotation is useless if pods keep using the old password until the next deploy, or if the rotation window causes connection failures.

What it does

  • Secrets Manager rotation for RDS uses either single user or alternating users strategy; alternating users avoids downtime.
  • Set ESO refreshInterval shorter than your rotation tolerance (for example 5 to 15 minutes) and watch API cost per request.
  • Use Stakater Reloader or annotation-based rollouts to restart pods on Secret change.
  • Applications that read secret files on each connection or support credential refresh avoid restarts.

Enable rotation

bashRotation with the RDS managed master secret
aws secretsmanager rotate-secret --secret-id shop/db \
  --rotation-lambda-arn arn:aws:lambda:us-east-1:111122223333:function:SecretsManagerRDSRotation \
  --rotation-rules AutomaticallyAfterDays=30
yamlReloader annotation on a Deployment
metadata:
  annotations:
    reloader.stakater.com/auto: "true"
Check yourself
What triggers a pod restart after a Secret changes?

A tool such as Reloader that watches Secrets and performs a rollout.

57.6

Alternatives and trade-offs

In plain words

ESO is one option. The AWS Secrets and Configuration Provider (ASCP) with the Secrets Store CSI driver mounts secrets directly into pods without creating a Kubernetes Secret.

The problem it solves

Teams must choose between convenience and exposure.

What it does

  • ESO: creates Kubernetes Secrets, works with env vars, many providers; the value exists in etcd.
  • CSI driver + ASCP: mounts files from Secrets Manager or Parameter Store; optional sync to Secrets; the pod's own identity fetches, so per-pod scoping is natural.
  • Sealed Secrets or SOPS: encrypted values committed to Git; good for GitOps but rotation is manual.
  • Use one approach per platform, document it, and ban plaintext secrets in manifests and CI variables.
Which approach
OptionESO
Choose whenmany apps need ordinary Secrets and env vars
Avoid whensecrets must never exist in etcd
OptionCSI driver and ASCP
Choose whensecrets should never be Kubernetes objects
Avoid whenyou need env vars and cannot restart on change
OptionSOPS
Choose whenGitOps with a small number of static secrets
Avoid whenyou need automatic rotation

Section 58 of 93

KMS and Secrets Manager

6 concepts · about 45 minutes

Encryption keys and secrets are the most sensitive objects in an account. KMS holds the keys; Secrets Manager holds credentials and uses KMS to protect them.

Goals
  • Explain envelope encryption and choose between AWS managed and customer managed keys
  • Write key policies and grants that separate administrators from users
  • Store, rotate and retrieve secrets with Secrets Manager and Parameter Store
58.1

Envelope encryption

In plain words

KMS never encrypts your large data directly. It encrypts a small data key; the data key encrypts your data. You store the encrypted data key beside the data.

The problem it solves

Sending gigabytes to a key service is slow and expensive, and you do not want plaintext keys saved anywhere.

What it does

  • GenerateDataKey returns a plaintext data key and the same key encrypted under a KMS key.
  • The service encrypts data with the plaintext key, discards it, and stores the encrypted copy.
  • To read, the service calls Decrypt on the encrypted data key (KMS checks the key policy and IAM) and decrypts the data locally.
  • S3, EBS, RDS, EKS secrets and Secrets Manager all use this pattern.

Try it

bashCreate a key and encrypt a small value
KEY=$(aws kms create-key --description "shop demo" --query KeyMetadata.KeyId --output text)
aws kms create-alias --alias-name alias/shop-demo --target-key-id "$KEY"
aws kms encrypt --key-id alias/shop-demo --plaintext fileb://<(printf 'hello') \
  --query CiphertextBlob --output text > cipher.b64
base64 --decode < cipher.b64 > cipher.bin
aws kms decrypt --ciphertext-blob fileb://cipher.bin --query Plaintext --output text | base64 --decode
Check yourself
Why use data keys instead of sending data to KMS?

KMS limits request size and rate; a local data key encrypts bulk data quickly and KMS protects only the small key.

58.2

Key types and rotation

In plain words

KMS keys come as AWS owned, AWS managed (aws/s3), or customer managed keys (CMKs). You get full control only with customer managed keys.

The problem it solves

Default keys cannot be shared across accounts, disabled on demand, or given a custom policy, so they fail many compliance requirements.

What it does

  • AWS managed keys rotate automatically (yearly) and cost nothing per key, but policy is fixed.
  • Customer managed keys have your own key policy, aliases, tags, optional automatic rotation (a period between 90 and 2560 days; check the current limits) and per-key monthly cost plus request charges.
  • Rotation keeps the same key ID; older key material stays to decrypt old data.
  • Symmetric keys (AES-256-GCM) are standard; asymmetric and HMAC keys exist for signing and verification.
  • Multi-Region keys share key material across Regions for DR and global tables.

Enable rotation

bashRotate a CMK yearly
aws kms enable-key-rotation --key-id alias/shop-demo --rotation-period-in-days 365
aws kms get-key-rotation-status --key-id alias/shop-demo
Check yourself
Does rotation change the key ID?

No; the key ID and ARN stay the same and old material is retained for decryption.

58.3

Key policies and grants

In plain words

Every KMS key has a key policy, and it is the primary access control. IAM policies only work if the key policy allows IAM to control the key.

The problem it solves

Without a clear split, the people who administer keys can also decrypt all data, and an admin leaving takes knowledge with them.

What it does

  • The default statement lets the account root enable IAM policies for the key.
  • Separate statements: key administrators (create, disable, schedule deletion) versus key users (Encrypt, Decrypt, GenerateDataKey).
  • kms:ViaService limits use to a specific service (for example only via RDS in us-east-1).
  • Grants give temporary, narrow permissions to AWS services such as EBS.
  • Schedule deletion has a 7 to 30 day wait; deleting a key makes data unrecoverable.

Policy

jsonKey policy for the shop RDS key
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Sid": "EnableIAM",
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Principal": {"AWS": "arn:aws:iam::111122223333:root"},
      "Action": "kms:*",
      "Resource": "*"
    },
    {
      "Sid": "AllowUseViaRds",
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Principal": {"AWS": "arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/ShopDbRole"},
      "Action": ["kms:Encrypt", "kms:Decrypt", "kms:GenerateDataKey*", "kms:DescribeKey"],
      "Resource": "*",
      "Condition": {"StringEquals": {"kms:ViaService": "rds.us-east-1.amazonaws.com"}}
    }
  ]
}
Danger

Never remove the account root statement from a key policy unless you are certain another principal can administer it; an unmanageable key cannot be repaired without AWS Support.

Check yourself
What does kms:ViaService do?

It restricts key use to requests made through the named AWS service.

58.4

Secrets Manager basics

In plain words

Secrets Manager stores credentials, API keys and certificates as versioned secrets, encrypted with KMS, with fine-grained IAM and optional automatic rotation.

The problem it solves

Hard-coded passwords in code, environment files or Terraform state leak and are never rotated.

What it does

  • A secret holds a string or JSON, with staging labels AWSCURRENT, AWSPREVIOUS, AWSPENDING.
  • Pay per secret per month plus per 10,000 API calls (check current pricing).
  • Resource policies allow cross-account access; replication copies a secret to other Regions.
  • Retrieval via SDK, CLI, ESO, CSI driver or Lambda extension; cache values in the client to cut cost and latency.
  • RDS and Aurora can create and rotate the master secret for you (--manage-master-user-password).

CLI

bashCreate, read and update a secret
aws secretsmanager create-secret --name shop/api-key --secret-string '{"key":"CHANGE_ME"}'
aws secretsmanager get-secret-value --secret-id shop/api-key --query SecretString --output text
aws secretsmanager put-secret-value --secret-id shop/api-key --secret-string '{"key":"NEW_VALUE"}'
aws secretsmanager describe-secret --secret-id shop/api-key --query VersionIdsToStages
Check yourself
Which staging label marks the active version?

AWSCURRENT.

58.5

Rotation with Lambda

In plain words

Rotation is a Lambda function that runs four steps: create a pending secret, set it in the database, test it, then finish by promoting it to current.

The problem it solves

Manual rotation is skipped. Automated rotation limits exposure from leaked credentials.

What it does

  • AWS provides rotation templates for RDS, Aurora, Redshift, DocumentDB; custom Lambdas cover anything else.
  • Single user strategy changes one user's password (short window of failures); alternating users keeps two users and swaps them (no downtime).
  • The Lambda needs network access to the database and to Secrets Manager (VPC endpoint).
  • Applications must re-read the secret on authentication failures or on a short cache TTL.

Schedule

bashRotate every 30 days
aws secretsmanager rotate-secret --secret-id shop/db \
  --rotation-lambda-arn arn:aws:lambda:us-east-1:111122223333:function:SecretsManagerRDSPostgreSQLRotationMultiUser \
  --rotation-rules ScheduleExpression="rate(30 days)"
Check yourself
Which rotation strategy avoids downtime?

Alternating users, because one valid user always remains while the other changes.

58.6

Parameter Store versus Secrets Manager

In plain words

Systems Manager Parameter Store holds configuration and, with SecureString, small secrets. It is cheaper but lacks built-in rotation.

The problem it solves

Not every value is a secret. Paying Secrets Manager prices for feature flags and endpoints wastes money.

What it does

  • Standard parameters are free (up to a quota); advanced parameters cost more and allow larger values and policies.
  • SecureString encrypts with KMS. Paths like /shop/prod/db/host allow hierarchical IAM.
  • Use Parameter Store for configuration and non-rotating secrets; Secrets Manager for credentials that rotate or need cross-account and replication.
  • Parameter Store can also reference Secrets Manager secrets by path /aws/reference/secretsmanager/<name>.

Use

bashParameter Store basics
aws ssm put-parameter --name /shop/prod/db/host --type String --value shop-db.example.internal
aws ssm put-parameter --name /shop/prod/feature-key --type SecureString --value CHANGE_ME
aws ssm get-parameters-by-path --path /shop/prod --with-decryption --recursive
Check yourself
When choose Secrets Manager over Parameter Store?

When you need automatic rotation, replication or cross-account sharing of credentials.

Section 59 of 93

IAM Identity Center, SCPs and access governance

6 concepts · about 50 minutes

Access governance means every human and machine has the least access needed, granted through one central place, with guardrails that no individual account can bypass.

Goals
  • Set up workforce access with IAM Identity Center permission sets and SSO profiles
  • Apply service control policies and permission boundaries as guardrails
  • Use IAM Access Analyzer to find external access and unused permissions
59.1

IAM Identity Center

In plain words

IAM Identity Center (successor to AWS SSO) gives your workforce single sign-on to all accounts in an Organization. Users sign in once through your identity provider (Astra Connect, Okta, Entra ID) and pick an account and role.

The problem it solves

Long-lived IAM users with access keys per account are hard to offboard, audit and rotate.

What it does

  • A permission set is a template of policies; assigning it to a user or group in an account creates a managed role AWSReservedSSO_<name>_<hash> there.
  • Identity sources: the built-in directory, Active Directory, or an external IdP via SAML and SCIM provisioning.
  • Sessions are short (1 to 12 hours) and temporary credentials are issued through the CLI.
  • Groups map to permission sets per account, so access reviews become group reviews.

CLI

bashConfigure and use an SSO profile
aws configure sso    # prompts for start URL, region, account and permission set
aws sso login --profile shop-prod-admin
aws sts get-caller-identity --profile shop-prod-admin
aws eks update-kubeconfig --name shop-prod --profile shop-prod-admin
Check yourself
What does Identity Center create in a member account?

An IAM role per assigned permission set, named AWSReservedSSO.

59.2

Permission sets and groups

In plain words

A permission set combines AWS managed policies, customer managed policies, an inline policy, a permissions boundary and a session duration.

The problem it solves

Hand-crafted roles per team and account lead to inconsistency and over-broad access.

What it does

  • Standard set: ReadOnly, Developer (edit in a namespace/workload scope), PlatformAdmin, BillingViewer, SecurityAudit.
  • Attach customer managed policies by name; they must exist in every target account.
  • Use attribute-based access control with IdP attributes (department, cost-center) passed as session tags.
  • Manage the whole thing as code (Terraform aws_ssoadmin_permission_set).

Terraform

hclPermission set with a managed policy
resource "aws_ssoadmin_permission_set" "dev" {
  name             = "Developer"
  instance_arn     = tolist(data.aws_ssoadmin_instances.this.arns)[0]
  session_duration = "PT8H"
}

resource "aws_ssoadmin_managed_policy_attachment" "dev_view" {
  instance_arn       = tolist(data.aws_ssoadmin_instances.this.arns)[0]
  managed_policy_arn = "arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/ReadOnlyAccess"
  permission_set_arn = aws_ssoadmin_permission_set.dev.arn
}
Check yourself
Why assign permission sets to groups rather than users?

Joiners and leavers then change group membership in the IdP, not AWS configuration.

59.3

Service control policies

In plain words

An SCP is an Organization policy that sets the maximum permissions for accounts in an OU. It never grants access; it only limits what IAM can allow.

The problem it solves

Even an account administrator could disable CloudTrail, leave the Organization, or use a Region you do not operate in.

What it does

  • Attach SCPs to the root, OUs or accounts; permissions are the intersection of the SCP chain and IAM.
  • They do not affect the management account or service-linked roles.
  • Typical guardrails: deny non-approved Regions, deny disabling CloudTrail/GuardDuty/Config, deny leaving the Organization, deny root user actions, require encryption.
  • Test in a sandbox OU first; a wrong deny can lock out automation.

Deny Regions

jsonDeny actions outside approved Regions
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Sid": "DenyOtherRegions",
      "Effect": "Deny",
      "NotAction": ["iam:*", "organizations:*", "route53:*", "cloudfront:*", "support:*", "sts:*"],
      "Resource": "*",
      "Condition": {
        "StringNotEquals": {"aws:RequestedRegion": ["us-east-1", "eu-west-1"]}
      }
    },
    {
      "Sid": "ProtectSecurityServices",
      "Effect": "Deny",
      "Action": ["cloudtrail:StopLogging", "cloudtrail:DeleteTrail", "guardduty:DeleteDetector", "config:StopConfigurationRecorder"],
      "Resource": "*"
    }
  ]
}
Check yourself
Does an SCP grant permissions?

No; it only restricts what IAM policies may allow.

59.4

Permission boundaries and least privilege

In plain words

A permissions boundary caps the permissions an IAM role can ever have, even if someone attaches AdministratorAccess to it.

The problem it solves

Developers need to create roles for their workloads without being able to create a role more powerful than themselves.

What it does

  • Allow role creation only when the new role carries a specific boundary policy (iam:PermissionsBoundary condition).
  • The boundary and the identity policy must both allow an action.
  • Good practice: start with Access Analyzer-generated policies from CloudTrail activity, then tighten.
  • Prefer roles and temporary credentials; avoid IAM users and access keys. Rotate or delete unused keys.

Policy

jsonCreate roles only with the boundary
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": ["iam:CreateRole", "iam:AttachRolePolicy", "iam:PutRolePolicy"],
      "Resource": "arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/shop-*",
      "Condition": {
        "StringEquals": {"iam:PermissionsBoundary": "arn:aws:iam::111122223333:policy/ShopBoundary"}
      }
    }
  ]
}
Check yourself
What stops a developer from creating a role with admin rights?

The boundary condition forces the new role to carry a boundary that caps its permissions.

59.5

IAM Access Analyzer

In plain words

Access Analyzer finds resources shared outside your account or Organization, validates policies, and reports unused access.

The problem it solves

A public S3 bucket, a role trusting an unknown account, or a forgotten admin role are invisible in day-to-day work.

What it does

  • External access findings for S3, IAM roles, KMS keys, SQS, Lambda, secrets and more.
  • Unused access findings list unused roles, users, keys and permissions (extra cost).
  • Policy validation and generation: check JSON for errors and create least-privilege policies from CloudTrail.
  • Findings go to Security Hub and EventBridge for alerts.

CLI

bashCreate an organisation analyzer and list findings
aws accessanalyzer create-analyzer --analyzer-name org-analyzer --type ORGANIZATION
aws accessanalyzer list-findings-v2 --analyzer-arn arn:aws:access-analyzer:us-east-1:111122223333:analyzer/org-analyzer \
  --filter '{"status":{"eq":["ACTIVE"]}}' --query 'findings[].[resourceType,resource]' --output table
Check yourself
What does external access analysis detect?

Resources shared outside your account or organisation, such as public buckets or cross-account trust.

59.6

Organizations, accounts and break-glass

In plain words

Multiple accounts are the strongest security boundary: separate workloads, environments and logging into different accounts under one Organization.

The problem it solves

One account for everything means one blast radius, one quota pool and tangled permissions.

What it does

  • Typical layout: management (billing only), security tooling, log archive, shared services/network, then workload accounts per environment.
  • AWS Control Tower or a landing zone sets baseline guardrails.
  • Lock the root user: MFA, no access keys, root access management features, alarm on root login.
  • Keep a break-glass role with MFA and strong alerting for when SSO is down.

Root alarm

bashShow who signed in as root recently
aws cloudtrail lookup-events --lookup-attributes AttributeKey=Username,AttributeValue=root --max-results 5 \
  --query 'Events[].[EventTime,EventName]' --output table
Check yourself
Why use several accounts?

Accounts limit blast radius, quotas and permissions between workloads and environments.

Section 60 of 93

GuardDuty, Security Hub and Inspector

5 concepts · about 50 minutes

Detection services answer: what is happening, what is vulnerable, and how do we respond. On AWS they are separate services that feed one another.

Goals
  • Enable threat detection with GuardDuty including EKS audit and runtime monitoring
  • Aggregate findings in Security Hub and automate response with EventBridge
  • Scan workloads continuously with Amazon Inspector
60.1

GuardDuty

In plain words

GuardDuty analyses CloudTrail events, VPC flow logs and DNS logs with threat intelligence and machine learning, and reports suspicious behaviour as findings.

The problem it solves

Compromised credentials, crypto mining and data exfiltration look like normal API calls unless something correlates them.

What it does

  • Enabled per Region and account; designate a delegated administrator and auto-enable members across the Organization.
  • No agents for core data sources. Optional protection plans: S3, EKS audit logs, EKS and ECS runtime monitoring, Lambda, RDS login activity, malware scanning of EBS.
  • Findings have severity (low, medium, high), a type like UnauthorizedAccess:IAMUser/InstanceCredentialExfiltration, and affected resources.
  • Billed by volume of analysed events (30 day free trial).

Enable

bashEnable GuardDuty with EKS protection
DET=$(aws guardduty create-detector --enable --query DetectorId --output text)
aws guardduty update-detector --detector-id "$DET" \
  --features '[{"Name":"EKS_AUDIT_LOGS","Status":"ENABLED"},{"Name":"S3_DATA_EVENTS","Status":"ENABLED"},{"Name":"EKS_RUNTIME_MONITORING","Status":"ENABLED","AdditionalConfiguration":[{"Name":"EKS_ADDON_MANAGEMENT","Status":"ENABLED"}]}]'
aws guardduty list-findings --detector-id "$DET" --finding-criteria '{"Criterion":{"severity":{"Gte":7}}}'
Check yourself
Does GuardDuty need agents on instances for its core detection?

No; it reads CloudTrail, flow and DNS logs directly.

60.2

GuardDuty for EKS

In plain words

Two protections cover Kubernetes: EKS audit log monitoring (analyses the API audit stream) and runtime monitoring (an agent add-on watching processes, files and network inside nodes).

The problem it solves

Attacks inside a cluster such as a container escape, a reverse shell or an anonymous API access do not appear in AWS API logs.

What it does

  • Audit log findings include Policy:Kubernetes/AnonymousAccessGranted, PrivilegeEscalation:Kubernetes/PrivilegedContainer.
  • Runtime findings include CryptoCurrency:Runtime/BitcoinTool.B, Execution:Runtime/ReverseShell.
  • Runtime monitoring installs the aws-guardduty-agent EKS add-on; it needs node resources and a VPC endpoint for private clusters.
  • Route findings to a response runbook: isolate the pod with a deny-all NetworkPolicy, snapshot, and rotate credentials.

Isolate a pod

yamlQuarantine NetworkPolicy applied by response automation
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: quarantine
  namespace: shop
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      quarantine: "true"
  policyTypes: ["Ingress", "Egress"]
bashLabel a suspicious pod
kubectl -n shop label pod orders-7d9c quarantine=true --overwrite
Check yourself
Which GuardDuty feature sees a reverse shell inside a container?

EKS runtime monitoring.

60.3

Security Hub

In plain words

Security Hub collects findings from GuardDuty, Inspector, Macie, Config, IAM Access Analyzer and partners into one format and one dashboard, and runs compliance checks against standards.

The problem it solves

Ten tools with ten consoles mean nobody looks at any of them. You need one prioritised list.

What it does

  • Standards: AWS Foundational Security Best Practices, CIS AWS Foundations, PCI DSS, NIST 800-53.
  • AWS Security Finding Format (ASFF) normalises findings; filters and insights group them.
  • Cross-account and cross-Region aggregation to a delegated administrator.
  • Automation rules update or suppress findings; custom actions send findings to EventBridge.
  • Newer Security Hub capabilities add correlation and exposure analysis (check the current feature set).

Commands

bashEnable standards and list failed controls
aws securityhub enable-security-hub --enable-default-standards
aws securityhub get-findings \
  --filters '{"ComplianceStatus":[{"Value":"FAILED","Comparison":"EQUALS"}],"SeverityLabel":[{"Value":"CRITICAL","Comparison":"EQUALS"}]}' \
  --max-items 5 --query 'Findings[].[Title,Resources[0].Id]' --output table
Check yourself
What is ASFF?

The AWS Security Finding Format, a common schema for findings from different tools.

60.4

Amazon Inspector

In plain words

Inspector scans EC2 instances, ECR container images and Lambda functions for software vulnerabilities and unintended network exposure.

The problem it solves

New CVEs are published daily; a point-in-time scan misses them.

What it does

  • Agentless or SSM-based scanning for EC2; ECR enhanced scanning for images; Lambda code and package scanning.
  • Continuous: re-evaluates when new CVEs arrive or software changes.
  • Risk score blends CVSS, exploitability and network reachability.
  • Findings include the package, fixed version and remediation.
  • Suppression rules and delegated administration support organisation-wide use.

CLI

bashEnable and list critical findings
aws inspector2 enable --resource-types EC2 ECR LAMBDA
aws inspector2 list-findings --filter-criteria '{"severity":[{"comparison":"EQUALS","value":"CRITICAL"}]}' \
  --max-results 5 --query 'findings[].[title,packageVulnerabilityDetails.vulnerabilityId]' --output table
Check yourself
What makes Inspector scanning continuous?

It re-evaluates resources when new vulnerabilities are published, not only at scan time.

60.5

Automated response with EventBridge

In plain words

EventBridge rules match findings and trigger Lambda, SSM Automation, Step Functions or notifications.

The problem it solves

A high-severity finding at night should not wait for someone to read a dashboard.

What it does

  • Match on source: aws.guardduty and severity above a threshold, then send to SNS/Chatbot and open a ticket.
  • Safe auto-remediation: disable an access key, attach a deny policy, isolate an instance with a quarantine security group, block a bucket public access.
  • Always log the action and keep a human approval step for destructive changes.
  • Test with GuardDuty sample findings (create-sample-findings).

Rule

jsonEventBridge pattern for high severity GuardDuty findings
{
  "source": ["aws.guardduty"],
  "detail-type": ["GuardDuty Finding"],
  "detail": {"severity": [{"numeric": [">=", 7]}]}
}
bashTest with sample findings
aws guardduty create-sample-findings --detector-id "$DET" --finding-types "UnauthorizedAccess:EC2/SSHBruteForce"
Check yourself
How can you test automation safely?

Generate GuardDuty sample findings and watch the rule fire.

Section 61 of 93

CloudTrail and AWS Config

6 concepts · about 45 minutes

CloudTrail records API calls. Config records resource configuration over time. Together they answer who did it, what changed and whether it is allowed.

Goals
  • Build an organisation trail that is tamper resistant and queryable
  • Use AWS Config rules and conformance packs to detect drift and noncompliance
  • Answer who did what and what changed using Trail, Lake and Config history
61.1

CloudTrail events and trails

In plain words

CloudTrail logs every AWS API call (console, CLI, SDK, other services) with the caller, time, source IP, request and response outcome.

The problem it solves

After an incident or an audit you need proof of who deleted a bucket or opened a security group.

What it does

  • Management events (control plane) are recorded for 90 days in the event history for free; a trail delivers them to S3 permanently.
  • Data events (S3 object access, Lambda invoke, DynamoDB item access) are off by default and billed per volume.
  • Insights events flag unusual API call rates.
  • An organisation trail from the management account covers all accounts and Regions.
  • Enable log file integrity validation and send logs to a dedicated, locked-down log archive account.

Create an organisation trail

bashMulti-Region organisation trail with validation
aws cloudtrail create-trail --name org-trail --s3-bucket-name org-trail-logs-111122223333 \
  --is-multi-region-trail --is-organization-trail --enable-log-file-validation \
  --kms-key-id alias/cloudtrail
aws cloudtrail start-logging --name org-trail
aws cloudtrail lookup-events --lookup-attributes AttributeKey=EventName,AttributeValue=DeleteBucket --max-results 5
Check yourself
How long is CloudTrail event history kept without a trail?

90 days for management events.

61.2

Protecting and querying logs

In plain words

Logs are evidence. Make them immutable and searchable.

The problem it solves

Attackers delete logs, and grepping gigabytes of JSON in S3 is slow.

What it does

  • Bucket policy allows only CloudTrail to write; enable versioning, S3 Object Lock or MFA delete, SSE-KMS and a lifecycle to Glacier.
  • SCP denies cloudtrail:StopLogging and DeleteTrail.
  • CloudTrail Lake is a managed event data store with SQL queries and retention up to years.
  • Alternatively use Athena over the S3 logs with a partitioned table.
  • Alert on sensitive events: root login, ConsoleLogin without MFA, IAM policy changes, CreateAccessKey.

Query

sqlWho deleted security groups last week (CloudTrail Lake)
SELECT eventTime, userIdentity.arn, sourceIPAddress, requestParameters
FROM <event-data-store-id>
WHERE eventName = 'DeleteSecurityGroup'
  AND eventTime > timestamp '2026-10-24 00:00:00'
ORDER BY eventTime DESC
LIMIT 50
Check yourself
Which control stops an administrator from turning logging off?

An SCP denying StopLogging and DeleteTrail, plus Object Lock on the bucket.

61.3

Reading a CloudTrail event

In plain words

Each event is a JSON record. A few fields answer most questions.

The problem it solves

Raw events are verbose and intimidating during an incident.

What it does

  • eventName and eventSource say what was called.
  • userIdentity shows the principal; for assumed roles sessionContext.sessionIssuer shows the underlying role, and for SSO the user name appears in the session name.
  • sourceIPAddress and userAgent identify where it came from.
  • errorCode of AccessDenied shows attempts that failed, which are valuable for detection.
  • requestParameters and responseElements show specifics such as the instance ID.

Example event

jsonTrimmed CloudTrail event
{
  "eventTime": "2026-10-30T08:35:12Z",
  "eventSource": "ec2.amazonaws.com",
  "eventName": "AuthorizeSecurityGroupIngress",
  "userIdentity": {
    "type": "AssumedRole",
    "arn": "arn:aws:sts::111122223333:assumed-role/AWSReservedSSO_Developer_abc123/alice"
  },
  "sourceIPAddress": "203.0.113.10",
  "requestParameters": {"groupId": "sg-0123456789abcdef0", "ipPermissions": {"items": [{"fromPort": 22, "toPort": 22, "ipRanges": {"items": [{"cidrIp": "0.0.0.0/0"}]}}]}}
}
Check yourself
What does sessionIssuer tell you?

Which IAM role an assumed-role session came from.

61.4

AWS Config recorder and history

In plain words

Config records the configuration of supported resources and every change, building a timeline per resource.

The problem it solves

CloudTrail says someone called ModifyDBInstance; it does not give you the full before and after configuration of the database.

What it does

  • A configuration recorder tracks resource types in each Region; a delivery channel sends snapshots and history to S3.
  • get-resource-config-history shows a resource at past times; relationships link a security group to its instances.
  • Advanced queries use SQL-like syntax across resources.
  • An aggregator consolidates accounts and Regions.
  • Config is billed per configuration item recorded, so record only what you need in non-production.

Commands

bashInspect a resource's history and query
aws configservice get-resource-config-history --resource-type AWS::EC2::SecurityGroup \
  --resource-id sg-0123456789abcdef0 --limit 3
aws configservice select-resource-config \
  --expression "SELECT resourceId, resourceType WHERE resourceType = 'AWS::S3::Bucket' AND configuration.publicAccessBlockConfiguration.blockPublicAcls = false"
Check yourself
What does Config give that CloudTrail does not?

The full configuration of a resource over time, not just the API call.

61.5

Config rules, conformance packs and remediation

In plain words

A Config rule evaluates resources as compliant or noncompliant. A conformance pack bundles many rules. Remediation actions fix findings with SSM Automation.

The problem it solves

Policies written in a wiki do not enforce themselves.

What it does

  • Managed rules such as s3-bucket-public-read-prohibited, encrypted-volumes, rds-instance-public-access-check, restricted-ssh.
  • Custom rules use Lambda or Guard policy-as-code.
  • Evaluation is triggered by configuration change or periodically.
  • Remediation can be automatic (for example, enable S3 block public access) or manual approval.
  • Findings flow to Security Hub; organisation conformance packs deploy standards across accounts.

Rule

bashAdd managed rules
aws configservice put-config-rule --config-rule '{
  "ConfigRuleName":"rds-no-public-access",
  "Source":{"Owner":"AWS","SourceIdentifier":"RDS_INSTANCE_PUBLIC_ACCESS_CHECK"}}'
aws configservice describe-compliance-by-config-rule --config-rule-names rds-no-public-access
hclTerraform
resource "aws_config_config_rule" "ebs_encrypted" {
  name = "encrypted-volumes"

  source {
    owner             = "AWS"
    source_identifier = "ENCRYPTED_VOLUMES"
  }
}
Check yourself
How does a custom Guard rule differ from a managed rule?

You write the evaluation logic as policy-as-code, while managed rules are prebuilt.

61.6

Investigation workflow

In plain words

Combine the tools: Config shows what changed, CloudTrail shows who changed it, GuardDuty shows whether it looked malicious.

The problem it solves

Without a routine, teams jump between consoles and lose time.

What it does

  • Start from the resource: Config timeline gives the exact time of change.
  • Query CloudTrail around that timestamp for the actor and source IP.
  • Check GuardDuty and Access Analyzer for related findings.
  • Decide: revert (infrastructure as code apply), revoke credentials, or accept.
  • Record the outcome in the incident ticket and improve the preventive control (SCP, Config rule).

Commands

bashCorrelate by time
aws cloudtrail lookup-events --lookup-attributes AttributeKey=ResourceName,AttributeValue=sg-0123456789abcdef0 \
  --start-time 2026-10-30T08:00:00Z --end-time 2026-10-30T09:00:00Z \
  --query 'Events[].[EventTime,EventName,Username]' --output table
Check yourself
In which order do you use Config and CloudTrail?

Config pinpoints what and when; CloudTrail then identifies who and from where.

Section 62 of 93

WAF, Shield, Macie and edge protection

6 concepts · about 45 minutes

Public applications face bots, injection attempts and floods. Data stores hold personal data. These services add layers around both.

Goals
  • Build WAF web ACLs with managed rules, rate limits and logging
  • Understand Shield Standard and Advanced and the role of CloudFront
  • Find sensitive data in S3 with Macie and apply data protection controls
62.1

AWS WAF web ACLs

In plain words

WAF inspects HTTP requests at an ALB, CloudFront, API Gateway or AppSync and allows, blocks, counts or challenges them based on rules.

The problem it solves

Application layer attacks (SQL injection, XSS, bad bots, scrapers) bypass network firewalls because they look like valid HTTPS.

What it does

  • A web ACL has ordered rules, each with an action; the default action applies if nothing matches.
  • AWS managed rule groups: Core rule set, Known bad inputs, SQL database, IP reputation, Bot Control, Account Takeover Prevention.
  • Rate-based rules limit requests per IP in a window (for example 2000 per 5 minutes).
  • Start new rules in Count mode, review logs, then switch to Block.
  • WAF capacity units (WCU) limit complexity; check the current quota.

Web ACL

hclRegional web ACL with managed rules and a rate limit
resource "aws_wafv2_web_acl" "shop" {
  name  = "shop"
  scope = "REGIONAL"

  default_action {
    allow {}
  }

  rule {
    name     = "aws-common"
    priority = 10
    override_action {
      none {}
    }
    statement {
      managed_rule_group_statement {
        name        = "AWSManagedRulesCommonRuleSet"
        vendor_name = "AWS"
      }
    }
    visibility_config {
      cloudwatch_metrics_enabled = true
      metric_name                = "aws-common"
      sampled_requests_enabled   = true
    }
  }

  rule {
    name     = "rate-limit"
    priority = 20
    action {
      block {}
    }
    statement {
      rate_based_statement {
        limit              = 2000
        aggregate_key_type = "IP"
      }
    }
    visibility_config {
      cloudwatch_metrics_enabled = true
      metric_name                = "rate-limit"
      sampled_requests_enabled   = true
    }
  }

  visibility_config {
    cloudwatch_metrics_enabled = true
    metric_name                = "shop"
    sampled_requests_enabled   = true
  }
}
Check yourself
Why start a new rule in Count mode?

To see what it would block in the logs before risking blocking real users.

62.2

WAF logging and tuning

In plain words

WAF logs every inspected request, including which rule matched, to CloudWatch Logs, S3 or Firehose.

The problem it solves

Managed rules produce false positives, and without logs you cannot tell why a user was blocked.

What it does

  • Log destinations must have names starting with aws-waf-logs-.
  • Redact sensitive fields (authorization headers, cookies) with redacted_fields.
  • Use labels and scope-down statements to exclude paths (for example allow large uploads on /upload).
  • Query blocked requests with Logs Insights; tune with rule exclusions rather than disabling whole groups.
  • Add Bot Control and Fraud Control only where justified; they cost extra.

Query

textLogs Insights query for blocked requests by rule
fields @timestamp, httpRequest.clientIp, httpRequest.uri, terminatingRuleId
| filter action = "BLOCK"
| stats count(*) as hits by terminatingRuleId, httpRequest.uri
| sort hits desc
| limit 20
Check yourself
What lets you keep a managed rule group but allow one path?

A rule exclusion or a scope-down statement.

62.3

AWS Shield

In plain words

Shield protects against DDoS attacks. Standard is automatic and free on all AWS resources; Advanced adds detection tuning, the response team, and cost protection.

The problem it solves

Volumetric floods saturate bandwidth, and application floods exhaust servers.

What it does

  • Standard defends against common network and transport layer (L3/L4) attacks on CloudFront, Route 53, ALB, NLB and Elastic IP.
  • Advanced is a subscription per organisation; protects named resources, gives near real-time metrics, access to the Shield Response Team, and credits for scaling charges during attacks.
  • Best practice: put CloudFront and Route 53 in front, hide origins (allow only CloudFront prefix list), scale on demand, and use WAF rate rules for L7.
  • Design for attack surface reduction: no direct public IPs on nodes, private subnets.

Lock the origin

hclAllow only CloudFront to reach the ALB
data "aws_ec2_managed_prefix_list" "cloudfront" {
  name = "com.amazonaws.global.cloudfront.origin-facing"
}

resource "aws_vpc_security_group_ingress_rule" "from_cloudfront" {
  security_group_id = aws_security_group.alb.id
  prefix_list_id    = data.aws_ec2_managed_prefix_list.cloudfront.id
  ip_protocol       = "tcp"
  from_port         = 443
  to_port           = 443
}
Check yourself
What does Shield Advanced add to Standard?

Tuned detection, access to the response team, and cost protection for attack-driven scaling.

62.4

Network Firewall and security groups

In plain words

Security groups filter by IP and port at the instance or pod level. AWS Network Firewall filters at the VPC edge with domain and signature rules.

The problem it solves

Security groups cannot allow "only *.amazonaws.com" or block known malicious domains for egress.

What it does

  • Security groups are stateful allow lists; reference other groups instead of CIDRs.
  • NACLs are stateless subnet filters; use sparingly.
  • Network Firewall supports stateful rules, domain allow lists (SNI), and Suricata-compatible rules, deployed in a dedicated inspection subnet.
  • Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall blocks lookups to malicious domains.
  • Egress control matters for EKS: restrict pods to required endpoints, since malware needs outbound access.

Domain allow list

jsonNetwork Firewall rule group (domain list)
{
  "RulesSource": {
    "RulesSourceList": {
      "Targets": [".amazonaws.com", ".example.com"],
      "TargetTypes": ["TLS_SNI", "HTTP_HOST"],
      "GeneratedRulesType": "ALLOWLIST"
    }
  }
}
Check yourself
Why is egress filtering valuable?

Compromised workloads need outbound access to download tools or exfiltrate data; blocking it limits damage.

62.5

Amazon Macie

In plain words

Macie scans S3 buckets for sensitive data (personal information, credentials, financial data) using managed and custom identifiers, and reports on bucket security posture.

The problem it solves

You cannot protect data you do not know you have, and a bucket of customer exports can be forgotten.

What it does

  • Inventory of buckets with public access, encryption and sharing status.
  • Sensitive data discovery jobs scan objects; automated discovery samples continuously.
  • Findings (policy and sensitive data) go to Security Hub and EventBridge.
  • Custom data identifiers use regex plus keywords.
  • Cost is per bucket and per GB inspected; scope jobs to relevant buckets.

Job

bashStart a discovery job
aws macie2 enable-macie
aws macie2 create-classification-job --job-type ONE_TIME --name scan-exports \
  --s3-job-definition '{"bucketDefinitions":[{"accountId":"111122223333","buckets":["shop-customer-exports"]}]}'
aws macie2 list-findings --max-results 5
Check yourself
What does Macie examine?

The contents and configuration of S3 buckets to find sensitive data and risky settings.

62.6

Data protection checklist

In plain words

A short list of controls that apply to every data store on a typical EKS application.

The problem it solves

Security is easy to promise and hard to verify; a checklist makes review repeatable.

What it does

  • Encrypt at rest with KMS (RDS, EBS, S3, DynamoDB, EFS) and in transit with TLS; enforce aws:SecureTransport in bucket policies.
  • Block public access at account level for S3.
  • Private subnets and VPC endpoints for AWS APIs; no public database endpoints.
  • Backups in a separate account or Region with immutability.
  • Least privilege IAM with Pod Identity or IRSA, no static keys.
  • Logging: CloudTrail, VPC flow logs, WAF logs, ALB logs, EKS audit logs.

Bucket policy

jsonDeny non-TLS access to a bucket
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Sid": "DenyInsecureTransport",
      "Effect": "Deny",
      "Principal": "*",
      "Action": "s3:*",
      "Resource": ["arn:aws:s3:::shop-customer-exports", "arn:aws:s3:::shop-customer-exports/*"],
      "Condition": {"Bool": {"aws:SecureTransport": "false"}}
    }
  ]
}
Check yourself
Which condition key forces TLS in S3 policies?

aws:SecureTransport.

Section 63 of 93

CloudWatch metrics and alarms

5 concepts · about 45 minutes

CloudWatch is the default telemetry store on AWS. Metrics are cheap time series; alarms turn them into action.

Goals
  • Use namespaces, dimensions, statistics and periods to read metrics correctly
  • Build alarms including composite alarms, anomaly detection and metric math
  • Publish custom metrics and wire alarms to notifications and automation
63.1

Metrics, namespaces and dimensions

In plain words

A metric is a time series identified by a namespace (AWS/RDS), a name (CPUUtilization) and dimensions (key-value labels such as DBInstanceIdentifier=shop-db).

The problem it solves

Hundreds of resources emit data points; you need a consistent way to pick exactly the series you mean.

What it does

  • AWS services publish basic metrics automatically at 1 or 5 minute resolution (some paid, finer).
  • Each unique combination of dimensions is a separate metric.
  • Statistics: Average, Sum, Minimum, Maximum, SampleCount and percentiles (p99).
  • Period is the aggregation window (60 seconds minimum, or 1 second for high-resolution custom metrics).
  • Retention: 1 minute data for 15 days, 5 minute data for 63 days, 1 hour data for 455 days (check the current retention).

Read metrics

bashQuery a metric with the CLI
aws cloudwatch list-metrics --namespace AWS/ApplicationELB --metric-name TargetResponseTime --max-items 3
aws cloudwatch get-metric-statistics --namespace AWS/ApplicationELB --metric-name TargetResponseTime \
  --dimensions Name=LoadBalancer,Value=app/shop/50dc6c495c0c9188 \
  --start-time "$(date -u -v-1H +%FT%TZ)" --end-time "$(date -u +%FT%TZ)" \
  --period 300 --extended-statistics p99
Check yourself
Why are two metrics with different dimensions distinct series?

Each dimension combination defines its own time series.

63.2

Alarms

In plain words

An alarm watches one metric (or a math expression) and changes state between OK, ALARM and INSUFFICIENT_DATA based on a threshold over several periods.

The problem it solves

Dashboards need a human watching. Alarms notify or act when thresholds are crossed.

What it does

  • EvaluationPeriods and DatapointsToAlarm (M out of N) reduce flapping.
  • TreatMissingData decides what missing data means: notBreaching, breaching, ignore, missing.
  • Actions: SNS topics, Auto Scaling policies, EC2 actions, Systems Manager OpsItems, Incident Manager.
  • Alarm on symptoms users feel (latency, error rate), not only causes (CPU).

Terraform

hcl5xx rate alarm on the ALB
resource "aws_cloudwatch_metric_alarm" "alb_5xx" {
  alarm_name          = "shop-alb-5xx"
  namespace           = "AWS/ApplicationELB"
  metric_name         = "HTTPCode_Target_5XX_Count"
  statistic           = "Sum"
  period              = 60
  evaluation_periods  = 5
  datapoints_to_alarm = 3
  threshold           = 10
  comparison_operator = "GreaterThanOrEqualToThreshold"
  treat_missing_data  = "notBreaching"
  dimensions = {
    LoadBalancer = var.alb_arn_suffix
  }
  alarm_actions = [aws_sns_topic.ops.arn]
  ok_actions    = [aws_sns_topic.ops.arn]
}
Check yourself
What does 3 datapoints out of 5 mean?

The alarm fires when at least 3 of the last 5 periods breach the threshold.

63.3

Metric math, anomaly detection and composite alarms

In plain words

Metric math computes new series, such as an error rate, from other metrics. Anomaly detection learns a normal band. Composite alarms combine alarms with AND/OR.

The problem it solves

Raw counts mislead (10 errors is fine at 1,000,000 requests and bad at 100), and many alarms firing together create noise.

What it does

  • Expression 100 * m1 / m2 gives error percentage from 5xx count and request count.
  • Anomaly detection alarms fire when a metric leaves its expected band, which suits seasonal traffic.
  • Composite: ALARM(high-latency) AND ALARM(high-errors) pages once, while individual alarms stay silent.
  • Use SEARCH expressions for fleet-wide dashboards.

Alarm JSON

jsonError percentage alarm input (put-metric-alarm --cli-input-json)
{
  "AlarmName": "shop-error-rate",
  "ComparisonOperator": "GreaterThanThreshold",
  "Threshold": 1.0,
  "EvaluationPeriods": 5,
  "DatapointsToAlarm": 3,
  "TreatMissingData": "notBreaching",
  "Metrics": [
    {"Id": "e1", "Expression": "100 * m1 / m2", "Label": "ErrorRate", "ReturnData": true},
    {"Id": "m1", "ReturnData": false, "MetricStat": {"Metric": {"Namespace": "AWS/ApplicationELB", "MetricName": "HTTPCode_Target_5XX_Count", "Dimensions": [{"Name": "LoadBalancer", "Value": "app/shop/50dc6c495c0c9188"}]}, "Period": 60, "Stat": "Sum"}},
    {"Id": "m2", "ReturnData": false, "MetricStat": {"Metric": {"Namespace": "AWS/ApplicationELB", "MetricName": "RequestCount", "Dimensions": [{"Name": "LoadBalancer", "Value": "app/shop/50dc6c495c0c9188"}]}, "Period": 60, "Stat": "Sum"}}
  ]
}
Check yourself
Why prefer a rate alarm over a raw count?

A rate stays meaningful as traffic changes, avoiding false alarms at peaks and missed ones at quiet times.

63.4

Custom metrics and the embedded metric format

In plain words

Applications can publish their own metrics with PutMetricData or by writing JSON logs in the Embedded Metric Format (EMF), which CloudWatch turns into metrics.

The problem it solves

Business signals such as orders per minute or queue depth are not in AWS metrics.

What it does

  • put-metric-data takes namespace, name, dimensions, value and unit; each unique dimension set is billed as a metric, so avoid high-cardinality dimensions like user ID.
  • EMF lines printed to stdout (picked up by the CloudWatch agent or Lambda) generate metrics without extra API calls.
  • Prometheus metrics can be scraped by the CloudWatch agent or sent to Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus.
  • Keep a small, reviewed set of SLO metrics: request rate, errors, latency, saturation.

Publish

bashPublish a custom metric
aws cloudwatch put-metric-data --namespace Shop --metric-name OrdersPlaced \
  --dimensions Environment=prod --value 12 --unit Count
jsonEMF log line
{
  "_aws": {
    "Timestamp": 1761826800000,
    "CloudWatchMetrics": [
      {"Namespace": "Shop", "Dimensions": [["Environment"]], "Metrics": [{"Name": "OrdersPlaced", "Unit": "Count"}]}
    ]
  },
  "Environment": "prod",
  "OrdersPlaced": 12
}
Check yourself
Why avoid user IDs as dimensions?

Each unique dimension value creates a new billable metric, causing huge cost and unusable dashboards.

63.5

Dashboards and notification routing

In plain words

Dashboards show golden signals across services; SNS and AWS Chatbot route alarms to people.

The problem it solves

During an incident people need one place to see health and the right channel to learn about failures.

What it does

  • Build a dashboard per service: traffic, errors, latency (p50 and p99), saturation, plus dependencies (RDS, Redis).
  • SNS topics fan out to email, SMS, HTTPS, Lambda, and AWS Chatbot for Slack or Teams.
  • Separate topics by severity: page for customer impact, ticket for the rest.
  • Cross-account observability links monitoring and workload accounts into one view.
  • Define dashboards as code (JSON or Terraform) so they are reviewed and recreated.

Topic

bashSNS topic with email subscription
aws sns create-topic --name ops-alerts
aws sns subscribe --topic-arn arn:aws:sns:us-east-1:111122223333:ops-alerts --protocol email --notification-endpoint oncall@example.com
aws cloudwatch put-dashboard --dashboard-name shop --dashboard-body file://dashboard.json
Check yourself
What should page a human?

Customer-impacting symptoms such as error rate or latency SLO breaches, not every resource warning.

← PreviousNext →
Section 64 of 93

CloudWatch Logs, Logs Insights and Container Insights

5 concepts · about 50 minutes

Logs answer why. On EKS the usual path is stdout, to a node agent, to CloudWatch Logs, with queries and metric filters on top.

Goals
  • Ship container logs to CloudWatch Logs and control retention and cost
  • Query logs with Logs Insights and turn patterns into metrics
  • Enable Container Insights and know when to choose Prometheus and Grafana instead
64.1

Log groups, streams and retention

In plain words

Logs are stored in log groups (one per application or source) that contain log streams (one per source instance). Retention and encryption are set on the group.

The problem it solves

Default retention is never expire, which silently builds large bills.

What it does

  • Set a retention period on every group (1 day to 10 years).
  • Encrypt with a KMS key when required.
  • Log classes: Standard (full features) and Infrequent Access (cheaper ingestion, fewer features).
  • Ingestion is the main cost, followed by storage; reduce noise with log levels and sampling.
  • Subscription filters stream logs to Kinesis, Firehose or Lambda; export to S3 for long-term archive.

Set retention everywhere

bashFind groups with no retention and fix them
aws logs describe-log-groups --query 'logGroups[?retentionInDays==`null`].logGroupName' --output text
aws logs put-retention-policy --log-group-name /aws/eks/shop-prod/cluster --retention-in-days 30
Check yourself
What is the usual hidden cost of CloudWatch Logs?

Log groups with no retention accumulate storage forever, and high-volume ingestion is billed per GB.

64.2

Shipping container logs from EKS

In plain words

Pods write to stdout. A DaemonSet agent (Fluent Bit, or the CloudWatch agent from the Observability add-on) reads node log files and ships them with Kubernetes metadata.

The problem it solves

Without an agent, logs vanish when pods are rescheduled.

What it does

  • The amazon-cloudwatch-observability add-on installs the CloudWatch agent and Fluent Bit and creates groups under /aws/containerinsights/<cluster>/.
  • Agents need an IAM role (CloudWatchAgentServerPolicy) via Pod Identity or IRSA.
  • Write structured JSON logs with level, trace ID and request ID.
  • Fargate uses the built-in log router configured via a ConfigMap.
  • Alternatives: ship to OpenSearch, Grafana Loki or a third party using Fluent Bit outputs.

Install

bashObservability add-on
aws eks create-addon --cluster-name shop-prod --addon-name amazon-cloudwatch-observability \
  --pod-identity-associations serviceAccount=cloudwatch-agent,roleArn=arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/cloudwatch-agent
kubectl -n amazon-cloudwatch get pods
Check yourself
Why log JSON?

Logs Insights and other tools can then filter by fields without brittle text parsing.

64.3

Logs Insights queries

In plain words

Logs Insights is an interactive query language for log groups: filter, parse, aggregate, sort.

The problem it solves

Grepping across many pods and streams is slow and misses context.

What it does

  • Commands: fields, filter, parse, stats, sort, limit, dedup, pattern.
  • Auto-discovers JSON fields in the log message (@message) so you can filter on level directly.
  • You pay per GB scanned, so narrow the time range and the group list.
  • Save queries and add them to dashboards; use anomaly or pattern to find new error shapes.

Queries

textTop errors by service in the last hour
fields @timestamp, kubernetes.labels.app as app, level, msg
| filter level = "error"
| stats count(*) as errors by app, msg
| sort errors desc
| limit 20
textp99 latency from request logs
fields @timestamp, duration_ms
| filter ispresent(duration_ms)
| stats pct(duration_ms, 99) as p99, avg(duration_ms) as avg by bin(5m)
bashRun a query from the CLI
aws logs start-query --log-group-name /aws/containerinsights/shop-prod/application \
  --start-time $(date -u -v-1H +%s) --end-time $(date -u +%s) \
  --query-string 'fields @timestamp, @message | filter @message like /error/ | limit 20'
Check yourself
What drives Logs Insights cost?

The amount of log data scanned by each query.

64.4

Metric filters and subscription filters

In plain words

A metric filter turns matching log lines into a CloudWatch metric. A subscription filter streams logs in near real time to another service.

The problem it solves

Applications log errors but do not publish metrics, so you cannot alarm on them.

What it does

  • Pattern like { $.level = "error" } increments a metric AppErrors; then alarm on it.
  • Metric filters apply to new events only, with values from JSON fields if needed.
  • Subscription filters (up to two per group) send to Firehose for S3/OpenSearch or Lambda for processing; use cross-account destinations to centralise logs.
  • Data protection policies can mask sensitive data patterns automatically.

Create

bashMetric filter for errors
aws logs put-metric-filter --log-group-name /aws/containerinsights/shop-prod/application \
  --filter-name app-errors --filter-pattern '{ $.level = "error" }' \
  --metric-transformations metricName=AppErrors,metricNamespace=Shop,metricValue=1,defaultValue=0
Check yourself
Do metric filters process historical logs?

No, only events ingested after the filter exists.

64.5

Container Insights

In plain words

Container Insights collects cluster, node, pod and container metrics (CPU, memory, network, restarts) and presents them in prebuilt dashboards, with optional enhanced observability for EKS.

The problem it solves

kubectl top shows only current values and no history; you need trends and per-namespace views.

What it does

  • Metrics land in the ContainerInsights namespace with dimensions ClusterName, Namespace, PodName, NodeName.
  • Enhanced observability adds more detail (per-container, control plane metrics, performance dashboards) at higher metric cost.
  • Cost control: metrics per pod multiply with churn; for large clusters consider Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus plus Managed Grafana, or a self-hosted stack.
  • Pair with Application Signals or OpenTelemetry (ADOT) for traces and service maps; X-Ray for tracing.
Observability stack
OptionContainer Insights
Choose whenquick start, AWS native alarms
Avoid whenvery high pod churn and cardinality
OptionPrometheus with AMP
Choose whenPromQL, SLOs, portable across clouds
Avoid whenyou want zero setup
OptionOpenTelemetry (ADOT)
Choose whentraces and metrics from apps
Avoid whenyou only need node metrics

Alarm on pod restarts

bashAlarm on container restarts
aws cloudwatch put-metric-alarm --alarm-name shop-pod-restarts \
  --namespace ContainerInsights --metric-name pod_number_of_container_restarts \
  --dimensions Name=ClusterName,Value=shop-prod Name=Namespace,Value=shop \
  --statistic Maximum --period 300 --evaluation-periods 1 --threshold 3 \
  --comparison-operator GreaterThanThreshold --alarm-actions arn:aws:sns:us-east-1:111122223333:ops-alerts
Check yourself
Why can Container Insights get expensive?

Metrics are produced per pod and per container, so churn and cardinality increase the metric count.
