Section 65 of 93

Well-Architected framework and the three-tier shop

5 concepts · about 45 minutes

The AWS Well-Architected Framework is a structured way to ask whether a workload is built well. It is not a certification and not a checklist to pass; it is a review that finds risks and ranks them.

Goals
  • Name the six pillars and the questions each asks
  • Run a Well-Architected review and track improvements
  • Describe the reference three-tier EKS application used in this section
65.1

The six pillars

In plain words

Six pillars group the questions: Operational Excellence, Security, Reliability, Performance Efficiency, Cost Optimization and Sustainability.

The problem it solves

Teams optimise what hurts today (an outage, a bill) and ignore the other dimensions until they fail.

What it does

  • Operational Excellence: run and improve with automation, small changes and learning from failure.
  • Security: protect data, identity and infrastructure; detect and respond.
  • Reliability: recover from failure and meet demand; design for failure.
  • Performance Efficiency: use the right resources and keep them right as needs change.
  • Cost Optimization: deliver value at the lowest price point; know where money goes.
  • Sustainability: reduce environmental impact through efficient use.
  • Trade-offs are explicit: more redundancy costs more; more controls slow delivery.

Tooling

bashWorkload reviews from the CLI
aws wellarchitected list-workloads --query 'WorkloadSummaries[].[WorkloadName,RiskCounts]'
aws wellarchitected list-lens-reviews --workload-id 0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef
Check yourself
Is Well-Architected a pass or fail audit?

No; it is a review that identifies and prioritises risks and trade-offs.

65.2

How a review works

In plain words

You pick a workload, answer the lens questions with your team, see high and medium risk items, and create an improvement plan.

The problem it solves

Reviews that are one-off documents get stale; the value is in repeating them.

What it does

  • The AWS Well-Architected Tool stores workloads, answers, risks and milestones; lenses include the Framework, Serverless, SaaS, Container Build, and others.
  • Review at design time, before launch, and at least yearly or after major changes.
  • Work in small sessions with the people who run the system, not only architects.
  • Convert each high risk item into a ticket with an owner and date.
  • Use Trusted Advisor, Config and Security Hub for automated evidence.

Check automated signals

bashTrusted Advisor checks via Support API (Business support or higher)
aws support describe-trusted-advisor-checks --language en --query 'checks[?category==`security`].[id,name]' --output table
Check yourself
How often should you repeat a review?

At least yearly and after major architecture changes.

65.3

The reference application

In plain words

Throughout this section the example is a shop with a web tier, an API tier and a data tier, running on EKS in a three-AZ VPC.

The problem it solves

Principles are abstract until they are applied to a concrete system with real services.

What it does

  • Edge: Route 53, CloudFront, WAF, ACM.
  • Web tier: ALB in public subnets, web pods in private subnets.
  • API tier: orders, catalog pods, Pod Identity for AWS access, ExternalDNS, cert-manager.
  • Data tier: Aurora PostgreSQL, ElastiCache, DynamoDB for sessions, S3 for media, in isolated subnets.
  • Platform: EKS on managed node group plus Karpenter, ECR, CloudWatch, GuardDuty, Security Hub.

Network layout

hclThree-AZ VPC with tiered subnets
module "vpc" {
  source  = "terraform-aws-modules/vpc/aws"
  version = "~> 5.0"

  name = "shop-prod"
  cidr = "10.20.0.0/16"
  azs  = ["us-east-1a", "us-east-1b", "us-east-1c"]

  public_subnets   = ["10.20.0.0/24", "10.20.1.0/24", "10.20.2.0/24"]
  private_subnets  = ["10.20.16.0/20", "10.20.32.0/20", "10.20.48.0/20"]
  database_subnets = ["10.20.64.0/24", "10.20.65.0/24", "10.20.66.0/24"]

  enable_nat_gateway     = true
  one_nat_gateway_per_az = true

  public_subnet_tags  = { "kubernetes.io/role/elb" = 1 }
  private_subnet_tags = { "kubernetes.io/role/internal-elb" = 1, "karpenter.sh/discovery" = "shop-prod" }
}
Check yourself
Where do database instances live?

In isolated database subnets with no route to the internet.

65.4

Operational excellence applied

In plain words

Make every change small, automated, observable and reversible.

The problem it solves

Manual changes cause outages and cannot be reviewed or repeated.

What it does

  • Infrastructure as code (Terraform) and GitOps (Argo CD or Flux) with pull requests.
  • CI pipeline: build image, scan, push to ECR with immutable tag, deploy to staging, run smoke tests, promote.
  • Observability: logs, metrics, traces, SLOs with alerts on symptoms.
  • Runbooks linked from alarms; game days; blameless post-incident reviews.
  • Progressive delivery (rolling, canary) with automatic rollback on SLO breach.

Argo CD application

yamlGitOps app for the shop
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Application
metadata:
  name: shop-prod
  namespace: argocd
spec:
  project: default
  source:
    repoURL: https://github.com/example/shop-config.git
    targetRevision: main
    path: overlays/prod
  destination:
    server: https://kubernetes.default.svc
    namespace: shop
  syncPolicy:
    automated:
      prune: true
      selfHeal: true
Check yourself
Why prefer pull requests for infrastructure changes?

They give review, history and the ability to revert a known state.

65.5

Security applied

In plain words

Apply least privilege and defence in depth at each tier.

The problem it solves

A single compromised pod or leaked key should not expose the database or the account.

What it does

  • Identity: SSO for people, Pod Identity for pods, no long-lived keys, permission boundaries, SCPs.
  • Network: private subnets, security groups for pods, default-deny NetworkPolicies, VPC endpoints, WAF and Shield at the edge.
  • Data: KMS everywhere, TLS in transit, Secrets Manager via External Secrets, S3 block public access.
  • Detection: CloudTrail, Config, GuardDuty with EKS protections, Security Hub, Inspector for images.
  • Response: runbooks and automated quarantine for high severity findings.

Pod security

yamlPod Security Admission labels on the namespace
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: shop
  labels:
    pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: restricted
    pod-security.kubernetes.io/audit: restricted
    pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn: restricted
Check yourself
Which Kubernetes mechanism enforces non-root, no privileged pods per namespace?

Pod Security Admission, with the restricted profile.

Section 66 of 93

Reliability, performance, cost and sustainability in the shop

6 concepts · about 50 minutes

Failures are normal: instances die, deployments break, AZs degrade. Reliability is the discipline of making those events boring.

Goals
  • Design a three-tier EKS workload that survives instance, pod and AZ failure
  • Scale pods, nodes and data tier with the right signals
  • Apply cost and sustainability levers without hurting reliability
66.1

Failure domains and static stability

In plain words

A failure domain is the largest thing that fails together: a pod, a node, an AZ, a Region, an account. Static stability means the system keeps working during a failure without needing new capacity or manual action.

The problem it solves

Systems that need to launch new capacity during an AZ outage fail exactly when the control plane and APIs are busiest.

What it does

  • Run at least three replicas across three AZs with topology spread, so losing one AZ leaves two thirds capacity.
  • Over-provision to survive an AZ loss: size each of three zones at 50 percent utilisation or use headroom (pause pods).
  • Avoid dependence on the control plane at failure time (for example, pre-provisioned NAT per AZ, pre-created replicas).
  • Keep zonal affinity: ALB cross-zone is on, but internal calls prefer same-zone to cut latency and cost.

Spread and headroom

yamlDeployment spread across zones and nodes
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: orders
  namespace: shop
spec:
  replicas: 6
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: orders
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: orders
    spec:
      topologySpreadConstraints:
        - maxSkew: 1
          topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
          whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule
          labelSelector:
            matchLabels:
              app: orders
        - maxSkew: 1
          topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname
          whenUnsatisfiable: ScheduleAnyway
          labelSelector:
            matchLabels:
              app: orders
      containers:
        - name: orders
          image: nginx:1.27
          resources:
            requests: {cpu: 500m, memory: 512Mi}
            limits: {memory: 512Mi}
Check yourself
What does static stability mean?

The workload continues to operate during a failure without launching new capacity or manual intervention.

66.2

Health, retries and graceful degradation

In plain words

Probes tell Kubernetes what is healthy; timeouts, retries with backoff and circuit breakers stop one failure from spreading.

The problem it solves

A slow dependency without timeouts exhausts threads in every caller and a minor issue becomes a full outage.

What it does

  • Readiness removes a pod from Service endpoints; liveness restarts a stuck container; startup protects slow starts. Do not put dependency checks in liveness.
  • Timeouts on every network call, retries only for idempotent operations, with exponential backoff and jitter, and retry budgets.
  • Circuit breakers and bulkheads; degrade features (cached catalog, queued orders) instead of failing whole requests.
  • Queues (SQS) decouple order intake from processing; use DLQs for poison messages.

Probes

yamlProbes for a service
containers:
  - name: orders
    image: nginx:1.27
    startupProbe:
      httpGet: {path: /healthz, port: 8080}
      failureThreshold: 30
      periodSeconds: 2
    readinessProbe:
      httpGet: {path: /ready, port: 8080}
      periodSeconds: 5
    livenessProbe:
      httpGet: {path: /healthz, port: 8080}
      periodSeconds: 10
      failureThreshold: 3
Check yourself
Why not check the database in a liveness probe?

A database outage would restart every pod and make the incident worse.

66.3

Scaling the tiers

In plain words

Scale pods with HPA (or KEDA for event signals), nodes with Karpenter, and data with replicas, caching and capacity settings.

The problem it solves

Traffic changes by hour and by campaign. Static sizing wastes money or fails at peak.

What it does

  • HPA on CPU, memory or custom metrics (requests per second via Prometheus adapter or KEDA).
  • KEDA scales to zero on SQS queue depth or schedules.
  • Karpenter adds nodes in about a minute; use low-priority pause pods for headroom.
  • Aurora readers scale reads (Application Auto Scaling for Aurora replicas); Serverless v2 scales compute.
  • ElastiCache and CloudFront offload reads; DynamoDB on-demand absorbs spikes.

HPA

yamlHPA on CPU with sensible bounds
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata:
  name: web
  namespace: shop
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    name: web
  minReplicas: 3
  maxReplicas: 30
  metrics:
    - type: Resource
      resource:
        name: cpu
        target:
          type: Utilization
          averageUtilization: 60
  behavior:
    scaleDown:
      stabilizationWindowSeconds: 300
Check yourself
What gives headroom while Karpenter launches nodes?

Low-priority pause pods that are evicted when real pods need the space.

66.4

Performance efficiency

In plain words

Choose the right resource type, measure, and keep reviewing as AWS releases new options.

The problem it solves

Defaults and old instance types drift out of line with the workload.

What it does

  • Use Graviton (arm64) instances for better price-performance where images support it.
  • Use CloudFront for static and cacheable content; ElastiCache for hot reads; S3 for media; gp3 volumes with explicit IOPS.
  • Set requests from measured usage (VPA recommendations); avoid CPU limits that throttle; keep memory limits equal to requests for predictability.
  • Load test before launch with realistic data and track p99, not only averages.
  • Use Performance Insights for SQL, X-Ray or OpenTelemetry traces for service latency.

Load test

bashQuick load test against staging
# k6, hey, or wrk are common choices
hey -z 60s -c 50 https://staging.shop.example.com/api/products
Check yourself
Why track p99 latency rather than the average?

Averages hide the slow tail that real users experience.

66.5

Cost and sustainability levers

In plain words

Cost and sustainability mostly push the same way: use less, and use it efficiently.

The problem it solves

Idle capacity costs money and energy. Unbounded logs and cross-AZ chatter add hidden spend.

What it does

  • Right-size and consolidate with Karpenter; use Spot for stateless pools; Graviton for efficiency.
  • Scale non-production to zero outside working hours.
  • Lifecycle S3 data to cheaper tiers; set log retention; expire old images.
  • Reduce data transfer: VPC endpoints, same-zone routing where possible, CloudFront.
  • Choose Regions with lower carbon intensity when latency and data residency allow.
  • Measure with the Customer Carbon Footprint Tool and cost allocation tags.

Scale dev to zero overnight

yamlKEDA cron scaler for a dev namespace
apiVersion: keda.sh/v1alpha1
kind: ScaledObject
metadata:
  name: web-office-hours
  namespace: shop-dev
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    name: web
  minReplicaCount: 0
  maxReplicaCount: 3
  triggers:
    - type: cron
      metadata:
        timezone: Asia/Kolkata
        start: 0 9 * * 1-5
        end: 0 19 * * 1-5
        desiredReplicas: "2"
Check yourself
Name one change that cuts both cost and energy use.

Right-sizing or removing idle capacity.

66.6

Pillar trade-offs and a review checklist

In plain words

Pillars compete: more redundancy raises cost, more controls slow releases. Decide per workload and write it down.

The problem it solves

Unspoken trade-offs become surprises in incidents and bills.

What it does

  • Tier workloads: tier 0 (payments, login) gets multi-AZ, tested DR, strict change control; tier 2 (internal tools) gets cheaper, simpler designs.
  • Record decisions in short architecture decision records (ADRs).
  • Revisit decisions at each review or incident.
Spend on resilience
OptionWarm standby
Choose whenrevenue loss per minute is high
Avoid whenthe app tolerates hours of downtime
OptionBackup and restore
Choose whenthe system is internal or rebuilt easily
Avoid whenRTO is under an hour

Section 67 of 93

Multi-AZ design for the three-tier shop

6 concepts · about 50 minutes

Availability Zones are separate data centre groups within a Region. Using three of them is the standard way to survive a facility problem without leaving the Region.

Goals
  • Lay out subnets, NAT, load balancers and nodes so one AZ can fail
  • Handle AZ failure in the data tier and avoid cross-AZ traffic costs
  • Test AZ loss with fault injection
67.1

What an AZ gives you

In plain words

An AZ is one or more data centres with independent power, cooling and networking, connected to others in the Region by fast links.

The problem it solves

A single data centre fault, power event or network problem must not take the application down.

What it does

  • Latency between AZs is low (single-digit milliseconds) so synchronous replication (Multi-AZ RDS, Aurora storage) is possible.
  • AZ names are per account mapped to physical zones; use AZ IDs (use1-az1) when coordinating across accounts.
  • Not all services are zonal: S3, DynamoDB, SQS are regional; EC2, EBS, NAT Gateway, subnets are zonal.
  • Regional services still have their own failure modes; check their SLAs.

List zones

bashZones and their IDs
aws ec2 describe-availability-zones --query 'AvailabilityZones[].[ZoneName,ZoneId,State]' --output table
Check yourself
Why use AZ IDs in cross-account work?

AZ names map to different physical zones in different accounts, but IDs are consistent.

67.2

Network layout across AZs

In plain words

Replicate each subnet tier in every AZ, give each AZ its own NAT Gateway, and route private subnets to the NAT in the same AZ.

The problem it solves

One NAT Gateway for the VPC is a single point of failure and a cross-AZ data cost.

What it does

  • Public subnets: ALB, NAT Gateways. Private subnets: nodes and pods. Database subnets: Aurora, ElastiCache.
  • One route table per private subnet pointing at the NAT in the same AZ.
  • Gateway endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB; interface endpoints for ECR, STS, Secrets Manager, CloudWatch Logs reduce NAT traffic.
  • ALB spans all AZs; enable cross-zone load balancing (default on for ALB).

Terraform routes

hclPrivate route per AZ to its own NAT
resource "aws_route" "private_default" {
  count                  = length(var.azs)
  route_table_id         = aws_route_table.private[count.index].id
  destination_cidr_block = "0.0.0.0/0"
  nat_gateway_id         = aws_nat_gateway.this[count.index].id
}

resource "aws_vpc_endpoint" "s3" {
  vpc_id            = var.vpc_id
  service_name      = "com.amazonaws.us-east-1.s3"
  vpc_endpoint_type = "Gateway"
  route_table_ids   = aws_route_table.private[*].id
}
Check yourself
Why one NAT Gateway per AZ?

It avoids a single point of failure and cross-AZ data processing for egress.

67.3

Compute and pod placement

In plain words

Spread nodes and pods across all AZs, keep spare capacity in each, and make volumes zone-aware.

The problem it solves

An EBS-backed pod cannot move to another AZ, and a node group confined to one AZ cannot reschedule after a failure.

What it does

  • Managed node groups and Karpenter span all subnets of the cluster; use topology spread on workloads.
  • PodDisruptionBudgets protect during drains; the AZ failure itself is an involuntary disruption.
  • For stateful sets on EBS, run multiple replicas across zones with application-level replication; the PV stays in its zone.
  • Use topology.kubernetes.io/zone labels for zone-aware routing; Kubernetes Topology Aware Routing (service.kubernetes.io/topology-mode: Auto) keeps traffic in-zone when endpoints are balanced.
  • Test: cordon and drain all nodes of one AZ in staging.

Topology aware routing

yamlKeep service traffic in-zone when possible
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: orders
  namespace: shop
  annotations:
    service.kubernetes.io/topology-mode: Auto
spec:
  selector:
    app: orders
  ports:
    - port: 80
      targetPort: 8080
Check yourself
Can an EBS volume follow a pod to another AZ?

No; an EBS volume is bound to one AZ.

67.4

Data tier failure behaviour

In plain words

Each data service handles AZ loss differently; know the recovery time and client behaviour of each.

The problem it solves

Assuming everything fails over instantly leads to long outages from DNS caching, connection pools and cold caches.

What it does

  • Aurora: reader promoted, service typically restored in under 60 seconds and often under 30; with no reader the instance is recreated, which AWS says typically takes under 10 minutes. Clients must reconnect to the cluster endpoint.
  • RDS Multi-AZ instance: standby promoted, typically 60 to 120 seconds (RDS user guide), via a DNS change.
  • ElastiCache with Multi-AZ: replica promoted; cache starts partially warm; apps must tolerate misses.
  • DynamoDB, S3, SQS: regionally replicated, no action needed.
  • EFS: regional; mount targets in each AZ; clients use the local AZ target.
  • Kafka (MSK): replication factor 3 with min.insync.replicas=2 across AZs.

Test failover

bashRehearse database failover in staging
aws rds failover-db-cluster --db-cluster-identifier shop-aurora-staging
aws elasticache test-failover --replication-group-id shop-cache-staging --node-group-id 0001
Check yourself
Why do clients matter during failover?

DNS caching, connection pools and retry logic decide how fast the application actually recovers.

67.5

Cross-AZ traffic costs and balance

In plain words

Traffic between AZs is billed per GB in each direction. Multi-AZ designs must watch chatty paths.

The problem it solves

A cluster that spreads microservice calls randomly can generate a large cross-AZ bill without any failure.

What it does

  • Data transfer between AZs in the same Region has a per-GB charge (check current pricing); within an AZ over private IPs it is free.
  • Sources of cross-AZ traffic: service-to-service calls, ALB cross-zone, replication, NAT from another AZ, Kafka consumers.
  • Reduce: Topology Aware Routing, keep consumers in the same AZ as brokers when possible (rack-aware fetching), same-AZ NAT, caching.
  • Do not sacrifice availability to save these costs for tier 0 services; measure first with VPC Flow Logs and Cost Explorer usage types (DataTransfer-Regional-Bytes).

Find it

bashCross-AZ spend in Cost Explorer
aws ce get-cost-and-usage --time-period Start=2026-10-01,End=2026-10-31 --granularity MONTHLY \
  --metrics UnblendedCost \
  --filter '{"Dimensions":{"Key":"USAGE_TYPE_GROUP","Values":["EC2: Data Transfer - Inter AZ"]}}'
Check yourself
Name two sources of hidden cross-AZ traffic.

Service calls spread across zones, and cross-zone load balancing or replication.

67.6

Fault injection and game days

In plain words

Prove the design works by breaking it on purpose in a controlled way.

The problem it solves

Untested redundancy often fails because of a missed dependency, a wrong timeout or a quota.

What it does

  • AWS Fault Injection Service (FIS) runs experiments such as stopping instances, throttling APIs, network disruption between subnets, and pod faults on EKS.
  • Use stop conditions linked to CloudWatch alarms so an experiment aborts if customers are affected.
  • Start in staging; define a hypothesis (error rate stays under 1 percent), run, learn, fix.
  • AWS Resilience Hub assesses an application against RTO and RPO targets.

Experiment template

jsonFIS template pausing network to one subnet (sketch)
{
  "description": "Disrupt connectivity of subnet in AZ b",
  "targets": {"subnets": {"resourceType": "aws:ec2:subnet", "resourceTags": {"Name": "shop-private-b"}, "selectionMode": "ALL"}},
  "actions": {"disrupt": {"actionId": "aws:network:disrupt-connectivity", "parameters": {"scope": "all", "duration": "PT5M"}, "targets": {"Subnets": "subnets"}}},
  "stopConditions": [{"source": "aws:cloudwatch:alarm", "value": "arn:aws:cloudwatch:us-east-1:111122223333:alarm:shop-error-rate"}],
  "roleArn": "arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/fis-experiment"
}
Check yourself
What is a stop condition in FIS?

An alarm that aborts the experiment if customer impact appears.

Section 68 of 93

Disaster recovery patterns

6 concepts · about 55 minutes

Multi-AZ covers a data centre failure. Disaster recovery covers losing a Region, an account compromise, ransomware or a bad deployment that corrupts data.

Goals
  • Define RTO and RPO and choose among backup and restore, pilot light, warm standby and active-active
  • Design DR for the EKS shop including data replication and traffic failover
  • Rehearse failover with a runbook and know the failback steps
68.1

RTO, RPO and the DR spectrum

In plain words

RPO (recovery point objective) is how much data you can lose, measured in time. RTO (recovery time objective) is how long recovery may take. Lower targets cost more.

The problem it solves

Without numbers, teams overbuild everything or discover too late that recovery takes days.

What it does

  • Get the targets from the business for each service tier, then pick the cheapest pattern that meets them.
  • AWS describes four strategies in increasing cost and speed: backup and restore, pilot light, warm standby, multi-site active-active.
  • Include dependencies: DNS, identity, secrets, container images, certificates, CI/CD, and people.
  • Also plan for non-regional disasters: account takeover, deletion, corrupted data. These need immutable backups in another account.

Record targets

yamlService tier targets (example)
tiers:
  tier0:
    services: [checkout, login]
    rpo: 1 minute
    rto: 15 minutes
    strategy: warm-standby
  tier1:
    services: [catalog, search]
    rpo: 15 minutes
    rto: 2 hours
    strategy: pilot-light
  tier2:
    services: [reports]
    rpo: 24 hours
    rto: 24 hours
    strategy: backup-restore
Check yourself
What does RPO measure?

The maximum acceptable amount of data loss, expressed as time.

68.2

Backup and restore

In plain words

Take regular backups, copy them to another Region and account, and rebuild the environment from infrastructure as code when needed.

The problem it solves

Cheap protection against Region loss and against deletion or ransomware.

What it does

  • AWS Backup plans centralise schedules, retention, cross-Region and cross-account copy, and Vault Lock for immutability. It covers RDS, Aurora, DynamoDB, EBS, EFS, S3, EKS (cluster state) and more.
  • Recreate the VPC, EKS and add-ons from Terraform and GitOps in the DR Region; restore data from backups.
  • RTO is dominated by rebuild time plus restore time; rehearse it.
  • ECR replication and Route 53 failover records are prerequisites.

Backup plan

hclAWS Backup plan with cross-Region copy
resource "aws_backup_vault" "primary" {
  name = "shop-primary"
}

resource "aws_backup_plan" "shop" {
  name = "shop-daily"

  rule {
    rule_name         = "daily"
    target_vault_name = aws_backup_vault.primary.name
    schedule          = "cron(0 3 * * ? *)"

    lifecycle {
      delete_after = 35
    }

    copy_action {
      destination_vault_arn = var.dr_vault_arn
      lifecycle {
        delete_after = 35
      }
    }
  }
}

resource "aws_backup_selection" "tagged" {
  plan_id      = aws_backup_plan.shop.id
  name         = "tagged-resources"
  iam_role_arn = var.backup_role_arn

  selection_tag {
    type  = "STRINGEQUALS"
    key   = "backup"
    value = "daily"
  }
}
Check yourself
Why copy backups to another account as well as another Region?

It protects against account compromise and deletion, not only a Region outage.

68.3

Pilot light

In plain words

Keep the data replicated and the core infrastructure defined in the DR Region, but keep compute switched off or at minimum size. On disaster, scale up.

The problem it solves

Backup and restore is too slow, but a full standby is too expensive.

What it does

  • Aurora Global Database secondary cluster (readers off or one small instance), DynamoDB global tables, S3 cross-Region replication, ECR replication.
  • A minimal EKS control plane exists (cluster fee) with zero or few nodes; manifests are synced by GitOps.
  • Failover steps: promote database, scale node pools and deployments, switch DNS.
  • RTO tens of minutes to hours; RPO seconds to minutes depending on replication.

Failover commands

bashPilot light activation (outline)
aws rds failover-global-cluster --global-cluster-identifier shop-global \
  --target-db-cluster-identifier arn:aws:rds:eu-west-1:111122223333:cluster:shop-aurora-eu --allow-data-loss
kubectl --context shop-dr scale deployment --all --replicas=3 -n shop
kubectl --context shop-dr patch nodepool general --type merge -p '{"spec":{"limits":{"cpu":"200"}}}'
aws route53 change-resource-record-sets --hosted-zone-id Z0123456789ABCDEFGHIJ --change-batch file://failover.json
Check yourself
What stays off in a pilot light?

Most compute; data replication and core definitions stay on.

68.4

Warm standby and active-active

In plain words

Warm standby runs a smaller but complete copy that can serve traffic at once and be scaled up. Active-active serves users from both Regions simultaneously.

The problem it solves

Tier 0 services cannot wait for scale-up and promotion steps.

What it does

  • Warm standby: DR cluster runs at 20 to 30 percent of production; Route 53 health checks fail over; scale with HPA and Karpenter.
  • Active-active: requires data layers that accept writes in both Regions (DynamoDB global tables, Aurora with write forwarding or sharded ownership, conflict handling) and idempotent business logic.
  • Global traffic: Route 53 latency or weighted records, Global Accelerator, CloudFront origin groups.
  • Most complex part is data consistency, not compute. Prefer active-passive unless you truly need active-active.

Route 53 failover records

hclPrimary and secondary failover records
resource "aws_route53_health_check" "primary" {
  fqdn              = "origin-a.shop.example.com"
  port              = 443
  type              = "HTTPS"
  resource_path     = "/healthz"
  failure_threshold = 3
  request_interval  = 10
}

resource "aws_route53_record" "primary" {
  zone_id         = var.zone_id
  name            = "shop.example.com"
  type            = "CNAME"
  ttl             = 60
  set_identifier  = "primary"
  records         = ["origin-a.shop.example.com"]
  health_check_id = aws_route53_health_check.primary.id

  failover_routing_policy {
    type = "PRIMARY"
  }
}

resource "aws_route53_record" "secondary" {
  zone_id        = var.zone_id
  name           = "shop.example.com"
  type           = "CNAME"
  ttl            = 60
  set_identifier = "secondary"
  records        = ["origin-b.shop.example.com"]

  failover_routing_policy {
    type = "SECONDARY"
  }
}
Check yourself
What is the hardest part of active-active?

Data consistency across Regions, including write conflicts.

68.5

DR for the EKS control plane and cluster state

In plain words

A second cluster is rebuilt from code. Application state lives in databases and object stores, not in the cluster.

The problem it solves

Teams back up etcd out of habit, but EKS does not expose etcd; the right approach is to treat clusters as disposable.

What it does

  • Keep cluster definition in Terraform and workloads in Git (Argo CD or Flux); a DR cluster syncs the same repository with region-specific overlays.
  • Stateful data: use managed databases; for PVs use EBS snapshots (via VolumeSnapshot or AWS Backup) copied to the DR Region; EFS replication; Velero for namespace-level backup of Kubernetes resources and volumes.
  • Secrets: Secrets Manager replication to the DR Region; External Secrets Operator in the DR cluster reads local replicas.
  • Certificates: cert-manager reissues; ACM certificates must exist in the DR Region.
  • Images: ECR replication.

Replicate secrets

bashReplicate a secret to the DR Region
aws secretsmanager replicate-secret-to-regions --secret-id shop/db \
  --add-replica-regions Region=eu-west-1,KmsKeyId=alias/shop-eu
bashVelero backup with schedule
velero schedule create shop-daily --schedule "0 2 * * *" --include-namespaces shop --ttl 720h
Check yourself
Why not rely on backing up etcd for DR?

EKS does not expose etcd; rebuild clusters from code and keep state in data stores.

68.6

Runbooks, rehearsals and failback

In plain words

A DR plan that was never exercised does not work. Write a runbook, run it, and record the actual times.

The problem it solves

Real disasters expose missing permissions, stale AMIs, expired certificates and forgotten dependencies.

What it does

  • Runbook: decision criteria and who decides, step by step commands, verification checks, communication plan, and rollback.
  • Rehearse at least twice a year in a game day; measure RTO and RPO against targets.
  • Failback: re-establish replication to the original Region, sync data, switch traffic during a quiet window. It is often harder than failover.
  • Keep DR credentials, break-glass access and the runbook available outside the failing Region and tooling.
  • AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery covers VM-based workloads; Resilience Hub validates the design.

Runbook skeleton

yamlDR runbook outline
name: shop-regional-failover
preconditions:
  - Incident commander approved
  - Replication lag below 60s or data loss accepted
steps:
  - promote Aurora secondary in eu-west-1
  - scale Karpenter NodePool limits in DR cluster
  - scale deployments to production counts
  - verify smoke tests against dr.shop.example.com
  - switch Route 53 failover record
verify:
  - checkout success rate above 99 percent
rollback:
  - restore record to primary if primary recovers within 15 minutes
Check yourself
Why is failback often harder than failover?

Data has changed in the DR Region and must be synchronised back before traffic can return safely.

Section 69 of 93

Cost visibility with Cost Explorer, CUR and tagging

5 concepts · about 45 minutes

You cannot reduce what you cannot attribute. Cost management starts with seeing who spends what, and that depends on tags and the right reports.

Goals
  • Read Cost Explorer with the right cost type and grouping
  • Activate cost allocation tags and enforce a tagging standard
  • Query the Cost and Usage Report with Athena or Data Exports
69.1

Billing basics and cost types

In plain words

AWS bills monthly per payer account, with usage priced by unit (instance-hour, GB-month, request). Different cost types answer different questions.

The problem it solves

Numbers differ between reports because of amortisation, credits and refunds, and teams argue over which is right.

What it does

  • Unblended: what was charged on the day of use. Blended: averaged across the organisation. Amortized: spreads upfront Savings Plan and RI fees across the term. Net amortized: includes discounts.
  • Use amortized or net amortized for team showback, unblended to reconcile invoices.
  • Consolidated billing in an Organization shares volume discounts and commitments across accounts.
  • Data in Cost Explorer lags by up to a day.

Query

bashMonthly cost by service
aws ce get-cost-and-usage --time-period Start=2026-10-01,End=2026-11-01 \
  --granularity MONTHLY --metrics AmortizedCost \
  --group-by Type=DIMENSION,Key=SERVICE \
  --query 'ResultsByTime[0].Groups[].[Keys[0],Metrics.AmortizedCost.Amount]' --output text | sort -k2 -nr | head
Check yourself
Which cost type suits team showback of Savings Plans?

Amortized (or net amortized), because upfront fees are spread across the term.

69.2

Cost Explorer

In plain words

Cost Explorer is the console and API to explore costs and usage over time, filtered and grouped by service, account, Region, usage type, tag and more.

The problem it solves

You need to find the biggest drivers and changes quickly without exporting data.

What it does

  • Group by Service first, then drill into Usage type (for example NatGateway-Bytes, DataTransfer-Regional-Bytes, BoxUsage).
  • Compare periods and use the forecast for month end.
  • Filters by linked account and tag give team views; saved reports keep them.
  • Hourly and resource-level granularity are optional (extra cost) for deep dives.
  • The get-cost-and-usage API costs a small amount per request.

Usage type breakdown

bashTop usage types for EC2 and VPC
aws ce get-cost-and-usage --time-period Start=2026-10-01,End=2026-11-01 --granularity MONTHLY \
  --metrics UnblendedCost --group-by Type=DIMENSION,Key=USAGE_TYPE \
  --filter '{"Dimensions":{"Key":"SERVICE","Values":["Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud - Compute","Amazon Virtual Private Cloud"]}}' \
  --query 'ResultsByTime[0].Groups[?Metrics.UnblendedCost.Amount>`50`].[Keys[0],Metrics.UnblendedCost.Amount]' --output table
Check yourself
Which grouping reveals NAT gateway data charges?

Usage type, such as NatGateway-Bytes.

69.3

Tagging strategy and cost allocation tags

In plain words

Tags are key-value labels on resources. Cost allocation tags must be activated in the Billing console before they appear in cost reports, and they apply from activation forward.

The problem it solves

Without tags, shared accounts produce one big number with no owner.

What it does

  • Standard keys: Owner, CostCenter, Environment, Application, Team. Keep a short, documented list with fixed values.
  • Enforce with tag policies (Organizations), SCPs requiring tags on create, Config rule required-tags, and Terraform default_tags.
  • Kubernetes resources: AWS load balancers and EBS volumes inherit tags via controller flags (--default-tags), but pod cost needs EKS split cost allocation or a tool.
  • AWS-generated tags (aws:createdBy) can also be activated.

Terraform default tags

hclProvider-wide tags
provider "aws" {
  region = "us-east-1"

  default_tags {
    tags = {
      Application = "shop"
      Environment = "prod"
      CostCenter  = "cc-1234"
      Owner       = "platform-team"
    }
  }
}
bashActivate tags
aws ce update-cost-allocation-tags-status --cost-allocation-tags-status \
  TagKey=Application,Status=Active TagKey=CostCenter,Status=Active TagKey=Environment,Status=Active
aws ce list-cost-allocation-tags --status Active
Check yourself
Do cost allocation tags apply to past costs?

No, only to usage after they are activated (backfill is a separate request).

69.4

Cost and Usage Report and Data Exports

In plain words

The Cost and Usage Report (CUR) is the most detailed dataset: one row per resource per line item per hour or day, delivered to S3 as Parquet or CSV. Data Exports is the newer interface that also offers CUR 2.0 and FOCUS formats.

The problem it solves

Cost Explorer cannot answer custom questions such as cost per pod label or per resource ID with joins to your CMDB.

What it does

  • Enable with resource IDs and hourly granularity for FinOps analysis.
  • Query with Athena; a Glue crawler or the provided CloudFormation creates tables.
  • Use columns line_item_unblended_cost, line_item_usage_type, line_item_resource_id, resource_tags_user_*, savings_plan_savings_plan_effective_cost.
  • Dashboards: QuickSight (CUDOS, CID dashboards) or Grafana.

Athena query

sqlCost by tag Application and service, last month
SELECT resource_tags_user_application AS application,
       line_item_product_code AS service,
       ROUND(SUM(line_item_unblended_cost), 2) AS cost
FROM cur_database.cur_table
WHERE year = '2026' AND month = '10'
  AND line_item_line_item_type = 'Usage'
GROUP BY 1, 2
ORDER BY cost DESC
LIMIT 25;
Check yourself
What does CUR give that Cost Explorer does not?

Line-item detail per resource and tag that you can join and query with SQL.

69.5

Kubernetes cost allocation

In plain words

EKS bills for nodes and volumes, not pods. To attribute spend to teams you need to divide node cost by pod resource use.

The problem it solves

Ten teams share a cluster; the bill shows EC2 and EBS only.

What it does

  • Split cost allocation data for Amazon EKS (enabled in Cost Management preferences) adds pod and namespace-level usage to CUR with Kubernetes labels as dimensions.
  • Open source OpenCost or Kubecost compute per namespace, label and workload costs using Prometheus and AWS pricing.
  • Allocate shared costs (control plane, system pods, idle) by an agreed rule: proportional to usage or even split.
  • Requests (not usage) are the fair basis for reserved capacity; track idle as a metric.
  • Label namespaces consistently: team, cost-center, app.

Install OpenCost

bashInstall OpenCost with Helm
helm repo add opencost https://opencost.github.io/opencost-helm-chart
helm upgrade --install opencost opencost/opencost -n opencost --create-namespace
kubectl -n opencost port-forward svc/opencost 9090:9090
Check yourself
Why can EC2 cost not be assigned to a team directly in a shared cluster?

Nodes run pods from many teams, so cost must be divided by pod resource use.

Section 70 of 93

Budgets, anomaly detection and cost governance

4 concepts · about 40 minutes

Bills should never surprise anyone. Budgets set expectations, anomaly detection finds surprises early, and guardrails stop expensive mistakes.

Goals
  • Create budgets with alerts and actions per account, tag and service
  • Detect unusual spend with Cost Anomaly Detection
  • Set up guardrails and a monthly FinOps routine
70.1

AWS Budgets

In plain words

A budget tracks cost, usage, Savings Plans coverage or utilisation against a target and sends alerts when actual or forecast spend crosses thresholds.

The problem it solves

You only discover overspend when the invoice arrives.

What it does

  • Types: cost, usage, RI utilisation and coverage, Savings Plans utilisation and coverage.
  • Filter by linked account, service, tag, Region.
  • Alerts at actual 80 and 100 percent and forecasted 100 percent, via email, SNS or Chatbot.
  • Budget actions can apply an IAM policy or SCP, or stop EC2/RDS instances when a threshold is crossed (with approval or automatically).
  • The first two budgets are free; more cost per day (check current pricing).

Create

jsonbudget.json
{
  "BudgetName": "shop-monthly",
  "BudgetLimit": {"Amount": "5000", "Unit": "USD"},
  "TimeUnit": "MONTHLY",
  "BudgetType": "COST",
  "CostFilters": {"TagKeyValue": ["user:Application$shop"]}
}
jsonnotifications.json
[
  {
    "Notification": {"NotificationType": "ACTUAL", "ComparisonOperator": "GREATER_THAN", "Threshold": 80, "ThresholdType": "PERCENTAGE"},
    "Subscribers": [{"SubscriptionType": "EMAIL", "Address": "finops@example.com"}]
  },
  {
    "Notification": {"NotificationType": "FORECASTED", "ComparisonOperator": "GREATER_THAN", "Threshold": 100, "ThresholdType": "PERCENTAGE"},
    "Subscribers": [{"SubscriptionType": "EMAIL", "Address": "finops@example.com"}]
  }
]
bashApply
aws budgets create-budget --account-id 111122223333 --budget file://budget.json --notifications-with-subscribers file://notifications.json
Check yourself
What is the benefit of a forecasted alert?

It warns before the limit is actually reached.

70.2

Cost Anomaly Detection

In plain words

Cost Anomaly Detection uses machine learning to flag unexpected spend by service, account, tag or cost category and ranks the likely root cause.

The problem it solves

A misconfigured autoscaler or a data transfer storm can cost thousands in a day, long before month end.

What it does

  • Monitors define the scope (AWS services, linked accounts, cost allocation tag, cost category).
  • Subscriptions send alerts above an absolute or percentage impact threshold, individually or as daily/weekly summaries.
  • Each anomaly shows impact and root causes (service, account, Region, usage type).
  • Free to use; pair with chat delivery for quick response.

Create

bashMonitor by service with an alert subscription
aws ce create-anomaly-monitor --anomaly-monitor '{"MonitorName":"services","MonitorType":"DIMENSIONAL","MonitorDimension":"SERVICE"}'
aws ce create-anomaly-subscription --anomaly-subscription '{
  "SubscriptionName":"finops-daily","Frequency":"DAILY",
  "MonitorArnList":["arn:aws:ce::111122223333:anomalymonitor/abcd"],
  "Subscribers":[{"Type":"EMAIL","Address":"finops@example.com"}],
  "ThresholdExpression":{"Dimensions":{"Key":"ANOMALY_TOTAL_IMPACT_ABSOLUTE","MatchOptions":["GREATER_THAN_OR_EQUAL"],"Values":["100"]}}}'
Check yourself
What does a monitor define?

The scope of spend the anomaly detection model watches.

70.3

Guardrails against expensive mistakes

In plain words

Prevention beats detection. Limit what can be created, where and how big.

The problem it solves

One engineer launching a large GPU instance or an unrestricted autoscaling group can cost more than a month of normal spend.

What it does

  • SCP denying expensive instance families or Regions in sandbox accounts.
  • Service Quotas as natural limits; keep them just above need.
  • Karpenter NodePool limits and EKS node group max sizes.
  • Auto-delete or shut down sandboxes on a schedule (AWS Instance Scheduler, Lambda, or aws-nuke style tools in sandbox only).
  • S3 lifecycle rules, log retention and ECR lifecycle by default through modules.
  • Review newly created resources with Config and tagging checks.

SCP for sandbox

jsonDeny large instance types in sandbox accounts
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Sid": "DenyLargeInstances",
      "Effect": "Deny",
      "Action": "ec2:RunInstances",
      "Resource": "arn:aws:ec2:*:*:instance/*",
      "Condition": {
        "StringNotLike": {"ec2:InstanceType": ["t3.*", "t4g.*", "m6i.large", "m6i.xlarge"]}
      }
    }
  ]
}
Check yourself
Why use preventive controls as well as budgets?

Budgets alert after spend occurs; guardrails stop the expensive action first.

70.4

A monthly FinOps routine

In plain words

FinOps is a habit: inform, optimise, operate. A short monthly review keeps spend aligned with value.

The problem it solves

Cost work done once decays; usage and prices change.

What it does

  • Review top 10 cost drivers and change from last month; ask the owner for each increase.
  • Track unit economics: cost per order, per request, per tenant, not only total.
  • Check commitment coverage and utilisation, idle resources (unattached EBS, idle load balancers, old snapshots) and rightsizing recommendations.
  • Record decisions and savings; set targets per team.
  • Share dashboards with engineering so cost is a design input, not a finance surprise.

Find idle resources

bashUnattached EBS volumes and idle Elastic IPs
aws ec2 describe-volumes --filters Name=status,Values=available \
  --query 'Volumes[].[VolumeId,Size,CreateTime]' --output table
aws ec2 describe-addresses --query 'Addresses[?AssociationId==`null`].[PublicIp,AllocationId]' --output table
Check yourself
What is a useful unit cost metric?

Cost per order, request or tenant, which ties spend to business value.

Section 71 of 93

Savings Plans, Reserved Instances and commitment strategy

5 concepts · about 45 minutes

On-demand is flexible but expensive. If you know some usage will run for a year or more, a commitment gives a discount in exchange for a promise to spend.

Goals
  • Compare Compute and EC2 Instance Savings Plans with Reserved Instances
  • Size commitments from stable baseline usage and monitor coverage and utilisation
  • Cover databases and other services and avoid common mistakes
71.1

Pricing models at a glance

In plain words

You can pay on-demand, commit to a steady spend, bid for spare capacity (Spot), or reserve specific capacity.

The problem it solves

Using only on-demand pays the highest price for predictable load; committing too much wastes money on unused hours.

What it does

  • On-demand: no commitment, highest unit price.
  • Savings Plans: commit to a USD per hour spend for 1 or 3 years; get discounted rates on matching usage.
  • Reserved Instances (RIs): commit to specific instance attributes; also discount; some offer capacity reservation (zonal).
  • Spot: spare capacity at a deep discount, interruptible.
  • Typical order of operation: reduce waste, rightsize, then commit to the stable baseline, then use Spot for flexible burst.

Look at recommendations

bashSavings Plans purchase recommendations
aws ce get-savings-plans-purchase-recommendation --savings-plans-type COMPUTE_SP \
  --term-in-years ONE_YEAR --payment-option NO_UPFRONT --lookback-period-in-days THIRTY_DAYS \
  --query 'SavingsPlansPurchaseRecommendation.SavingsPlansPurchaseRecommendationSummary'
Check yourself
What is the usual order: commit or rightsize first?

Rightsize first, then commit to the stable baseline.

71.2

Savings Plan types

In plain words

Compute Savings Plans apply across EC2 families, Regions, OS, tenancy, Fargate and Lambda. EC2 Instance Savings Plans give a deeper discount for a chosen family in a Region. SageMaker and database plans also exist.

The problem it solves

Karpenter and Fargate shift instance types constantly; a commitment tied to one instance type would go unused.

What it does

  • Compute SP: most flexible; fits EKS with Karpenter, Graviton migration, Fargate. Discount is lower than instance-specific options.
  • EC2 Instance SP: commit to a family (like m6i) in a Region; flexible on size, OS and tenancy. Higher discount, less flexible.
  • Database Savings Plans (check availability) cover some RDS and Aurora usage for flexibility across engines and instance types.
  • Payment: all upfront, partial upfront, no upfront; more upfront gives a bigger discount.
  • Commitment is hourly: unused commitment in an hour is lost; it does not carry over.

Purchase

bashBuy a one-year compute plan (example)
aws savingsplans create-savings-plan --savings-plan-offering-id <offering-id> --commitment 4.00 \
  --client-token "$(uuidgen)"
aws savingsplans describe-savings-plans --states active
Check yourself
Which plan type suits Karpenter with changing instance types?

Compute Savings Plans.

71.3

Reserved Instances and what is left of them

In plain words

RIs reserve a specific instance type, platform and scope (Regional or zonal) for 1 or 3 years. Standard RIs give the best discount; Convertible RIs can be exchanged.

The problem it solves

Existing estates and some services (RDS, ElastiCache, OpenSearch, Redshift) still use RIs or reserved nodes.

What it does

  • Regional RIs apply to any AZ in the Region with size flexibility within a family (for Linux), no capacity reservation.
  • Zonal RIs reserve capacity in one AZ.
  • Standard RIs can be sold on the RI Marketplace; Convertible can be exchanged for equal or greater value.
  • For EC2, Savings Plans are generally simpler; use RIs for RDS, ElastiCache and OpenSearch where Savings Plans do not apply (check the current list).
  • Use On-Demand Capacity Reservations when you need guaranteed capacity without a term.
What to buy
OptionCompute Savings Plan
Choose whenEKS and EC2 with changing families, Fargate
Avoid whenyou need guaranteed capacity in a zone
OptionEC2 Instance Savings Plan
Choose whenstable family and Region
Avoid whenyou plan to migrate families soon
OptionReserved nodes for RDS or ElastiCache
Choose whenstable database sizes
Avoid whenyou may move to Aurora Serverless
OptionCapacity Reservation
Choose whenscheduled events needing capacity
Avoid whenyou want a discount alone

RDS reservation

bashFind reserved DB instance offerings
aws rds describe-reserved-db-instances-offerings --db-instance-class db.r6g.large \
  --product-description postgresql --duration 31536000 --offering-type "No Upfront" \
  --query 'ReservedDBInstancesOfferings[].[ReservedDBInstancesOfferingId,FixedPrice,RecurringCharges[0].RecurringChargeAmount]'
Check yourself
Which services still rely on reserved nodes rather than Savings Plans?

Typically RDS, ElastiCache and OpenSearch (check current coverage).

71.4

Sizing a commitment

In plain words

Commit to the level of usage you are certain to have, not the average and certainly not the peak.

The problem it solves

Overcommitting locks in waste for years; undercommitting leaves savings on the table.

What it does

  • Look at the minimum hourly usage over 30 to 90 days after rightsizing; commit up to about 70 to 80 percent of that baseline at first.
  • Stagger purchases (for example quarterly) to spread expiry and adapt to change.
  • Choose 1 year for uncertain workloads, 3 years for stable platforms.
  • Account for planned migrations (Graviton, Aurora Serverless, Fargate) and shutdowns.
  • Commitments are shared across the Organization by default; the management account can disable sharing for specific accounts.

Check utilisation and coverage

bashSavings Plans utilisation and coverage
aws ce get-savings-plans-utilization --time-period Start=2026-10-01,End=2026-10-31 \
  --query 'Total.Utilization.UtilizationPercentage'
aws ce get-savings-plans-coverage --time-period Start=2026-10-01,End=2026-10-31 \
  --query 'SavingsPlansCoverages[].Coverage.CoveragePercentage' --output text
Check yourself
What number should a first commitment be sized from?

The stable minimum hourly usage after rightsizing, not the average or the peak.

71.5

Monitoring and avoiding mistakes

In plain words

Commitments need ongoing care: watch utilisation (are we using what we bought) and coverage (how much eligible usage is covered).

The problem it solves

Team changes quietly drop usage and the commitment is wasted for months.

What it does

  • Alert when utilisation falls below about 95 percent or coverage below target using Budgets.
  • Review expirations 60 days ahead; renew with fresh data.
  • Common mistakes: buying before rightsizing, tying to one family before a Graviton move, forgetting non-production shutdown, ignoring Fargate/Lambda eligibility, committing in a member account that leaves the Organization.
  • Understand that Savings Plans apply first to the usage with the highest discount.
  • Consider third-party or AWS automation for rolling purchases, but keep human approval.

Budget for utilisation

bashSavings Plans utilisation budget
aws budgets create-budget --account-id 111122223333 --budget '{
  "BudgetName":"sp-utilization","BudgetType":"SAVINGS_PLANS_UTILIZATION","TimeUnit":"MONTHLY",
  "BudgetLimit":{"Amount":"95","Unit":"PERCENTAGE"}}' \
  --notifications-with-subscribers '[{"Notification":{"NotificationType":"ACTUAL","ComparisonOperator":"LESS_THAN","Threshold":95,"ThresholdType":"PERCENTAGE"},"Subscribers":[{"SubscriptionType":"EMAIL","Address":"finops@example.com"}]}]'
Check yourself
What does low utilisation mean?

You are paying for commitment you are not using.

Section 72 of 93

Rightsizing, Spot and efficient compute

5 concepts · about 50 minutes

The cheapest resource is the one you do not run. Rightsizing removes waste first; then Spot and efficient hardware lower the price of what remains.

Goals
  • Rightsize EC2, EKS pods and databases using measured utilisation
  • Run stateless workloads on Spot safely with diversification and interruption handling
  • Use Graviton, gp3 and storage choices to reduce unit cost
72.1

Rightsizing EC2 and databases

In plain words

Rightsizing matches instance size to measured usage. Many instances run at under 20 percent CPU.

The problem it solves

Sizes chosen at launch "to be safe" persist for years.

What it does

  • AWS Compute Optimizer recommends instance types for EC2, EBS volumes, Lambda, ECS on Fargate and Auto Scaling groups using at least 30 hours of metrics (extended lookback is available).
  • Cost Explorer rightsizing lists idle and underused instances.
  • For RDS, use Performance Insights and CloudWatch: CPU, memory (FreeableMemory), connections, IOPS.
  • Memory metrics for EC2 need the CloudWatch agent; without it, recommendations ignore memory.
  • Change one step at a time and compare p99 latency before and after.

Recommendations

bashUnderprovisioned and overprovisioned EC2
aws compute-optimizer get-ec2-instance-recommendations \
  --query 'instanceRecommendations[?finding==`OVER_PROVISIONED`].[instanceArn,currentInstanceType,recommendationOptions[0].instanceType]' --output table
Check yourself
Why install the CloudWatch agent for rightsizing?

EC2 does not report memory by default, so recommendations without it ignore memory use.

72.2

Rightsizing Kubernetes requests

In plain words

Pod requests drive node count. Inflated requests waste nodes; low requests cause throttling and eviction.

The problem it solves

Teams copy YAML with requests of 1 CPU and 2 GiB, then use 50m and 300 MiB.

What it does

  • Measure real usage with Prometheus or Container Insights (p95 CPU, max memory over 2 weeks).
  • Vertical Pod Autoscaler in recommendation mode (updateMode: "Off") suggests values without restarting pods.
  • Goldilocks shows VPA recommendations per namespace.
  • Set CPU request near typical usage; avoid CPU limits unless needed (they throttle); set memory limit equal to request.
  • Re-check after load changes. Cluster-wide, compare requested versus used CPU: high gaps mean waste.

VPA in recommend-only mode

yamlVPA that only recommends
apiVersion: autoscaling.k8s.io/v1
kind: VerticalPodAutoscaler
metadata:
  name: orders
  namespace: shop
spec:
  targetRef:
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    name: orders
  updatePolicy:
    updateMode: "Off"
bashRead recommendations
kubectl -n shop get vpa orders -o jsonpath='{.status.recommendation.containerRecommendations}'
kubectl top pods -n shop --containers
Check yourself
What does updateMode Off do?

It computes recommendations without changing running pods.

72.3

Spot instances

In plain words

Spot instances use spare EC2 capacity at a large discount, but AWS can reclaim them with two minutes' notice.

The problem it solves

Stateless workers do not need guaranteed capacity, yet are billed at on-demand prices.

What it does

  • Good fits: stateless web replicas (with spread), batch jobs, CI runners, data processing, dev and test.
  • Bad fits: databases, single replica services, long jobs without checkpointing.
  • Diversify: many instance types, sizes and AZs; Spot placement score helps choose.
  • Handle interruption: draining on notice, PDBs, replicas in several pools, checkpoints, SQS for work.
  • Spot price is stable and no longer needs bidding; set only a max price if needed.

Node group on Spot

yamleksctl Spot managed node group
apiVersion: eksctl.io/v1alpha5
kind: ClusterConfig
metadata:
  name: shop-prod
  region: us-east-1
managedNodeGroups:
  - name: spot-workers
    spot: true
    instanceTypes: ["m6i.large", "m5.large", "m6a.large", "m7i.large", "m5a.large"]
    minSize: 0
    maxSize: 20
    labels: {lifecycle: spot}
    taints:
      - key: spot
        value: "true"
        effect: NoSchedule
bashCheck placement scores
aws ec2 get-spot-placement-scores --instance-types m6i.large m5.large m6a.large \
  --target-capacity 20 --region-names us-east-1 --single-availability-zone false
Check yourself
How many minutes of notice does a Spot interruption give?

Two minutes.

72.4

Graviton, storage and other unit-cost levers

In plain words

Cheaper hardware and better storage choices lower cost per unit of work without reducing capacity.

The problem it solves

Older generations and over-provisioned storage silently cost more.

What it does

  • Graviton (arm64) offers better price-performance; many images are multi-arch. Build with docker buildx --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 and let Karpenter pick.
  • Prefer current generation instances (m7, c7 families), which are usually cheaper per unit.
  • gp3 is cheaper than gp2 and lets you tune IOPS and throughput; migrate volumes online with modify-volume.
  • Delete unattached volumes, old snapshots, and unused AMIs.
  • S3 Intelligent-Tiering and lifecycle rules reduce storage costs; delete incomplete multipart uploads.
  • For Lambda and Fargate, ARM also reduces price.

Convert gp2 to gp3

bashList gp2 volumes and convert one
aws ec2 describe-volumes --filters Name=volume-type,Values=gp2 --query 'Volumes[].[VolumeId,Size]' --output table
# aws ec2 modify-volume --volume-id vol-0123456789abcdef0 --volume-type gp3
bashMulti-arch build
docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 -t 111122223333.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/shop/web:1.4.3 --push .
Check yourself
Why build multi-architecture images?

They let the same image run on cheaper Graviton nodes as well as x86.

72.5

Scheduling off-hours and scaling to zero

In plain words

Development and test environments rarely need to run at night or on weekends.

The problem it solves

A non-production cluster running 24/7 costs about three times what is needed.

What it does

  • Scale Karpenter-managed workloads to zero replicas (KEDA cron, CronJobs patching deployments); nodes drain and consolidate away.
  • For managed node groups, schedule desired size to 0 with Auto Scaling scheduled actions.
  • Stop RDS instances (up to seven days) or use Aurora Serverless v2 with low minimum; schedule with EventBridge Scheduler.
  • AWS Instance Scheduler solution automates start and stop by tag.
  • Keep the EKS control plane (fixed hourly cost) or use shared dev clusters per team.

Scheduled node group scaling

bashScheduled actions for a dev node group ASG
aws autoscaling put-scheduled-update-group-action --auto-scaling-group-name eks-dev-general \
  --scheduled-action-name night-off --recurrence "30 13 * * 1-5" --min-size 0 --desired-capacity 0
aws autoscaling put-scheduled-update-group-action --auto-scaling-group-name eks-dev-general \
  --scheduled-action-name morning-on --recurrence "0 3 * * 1-5" --min-size 2 --desired-capacity 2
Check yourself
What cost remains when a dev cluster is scaled to zero nodes?

The EKS control plane fee, storage and other fixed resources.

Section 73 of 93

Data transfer and networking costs

5 concepts · about 45 minutes

Data transfer is the line item that surprises teams most: it has many rules and is billed in many places. Prices vary by Region, so check the current pricing page and use the principles here.

Goals
  • Identify which data flows are free, charged per GB or charged per hour
  • Reduce NAT Gateway, cross-AZ and internet egress costs with endpoints and caching
  • Find the top transfer cost drivers with Cost Explorer and VPC Flow Logs
73.1

The pricing rules

In plain words

Roughly: data in from the internet is free, data out to the internet is charged per GB, traffic between AZs in a Region is charged per GB, and traffic inside one AZ over private IPs is free.

The problem it solves

Architects draw boxes without arrows' price tags; the invoice later shows transfer costs rivalling compute.

What it does

  • Inbound from the internet: free.
  • Outbound to the internet: charged per GB with a small free tier and volume tiers.
  • Cross-AZ in the same Region: charged per GB, billed on both sides.
  • Cross-Region: charged per GB from the source Region.
  • Same AZ, private IP: free. Using public or Elastic IPs between instances in the same AZ is billed like cross-AZ.
  • Many services add their own processing charge (NAT Gateway, Transit Gateway, load balancers, PrivateLink).

Read the usage types

bashCost of data transfer by usage type
aws ce get-cost-and-usage --time-period Start=2026-10-01,End=2026-11-01 --granularity MONTHLY \
  --metrics UnblendedCost --group-by Type=DIMENSION,Key=USAGE_TYPE \
  --filter '{"Dimensions":{"Key":"USAGE_TYPE_GROUP","Values":["EC2: Data Transfer - Internet (Out)","EC2: Data Transfer - Inter AZ","EC2: Data Transfer - Region to Region (Out)","EC2: NAT Gateway - Data Processed"]}}' \
  --query 'ResultsByTime[0].Groups[].[Keys[0],Metrics.UnblendedCost.Amount]' --output table
Check yourself
Is traffic between two instances in the same AZ always free?

Only over private IPs; using public or Elastic IPs is charged.

73.2

NAT Gateway costs

In plain words

A NAT Gateway charges an hourly fee plus a per-GB data processing charge on everything that passes through, in addition to normal data transfer.

The problem it solves

Private nodes pulling images, calling S3 or DynamoDB, and shipping logs push terabytes through NAT.

What it does

  • Add gateway endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB (free); traffic bypasses NAT.
  • Add interface endpoints for ECR (api, dkr), STS, Secrets Manager, CloudWatch Logs, SSM; they cost per hour per AZ plus per GB, which is usually lower than NAT per GB at high volume.
  • Use ECR pull-through cache and node image caching to reduce pulls.
  • Find big talkers with VPC Flow Logs or NAT Gateway metrics (BytesOutToDestination).
  • Keep a NAT per AZ for reliability, accepting the hourly cost; remove NATs in dev AZs if resilience is not needed.

Endpoints

hclInterface endpoints for ECR and STS
locals {
  interface_services = ["ecr.api", "ecr.dkr", "sts", "secretsmanager", "logs"]
}

resource "aws_vpc_endpoint" "interface" {
  for_each            = toset(local.interface_services)
  vpc_id              = var.vpc_id
  service_name        = "com.amazonaws.us-east-1.${each.key}"
  vpc_endpoint_type   = "Interface"
  subnet_ids          = var.private_subnet_ids
  security_group_ids  = [var.endpoint_sg_id]
  private_dns_enabled = true
}
Check yourself
Which endpoint type is free?

Gateway endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB.

73.3

Internet egress and CloudFront

In plain words

Serving users directly from EC2 or ALB incurs internet egress at the standard rate. CloudFront often costs less per GB and reduces origin load.

The problem it solves

Media and API responses leaving through the ALB form a large and growing part of the bill.

What it does

  • Data transfer from AWS origins (S3, ALB) to CloudFront is free; you pay CloudFront rates to users, usually lower with volume discounts and free tier.
  • Cache static and cacheable API responses; compress (gzip, brotli) responses.
  • CloudFront security savings bundle and committed-use pricing exist (check current offer).
  • Serve images through an image optimiser; avoid sending large JSON unnecessarily (pagination, field selection).
  • Direct Connect or Private connectivity reduce egress for hybrid traffic.

Compression and caching

hclCloudFront cache policy with compression
resource "aws_cloudfront_cache_policy" "static" {
  name        = "shop-static"
  default_ttl = 86400
  max_ttl     = 31536000
  min_ttl     = 0

  parameters_in_cache_key_and_forwarded_to_origin {
    enable_accept_encoding_gzip   = true
    enable_accept_encoding_brotli = true
    cookies_config {
      cookie_behavior = "none"
    }
    headers_config {
      header_behavior = "none"
    }
    query_strings_config {
      query_string_behavior = "none"
    }
  }
}
Check yourself
Is transfer from an S3 origin to CloudFront charged?

No, origin-to-CloudFront transfer from AWS origins is free; CloudFront to users is billed.

73.4

Cross-AZ and cross-Region traffic in practice

In plain words

Distributed systems send data between zones constantly: service calls, replication, consumers, backups.

The problem it solves

Cross-AZ costs scale with traffic volume and are invisible without measurement.

What it does

  • Enable Topology Aware Routing on Services and prefer same-zone targets; ALB cross-zone load balancing introduces cross-AZ hops (acceptable for availability).
  • Kafka: rack-aware consumers (follower fetching) reduce cross-AZ reads.
  • Databases: send reads to a same-AZ replica only if the driver supports it; otherwise accept the cost.
  • Cross-Region: replicate only what you need, compress, and schedule bulk copies; use S3 Replication Time Control only where required.
  • Measure with Flow Logs enriched with AZ info or tools like Kubecost network cost allocation.

VPC Flow Logs for analysis

bashEnable flow logs to S3 with AZ details
aws ec2 create-flow-logs --resource-type VPC --resource-ids vpc-0123456789abcdef0 \
  --traffic-type ALL --log-destination-type s3 \
  --log-destination arn:aws:s3:::shop-flow-logs/prod/ \
  --log-format '${srcaddr} ${dstaddr} ${bytes} ${az-id} ${pkt-src-aws-service} ${flow-direction}'
Check yourself
What is one way to keep Kubernetes service traffic in-zone?

Topology Aware Routing on the Service.

73.5

A checklist for transfer savings

In plain words

Work through the big levers in order of effort versus payoff.

The problem it solves

Without a list, teams optimise small items first.

What it does

    1. S3 and DynamoDB gateway endpoints everywhere (free, immediate).
    1. Interface endpoints for ECR, STS, Secrets Manager, Logs where NAT volume is high.
    1. CloudFront in front of public content and APIs where cacheable.
    1. Topology Aware Routing and consumer placement.
    1. Compress logs and responses; sample verbose logs; lower retention.
    1. Review cross-Region replication and backup copies.
    1. Keep dev environments on one AZ and one NAT, if acceptable.
  • Re-run the usage-type report monthly and track GB per request or per order.

Quick NAT check

bashNAT gateway bytes in the last day
aws cloudwatch get-metric-statistics --namespace AWS/NATGateway --metric-name BytesOutToDestination \
  --dimensions Name=NatGatewayId,Value=nat-0123456789abcdef0 \
  --start-time "$(date -u -v-1d +%FT%TZ)" --end-time "$(date -u +%FT%TZ)" --period 86400 --statistics Sum

Which saving is free and immediate?

Adding S3 and DynamoDB gateway endpoints.
