Section 74 of 93

CloudFormation stacks, change sets and drift

7 concepts · about 55 minutes

CloudFormation is AWS's native infrastructure as code. Even if you use Terraform, you will meet it in Control Tower, Service Catalog, SAM and CDK.

Goals
  • Write a CloudFormation template with parameters, conditions, outputs and intrinsic functions
  • Preview and apply updates safely with change sets and stack policies
  • Detect drift and use StackSets for multi-account deployment
74.1

Templates and stacks

In plain words

A template (YAML or JSON) declares resources. A stack is the deployed instance of a template, managed as one unit.

The problem it solves

Clicking resources in the console cannot be reviewed, repeated or rolled back.

What it does

  • Sections: Parameters, Mappings, Conditions, Resources (required), Outputs, Rules.
  • Creating, updating or deleting the stack changes all its resources together; failure rolls back by default.
  • Each resource has a logical ID and a physical ID. Renaming a logical ID replaces the resource.
  • Stacks live in one account and Region.

A bucket template

yamlbucket.yaml
AWSTemplateFormatVersion: "2010-09-09"
Parameters:
  Env:
    Type: String
    AllowedValues: [dev, prod]
Conditions:
  IsProd: !Equals [!Ref Env, prod]
Resources:
  Data:
    Type: AWS::S3::Bucket
    DeletionPolicy: Retain
    Properties:
      BucketEncryption:
        ServerSideEncryptionConfiguration:
          - ServerSideEncryptionByDefault:
              SSEAlgorithm: aws:kms
      VersioningConfiguration:
        Status: !If [IsProd, Enabled, Suspended]
Outputs:
  BucketName:
    Value: !Ref Data
    Export:
      Name: !Sub "${AWS::StackName}-bucket"
bashDeploy
aws cloudformation deploy --template-file bucket.yaml --stack-name data-dev --parameter-overrides Env=dev
Check yourself
What happens if you rename a resource's logical ID?

CloudFormation creates a new resource and deletes the old one.

74.2

Intrinsic functions and pseudo parameters

In plain words

Intrinsic functions such as !Ref, !GetAtt, !Sub, !Join, !Select and !ImportValue compute values at deploy time.

The problem it solves

Templates must reference other resources and account facts without hard coding.

What it does

  • !Ref returns an ID or parameter value; !GetAtt returns an attribute such as an ARN.
  • !Sub substitutes ${Var} and pseudo parameters like ${AWS::Region}, ${AWS::AccountId}, ${AWS::StackName}.
  • Fn::ImportValue reads exports of another stack; this creates a hard dependency that blocks changing the export.
  • Fn::ForEach (with the LanguageExtensions transform) loops, and SSM parameter types read values at deploy time.
  • Dynamic references {{resolve:ssm:/path}} and {{resolve:secretsmanager:...}} avoid putting secrets in templates.

Lambda using a role

yamlfunction.yaml
Resources:
  Role:
    Type: AWS::IAM::Role
    Properties:
      AssumeRolePolicyDocument:
        Version: "2012-10-17"
        Statement:
          - Effect: Allow
            Principal: {Service: lambda.amazonaws.com}
            Action: sts:AssumeRole
      ManagedPolicyArns:
        - arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/service-role/AWSLambdaBasicExecutionRole
  Fn:
    Type: AWS::Lambda::Function
    Properties:
      FunctionName: !Sub "${AWS::StackName}-fn"
      Runtime: python3.12
      Handler: index.handler
      Role: !GetAtt Role.Arn
      Code:
        ZipFile: |
          def handler(event, context):
              return "ok"
74.3

Change sets and stack policies

In plain words

A change set shows exactly what an update will add, modify, replace or remove before you apply it. A stack policy blocks updates to protected resources.

The problem it solves

A small template edit can silently replace a database and lose data.

What it does

  • Review the Replacement column: True means the resource is recreated.
  • Apply change sets in CI after a human or policy review.
  • Stack policy denies Update:Replace and Update:Delete on critical resources.
  • DeletionPolicy: Retain or Snapshot and UpdateReplacePolicy protect data.
  • Termination protection stops accidental stack deletion.

Preview with CLI

bashChange set
aws cloudformation create-change-set --stack-name data-prod --change-set-name pr-42 \
  --template-body file://bucket.yaml --parameters ParameterKey=Env,ParameterValue=prod
aws cloudformation describe-change-set --stack-name data-prod --change-set-name pr-42 \
  --query 'Changes[].ResourceChange.[LogicalResourceId,Action,Replacement]' --output table
aws cloudformation execute-change-set --stack-name data-prod --change-set-name pr-42
Check yourself
Which column warns that an update recreates a resource?

Replacement set to True.

74.4

Drift detection

In plain words

Drift is when real resources differ from what the stack template says, usually because someone changed them by hand.

The problem it solves

Manual hotfixes make environments differ and the next update may overwrite them or fail.

What it does

  • Run drift detection per stack; results list resources as IN_SYNC, MODIFIED or DELETED with property differences.
  • Not all resource types or properties are supported.
  • Fix by updating the template to match intent, or revert the resource, then update the stack. Use resource import to bring existing resources under management.
  • Detect regularly and alert; prevent drift with SCPs that restrict console writes.

Detect

bashDrift
aws cloudformation detect-stack-drift --stack-name data-prod
aws cloudformation describe-stack-resource-drifts --stack-name data-prod \
  --stack-resource-drift-status-filters MODIFIED DELETED
74.5

Nested stacks, exports and StackSets

In plain words

Nested stacks compose templates. StackSets deploy one template to many accounts and Regions.

The problem it solves

Giant templates are slow and risky, and baseline resources are needed in every account.

What it does

  • Nested stack: a resource of type AWS::CloudFormation::Stack pointing to a template in S3; good for reuse in one deployment.
  • Cross-stack references through exports are rigid; prefer SSM parameters for loosely coupled sharing.
  • StackSets with service-managed permissions integrate with AWS Organizations and auto-deploy to new accounts in target OUs.
  • Control rollout with failure tolerance and max concurrent accounts.

Create service-managed StackSet

bashStackSet
aws cloudformation create-stack-set --stack-set-name baseline --template-body file://baseline.yaml \
  --permission-model SERVICE_MANAGED --auto-deployment Enabled=true,RetainStacksOnAccountRemoval=false \
  --capabilities CAPABILITY_NAMED_IAM
aws cloudformation create-stack-instances --stack-set-name baseline \
  --deployment-targets OrganizationalUnitIds=ou-abcd-11111111 --regions eu-west-1
Check yourself
Why prefer SSM parameters over exports for sharing?

Exports lock the producing stack; parameters decouple lifecycles.

74.6

Custom resources, macros and hooks

In plain words

Custom resources run your Lambda during stack operations. Macros transform templates. Hooks validate resources before provisioning.

The problem it solves

Some tasks (look up an AMI, seed data) or policies (all buckets must be encrypted) are not supported by native resources.

What it does

  • Custom resource: Lambda receives Create, Update, Delete events and must return a response to the pre-signed URL or the stack hangs until timeout. cfn-response or CDK Provider framework handles this.
  • Macros (like AWS::Serverless for SAM) rewrite templates.
  • CloudFormation Guard and Hooks enforce rules at deploy time; cfn-lint checks templates in CI.
  • Registry extensions add third-party resource types.

CI checks

bashLint and guard
cfn-lint bucket.yaml
cfn-guard validate --data bucket.yaml --rules rules.guard
74.7

Troubleshooting stack failures

In plain words

Most failures are permissions, quotas, name conflicts, dependency order or a rollback loop.

The problem it solves

Stacks stuck in ROLLBACK_FAILED or UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED block everyone.

What it does

  • Read the stack events, first failed resource at the bottom of the time order, for the real error.
  • CREATE_FAILED rolls back and leaves the stack in ROLLBACK_COMPLETE; delete and recreate.
  • UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED: fix the cause (often a manually deleted resource) and use continue-update-rollback, optionally skipping resources.
  • Use --disable-rollback in dev to keep failed resources for inspection.
  • Always pass a service role with least privilege for deployments.

Find the failure

bashFailed events
aws cloudformation describe-stack-events --stack-name data-prod \
  --query "StackEvents[?contains(ResourceStatus,'FAILED')].[Timestamp,LogicalResourceId,ResourceStatusReason]" --output table
Check yourself
Which command resumes a stuck UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED stack?

continue-update-rollback.

← PreviousNext →
Section 75 of 93

AWS CDK constructs and pipelines

7 concepts · about 50 minutes

The AWS Cloud Development Kit lets you define infrastructure in TypeScript, Python, Java, C# or Go and synthesizes CloudFormation templates.

Goals
  • Explain apps, stacks and the three construct levels
  • Synthesize, diff and deploy a CDK app and understand bootstrapping
  • Test constructs and package reusable platform patterns
75.1

What CDK is

In plain words

CDK is a framework where you write code that creates objects called constructs. Running cdk synth turns them into CloudFormation templates, and cdk deploy applies them.

The problem it solves

YAML templates have no loops, types, functions or unit tests, so large estates become copy and paste.

What it does

  • Languages: TypeScript (primary), Python, Java, .NET, Go.
  • A CDK app contains one or more stacks; each stack becomes a CloudFormation stack.
  • You get real programming constructs, IDE completion and package sharing.
  • The result is still CloudFormation, so rollback, drift detection and change sets all apply.

A small app in Python

pythonapp.py
import aws_cdk as cdk
from aws_cdk import aws_s3 as s3, aws_lambda as _lambda

class ShopStack(cdk.Stack):
    def __init__(self, scope, id, **kwargs):
        super().__init__(scope, id, **kwargs)
        bucket = s3.Bucket(self, "Uploads",
                           versioned=True,
                           encryption=s3.BucketEncryption.S3_MANAGED,
                           block_public_access=s3.BlockPublicAccess.BLOCK_ALL)
        fn = _lambda.Function(self, "Resize",
                              runtime=_lambda.Runtime.PYTHON_3_12,
                              handler="index.handler",
                              code=_lambda.Code.from_asset("lambda"))
        bucket.grant_read(fn)

app = cdk.App()
ShopStack(app, "Shop", env=cdk.Environment(account="111122223333", region="eu-west-1"))
app.synth()
Check yourself
What does cdk synth produce?

CloudFormation templates (a cloud assembly).

75.2

Construct levels L1, L2 and L3

In plain words

L1 constructs map one to one to CloudFormation resources (CfnBucket). L2 add sensible defaults and helper methods. L3 (patterns) combine several resources into a solution.

The problem it solves

Raw resources need lots of repeated wiring such as IAM policies and security groups.

What it does

  • L1: names start with Cfn, generated from the CloudFormation spec; use as an escape hatch.
  • L2: s3.Bucket, lambda.Function; grant methods such as bucket.grantRead(fn) create least-privilege IAM automatically.
  • L3 or patterns: for example ApplicationLoadBalancedFargateService creates cluster, service, ALB and roles.
  • Your platform team can publish its own L3 constructs with company defaults.

Escape hatch

pythonescape.py
from aws_cdk import Stack, aws_s3 as s3
from constructs import Construct


class DataStack(Stack):
    def __init__(self, scope: Construct, construct_id: str, **kwargs) -> None:
        super().__init__(scope, construct_id, **kwargs)
        bucket = s3.Bucket(self, "Data", versioned=True)
        # drop to the L1 resource only for a property the L2 construct does not expose
        cfn_bucket = bucket.node.default_child
        cfn_bucket.add_property_override("ObjectLockEnabled", True)
Check yourself
Which level should you reach for first?

L2, dropping to L1 only when a feature is missing.

75.3

Bootstrapping and environments

In plain words

Before first deploy, cdk bootstrap creates a CDKToolkit stack in each account and Region with an assets bucket, ECR repository and roles.

The problem it solves

CDK must upload Lambda code and Docker images before CloudFormation can use them, and needs roles to deploy.

What it does

  • Bootstrap once per account and Region: cdk bootstrap aws://111122223333/eu-west-1.
  • Creates deploy, file publishing, image publishing and lookup roles; cross-account deployments trust the pipeline account.
  • Modern bootstrap supports least-privilege customisation and permission boundaries.
  • Environment-agnostic stacks cannot look up VPCs or AZs; set env for those.

Commands

bashBootstrap and deploy
cdk bootstrap aws://111122223333/eu-west-1
cdk diff
cdk deploy Shop --require-approval broadening
75.4

Diff, deploy and context

In plain words

cdk diff compares your code against the deployed stack. Context caches lookups such as VPC IDs in cdk.context.json.

The problem it solves

Without a preview, a refactor can replace resources unexpectedly, and lookups that change between runs make builds non-repeatable.

What it does

  • Commit cdk.context.json so synthesis is deterministic.
  • --require-approval broadening pauses when IAM or security group access widens.
  • Changing a construct ID changes the logical ID, which replaces the resource. Use overrideLogicalId or keep IDs stable.
  • cdk watch hot-swaps Lambda or ECS changes in development. Not for production.

Pin context

jsoncdk.context.json
{
  "vpc-provider:account=111122223333:filter.vpc-id=vpc-0abc123:region=eu-west-1:returnAsymmetricSubnets=true": {
    "vpcId": "vpc-0abc123"
  }
}
Check yourself
Why commit cdk.context.json?

Lookups stay stable so builds are repeatable.

75.5

Testing and aspects

In plain words

You can unit test synthesized templates, and use Aspects to enforce rules across all constructs.

The problem it solves

Infrastructure mistakes are found in production unless they are tested like application code.

What it does

  • Assertions module: check the template contains a resource with given properties, or snapshot test.
  • Aspects visit every construct; use them to add tags, enforce encryption or block public buckets.
  • cdk-nag applies rule packs such as AWS Solutions checks.
  • Integration tests with the integ-tests library deploy to a real account.

Assertion test

pythontest_shop.py
import aws_cdk as cdk
from aws_cdk.assertions import Template
from shop.shop_stack import ShopStack

def test_bucket_is_encrypted():
    app = cdk.App()
    template = Template.from_stack(ShopStack(app, "Test"))
    template.has_resource_properties("AWS::S3::Bucket", {
        "BucketEncryption": {"ServerSideEncryptionConfiguration": [{"ServerSideEncryptionByDefault": {"SSEAlgorithm": "AES256"}}]}
    })
75.6

CDK Pipelines

In plain words

CDK Pipelines creates a self-mutating CodePipeline that builds, tests and deploys your CDK app across stages and accounts.

The problem it solves

Hand-written deployment pipelines drift from the infrastructure they deploy.

What it does

  • Pipeline stages: Source, Build (synth), UpdatePipeline (self-mutate), Assets, then your deployment waves.
  • Add manual approval or validation steps between environments.
  • Cross-account deployment uses the bootstrapped roles, with cross-account KMS for artifacts.
  • Alternative: run cdk deploy from GitHub Actions or another CI with OIDC.

Pipeline skeleton

pythonpipeline.py
from aws_cdk import pipelines, Stack

class PipelineStack(Stack):
    def __init__(self, scope, id, **kwargs):
        super().__init__(scope, id, **kwargs)
        pipeline = pipelines.CodePipeline(self, "Pipeline",
            synth=pipelines.ShellStep("Synth",
                input=pipelines.CodePipelineSource.connection("org/shop", "main",
                    connection_arn="arn:aws:codeconnections:eu-west-1:111122223333:connection/abc"),
                commands=["pip install -r requirements.txt", "npx cdk synth"]))
Check yourself
What does the self mutate stage do?

Updates the pipeline itself when its definition in code changes.

75.7

Sharing constructs and CDK vs Terraform

In plain words

Publish well-tested constructs as packages so teams reuse your standards. Choose CDK or Terraform by team skills and estate.

The problem it solves

Every team re-solves the same patterns differently, and tool choice debates stall projects.

What it does

  • Package constructs with jsii for multiple languages, or publish a single language to a private registry such as CodeArtifact.
  • Version constructs with semantic versioning and a changelog; use snapshot tests.
  • CDK strengths: AWS-first, types, CloudFormation rollback, strong L2 defaults. Terraform strengths: multi-cloud, large provider ecosystem, plan output, state portability.
  • CDK for Terraform (CDKTF) exists, but check its current status before adopting it.
  • Mixed estates are fine: bridge them with SSM parameters.
IaC tool
OptionCDK
Choose whenAWS-centric dev teams who like code
Avoid whenyou must manage many non-AWS providers
OptionTerraform
Choose whenmulti-cloud or platform team standard
Avoid whenyour team wants L3 patterns with generated IAM
OptionCloudFormation
Choose whenyou use SAM, StackSets or Service Catalog
Avoid whenyou need loops and abstractions

Section 76 of 93

CodeBuild and CodePipeline

7 concepts · about 50 minutes

CodeBuild is a managed build service. CodePipeline orchestrates stages from source to production. Together they give an AWS-native CI/CD path.

Goals
  • Write a buildspec and run CodeBuild with caching, secrets and a least-privilege role
  • Model a release flow in CodePipeline with stages, approvals and cross-account deployment
  • Trigger pipelines from source events and troubleshoot failures
76.1

CodeBuild projects

In plain words

A CodeBuild project runs commands from a buildspec in a fresh container and bills by the build minute.

The problem it solves

Self-hosted CI servers need patching, scaling and idle capacity.

What it does

  • Choose a compute type, an AWS-provided or custom image, and a service role.
  • Source: CodeConnections (GitHub, Bitbucket, GitLab), CodeCommit, S3.
  • Outputs: artifacts to S3, test and coverage reports, logs in CloudWatch.
  • Build in a VPC to reach private resources; compute can be on-demand EC2 or Lambda for short builds; check the current compute options.
  • Also runs GitHub Actions self-hosted runners in recent versions; check the current docs.

Project in Terraform

hclcodebuild.tf
resource "aws_codebuild_project" "app" {
  name         = "app-build"
  service_role = aws_iam_role.codebuild.arn
  artifacts {
    type = "CODEPIPELINE"
  }
  environment {
    compute_type    = "BUILD_GENERAL1_SMALL"
    image           = "aws/codebuild/amazonlinux2-x86_64-standard:5.0"
    type            = "LINUX_CONTAINER"
    privileged_mode = true
  }
  source {
    type = "CODEPIPELINE"
  }
}
Note

Privileged mode is needed only to run Docker inside the build. Leave it off otherwise.

Check yourself
How is CodeBuild billed?

By build minutes at the chosen compute size.

76.2

The buildspec

In plain words

buildspec.yml defines phases, environment variables, artifacts and cache.

The problem it solves

Builds must be repeatable and versioned alongside the code.

What it does

  • Phases: install, pre_build, build, post_build; a failing phase stops the build (post_build still runs).
  • env.parameter-store and env.secrets-manager inject secrets at runtime without exposing them in the project.
  • cache paths (S3 or local) speed up dependency downloads.
  • reports upload JUnit or coverage data.

Example

yamlbuildspec.yml
version: 0.2
env:
  parameter-store:
    NPM_TOKEN: /ci/npm-token
phases:
  install:
    runtime-versions:
      nodejs: 20
  pre_build:
    commands:
      - npm ci
      - npm test
  build:
    commands:
      - npm run build
artifacts:
  files:
    - "dist/**/*"
cache:
  paths:
    - node_modules/**/*
reports:
  unit:
    files:
      - "junit.xml"
    file-format: JUNITXML
Check yourself
Which phase still runs after a failed build phase?

post_build.

76.3

Building and pushing container images

In plain words

CodeBuild commonly builds a Docker image and pushes it to ECR with an immutable tag.

The problem it solves

Images pushed with a mutable latest tag cannot be traced or rolled back.

What it does

  • Tag with the commit SHA from CODEBUILD_RESOLVED_SOURCE_VERSION.
  • Authenticate with aws ecr get-login-password.
  • Scan on push in ECR and enable immutable tags.
  • Output an imagedefinitions.json file so CodePipeline can deploy to ECS.

Commands

bashBuild and push
TAG=${CODEBUILD_RESOLVED_SOURCE_VERSION:0:8}
aws ecr get-login-password | docker login --username AWS --password-stdin 111122223333.dkr.ecr.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com
docker build -t 111122223333.dkr.ecr.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/web:$TAG .
docker push 111122223333.dkr.ecr.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/web:$TAG
printf '[{"name":"web","imageUri":"%s"}]' "111122223333.dkr.ecr.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/web:$TAG" > imagedefinitions.json
76.4

CodePipeline stages and actions

In plain words

A pipeline is a series of stages, each with actions (source, build, test, approval, deploy, invoke) that pass artifacts forward.

The problem it solves

Releases need a visible, gated, auditable path from commit to production.

What it does

  • V2 pipelines support variables, triggers with Git tag and branch filters, and stage-level conditions; check the current features.
  • Actions in a stage can run in parallel using runOrder.
  • Manual approval actions notify through SNS.
  • Artifacts are stored in an S3 artifact bucket, encrypted with KMS.

Pipeline skeleton

hclpipeline.tf
resource "aws_codepipeline" "app" {
  name          = "app"
  role_arn      = aws_iam_role.pipeline.arn
  pipeline_type = "V2"
  artifact_store {
    location = aws_s3_bucket.artifacts.bucket
    type     = "S3"
  }
  stage {
    name = "Source"
    action {
      name             = "Source"
      category         = "Source"
      owner            = "AWS"
      provider         = "CodeStarSourceConnection"
      version          = "1"
      output_artifacts = ["src"]
      configuration = {
        ConnectionArn    = aws_codestarconnections_connection.github.arn
        FullRepositoryId = "org/app"
        BranchName       = "main"
      }
    }
  }
  stage {
    name = "Build"
    action {
      name             = "Build"
      category         = "Build"
      owner            = "AWS"
      provider         = "CodeBuild"
      version          = "1"
      input_artifacts  = ["src"]
      output_artifacts = ["build"]
      configuration = {
        ProjectName = aws_codebuild_project.app.name
      }
    }
  }
}
Check yourself
How are artifacts passed between stages?

Through an encrypted S3 artifact store.

76.5

Cross-account and cross-Region deployment

In plain words

Pipelines usually live in a tooling account and deploy into workload accounts by assuming roles there.

The problem it solves

Giving every workload account its own pipeline is expensive, and shared admin credentials are risky.

What it does

  • Artifact bucket uses a customer managed KMS key whose policy allows the target account roles.
  • The action's role_arn is a deploy role in the target account that trusts the pipeline role.
  • Keep the deployment role scoped to what the stage deploys.
  • Cross-Region pipelines need an artifact bucket in each Region.

Trust policy for the deploy role

jsondeploy-role-trust.json
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [{
    "Effect": "Allow",
    "Principal": {"AWS": "arn:aws:iam::222233334444:role/pipeline-role"},
    "Action": "sts:AssumeRole"
  }]
}
76.6

Triggers, approvals and notifications

In plain words

Pipelines start on source changes and can pause for approval, with events sent to chat or email.

The problem it solves

Unwatched pipelines fail silently and ungated ones deploy mistakes straight to production.

What it does

  • Triggers filter by branch, tag and file paths (V2).
  • Approval actions can include a URL and comment; only IAM principals with the approval permission can respond.
  • Notification rules send pipeline events to SNS or AWS Chatbot.
  • EventBridge pipeline execution state change events allow custom automation.

Rule

hclnotify.tf
resource "aws_cloudwatch_event_rule" "pipeline_failed" {
  name = "pipeline-failed"
  event_pattern = jsonencode({
    source        = ["aws.codepipeline"]
    "detail-type" = ["CodePipeline Pipeline Execution State Change"]
    detail        = { state = ["FAILED"] }
  })
}
Check yourself
Who can approve a manual approval action?

Principals whose IAM policy allows codepipeline:PutApprovalResult on it.

76.7

Troubleshooting builds and pipelines

In plain words

Failures cluster around permissions, missing artifacts, network access and buildspec errors.

The problem it solves

Pipelines fail with terse messages that hide the actual cause.

What it does

  • AccessDenied on S3 or KMS: the service role or the artifact bucket key policy.
  • YAML_FILE_ERROR: buildspec syntax error; lint locally.
  • Build cannot reach the internet in a VPC: needs NAT or endpoints.
  • Docker rate limit pulling base images: use ECR pull-through cache.
  • Use the action's execution details and the CodeBuild logs; retry only the failed stage when safe.

Fetch last build log

bashLatest build
ID=$(aws codebuild list-builds-for-project --project-name app-build --query 'ids[0]' --output text)
aws codebuild batch-get-builds --ids "$ID" --query 'builds[0].[buildStatus,currentPhase,phases[?phaseStatus==`FAILED`].contexts[].message]'

Section 77 of 93

CodeDeploy deployment strategies

7 concepts · about 45 minutes

CodeDeploy automates application releases so that a bad version is caught and rolled back before all users see it.

Goals
  • Describe CodeDeploy for EC2, Lambda and ECS compute platforms
  • Write an appspec and choose in-place, rolling, canary and blue/green configurations
  • Wire alarms and hooks for automatic rollback
77.1

What CodeDeploy does

In plain words

CodeDeploy coordinates releasing a new revision to a fleet, a Lambda alias or an ECS service, following an appspec file and a deployment configuration.

The problem it solves

Scripts that SSH to servers cannot shift traffic gradually, check health or roll back reliably.

What it does

  • Three compute platforms: EC2 or on-premises (agent based), AWS Lambda, Amazon ECS.
  • An application holds deployment groups; a deployment applies a revision.
  • Integrates with Auto Scaling groups, load balancers, CloudWatch alarms and SNS.
  • No extra charge for EC2, Lambda or ECS targets; on-premises instances are billed (check current pricing).

Application and group

bashCreate
aws deploy create-application --application-name shop --compute-platform ECS
aws deploy create-deployment --application-name shop --deployment-group-name prod \
  --revision revisionType=S3,s3Location={bucket=artifacts,key=appspec.zip,bundleType=zip}
Check yourself
Which platforms does CodeDeploy support?

EC2 or on-premises, Lambda and ECS.

77.2

In-place and rolling deployments on EC2

In plain words

An in-place deployment stops the app on each instance, installs the new revision and restarts it, in batches.

The problem it solves

You need to update long-lived servers without taking everything down at once.

What it does

  • Configs: OneAtATime, HalfAtATime, AllAtOnce or custom minimum healthy hosts.
  • Instances are deregistered from the load balancer during update, then re-registered after validation.
  • Capacity drops during the update; plan for the minimum healthy percentage.
  • Example: 10 instances with HalfAtATime updates 5 at a time, so capacity is 50 percent while a batch is running.

appspec for EC2

yamlappspec.yml
version: 0.0
os: linux
files:
  - source: /
    destination: /opt/shop
hooks:
  BeforeInstall:
    - location: scripts/stop.sh
      timeout: 60
  AfterInstall:
    - location: scripts/configure.sh
      timeout: 120
  ApplicationStart:
    - location: scripts/start.sh
      timeout: 60
  ValidateService:
    - location: scripts/health.sh
      timeout: 120
Check yourself
10 instances, HalfAtATime. Capacity during a batch?

50 percent (5 of 10 serving).

77.3

Blue/green deployments

In plain words

Blue/green creates a complete new environment (green), tests it, then moves traffic from blue and keeps blue for quick rollback.

The problem it solves

In-place changes alter the running version, so rollback means redeploying and capacity dips.

What it does

  • EC2: copies the Auto Scaling group, installs the revision, then shifts the load balancer.
  • ECS: creates a replacement task set behind a second target group, then moves the listener.
  • You can pay for double capacity during the window; set the termination wait time for the blue environment.
  • Rollback is switching traffic back, which takes seconds.

ECS appspec

yamlappspec-ecs.yml
version: 0.0
Resources:
  - TargetService:
      Type: AWS::ECS::Service
      Properties:
        TaskDefinition: "arn:aws:ecs:eu-west-1:111122223333:task-definition/web:13"
        LoadBalancerInfo:
          ContainerName: "web"
          ContainerPort: 8080
Hooks:
  - AfterAllowTestTraffic: "arn:aws:lambda:eu-west-1:111122223333:function:smoke-test"
77.4

Canary and linear traffic shifting

In plain words

Canary sends a small percentage first, then the rest. Linear adds a fixed percentage on an interval.

The problem it solves

All-at-once shifts expose every user to a bad release.

What it does

  • Predefined configs, for example CodeDeployDefault.LambdaCanary10Percent5Minutes and CodeDeployDefault.ECSLinear10PercentEvery1Minutes.
  • Canary 10 percent for 5 minutes then 100: total shift time about 5 minutes.
  • Linear 10 percent every 1 minute reaches 100 percent after 10 steps, about 9 to 10 minutes.
  • Combine with alarms and pre/post traffic hooks that run tests.

Lambda appspec

yamlappspec-lambda.yml
version: 0.0
Resources:
  - orders:
      Type: AWS::Lambda::Function
      Properties:
        Name: "orders"
        Alias: "live"
        CurrentVersion: "12"
        TargetVersion: "13"
Hooks:
  - BeforeAllowTraffic: "orders-pre-traffic-check"
  - AfterAllowTraffic: "orders-post-traffic-check"
Check yourself
How long does Linear10PercentEvery1Minute take to reach 100 percent?

About 10 minutes (ten steps of one minute), the last step completing the shift.

77.5

Alarms and automatic rollback

In plain words

CodeDeploy can watch CloudWatch alarms and automatically roll back if they fire.

The problem it solves

Humans notice errors late; a bad version keeps serving traffic.

What it does

  • Attach up to the quota number of alarms to a deployment group (check the current quota).
  • Rollback on deployment failure or alarm threshold.
  • Good alarms: 5xx rate, p99 latency, Lambda errors, business metrics.
  • Rollback redeploys the last good revision (EC2) or restores traffic (blue/green).

Group settings

hcldeploy-group.tf
resource "aws_codedeploy_deployment_group" "web" {
  app_name               = aws_codedeploy_app.shop.name
  deployment_group_name  = "prod"
  service_role_arn       = aws_iam_role.codedeploy.arn
  deployment_config_name = "CodeDeployDefault.OneAtATime"
  alarm_configuration {
    enabled = true
    alarms  = [aws_cloudwatch_metric_alarm.errors.alarm_name]
  }
  auto_rollback_configuration {
    enabled = true
    events  = ["DEPLOYMENT_FAILURE", "DEPLOYMENT_STOP_ON_ALARM"]
  }
}
77.6

Lifecycle hooks and agent

In plain words

Hooks run scripts or Lambda functions at defined points; EC2 deployments need the CodeDeploy agent installed.

The problem it solves

A deployment must run migrations, health checks and warm-up in the right order.

What it does

  • EC2 hook order: ApplicationStop, DownloadBundle, BeforeInstall, Install, AfterInstall, ApplicationStart, ValidateService (plus load balancer hooks).
  • Lambda and ECS use Lambda-based hooks that report Succeeded or Failed via PutLifecycleEventHookExecutionStatus.
  • Install the agent through Systems Manager Distributor or user data, and give the instance profile S3 read access to the bundle.
  • Keep hooks idempotent.

Hook report

pythonhook.py
import boto3

codedeploy = boto3.client("codedeploy")

def handler(event, context):
    status = "Succeeded"  # replace with real checks
    codedeploy.put_lifecycle_event_hook_execution_status(
        deploymentId=event["DeploymentId"],
        lifecycleEventHookExecutionId=event["LifecycleEventHookExecutionId"],
        status=status)
Check yourself
What must a Lambda hook call back to CodeDeploy?

PutLifecycleEventHookExecutionStatus with Succeeded or Failed.

77.7

Choosing a deployment strategy

In plain words

Pick by risk, cost of duplicate capacity and how quickly you must roll back.

The problem it solves

Using the same strategy for everything wastes money or accepts needless risk.

What it does

  • Internal tools and dev: in-place, all at once.
  • Stateless services: rolling or canary.
  • Customer-facing critical paths: blue/green canary with alarms.
  • Stateful changes: expand and contract migrations so old and new versions both run against the schema.
  • Kubernetes users have rollout controllers (Argo Rollouts) instead; CodeDeploy covers ECS, EC2 and Lambda.
Strategy
OptionIn-place
Choose whendev and low risk with spare capacity
Avoid whenstrict uptime requirements
OptionRolling
Choose whenstateless fleets with health checks
Avoid whenschema changes incompatible with old version
OptionBlue/green canary
Choose whenproduction APIs with alarms
Avoid whencost of duplicate capacity is prohibited

Section 78 of 93

Systems Manager operations toolkit

7 concepts · about 50 minutes

Systems Manager (SSM) is the operations hub for EC2, on-premises servers and containers. It replaces login keys, ad-hoc scripts and spreadsheets of patch levels.

Goals
  • Manage fleets with the SSM Agent, managed nodes and Session Manager
  • Store configuration in Parameter Store and patch with Patch Manager
  • Automate runbooks with Automation and Run Command
78.1

Managed nodes and the SSM Agent

In plain words

A managed node is a machine running the SSM Agent whose IAM role lets it talk to Systems Manager.

The problem it solves

Operating a fleet by logging in to each server does not scale or leave an audit trail.

What it does

  • The agent is preinstalled on Amazon Linux and many AMIs.
  • The instance profile needs the managed policy AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore.
  • The node needs outbound HTTPS to the ssm, ssmmessages and ec2messages endpoints, through NAT or three interface VPC endpoints.
  • Default Host Management Configuration can grant the role to instances account-wide.
  • Fleet Manager lists nodes and their agent versions.

Check the fleet

bashWhich nodes are online
aws ssm describe-instance-information \
  --query 'InstanceInformationList[].[InstanceId,PingStatus,PlatformName,AgentVersion]' --output table
Check yourself
An instance does not appear in Fleet Manager. Name three causes.

Missing role permissions, no network path to the SSM endpoints, or the agent not running.

78.2

Session Manager

In plain words

Session Manager gives a shell on an instance through the AWS API, with no inbound ports, bastion hosts or key pairs.

The problem it solves

Classic remote login needs open port 22, key distribution and offers poor auditing.

What it does

  • Access controlled by IAM (ssm:StartSession) with conditions on tags, so a team can reach only its own instances.
  • Sessions can log to CloudWatch Logs or S3 and are recorded in CloudTrail.
  • Port forwarding reaches private databases with the document AWS-StartPortForwardingSessionToRemoteHost.
  • Requires the Session Manager plugin for the CLI.

Allow only tagged instances

jsonsession-policy.json
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [{
    "Effect": "Allow",
    "Action": "ssm:StartSession",
    "Resource": "arn:aws:ec2:eu-west-1:111122223333:instance/*",
    "Condition": {"StringEquals": {"ssm:resourceTag/Team": "payments"}}
  }]
}
bashPort forward to a private database
aws ssm start-session --target i-0123456789abcdef0 \
  --document-name AWS-StartPortForwardingSessionToRemoteHost \
  --parameters host=db.internal,portNumber=5432,localPortNumber=15432
Check yourself
How do you restrict engineers to their own team's instances?

An IAM condition on ssm:resourceTag for StartSession.

78.3

Parameter Store

In plain words

Parameter Store is a hierarchical key value store for configuration and secrets, with versions and IAM access.

The problem it solves

Configuration hard coded in images or environment files is hard to change and audit.

What it does

  • Types: String, StringList, SecureString (KMS encrypted).
  • Hierarchy such as /shop/prod/db/host allows IAM policies on a path and get-parameters-by-path.
  • Standard parameters have no charge; advanced parameters allow bigger values and policies such as expiry (check current pricing).
  • Public parameters hold the latest AMI IDs, for example /aws/service/ami-amazon-linux-latest/al2023-ami-kernel-default-x86_64.
  • Secrets Manager adds automatic rotation; use it for database credentials.

Write and read

bashParameters
aws ssm put-parameter --name /shop/prod/db/host --type String --value db.internal --overwrite
aws ssm put-parameter --name /shop/prod/db/password --type SecureString --value "$PW"
aws ssm get-parameters-by-path --path /shop/prod --recursive --with-decryption
hclparam.tf
data "aws_ssm_parameter" "al2023" {
  name = "/aws/service/ami-amazon-linux-latest/al2023-ami-kernel-default-x86_64"
}
78.4

Run Command and State Manager

In plain words

Run Command runs a document (script) on many nodes at once. State Manager keeps nodes in a desired state by applying documents on a schedule.

The problem it solves

Fleet-wide changes through login loops are slow, unaudited and fail halfway.

What it does

  • Target by instance IDs, tags or resource groups; control with max-concurrency and max-errors.
  • Output goes to S3 or CloudWatch Logs.
  • Documents: AWS-RunShellScript, AWS-RunPowerShellScript, AWS-ConfigureAWSPackage and your own.
  • State Manager associations install agents and enforce configuration, for example the CloudWatch agent on every node.

Run on tagged nodes

bashRun Command
aws ssm send-command --document-name AWS-RunShellScript \
  --targets Key=tag:Env,Values=prod --max-concurrency 10% --max-errors 1 \
  --parameters 'commands=["systemctl is-active nginx"]'
Check yourself
Which two settings limit the blast radius of Run Command?

max-concurrency and max-errors.

78.5

Patch Manager

In plain words

Patch Manager scans nodes for missing OS patches and installs them in maintenance windows, using patch baselines.

The problem it solves

Unpatched servers are a leading cause of breaches, and manual patching drifts.

What it does

  • A patch baseline defines approved classifications, severities and auto-approval delay (for example 7 days after release).
  • Patch groups or tags attach nodes to a baseline.
  • Two operations: Scan (report) and Install; schedule through a maintenance window or a patch policy in Quick Setup, which can span an organization.
  • Compliance reports show per-node missing patches.
  • Immutable fleets patch by building new AMIs instead; combine with Image Builder.

Baseline

hclpatch.tf
resource "aws_ssm_patch_baseline" "linux" {
  name             = "al2023-security"
  operating_system = "AMAZON_LINUX_2023"
  approval_rule {
    approve_after_days = 7
    patch_filter {
      key    = "CLASSIFICATION"
      values = ["Security"]
    }
    patch_filter {
      key    = "SEVERITY"
      values = ["Critical", "Important"]
    }
  }
}
Check yourself
What does approve_after_days do?

Waits that many days after a patch is released before the baseline approves it.

78.6

Automation runbooks

In plain words

Automation runs multi-step runbooks that call AWS APIs, with approvals, branching and rate control.

The problem it solves

Operational procedures, such as restoring from a snapshot, live in wikis and are done differently by each person.

What it does

  • AWS-owned runbooks exist for many tasks, such as AWS-RestartEC2Instance, AWS-CreateImage, AWS-UpdateLinuxAmi.
  • Custom runbooks in YAML or JSON with actions like aws:executeAwsApi, aws:runCommand, aws:approve.
  • Run with an assume role so people need not have wide permissions.
  • Trigger from EventBridge, Config remediation or OpsCenter.

Simple runbook

yamlrestart-runbook.yaml
schemaVersion: "0.3"
description: Stop and start an instance
assumeRole: "{{ AutomationAssumeRole }}"
parameters:
  AutomationAssumeRole:
    type: String
  InstanceId:
    type: String
mainSteps:
  - name: stop
    action: aws:changeInstanceState
    inputs:
      InstanceIds:
        - "{{ InstanceId }}"
      DesiredState: stopped
  - name: start
    action: aws:changeInstanceState
    inputs:
      InstanceIds:
        - "{{ InstanceId }}"
      DesiredState: running
78.7

Maintenance windows, Inventory and Change Manager

In plain words

Maintenance windows schedule tasks. Inventory lists software. Change Manager adds approval workflows.

The problem it solves

Changes must happen at agreed times with a record of what and who.

What it does

  • Maintenance windows: cron schedule, duration, cutoff and registered targets with tasks (Run Command, Automation, Lambda, Step Functions).
  • Inventory collects applications, network settings and files into a queryable store, aggregated by Resource Data Sync to S3.
  • Change Manager needs approvers and change calendars to block changes during freezes.
  • Explorer and OpsCenter give a dashboard and an operational issue queue.
  • Multi-account use is through a delegated administrator and Quick Setup.

Window

hclwindow.tf
resource "aws_ssm_maintenance_window" "sunday" {
  name     = "sunday-patching"
  schedule = "cron(0 2 ? * SUN *)"
  duration = 3
  cutoff   = 1
}

Duration 3 hours with cutoff 1 hour means no new task starts after 2 hours into the window.

Check yourself
Window duration 3 h and cutoff 1 h. When does the last task start?

At most 2 hours after the window starts.

← PreviousNext →
Section 79 of 93

AWS Backup and Elastic Disaster Recovery

7 concepts · about 50 minutes

Backups protect against deletion and corruption. Disaster recovery protects against the loss of a site or Region. This section covers the AWS services for both.

Goals
  • Build centralised backup plans with vaults, lifecycle, copies and Vault Lock
  • Choose between backup restore, pilot light, warm standby and Elastic Disaster Recovery
  • Test restores and measure RPO and RTO
79.1

AWS Backup plans and vaults

In plain words

AWS Backup is one service to schedule, retain and monitor backups for EBS, RDS, Aurora, DynamoDB, EFS, FSx, S3, EC2 and more.

The problem it solves

Each service has its own backup settings, so coverage is inconsistent and nobody can prove it.

What it does

  • A backup plan has rules for schedule, window, lifecycle (cold storage, expiry) and copy actions.
  • A vault stores recovery points and is encrypted with a KMS key.
  • Resources are chosen by tag such as backup=daily, so new resources are covered automatically.
  • Continuous backup with point-in-time recovery exists for some services; check the supported list.

Plan in Terraform

hclbackup.tf
resource "aws_backup_vault" "main" {
  name        = "main"
  kms_key_arn = aws_kms_key.backup.arn
}

resource "aws_backup_plan" "daily" {
  name = "daily"
  rule {
    rule_name         = "daily-35d"
    target_vault_name = aws_backup_vault.main.name
    schedule          = "cron(0 3 * * ? *)"
    lifecycle {
      delete_after = 35
    }
  }
}

resource "aws_backup_selection" "tagged" {
  name         = "tagged"
  plan_id      = aws_backup_plan.daily.id
  iam_role_arn = aws_iam_role.backup.arn
  selection_tag {
    type  = "STRINGEQUALS"
    key   = "backup"
    value = "daily"
  }
}
Check yourself
How do new resources get included automatically?

A tag based selection in the backup plan.

79.2

Cross-account copies and Vault Lock

In plain words

Copy recovery points to another account and Region, and lock the vault so even administrators cannot delete them early.

The problem it solves

Ransomware or a compromised admin can delete backups that live beside the data.

What it does

  • A copy rule sends recovery points to a vault in a separate backup account and a second Region.
  • Vault Lock in compliance mode enforces minimum and maximum retention; after the grace period it cannot be removed.
  • Organization backup policies apply plans across accounts.
  • Logically air-gapped vaults are an additional option; check current documentation.

Vault Lock

bashLock a vault
aws backup put-backup-vault-lock-configuration --backup-vault-name main \
  --min-retention-days 7 --max-retention-days 365 --changeable-for-days 3
Danger

After the changeable period ends, compliance mode cannot be undone. Test in a non production vault first.

Check yourself
What is the benefit of a separate backup account?

A compromise of a workload account cannot delete its own backups.

79.3

RPO, RTO and restore time

In plain words

RPO is how much data you can lose, measured in time. RTO is how long you can be down. They drive the design and its cost.

The problem it solves

Without numbers, teams buy too little protection or an expensive design they do not need.

What it does

  • Daily backup gives RPO up to 24 hours; hourly up to 1 hour; continuous backup seconds to minutes.
  • RTO includes detection, decision, restore time and validation.
  • Worked estimate: a 2 TB restore at an effective 100 MB per second is 2,000,000 MB / 100 = 20,000 s, about 5.6 hours.
  • Test restores to measure real RTO.

Estimate in Python

pythonrto.py
size_mb = 2 * 1000 * 1000
rate_mb_s = 100
seconds = size_mb / rate_mb_s
print(seconds, seconds / 3600)
Check yourself
Daily backups give what worst case RPO?

Up to 24 hours.

79.4

DR strategies

In plain words

Four classic strategies trade cost against recovery speed: backup and restore, pilot light, warm standby and multi-site active-active.

The problem it solves

Choosing the same DR level for every workload either wastes money or leaves critical systems exposed.

What it does

  • Backup and restore: cheapest, RTO hours to a day.
  • Pilot light: data replicated and core services such as the database running; scale out on disaster.
  • Warm standby: a scaled-down full copy running; scale up on failover.
  • Active-active: every Region serves traffic; lowest RTO, highest cost and complexity.
DR level
OptionBackup and restore
Choose wheninternal systems with hours of tolerance
Avoid whenrevenue systems with minutes of tolerance
OptionPilot light
Choose whenimportant systems
Avoid whenstrict minutes-level RTO
OptionWarm standby
Choose whencustomer facing with minutes of tolerance
Avoid whenbudget cannot carry a second stack
OptionActive-active
Choose whennear zero downtime is a requirement
Avoid whendata model cannot handle multi-writer conflicts
Check yourself
Which strategy keeps a scaled-down full environment running?

Warm standby.

79.5

AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery

In plain words

AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery (DRS) continuously replicates servers at block level into a low-cost staging area in AWS and launches recovery instances on demand.

The problem it solves

Running a second copy of every server is costly, but restoring from nightly backups is too slow.

What it does

  • An agent on the source server replicates disks to replication servers and EBS volumes in a staging subnet. Typical RPO is seconds and RTO minutes.
  • Launch templates define instance type, subnet and security groups for recovery.
  • Point-in-time snapshots allow recovery to before corruption.
  • Drills launch recovery instances without interrupting replication; failback returns data to the source.

Start a drill

bashDRS commands
aws drs initialize-service
aws drs describe-source-servers --query 'items[].[sourceServerID,dataReplicationInfo.dataReplicationState]'
aws drs start-recovery --is-drill --source-servers sourceServerID=s-1234567890abcdef0
Check yourself
Does DRS need a full duplicate fleet running?

No. Only low-cost staging resources run until recovery.

79.6

Testing recovery

In plain words

A recovery plan is real only after it has been exercised with measured results.

The problem it solves

Teams discover broken runbooks, missing permissions and expired keys during the real outage.

What it does

  • AWS Backup restore testing plans restore and validate automatically on a schedule.
  • Script failover with Step Functions or Systems Manager Automation.
  • Use Route 53 health checks and Application Recovery Controller routing controls for deliberate DNS switching.
  • Record actual RPO and RTO, fix gaps, retest.

Restore test plan

hclrestore-test.tf
resource "aws_backup_restore_testing_plan" "weekly" {
  name                = "weekly"
  schedule_expression = "cron(0 5 ? * SUN *)"
  start_window_hours  = 4
  recovery_point_selection {
    algorithm            = "LATEST_WITHIN_WINDOW"
    include_vaults       = ["*"]
    recovery_point_types = ["SNAPSHOT"]
    lookback_window_days = 7
  }
}
79.7

Backup monitoring and cost

In plain words

Monitor job success, alarm on failures and watch storage growth, because backup storage accumulates silently.

The problem it solves

A backup that failed three weeks ago is discovered only when needed.

What it does

  • EventBridge emits job state events; alarm on failed jobs.
  • Backup Audit Manager checks coverage and retention against policy.
  • Cost drivers: warm storage per GB-month, cold storage with a minimum retention, cross-Region transfer and restore charges.
  • Incremental estimate: 5 TB, 2 percent daily change, 35 days gives about 5 + 0.02 x 5 x 35 = 8.5 TB.

Failed jobs

bashFailed backup jobs
aws backup list-backup-jobs --by-state FAILED --query 'BackupJobs[].[ResourceArn,StatusMessage]' --output table
Check yourself
Compute the estimate for 5 TB, 2 percent daily change, 35 days.

5 + 0.02 x 5 x 35 = 8.5 TB.

Section 80 of 93

Direct Connect and Site-to-Site VPN

6 concepts · about 55 minutes

Hybrid architectures need a reliable path between the data centre and AWS. VPN is quick and encrypted over the internet. Direct Connect is a private circuit with predictable performance.

Goals
  • Compare Site-to-Site VPN, Direct Connect and combined designs
  • Design resilient hybrid connectivity with BGP and multiple links
  • Choose between private, transit and public virtual interfaces
80.1

Site-to-Site VPN

In plain words

A Site-to-Site VPN creates two IPsec tunnels between your customer gateway device and AWS over the internet.

The problem it solves

You need encrypted connectivity within minutes, without ordering a circuit.

What it does

  • Each connection has two tunnels in different AZs; configure both on your device.
  • Terminates on a virtual private gateway (one VPC) or a transit gateway (many VPCs).
  • Routing is dynamic BGP (preferred) or static.
  • Each tunnel has a bandwidth limit (about 1.25 Gbps; check the current quota). ECMP on a transit gateway can aggregate tunnels.
  • Accelerated VPN uses Global Accelerator edge locations for steadier performance.

Terraform

hclvpn.tf
resource "aws_customer_gateway" "dc" {
  bgp_asn    = 65010
  ip_address = "203.0.113.10"
  type       = "ipsec.1"
}

resource "aws_vpn_connection" "dc" {
  customer_gateway_id = aws_customer_gateway.dc.id
  transit_gateway_id  = aws_ec2_transit_gateway.main.id
  type                = "ipsec.1"
  static_routes_only  = false
}
Check yourself
Why configure both tunnels?

AWS can take one down for maintenance; both give redundancy.

80.2

Direct Connect basics

In plain words

AWS Direct Connect is a dedicated private network connection from your site to an AWS Direct Connect location.

The problem it solves

Internet VPN performance varies, and large transfers over the internet are slow and costly.

What it does

  • Dedicated connections (1, 10, 100 Gbps and more where offered) or hosted connections from partners at smaller speeds.
  • Lead time is weeks, so order early.
  • Traffic is not encrypted by default; add MACsec on supported ports or run an IPsec VPN over it.
  • Data transfer out is cheaper than internet egress; check current rates.
  • Needs a cross connect in a colocation facility, or a partner.

Describe connections

bashConnections
aws directconnect describe-connections --query 'connections[].[connectionName,bandwidth,connectionState,location]' --output table
80.3

Virtual interfaces and the Direct Connect gateway

In plain words

A virtual interface (VIF) is a VLAN with a BGP session on a Direct Connect connection. A Direct Connect gateway lets one VIF reach VPCs in many Regions.

The problem it solves

One physical link must carry private VPC traffic, transit gateway traffic and public AWS service traffic.

What it does

  • Private VIF: to a VPC through a virtual private gateway or Direct Connect gateway.
  • Transit VIF: to a transit gateway through a Direct Connect gateway; best for many VPCs.
  • Public VIF: reach AWS public endpoints such as S3 using public IPs.
  • The Direct Connect gateway does not provide VPC to VPC transit by itself.
  • BGP prefix limits apply; summarise routes (check current quotas).

Gateway association

hcldx-gateway.tf
resource "aws_dx_gateway" "main" {
  name            = "main"
  amazon_side_asn = 64512
}

resource "aws_dx_gateway_association" "tgw" {
  dx_gateway_id         = aws_dx_gateway.main.id
  associated_gateway_id = aws_ec2_transit_gateway.main.id
  allowed_prefixes      = ["10.0.0.0/16", "10.1.0.0/16"]
}
Check yourself
Which VIF type serves many VPCs through a transit gateway?

A transit VIF.

80.4

Resilience models

In plain words

AWS recommends resilience levels from development up to maximum resiliency, based on the number of locations and links.

The problem it solves

A single link and location is a single point of failure for the whole data centre connection.

What it does

  • Maximum resiliency: two locations with two devices each, so four connections. Survives device, link and location failure.
  • High resiliency: two locations with one connection each. Survives a location failure.
  • Development and test: one connection with a VPN backup.
  • Add a Site-to-Site VPN as a backup path with lower BGP preference.
  • The SLA applies only to supported resilient designs; check the current text.
Resilience level
OptionMaximum
Choose whenproduction that cannot lose connectivity
Avoid whena lab environment
OptionHigh
Choose whenproduction with some tolerance for device failure
Avoid whensingle device failure is unacceptable
OptionDev and test
Choose whennon critical workloads
Avoid whenany production dependency
80.5

BGP routing and path selection

In plain words

BGP exchanges routes between your router and AWS. When several paths exist, the most specific route and the documented preference order decide.

The problem it solves

Traffic must take the intended path and fail over predictably.

What it does

  • Longest prefix match wins first. For equal prefixes AWS prefers Direct Connect over VPN (check the current preference documentation).
  • Influence inbound traffic with AS path prepending or communities, outbound with local preference.
  • Use BFD for fast failure detection and BGP MD5 authentication.
  • Example: if 10.0.0.0/8 is advertised on Direct Connect and 10.0.0.0/16 on VPN, traffic to 10.0.1.5 takes the VPN because the /16 is more specific.

Inspect propagated routes

bashTGW routes
aws ec2 search-transit-gateway-routes --transit-gateway-route-table-id tgw-rtb-0abc \
  --filters Name=type,Values=propagated --query 'Routes[].[DestinationCidrBlock,State]'
Check yourself
For 10.0.1.5, which wins, the /8 on DX or the /16 on VPN?

The /16 on VPN, because longest prefix wins.

80.6

Hybrid DNS and monitoring

In plain words

Name resolution must work both ways, and the links must be monitored.

The problem it solves

Connectivity without DNS means services still cannot find one another, and a silent tunnel failure goes unnoticed.

What it does

  • Route 53 Resolver inbound endpoints accept queries from on-premises; outbound endpoints with rules forward corporate domains to on-premises DNS.
  • Place endpoints in at least two AZs.
  • Monitor ConnectionState, ConnectionBpsEgress and VPN TunnelState; alarm on state changes.
  • Usual production design: Direct Connect primary and VPN backup.

Forwarding rule and alarm

hclresolver.tf
resource "aws_route53_resolver_rule" "corp" {
  domain_name          = "corp.example.com"
  rule_type            = "FORWARD"
  resolver_endpoint_id = aws_route53_resolver_endpoint.out.id
  target_ip {
    ip = "10.200.0.2"
  }
}

resource "aws_cloudwatch_metric_alarm" "tunnel" {
  alarm_name          = "vpn-tunnel-down"
  namespace           = "AWS/VPN"
  metric_name         = "TunnelState"
  dimensions          = { VpnId = "vpn-0abc123" }
  statistic           = "Maximum"
  period              = 60
  evaluation_periods  = 3
  threshold           = 1
  comparison_operator = "LessThanThreshold"
}
Check yourself
Which design is usual for production hybrid?

Direct Connect primary with VPN backup, or two resilient Direct Connect locations.
