Section 81 of 93

Transit Gateway deep dive

6 concepts · about 50 minutes

A Transit Gateway (TGW) is a regional router that connects VPCs, VPNs and Direct Connect through one hub, replacing a mesh of peerings.

Goals
  • Explain attachments, route tables, associations and propagation
  • Design segmented networks and inspection VPCs with multiple route tables
  • Peer Regions, share the gateway with RAM and reason about cost
81.1

Why a transit gateway

In plain words

A TGW is a hub. Each network attaches once, and the hub routes between them.

The problem it solves

VPC peering is not transitive. N VPCs fully meshed need N x (N - 1) / 2 peerings.

What it does

  • Worked count: 10 VPCs need 10 x 9 / 2 = 45 peerings, but only 10 TGW attachments.
  • Attachment types: VPC, VPN, Direct Connect gateway, peering (another TGW), and Connect (SD-WAN).
  • Bandwidth per VPC attachment is limited (check the current quota); you pay per attachment-hour and per GB processed.
  • Regional resource; use TGW peering for multiple Regions.

Gateway and attachment

hcltgw.tf
resource "aws_ec2_transit_gateway" "main" {
  description                     = "main"
  amazon_side_asn                 = 64512
  default_route_table_association = "disable"
  default_route_table_propagation = "disable"
}

resource "aws_ec2_transit_gateway_vpc_attachment" "app" {
  transit_gateway_id = aws_ec2_transit_gateway.main.id
  vpc_id             = aws_vpc.app.id
  subnet_ids         = aws_subnet.tgw[*].id
}
Check yourself
How many peerings does a full mesh of 10 VPCs need?

45.

81.2

Route tables, associations and propagation

In plain words

Each attachment is associated with one TGW route table that decides where its traffic goes. An attachment can propagate its routes into any number of tables.

The problem it solves

Without separate tables every attachment can reach every other one, which breaks segmentation.

What it does

  • Association: which table is used for traffic entering from that attachment (one only).
  • Propagation: which tables learn this attachment's CIDRs automatically.
  • Static routes can be added, including blackhole routes.
  • Default tables are convenient but disable them when you want explicit segmentation.

Associate and propagate

hcltgw-routes.tf
resource "aws_ec2_transit_gateway_route_table" "prod" {
  transit_gateway_id = aws_ec2_transit_gateway.main.id
}

resource "aws_ec2_transit_gateway_route_table_association" "prod_vpc" {
  transit_gateway_attachment_id  = aws_ec2_transit_gateway_vpc_attachment.app.id
  transit_gateway_route_table_id = aws_ec2_transit_gateway_route_table.prod.id
}

resource "aws_ec2_transit_gateway_route_table_propagation" "shared_to_prod" {
  transit_gateway_attachment_id  = aws_ec2_transit_gateway_vpc_attachment.shared.id
  transit_gateway_route_table_id = aws_ec2_transit_gateway_route_table.prod.id
}
Check yourself
How many route tables can one attachment be associated with?

One.

81.3

Segmentation patterns

In plain words

Use separate route tables to isolate environments while sharing common services.

The problem it solves

Prod and dev must not talk, but both need DNS, logging and package mirrors.

What it does

  • Prod table: routes to prod VPCs and shared services only.
  • Dev table: routes to dev VPCs and shared services only.
  • Shared services VPC propagates into both tables, while prod and dev do not propagate into each other.
  • Verify with Network Manager Route Analyzer and VPC Reachability Analyzer.
Segmentation
OptionSeparate tables
Choose whenenvironments, compliance zones
Avoid whena tiny network with one team
OptionSingle default table
Choose whena lab
Avoid whenany regulated workload
81.4

Centralised inspection and egress

In plain words

Send traffic through a central inspection VPC with firewalls, or through a central NAT, using appliance mode and route design.

The problem it solves

Each VPC running its own firewall and NAT is costly and inconsistent.

What it does

  • Spokes route 0.0.0.0/0 to the TGW; the TGW forwards to the inspection VPC attachment.
  • Enable appliance mode on the inspection attachment so both directions of a flow use the same AZ and the stateful firewall sees both.
  • Egress VPC holds NAT gateways in each AZ and routes back to the TGW.
  • Watch cross-AZ and TGW data processing charges.

Appliance mode

hclappliance.tf
resource "aws_ec2_transit_gateway_vpc_attachment" "inspection" {
  transit_gateway_id     = aws_ec2_transit_gateway.main.id
  vpc_id                 = aws_vpc.inspection.id
  subnet_ids             = aws_subnet.inspection_tgw[*].id
  appliance_mode_support = "enable"
}
Check yourself
Why enable appliance mode?

So both directions of a flow stay in the same AZ and a stateful appliance sees them.

81.5

Inter-Region peering and sharing

In plain words

TGW peering links gateways in different Regions. AWS RAM shares a gateway with other accounts.

The problem it solves

Multi-Region and multi-account networks need one coherent fabric.

What it does

  • Peering attachments use static routes only (no propagation across peering).
  • Traffic stays on the AWS backbone and is encrypted at the physical layer.
  • Share the TGW to the whole organization with RAM, so each account creates its own VPC attachment, which the owner can auto-accept.
  • Keep the TGW in a dedicated network account.

Share with RAM

bashShare the gateway
aws ram create-resource-share --name tgw-share \
  --resource-arns arn:aws:ec2:eu-west-1:111122223333:transit-gateway/tgw-0abc123 \
  --principals arn:aws:organizations::111122223333:organization/o-exampleorgid
81.6

Cost, limits and troubleshooting

In plain words

Costs have an hourly attachment fee and a per GB processing fee. Troubleshooting follows the route chain.

The problem it solves

Surprise bills and silent blackholes are the common TGW incidents.

What it does

  • Estimate: 20 attachments x 730 hours x hourly price, plus GB x per GB price. Check the current prices.
  • Overlapping CIDRs cannot be routed; plan addresses centrally.
  • Debug: VPC route table to TGW, TGW association table has a route, return route exists, security groups and NACLs allow.
  • Use Flow Logs on attachments and Reachability Analyzer.

Reachability

bashAnalyze a path
aws ec2 create-network-insights-path --source eni-0aaa --destination eni-0bbb --protocol tcp --destination-port 443
Check yourself
Why might traffic reach the destination but replies fail?

A missing return route in the destination VPC or TGW table.

← PreviousNext →
Section 82 of 93

Network Firewall and Global Accelerator

7 concepts · about 45 minutes

Network Firewall inspects traffic inside your VPCs. Global Accelerator improves how users reach your endpoints. Both operate at the network layer.

Goals
  • Deploy AWS Network Firewall with stateless and stateful rule groups
  • Place firewall endpoints in distributed and centralised designs
  • Use Global Accelerator for static anycast entry points and fast failover
82.1

What Network Firewall is

In plain words

AWS Network Firewall is a managed, stateful network firewall and intrusion prevention service deployed as endpoints in your VPC subnets.

The problem it solves

Security groups and NACLs cannot filter by domain name, inspect protocols or block known bad signatures.

What it does

  • Rule engines: stateless (fast, 5-tuple) then stateful (Suricata compatible rules, domain lists, protocol detection).
  • Scales automatically; one firewall endpoint per AZ.
  • Logs alert and flow records to S3, CloudWatch Logs or Firehose.
  • Managed rule groups from AWS cover threat signatures and domain reputation; check current groups.

Policy outline

hclfirewall.tf
resource "aws_networkfirewall_firewall_policy" "main" {
  name = "main"
  firewall_policy {
    stateless_default_actions          = ["aws:forward_to_sfe"]
    stateless_fragment_default_actions = ["aws:forward_to_sfe"]
    stateful_rule_group_reference {
      resource_arn = aws_networkfirewall_rule_group.domains.arn
    }
  }
}
Check yourself
Which service filters traffic by domain name inside a VPC?

Network Firewall (stateful domain list rules).

82.2

Rule groups and domain filtering

In plain words

A rule group is a reusable set of rules. Stateful groups can allow or deny by domain list, or use Suricata rule strings.

The problem it solves

Workloads should only reach approved external domains, and egress must be controlled without maintaining IP lists.

What it does

  • Domain list rule groups match the TLS SNI or HTTP host header for chosen protocols.
  • Default action drop established with alert logging blocks unmatched flows (strict rule order).
  • Capacity is fixed when a rule group is created, so size it with headroom.
  • Suricata rules allow custom signatures.

Allow list

hcldomains.tf
resource "aws_networkfirewall_rule_group" "domains" {
  name     = "allowed-domains"
  type     = "STATEFUL"
  capacity = 100
  rule_group {
    rules_source {
      rules_source_list {
        generated_rules_type = "ALLOWLIST"
        target_types         = ["HTTP_HOST", "TLS_SNI"]
        targets              = [".amazonaws.com", "github.com"]
      }
    }
  }
}
Check yourself
Why size rule group capacity with headroom?

Capacity is fixed at creation and cannot be raised later.

82.3

Firewall deployment models

In plain words

Deploy firewall endpoints in each VPC (distributed) or in one inspection VPC reached through a transit gateway (centralised).

The problem it solves

The right placement depends on how many VPCs you have and who owns policy.

What it does

  • Distributed: endpoint in each VPC, local policy; more endpoints to pay for, less transit traffic.
  • Centralised: one inspection VPC with TGW appliance mode; consistent policy, extra hop and TGW data charges.
  • Ingress needs an edge route table to send internet gateway traffic through the endpoint first.
  • Compare with Gateway Load Balancer for third party appliances.
Placement
OptionDistributed
Choose whenfew VPCs with team-owned rules
Avoid whenmany accounts needing one policy
OptionCentralised
Choose whenmany VPCs and a security team
Avoid whenvery high cross-AZ transit volume
OptionThird party via GWLB
Choose whenyou must use a vendor firewall
Avoid whena managed AWS option satisfies needs
82.4

Logging and tuning

In plain words

Send alert and flow logs somewhere searchable, then tune rules from real traffic.

The problem it solves

A new firewall in drop mode breaks applications that nobody listed.

What it does

  • Start in alert mode, analyse in Athena or CloudWatch Logs Insights, then move to drop.
  • Log fields include the matching rule SID and action.
  • Review monthly; remove stale domains.
  • Cost: hourly endpoint charge per AZ plus per GB processed; check the current prices.

Logging config

hclfw-logging.tf
resource "aws_networkfirewall_logging_configuration" "main" {
  firewall_arn = aws_networkfirewall_firewall.main.arn
  logging_configuration {
    log_destination_config {
      log_destination      = { logGroup = "/nfw/alerts" }
      log_destination_type = "CloudWatchLogs"
      log_type             = "ALERT"
    }
  }
}
Check yourself
Why start in alert mode?

To learn legitimate traffic before blocking it.

82.5

Global Accelerator basics

In plain words

AWS Global Accelerator gives your application two static anycast IP addresses that route users onto the AWS backbone at the nearest edge location.

The problem it solves

Internet paths vary, DNS caching slows failover, and clients or firewalls may need fixed IP addresses.

What it does

  • Listeners accept TCP or UDP on chosen ports; endpoint groups per Region hold endpoints (ALB, NLB, EC2, Elastic IP).
  • Health checks and traffic dials move traffic away from unhealthy endpoints within seconds, with no DNS TTL wait.
  • Client IP preservation is available for some endpoint types.
  • Billed by hour per accelerator plus a data transfer premium; check current pricing.

Terraform

hclga.tf
resource "aws_globalaccelerator_accelerator" "web" {
  name            = "web"
  ip_address_type = "IPV4"
  enabled         = true
}

resource "aws_globalaccelerator_listener" "https" {
  accelerator_arn = aws_globalaccelerator_accelerator.web.id
  protocol        = "TCP"
  port_range {
    from_port = 443
    to_port   = 443
  }
}
Check yourself
Why does failover not wait for DNS TTL?

Clients use fixed anycast IPs and Global Accelerator itself reroutes.

82.6

Global Accelerator versus CloudFront and Route 53

In plain words

CloudFront caches HTTP content at the edge. Route 53 answers DNS. Global Accelerator speeds up and stabilises any TCP or UDP path.

The problem it solves

Teams pick one for everything and miss the better fit.

What it does

  • CloudFront: cacheable web content, WAF, edge functions, HTTP only.
  • Global Accelerator: non-HTTP (gaming, IoT, VoIP), static IPs, instant regional failover for dynamic apps.
  • Route 53: low-cost DNS-level routing (latency, weighted, failover); subject to DNS caching.
  • Combine them: CloudFront for assets plus Global Accelerator for an API with fixed IPs.
Edge choice
OptionCloudFront
Choose whencontent is cacheable HTTP
Avoid whenyou need fixed IPs for a TCP service
OptionGlobal Accelerator
Choose whenstatic IP or non-HTTP traffic
Avoid whencaching would solve the problem
OptionRoute 53 only
Choose whensimple multi-Region failover with tolerable TTL
Avoid whenseconds-level failover is required
82.7

Multi-Region failover with Global Accelerator

In plain words

Place endpoint groups in two Regions and use traffic dials and health checks to steer traffic.

The problem it solves

A Region impairment should shift users automatically and deployments should shift traffic gradually.

What it does

  • Each endpoint group has a traffic dial (0 to 100 percent); set one to 0 to drain a Region.
  • Endpoint weights balance inside a group.
  • Health checks (TCP, HTTP, HTTPS) decide endpoint health.
  • Example: dial eu-west-1 at 90 and us-east-1 at 10 sends a small share to the second Region for warm-up.

Endpoint group

hclga-group.tf
resource "aws_globalaccelerator_endpoint_group" "eu" {
  listener_arn          = aws_globalaccelerator_listener.https.id
  endpoint_group_region = "eu-west-1"
  traffic_dial_percentage = 90
  health_check_protocol = "HTTPS"
  health_check_path     = "/healthz"
  endpoint_configuration {
    endpoint_id = aws_lb.web.arn
    weight      = 128
  }
}
Check yourself
How do you drain a Region for maintenance?

Set its endpoint group traffic dial to 0.

← PreviousNext →
Section 83 of 93

CloudFront deep dive

7 concepts · about 55 minutes

CloudFront is a global content delivery network. Correct cache keys and secure origins make the difference between a fast, cheap site and an expensive one.

Goals
  • Configure distributions, origins, behaviors and cache policies
  • Secure origins with Origin Access Control, signed URLs and WAF
  • Use CloudFront Functions and Lambda@Edge and troubleshoot cache hit ratio
83.1

Distributions, origins and behaviors

In plain words

A distribution has one or more origins (S3, ALB, custom HTTP) and behaviors that map URL path patterns to an origin and cache settings.

The problem it solves

Users far from the origin see latency, and the origin carries every request.

What it does

  • Edge locations cache responses; regional edge caches add a second tier.
  • Default behavior * plus path behaviors such as /api/* and /static/*.
  • Viewer protocol policy (redirect to HTTPS), allowed methods, compression, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3.
  • Custom domain needs an ACM certificate in us-east-1.

Terraform sketch

hclcf.tf
resource "aws_cloudfront_distribution" "site" {
  enabled             = true
  default_root_object = "index.html"
  aliases             = ["www.example.com"]

  origin {
    domain_name              = aws_s3_bucket.site.bucket_regional_domain_name
    origin_id                = "s3-site"
    origin_access_control_id = aws_cloudfront_origin_access_control.site.id
  }

  default_cache_behavior {
    target_origin_id       = "s3-site"
    viewer_protocol_policy = "redirect-to-https"
    allowed_methods        = ["GET", "HEAD"]
    cached_methods         = ["GET", "HEAD"]
    cache_policy_id        = "658327ea-f89d-4fab-a63d-7e88639e58f6"
    compress               = true
  }

  restrictions {
    geo_restriction {
      restriction_type = "none"
    }
  }

  viewer_certificate {
    acm_certificate_arn = aws_acm_certificate.site.arn
    ssl_support_method  = "sni-only"
  }
}
Note

The cache policy ID above is the AWS managed CachingOptimized policy; check the current ID in the console or documentation.

Check yourself
In which Region must a CloudFront ACM certificate live?

us-east-1.

83.2

Cache keys, TTLs and invalidation

In plain words

The cache key decides which requests share one cached object. TTLs decide how long it lives.

The problem it solves

A cache key that includes needless headers or query strings fragments the cache and the hit ratio collapses.

What it does

  • Cache policies choose which headers, cookies and query strings are in the key and set min, default and max TTL.
  • Origin request policies forward values to the origin without adding them to the key.
  • Respect origin Cache-Control; for static assets use content-hashed filenames and long TTLs.
  • Invalidation (/*) removes objects; paths are billed after a free monthly allowance (check current terms). Prefer versioned file names.
  • Hit ratio example: 900 hits out of 1,000 requests is 90 percent.

Invalidate

bashInvalidate a path
aws cloudfront create-invalidation --distribution-id E1ABCDEF12345 --paths "/index.html" "/config.json"
Check yourself
Better than invalidating on every deploy?

Content-hashed file names with long TTLs.

83.3

Securing origins

In plain words

Origin Access Control (OAC) lets only CloudFront read a private S3 bucket. For ALB origins, restrict by secret header or managed prefix list.

The problem it solves

If the origin is reachable directly, users bypass WAF, caching and geo rules.

What it does

  • S3: bucket policy allows cloudfront.amazonaws.com with condition AWS:SourceArn equal to the distribution.
  • ALB: security group allows the AWS-managed CloudFront origin-facing prefix list; add a custom header check for stronger assurance.
  • VPC origins let CloudFront reach private ALBs or EC2 without public IPs; check current support.
  • HTTPS between CloudFront and origin with a valid certificate.

Bucket policy for OAC

jsonoac-policy.json
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [{
    "Effect": "Allow",
    "Principal": {"Service": "cloudfront.amazonaws.com"},
    "Action": "s3:GetObject",
    "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::example-site/*",
    "Condition": {"StringEquals": {"AWS:SourceArn": "arn:aws:cloudfront::111122223333:distribution/E1ABCDEF12345"}}
  }]
}
Check yourself
How does an S3 policy bind access to one distribution?

A condition on AWS:SourceArn.

83.4

Signed URLs, cookies and WAF

In plain words

Signed URLs and cookies restrict who may fetch content. AWS WAF filters malicious requests at the edge.

The problem it solves

Paid or private content must not be shareable by anyone with the URL, and bots can hammer your origin.

What it does

  • Use key groups with public keys (not the old account-level trusted signers); sign with the private key in your app.
  • Policies include expiry, IP range, and path.
  • WAF web ACL with managed rules, rate-based rules and geo or bot control attaches to the distribution (global scope).
  • Security headers via response headers policies.

Attach WAF

hclcf-waf.tf
resource "aws_wafv2_web_acl" "edge" {
  name  = "edge"
  scope = "CLOUDFRONT"
  default_action {
    allow {}
  }
  rule {
    name     = "rate"
    priority = 1
    action {
      block {}
    }
    statement {
      rate_based_statement {
        limit              = 2000
        aggregate_key_type = "IP"
      }
    }
    visibility_config {
      cloudwatch_metrics_enabled = true
      metric_name                = "rate"
      sampled_requests_enabled   = true
    }
  }
  visibility_config {
    cloudwatch_metrics_enabled = true
    metric_name                = "edge"
    sampled_requests_enabled   = true
  }
}
83.5

Edge compute with Functions and Lambda@Edge

In plain words

Run small code at the edge. CloudFront Functions are tiny JavaScript for viewer events. Lambda@Edge is full Lambda for viewer and origin events.

The problem it solves

URL rewrites, redirects, header edits and simple auth should not need a trip to the origin.

What it does

  • CloudFront Functions: sub-millisecond, viewer request and response only, no network access, tiny size limits; ideal for rewrites and header manipulation.
  • Lambda@Edge: origin events too, network calls, larger code; deployed from us-east-1, higher cost and latency.
  • CloudFront KeyValueStore lets functions read small config data.
  • Test with the built-in test events.

SPA rewrite function

javascriptrewrite.js
function handler(event) {
  var request = event.request;
  if (!request.uri.includes('.')) {
    request.uri = '/index.html';
  }
  return request;
}
Check yourself
Which option can call an external API?

Lambda@Edge, not CloudFront Functions.

83.6

Origin failover and performance

In plain words

Origin groups fail over to a secondary origin on selected status codes. Compression, HTTP/3 and Origin Shield improve performance.

The problem it solves

A failing origin returns errors to every user, and many edge locations hitting one origin raises load.

What it does

  • Origin group: primary and secondary origin, failover on 500, 502, 503, 504 (for GET, HEAD, OPTIONS).
  • Origin Shield adds a central cache layer in one chosen Region to collapse requests; extra cost, enable for expensive origins.
  • Brotli and gzip compression, connection keep-alive timeouts, and custom error pages with error caching TTL.
  • Continuous deployment lets you send a share of traffic to a staging distribution.

Real-time check

bashCheck headers
curl -sI https://www.example.com/app.js | grep -iE 'x-cache|age|via|cache-control'
Check yourself
What header shows a cache hit?

X-Cache: Hit from cloudfront.

83.7

Logging, cost and troubleshooting

In plain words

Standard logs, real-time logs and CloudWatch metrics show hit ratio, errors and bytes.

The problem it solves

Low hit ratios and surprise transfer bills are usually discovered late.

What it does

  • Standard access logs to S3; real-time logs to Kinesis for immediate analysis; additional metrics for cache hit rate and origin latency.
  • Costs: data transfer out per GB by price class, requests per 10,000, invalidations, functions, WAF, logging. Price classes limit which edge locations serve you; check current definitions.
  • Egress example: 10 TB per month at a rate of R per GB costs 10,000 x R; compute with the current tiered rate.
  • 403 from S3 origin: policy or OAC mismatch. 502/504: origin TLS or timeout. Stale content: TTL or cache key.

Metrics alarm

hclcf-alarm.tf
resource "aws_cloudwatch_metric_alarm" "errors" {
  provider            = aws.us_east_1
  alarm_name          = "cf-5xx"
  namespace           = "AWS/CloudFront"
  metric_name         = "5xxErrorRate"
  dimensions          = { DistributionId = "E1ABCDEF12345", Region = "Global" }
  statistic           = "Average"
  period              = 300
  evaluation_periods  = 2
  threshold           = 5
  comparison_operator = "GreaterThanThreshold"
}

Section 84 of 93

Migrating an Organization to a Control Tower landing zone

7 concepts · about 55 minutes

Many teams start with a hand-built Organization and later want a managed landing zone. This section shows a safe migration path.

Goals
  • Assess an existing Organization before enabling Control Tower
  • Enrol existing accounts and OUs with Account Factory and baselines
  • Apply controls, customise with AFT or Customizations for Control Tower and plan rollback
84.1

What Control Tower adds

In plain words

AWS Control Tower sets up a multi-account landing zone with a log archive account, an audit account, IAM Identity Center, baseline CloudTrail and Config, and controls (guardrails).

The problem it solves

Hand-built baselines drift and every new account needs the same logging, access and guardrail steps repeated.

What it does

  • Home Region is fixed at setup; governed Regions are selectable.
  • Security OU holds Log Archive and Audit accounts; Sandbox OU is optional.
  • Controls: preventive (SCP or RCP), detective (Config rules) and proactive (CloudFormation hooks).
  • Account Factory vends new accounts with a baseline; enrolment brings existing accounts under governance.

Check status

bashLanding zone
aws controltower list-landing-zones
aws organizations list-roots --query 'Roots[].[Id,Name]'
Check yourself
Which two accounts does Control Tower create for logging and audit?

Log Archive and Audit.

84.2

Pre-migration assessment

In plain words

Inventory what already exists so Control Tower does not collide with your current setup.

The problem it solves

Existing CloudTrail, Config recorders, roles and Regions can block or complicate enrolment.

What it does

  • List OUs, accounts, SCPs and delegated administrators.
  • Existing AWS Config recorders and delivery channels in target Regions may need to be removed or adapted before enrolment, because Control Tower manages them (check the current prerequisites).
  • Existing IAM Identity Center configuration, organization trail and StackSets with conflicting names.
  • Decide the home Region and governed Regions; they are costly to change.
  • Document exceptions; plan a pilot OU first.

Inventory scripts

bashInventory
aws organizations list-accounts --query 'Accounts[].[Id,Name,Status]' --output table
aws organizations list-policies --filter SERVICE_CONTROL_POLICY --query 'Policies[].[Name,AwsManaged]' --output table
aws configservice describe-configuration-recorders --region eu-west-1
Check yourself
Why choose the home Region carefully?

It is hard to change later and hosts Control Tower resources.

84.3

Enabling the landing zone

In plain words

Set up Control Tower from the management account, creating or reusing the Security OU accounts.

The problem it solves

Wrong inputs at this step lock in bad choices such as Region and logging retention.

What it does

  • Requires an Organization with all features and a management account.
  • You can reuse existing account emails for Log Archive and Audit or let Control Tower create them.
  • Choose log retention periods and KMS encryption for logs.
  • Takes roughly an hour; monitor the setup status.
  • Landing zone updates are applied through the console or API, and changes in drift must be repaired.

Landing zone API shape

bashCreate landing zone
aws controltower create-landing-zone --version 3.3 \
  --manifest file://landing-zone-manifest.json
Note

Check the current landing zone version and manifest format in the documentation before running this.

84.4

Enrolling existing accounts and OUs

In plain words

Enrolment installs the Control Tower baseline in an existing account so it follows the same guardrails as new ones.

The problem it solves

Hundreds of legacy accounts cannot be recreated, yet they need the same governance.

What it does

  • Register an OU first (applies baseline and controls to its accounts), or enrol single accounts through Account Factory.
  • Prerequisites: the account has the AWSControlTowerExecution role trusting the management account, no conflicting Config or CloudTrail, and enough free quota.
  • Enrol the pilot OU, test workloads, then move to production OUs in waves.
  • Account moves between OUs inherit that OU's controls and SCPs, so review before moving.

Execution role trust

jsonexecution-role-trust.json
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [{
    "Effect": "Allow",
    "Principal": {"AWS": "arn:aws:iam::111122223333:root"},
    "Action": "sts:AssumeRole"
  }]
}
bashEnrol an OU
aws controltower enable-baseline \
  --baseline-identifier arn:aws:controltower:eu-west-1::baseline/17BSJV3IGJ2QSGA2 \
  --baseline-version 4.0 \
  --target-identifier arn:aws:organizations::111122223333:ou/o-exampleorgid/ou-abcd-11111111
Check yourself
Which role must exist in an account before it can be enrolled?

AWSControlTowerExecution.

84.5

Controls and SCP migration

In plain words

Replace homemade SCPs with Control Tower controls where an equivalent exists, and keep custom SCPs for the rest.

The problem it solves

Two overlapping sets of preventive policies confuse troubleshooting and may hit the SCP size limit.

What it does

  • Mandatory controls always apply; strongly recommended and elective controls are chosen per OU.
  • Control Tower SCPs are managed by Control Tower; do not edit them manually.
  • Custom SCPs remain allowed, attached separately; test with the policy simulator and a sandbox account.
  • Detective controls surface non-compliance as Config findings in the dashboard.
  • Check the current control catalogue; it grows.

Enable a control

bashControl
aws controltower enable-control \
  --control-identifier arn:aws:controltower:eu-west-1::control/AWS-GR_RESTRICT_ROOT_USER \
  --target-identifier arn:aws:organizations::111122223333:ou/o-exampleorgid/ou-abcd-11111111
84.6

Customisation with AFT and CfCT

In plain words

Account Factory for Terraform (AFT) and Customizations for Control Tower (CfCT) add your own baselines, networking and roles to new accounts.

The problem it solves

The Control Tower baseline is intentionally small; real accounts need VPCs, roles and tooling.

What it does

  • AFT: a Terraform pipeline triggered by account request files in Git; runs global and per-account customisations.
  • CfCT: CloudFormation StackSets and SCPs from a manifest, triggered by Control Tower lifecycle events.
  • Choose one approach to avoid duplication; AFT suits Terraform shops.
  • Run both from a dedicated deployment account, not the management account.

Account request module

hclaccount-request.tf
module "payments_prod" {
  source = "./modules/aft-account-request"

  control_tower_parameters = {
    AccountEmail              = "aws-payments-prod@example.com"
    AccountName               = "payments-prod"
    ManagedOrganizationalUnit = "Workloads/Prod"
    SSOUserEmail              = "platform@example.com"
    SSOUserFirstName          = "Platform"
    SSOUserLastName           = "Team"
  }

  account_tags = {
    owner = "payments"
    env   = "prod"
  }
}
Check yourself
What triggers AFT to build an account?

A merged account request file in Git.

84.7

Rollback, drift and operations

In plain words

Plan how to repair drift and what to do if enrolment fails.

The problem it solves

Manual changes to Control Tower resources put the landing zone or an OU into a drifted state.

What it does

  • Common drift: moved accounts, edited managed SCPs or removed roles; the dashboard shows it and offers repair.
  • Failed enrolment leaves the account in a failed state; fix the cause then retry.
  • Decommissioning a landing zone is possible but heavy; do not treat it as a casual rollback.
  • Keep the management account nearly empty; root access protected with MFA.
  • Re-run landing zone updates after Control Tower releases new versions.

Check drift

bashDrift status
aws controltower list-enabled-baselines --query 'enabledBaselines[].[baselineIdentifier,statusSummary.status]' --output table

Section 85 of 93

AWS Service Catalog

7 concepts · about 40 minutes

Service Catalog lets a platform team publish approved infrastructure patterns that other teams launch on their own, without granting them broad permissions.

Goals
  • Publish approved products as portfolios built from CloudFormation or Terraform
  • Control launch with launch constraints, template constraints and tag options
  • Share portfolios across an Organization and manage product versions
85.1

Portfolios and products

In plain words

A product is an approved template (for example a standard S3 bucket or a three-tier stack). A portfolio groups products and decides who can launch them.

The problem it solves

Developers either wait for tickets or receive wide permissions and build non-compliant resources.

What it does

  • Products are CloudFormation templates, or Terraform configurations through the Terraform Open Source or Terraform Cloud engine (check the current engine support).
  • Each product has versions, so you can ship fixes and deprecate old ones.
  • Access is granted to IAM users, groups or roles at portfolio level.
  • Launches create a provisioned product that can be updated, terminated and tracked.

Define a product

hclcatalog.tf
resource "aws_servicecatalog_portfolio" "platform" {
  name          = "platform-approved"
  description   = "Approved building blocks"
  provider_name = "platform-team"
}

resource "aws_servicecatalog_product" "bucket" {
  name  = "secure-bucket"
  owner = "platform-team"
  type  = "CLOUD_FORMATION_TEMPLATE"
  provisioning_artifact_parameters {
    name         = "v1"
    type         = "CLOUD_FORMATION_TEMPLATE"
    template_url = "https://example-artifacts.s3.amazonaws.com/secure-bucket-v1.yaml"
  }
}

resource "aws_servicecatalog_product_portfolio_association" "bucket" {
  portfolio_id = aws_servicecatalog_portfolio.platform.id
  product_id   = aws_servicecatalog_product.bucket.id
}
Check yourself
What is a provisioned product?

The running instance created when a user launches a product.

85.2

Launch constraints and least privilege

In plain words

A launch constraint names an IAM role that Service Catalog assumes to create the resources, so the end user needs no permissions beyond launching.

The problem it solves

Without it, the user would need create rights for every resource in the template, defeating governance.

What it does

  • The launch role holds only what the product needs.
  • The user needs servicecatalog:* style permissions for launching and access to the portfolio, but not the underlying service actions.
  • Auditing: CloudTrail shows the launching user and the assumed role.
  • Constrain the role with a permissions boundary and trust only servicecatalog.amazonaws.com.

Launch role trust

jsonlaunch-trust.json
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [{
    "Effect": "Allow",
    "Principal": {"Service": "servicecatalog.amazonaws.com"},
    "Action": "sts:AssumeRole"
  }]
}
Check yourself
Why does a launch constraint help least privilege?

The user needs no direct create permissions. The service assumes a scoped role.

85.3

Template constraints and parameters

In plain words

Template constraints restrict the parameter values users may pick, for example instance sizes or Regions.

The problem it solves

A flexible template lets users choose an expensive or non-compliant option.

What it does

  • Rules use conditions on parameters, such as InstanceType in an approved list.
  • Combined with AllowedValues and AllowedPattern in the template itself.
  • Use tag options to enforce tag keys and values chosen from a list.
  • Service Catalog applies portfolio tags automatically to launched resources.

Rule

jsontemplate-rule.json
{
  "Rules": {
    "SmallOnly": {
      "Assertions": [{
        "Assert": {"Fn::Contains": [["t3.small", "t3.medium"], {"Ref": "InstanceType"}]},
        "AssertDescription": "Only t3.small or t3.medium are allowed"
      }]
    }
  }
}
85.4

Sharing across accounts

In plain words

Portfolios can be shared with accounts or an entire Organization so every account sees the same catalog.

The problem it solves

Copying products by hand to each account causes version drift.

What it does

  • Share from the management or delegated administrator account to accounts, OUs or the Organization.
  • Imported portfolios in recipient accounts stay in sync with the source; recipients add their own access.
  • Share launch roles by name: the role must exist in each recipient account (create it with a StackSet).
  • Product updates propagate; users choose when to update provisioned products.

Share to an Organization

bashShare portfolio
aws servicecatalog create-portfolio-share --portfolio-id port-abc123def456 \
  --organization-node Type=ORGANIZATION,Value=o-exampleorgid
Check yourself
What must exist in each recipient account for a shared launch role?

A role with the same name.

85.5

Versions, updates and lifecycle

In plain words

Each product has numbered versions. Users update provisioned products to a newer version through a change set.

The problem it solves

Bug fixes and security improvements must reach existing deployments without surprise replacements.

What it does

  • Mark old versions inactive so new launches cannot choose them.
  • Updates use CloudFormation change sets; review replacements for stateful resources.
  • Notifications through SNS on provisioned product events.
  • Use provisioning artifacts from Git via CI: validate with cfn-lint, then publish a new version automatically.

Create a version

bashNew version
aws servicecatalog create-provisioning-artifact --product-id prod-abc123def456 \
  --parameters 'Name=v2,Type=CLOUD_FORMATION_TEMPLATE,Info={LoadTemplateFromURL=https://example-artifacts.s3.amazonaws.com/secure-bucket-v2.yaml}'
85.6

Service Catalog versus other approaches

In plain words

Service Catalog sits between a free-for-all and fully central ticket-based provisioning.

The problem it solves

Teams need to decide whether a catalog, a module registry or a self-service portal best fits their culture.

What it does

  • Catalog: console and API self-service with IAM controls, native to AWS and Control Tower.
  • Terraform module registry plus pipeline: developer-friendly Git workflow, policy as code with Sentinel or OPA.
  • Backstage or an internal portal can sit on top of either.
  • Many organizations use Service Catalog for guarded foundational products and Terraform for application stacks.
Self-service model
OptionService Catalog
Choose whennon-engineers or many accounts need guarded launches
Avoid whena pure Git workflow already works
OptionModule registry with pipeline
Choose whenengineers own infrastructure in Git
Avoid whenusers lack Git or CI access
OptionInternal portal over both
Choose whenyou want one front door
Avoid whenno platform team exists
Check yourself
When prefer Service Catalog?

When you want guarded self-service launches with launch roles and portfolios across accounts.

85.7

AppRegistry and governance

In plain words

AWS Service Catalog AppRegistry groups resources into applications with metadata, so cost, compliance and ownership roll up to an application.

The problem it solves

Resources belong to apps, but accounts see flat lists of resources.

What it does

  • Create an application, associate CloudFormation stacks or tag-based resources, and attach attribute groups (owner, tier, data classification).
  • The awsApplication tag is added automatically to associated resources, useful for cost allocation.
  • Integrates with Systems Manager application manager and myApplications.
  • Use with Budgets and cost allocation tags.

Create an application

bashAppRegistry
aws servicecatalog-appregistry create-application --name shop --description "Shop platform"

Section 86 of 93

Resilience Hub and Fault Injection Service

6 concepts · about 45 minutes

Resilience is a claim until you test it. Resilience Hub compares your architecture with targets. Fault Injection Service (FIS) breaks things on purpose, safely.

Goals
  • Assess an application against RTO and RPO targets with Resilience Hub
  • Run controlled failure experiments with AWS Fault Injection Service
  • Build game days with stop conditions, alarms and clear hypotheses
86.1

Resilience Hub assessments

In plain words

AWS Resilience Hub analyses an application's resources against resilience policies you set and reports gaps with recommendations.

The problem it solves

Teams state RTO and RPO targets, but nobody checks that the deployed architecture can meet them.

What it does

  • Define an application from CloudFormation stacks, Terraform state, AppRegistry, tags or Resource Groups.
  • A resilience policy sets RTO and RPO for four disruption types: application, infrastructure, AZ and Region.
  • The assessment estimates achievable RTO and RPO per type and flags resources that miss the targets.
  • Recommendations cover alarms, SOPs and FIS tests.

Create a policy

bashPolicy
aws resiliencehub create-resiliency-policy --policy-name tier1 --tier MissionCritical \
  --policy 'AZ={rtoInSecs=300,rpoInSecs=0},Hardware={rtoInSecs=300,rpoInSecs=0},Software={rtoInSecs=300,rpoInSecs=0},Region={rtoInSecs=3600,rpoInSecs=300}'
Check yourself
Name the four disruption types in a policy.

Application (software), infrastructure (hardware), Availability Zone and Region.

86.2

Operational recommendations

In plain words

Resilience Hub produces more than design advice. It suggests alarms, standard operating procedures and tests.

The problem it solves

A resilient design still fails if nobody knows the recovery steps or gets alerted.

What it does

  • Alarm recommendations as CloudFormation you can adopt.
  • SOP recommendations as Systems Manager documents for recovery tasks.
  • FIS experiment templates mapped to the risks found.
  • Drift detection between assessments flags design changes.

List assessments

bashAssessments
aws resiliencehub list-app-assessments --query 'assessmentSummaries[].[appArn,assessmentStatus,complianceStatus]' --output table
86.3

FIS experiment templates

In plain words

AWS Fault Injection Service runs fault actions on your resources according to an experiment template.

The problem it solves

Real failures are rare and unpredictable, so recovery code and runbooks go untested until a real outage.

What it does

  • Template: actions, targets (selected by tag, ARN or filter), stop conditions and an IAM role.
  • Actions include stopping or terminating EC2 instances, CPU or memory stress through SSM, network latency or blackhole, throttling APIs, failing over RDS or Aurora, interrupting Spot, and Kubernetes pod faults for EKS. Check the current action list.
  • Scenario library has prebuilt multi-action tests such as AZ power interruption; check availability.
  • Experiments record start, end and results; you pay per action-minute.

Template

jsonfis-template.json
{
  "description": "Stop 25 percent of tagged web instances",
  "targets": {
    "WebInstances": {
      "resourceType": "aws:ec2:instance",
      "resourceTags": {"Role": "web"},
      "selectionMode": "PERCENT(25)"
    }
  },
  "actions": {
    "StopInstances": {
      "actionId": "aws:ec2:stop-instances",
      "parameters": {"startInstancesAfterDuration": "PT5M"},
      "targets": {"Instances": "WebInstances"}
    }
  },
  "stopConditions": [
    {"source": "aws:cloudwatch:alarm", "value": "arn:aws:cloudwatch:eu-west-1:111122223333:alarm:web-5xx-high"}
  ],
  "roleArn": "arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/fis-experiment",
  "tags": {"Name": "web-instance-loss"}
}
bashCreate and start
aws fis create-experiment-template --cli-input-json file://fis-template.json
aws fis start-experiment --experiment-template-id EXT1a2b3c4d5e6f7
Check yourself
What aborts an experiment automatically?

A stop condition, usually a CloudWatch alarm.

86.4

Stop conditions and safety

In plain words

Experiments must be bounded. Stop conditions, narrow targets and a dedicated role keep them safe.

The problem it solves

A chaos test that spreads past its target becomes an outage.

What it does

  • Stop condition alarms on user-facing symptoms such as error rate or latency.
  • Targets limited by tags and a percentage; start in a non-production environment.
  • The FIS role has least privilege and is only assumable by fis.amazonaws.com.
  • Notify the team, record the hypothesis, and have a rollback.
  • Use SCPs to restrict who can start experiments in production.

FIS role trust

jsonfis-trust.json
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [{
    "Effect": "Allow",
    "Principal": {"Service": "fis.amazonaws.com"},
    "Action": "sts:AssumeRole",
    "Condition": {"StringEquals": {"aws:SourceAccount": "111122223333"}}
  }]
}
86.5

AZ failure and database failover tests

In plain words

Two high-value tests simulate losing an AZ and forcing a database failover.

The problem it solves

Multi-AZ designs often hide single points of failure such as one NAT gateway per VPC or a hard coded AZ.

What it does

  • AZ impairment: network disruption against subnets in one AZ, plus stopping instances there; observe the load balancer and Auto Scaling replacing capacity.
  • Aurora or RDS failover action: measure application reconnect time and connection pool behaviour.
  • Check that clients retry with backoff and that DNS TTLs are short enough.
  • Compare measured recovery with your RTO.

Aurora failover action

jsonfis-aurora.json
{
  "description": "Fail over the Aurora cluster",
  "targets": {
    "Cluster": {
      "resourceType": "aws:rds:cluster",
      "resourceArns": ["arn:aws:rds:eu-west-1:111122223333:cluster:shop-aurora"],
      "selectionMode": "ALL"
    }
  },
  "actions": {
    "Failover": {
      "actionId": "aws:rds:failover-db-cluster",
      "targets": {"Clusters": "Cluster"}
    }
  },
  "stopConditions": [{"source": "none"}],
  "roleArn": "arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/fis-experiment"
}
Check yourself
Which hidden single points of failure do AZ tests often reveal?

A single NAT gateway, hard coded AZs, or single-AZ dependencies.

86.6

Game days and continuous validation

In plain words

A game day is a planned exercise where a team runs failures and practises response. Continuous experiments keep results fresh.

The problem it solves

One-off tests decay as the system changes.

What it does

  • Write a hypothesis, for example "if one AZ is lost, error rate stays under 1 percent and recovers in 5 minutes".
  • Run in staging first, then in production at a quiet time with the team watching dashboards.
  • Schedule recurring experiments with EventBridge Scheduler or run FIS from a pipeline step.
  • Capture findings as tickets, fix, and rerun.
  • Link results to Resilience Hub assessments to prove the RTO and RPO.

Schedule an experiment

hclfis-schedule.tf
resource "aws_scheduler_schedule" "weekly_fis" {
  name                = "weekly-fis-staging"
  schedule_expression = "cron(0 10 ? * TUE *)"
  flexible_time_window {
    mode = "OFF"
  }
  target {
    arn      = "arn:aws:scheduler:::aws-sdk:fis:startExperiment"
    role_arn = aws_iam_role.scheduler.arn
    input = jsonencode({
      ExperimentTemplateId = "EXT1a2b3c4d5e6f7"
      ClientToken          = "weekly"
    })
  }
}
Check yourself
What makes a game day useful?

A clear hypothesis, bounded failure, measurement and follow-up fixes.

Section 87 of 93

Trusted Advisor and Compute Optimizer

6 concepts · about 40 minutes

AWS offers built-in advice. Trusted Advisor looks across the account for risks and waste. Compute Optimizer uses utilisation metrics to suggest better sizes.

Goals
  • Use Trusted Advisor checks for cost, security, fault tolerance, performance and service limits
  • Read Compute Optimizer recommendations for EC2, EBS, Lambda, ECS on Fargate and Auto Scaling
  • Turn recommendations into automated, tracked improvements
87.1

What Trusted Advisor checks

In plain words

Trusted Advisor inspects your account against best practice checks in categories: cost optimization, performance, security, fault tolerance, service limits and operational excellence.

The problem it solves

Teams do not know which of thousands of settings matter most.

What it does

  • Core checks are available to all accounts (for example S3 bucket permissions, security groups with unrestricted access, MFA on root, service quotas).
  • The full check set requires a Business, Enterprise On-Ramp or Enterprise support plan (check the current plans).
  • Findings show status (OK, warning, action needed), affected resources and recommended actions.
  • Organizational view aggregates all accounts from the management or delegated administrator account.

Read checks

bashTrusted Advisor via API
aws support describe-trusted-advisor-checks --language en --region us-east-1 \
  --query 'checks[?category==`cost_optimizing`].[id,name]' --output table
Check yourself
Which Trusted Advisor check category warns before you hit quotas?

Service limits.

87.2

Automating Trusted Advisor

In plain words

Trusted Advisor publishes status changes to EventBridge, so findings can raise tickets or trigger remediation.

The problem it solves

A dashboard nobody opens does not reduce risk.

What it does

  • The EventBridge event Trusted Advisor Check Item Refresh Notification carries the check and status.
  • Route to SNS, chat or a ticket system, or invoke Lambda or SSM Automation to remediate.
  • Weekly email summary and organizational reports to S3.
  • Prioritise by severity and cost saving; track with an owner and a due date.
  • Combine with Security Hub and Config for findings with automated fixes.

Rule

hclta-rule.tf
resource "aws_cloudwatch_event_rule" "ta" {
  name = "trusted-advisor-red"
  event_pattern = jsonencode({
    source        = ["aws.trustedadvisor"]
    "detail-type" = ["Trusted Advisor Check Item Refresh Notification"]
    detail        = { status = ["ERROR"] }
  })
}
Note

Trusted Advisor events are delivered in us-east-1, so create this rule in that Region.

87.3

How Compute Optimizer works

In plain words

Compute Optimizer analyses CloudWatch utilisation history with machine learning and recommends better configurations.

The problem it solves

Right-sizing by guesswork either wastes money or risks performance.

What it does

  • Covers EC2 instances, Auto Scaling groups, EBS volumes, Lambda functions, ECS services on Fargate, commercial software licences and RDS (check the current resource list).
  • Needs opt-in, either per account or for the whole Organization.
  • Default look-back is 14 days; enhanced infrastructure metrics extend to 93 days (paid) and memory metrics need the CloudWatch agent for EC2.
  • Each finding is Under-provisioned, Over-provisioned or Optimized, with up to three options, expected savings and a performance risk score.

Enable and read

bashCompute Optimizer
aws compute-optimizer update-enrollment-status --status Active
aws compute-optimizer get-ec2-instance-recommendations \
  --query 'instanceRecommendations[].[instanceArn,finding,recommendationOptions[0].instanceType]' --output table
Check yourself
Which metric needs the CloudWatch agent for EC2 recommendations?

Memory utilisation.

87.4

Acting on recommendations safely

In plain words

A recommendation is a hypothesis. Test it on a copy or in a canary before you change production.

The problem it solves

Blindly applying a smaller size can break a latency-sensitive workload or one with spiky memory.

What it does

  • Check the performance risk score and the peak, not only the average.
  • Change one tier of size at a time, watch p99 latency and error rates.
  • For Auto Scaling groups change the launch template and use instance refresh.
  • Lambda: use the recommended memory then confirm duration and cost with real traffic.
  • Worked example: moving from m5.2xlarge to m5.xlarge halves vCPU and memory, so the hourly price is about half; for 20 instances at 730 hours check the saving as 20 x 730 x (old rate minus new rate) with current prices.

Refresh after template change

bashInstance refresh
aws autoscaling start-instance-refresh --auto-scaling-group-name web \
  --preferences '{"MinHealthyPercentage":90,"InstanceWarmup":120}'
87.5

Cost Optimization Hub and Savings Plans

In plain words

Cost Optimization Hub consolidates savings opportunities from many sources, including Compute Optimizer, idle resources and commitment recommendations.

The problem it solves

Savings ideas are scattered across several consoles.

What it does

  • One list across accounts and Regions with estimated monthly savings and effort level.
  • Includes rightsizing, idle resource deletion, Graviton migration, Savings Plans and Reserved Instance recommendations.
  • Filter by account, tag or action type; export to S3 via Data Exports.
  • Review commitment purchases together with rightsizing: rightsize first, then commit.
Order of work
OptionDelete idle first
Choose whenresources have no traffic
Avoid whenthey are quiet DR standbys
OptionRight-size second
Choose whenutilisation is consistently low
Avoid whenspiky workloads need headroom
OptionCommit last
Choose whenthe baseline is stable
Avoid whenarchitecture changes are planned soon

Query recommendations

bashHub
aws cost-optimization-hub list-recommendations --max-results 5
Check yourself
Why rightsize before buying Savings Plans?

A commitment sized to wasteful usage locks in the waste.

87.6

Governance and reporting

In plain words

Put recommendations into a regular review with owners, so improvements actually happen.

The problem it solves

Recommendations pile up without accountability.

What it does

  • Assign each finding to the owning team by tag.
  • Monthly review: top savings, security risks, quota warnings.
  • Track realised savings versus estimated; keep an exceptions list with expiry.
  • Feed into Well-Architected reviews and FinOps reporting.
  • Use Organizations delegated administrators for Trusted Advisor, Compute Optimizer and Cost Optimization Hub so central teams see all accounts.

Delegate administration

bashDelegated admin
aws organizations register-delegated-administrator --account-id 444455556666 \
  --service-principal compute-optimizer.amazonaws.com

Section 88 of 93

AWS Config rules and conformance packs

6 concepts · about 45 minutes

AWS Config records what your resources look like and checks them against rules. This section goes beyond recording to compliance at scale.

Goals
  • Record resource configuration and evaluate it with managed and custom Config rules
  • Deploy conformance packs and aggregators across an Organization
  • Remediate non-compliance automatically with Systems Manager Automation
88.1

Config recorder, rules and evaluations

In plain words

The configuration recorder stores a history of resource configuration items. Rules evaluate those items and mark each resource compliant or non-compliant.

The problem it solves

You cannot answer "which of my buckets are unencrypted right now, and since when" from the console alone.

What it does

  • The recorder runs per account and Region; choose all supported resources or a list.
  • A managed rule such as s3-bucket-server-side-encryption-enabled is provided by AWS (many exist).
  • Triggers: configuration change or periodic.
  • Config stores timelines so you can see changes and compliance history.
  • Cost depends on configuration items recorded and rule evaluations; check current pricing.

Managed rule

hclconfig-rule.tf
resource "aws_config_config_rule" "s3_encrypted" {
  name = "s3-bucket-sse-enabled"
  source {
    owner             = "AWS"
    source_identifier = "S3_BUCKET_SERVER_SIDE_ENCRYPTION_ENABLED"
  }
}
Check yourself
Which two triggers can a Config rule use?

Configuration change and periodic.

88.2

Custom rules with Lambda and Guard

In plain words

When no managed rule fits, write a custom Lambda rule or a Guard policy-as-code rule.

The problem it solves

Company-specific standards, such as a required tag format, are not covered by managed rules.

What it does

  • Custom Lambda: receives the configuration item and reports the evaluation with PutEvaluations.
  • Custom policy (Guard): write the rule in the CloudFormation Guard DSL; no Lambda to maintain.
  • Test locally with cfn-guard.
  • Prefer Guard for simple property checks, Lambda for logic needing outside data.

Guard rule

texttags.guard
rule s3_has_owner_tag when resourceType == "AWS::S3::Bucket" {
  configuration.tags exists
  some configuration.tags[*].key == "Owner"
}
88.3

Conformance packs

In plain words

A conformance pack is a bundle of Config rules and remediation actions deployed together as a single template.

The problem it solves

Managing hundreds of individual rules across accounts is tedious and inconsistent.

What it does

  • Defined in a YAML template like CloudFormation; AWS publishes sample packs for frameworks such as CIS, PCI DSS and NIST, and operational best practices (check the current list).
  • Deploy to one account or across an Organization from the management or delegated administrator account.
  • Shows a compliance score per pack.
  • Updating the template updates all member accounts.

Pack template

yamlpack.yaml
Resources:
  S3Encrypted:
    Type: AWS::Config::ConfigRule
    Properties:
      ConfigRuleName: s3-sse-enabled
      Source:
        Owner: AWS
        SourceIdentifier: S3_BUCKET_SERVER_SIDE_ENCRYPTION_ENABLED
  RootMfa:
    Type: AWS::Config::ConfigRule
    Properties:
      ConfigRuleName: root-mfa-enabled
      Source:
        Owner: AWS
        SourceIdentifier: ROOT_ACCOUNT_MFA_ENABLED
bashDeploy to the Organization
aws configservice put-organization-conformance-pack --organization-conformance-pack-name baseline \
  --template-body file://pack.yaml
Check yourself
Where do you deploy an organization conformance pack from?

The management account or a delegated administrator.

88.4

Aggregators and advanced queries

In plain words

An aggregator collects Config data from many accounts and Regions into one view. Advanced queries use SQL-like syntax over resource configuration.

The problem it solves

Each account's Config data is separate, so central teams cannot search the estate.

What it does

  • Aggregator in a central account, authorised per account or via Organizations.
  • Query across all accounts: "all EC2 instances not using IMDSv2".
  • Compliance dashboards by rule, account and Region.
  • Pair with Security Hub for findings and with Athena for long term analysis of delivered snapshots.

SQL query

bashAdvanced query
aws configservice select-aggregate-resource-config \
  --configuration-aggregator-name org-agg \
  --expression "SELECT accountId, resourceId WHERE resourceType = 'AWS::EC2::Instance' AND configuration.metadataOptions.httpTokens = 'optional'"
Check yourself
What does an aggregator give a central team?

A single place to see configuration and compliance across accounts and Regions.

88.5

Automatic remediation

In plain words

A Config rule can trigger an SSM Automation runbook to fix a non-compliant resource, automatically or after approval.

The problem it solves

Detecting issues without fixing them leaves a growing backlog.

What it does

  • Use AWS-owned runbooks such as AWS-EnableS3BucketEncryption, or your own.
  • Automatic remediation retries a few times; manual remediation waits for a click.
  • The remediation role needs only the permissions the fix requires.
  • Be careful with destructive fixes; prefer remediating configuration (encryption, tags) over deletion.

Remediation config

hclremediation.tf
resource "aws_config_remediation_configuration" "s3_encrypt" {
  config_rule_name = aws_config_config_rule.s3_encrypted.name
  target_type      = "SSM_DOCUMENT"
  target_id        = "AWS-EnableS3BucketEncryption"
  automatic        = true
  maximum_automatic_attempts = 3
  retry_attempt_seconds      = 60
  parameter {
    name           = "BucketName"
    resource_value = "RESOURCE_ID"
  }
  parameter {
    name         = "SSEAlgorithm"
    static_value = "AES256"
  }
  parameter {
    name         = "AutomationAssumeRole"
    static_value = "arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/config-remediation"
  }
}
88.6

Config versus Control Tower, Security Hub and cost

In plain words

Config is the detective data layer. Control Tower, Security Hub and others consume it.

The problem it solves

Teams enable several overlapping tools and pay twice for the same data.

What it does

  • Control Tower detective controls are Config rules that it manages; do not duplicate them.
  • Security Hub standards use Config rules under the hood and require Config to be on.
  • Reduce cost by recording only needed resource types and excluding high-churn ones, or by using periodic recording for chatty resources.
  • Cost sketch: recorded items per month x price per item + evaluations x price per evaluation; check the current rates.
  • Keep delivery to S3 and use lifecycle rules for history.

Recorder with exclusions

hclrecorder.tf
resource "aws_config_configuration_recorder" "main" {
  name     = "default"
  role_arn = aws_iam_role.config.arn
  recording_group {
    all_supported = false
    resource_types = ["AWS::EC2::Instance", "AWS::S3::Bucket", "AWS::IAM::Role", "AWS::RDS::DBInstance"]
  }
}
Check yourself
Why trim recorded resource types?

To reduce cost by skipping resources and churn you never evaluate.

Section 89 of 93

Amazon VPC Lattice

7 concepts · about 45 minutes

VPC Lattice is an application networking layer. It connects services across VPCs and accounts with built-in discovery, routing and authorisation, without managing overlapping networks.

Goals
  • Explain services, service networks, listeners and target groups in VPC Lattice
  • Secure service to service calls with auth policies and SigV4
  • Compare Lattice with PrivateLink, Transit Gateway and a service mesh
89.1

Why Lattice exists

In plain words

Lattice lets one service call another by name, across VPCs and accounts, with routing and access control handled by AWS.

The problem it solves

Connecting many services across VPCs normally needs peering or a transit gateway, non-overlapping CIDRs, DNS plumbing and per-service security groups.

What it does

  • Works at layer 7 (HTTP, HTTPS, gRPC) and also TCP in recent releases; check the current protocol support.
  • Overlapping IP ranges are fine, because clients reach a Lattice-provided address, not the target IP.
  • Targets can be instances, IPs, Lambda functions, ALBs and Kubernetes pods through the Gateway API controller.
  • Billed per service, per GB processed and per request; check current pricing.

List

bashInspect
aws vpc-lattice list-service-networks
aws vpc-lattice list-services --query 'items[].[name,dnsEntry.domainName]' --output table
Check yourself
Can two VPCs with overlapping CIDRs use Lattice?

Yes, since clients connect through Lattice rather than routing to target IPs.

89.2

Services, listeners, rules and target groups

In plain words

A service has listeners (protocol and port). Rules match requests and forward to target groups, like a managed ALB for service to service traffic.

The problem it solves

Each team re-implements routing, weights and health checks differently.

What it does

  • Rule conditions: path, header, method; actions: forward with weights or fixed response.
  • Weighted forwarding supports canary releases between two target groups.
  • Health checks per target group.
  • A custom domain name and certificate can be attached.

Terraform

hcllattice-service.tf
resource "aws_vpclattice_service" "orders" {
  name      = "orders"
  auth_type = "AWS_IAM"
}

resource "aws_vpclattice_target_group" "v1" {
  name = "orders-v1"
  type = "IP"
  config {
    port           = 8080
    protocol       = "HTTP"
    vpc_identifier = aws_vpc.app.id
  }
}

resource "aws_vpclattice_listener" "https" {
  name               = "http"
  protocol           = "HTTP"
  port               = 80
  service_identifier = aws_vpclattice_service.orders.id
  default_action {
    forward {
      target_groups {
        target_group_identifier = aws_vpclattice_target_group.v1.id
        weight                  = 100
      }
    }
  }
}
89.3

Service networks and associations

In plain words

A service network is a logical boundary. Services and VPCs are associated with it, and associated VPCs can reach the associated services.

The problem it solves

You need a simple way to say which VPCs may reach which services.

What it does

  • Associate services with a network, and VPCs with the same network.
  • Share networks across accounts using AWS RAM.
  • Security groups on the VPC association restrict which clients in the VPC may call.
  • Alternative for single-service sharing: a service-level association or a resource gateway for databases and TCP resources; check current features.

Associate a VPC

hclassoc.tf
resource "aws_vpclattice_service_network" "main" {
  name      = "shop"
  auth_type = "AWS_IAM"
}

resource "aws_vpclattice_service_network_vpc_association" "app" {
  vpc_identifier             = aws_vpc.app.id
  service_network_identifier = aws_vpclattice_service_network.main.id
  security_group_ids         = [aws_security_group.lattice_clients.id]
}
Check yourself
How are service networks shared between accounts?

With AWS RAM.

89.4

Auth policies and SigV4

In plain words

Lattice evaluates auth policies (resource policies in IAM policy language) on service networks and services, for clients that sign requests with SigV4.

The problem it solves

Network reachability alone does not say whether this caller may use this API.

What it does

  • Auth type AWS_IAM requires signed requests; NONE allows any caller in the network.
  • Policies can allow by principal, org ID, path and method using vpc-lattice-svcs: condition keys.
  • The network-level policy is evaluated first, then the service-level policy; both must allow.
  • Pods and functions sign with their workload identity, so policies refer to roles, not IPs.

Policy

jsonauth-policy.json
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [{
    "Effect": "Allow",
    "Principal": "*",
    "Action": "vpc-lattice-svcs:Invoke",
    "Resource": "*",
    "Condition": {
      "StringEquals": {"aws:PrincipalOrgID": "o-exampleorgid"},
      "StringLike": {"vpc-lattice-svcs:RequestPath": "/orders/*"}
    }
  }]
}
bashApply policy
aws vpc-lattice put-auth-policy --resource-identifier svc-0abc123 --policy file://auth-policy.json
Check yourself
Which auth type requires signed requests?

AWS_IAM.

89.5

Lattice with Kubernetes

In plain words

The AWS Gateway API Controller maps Kubernetes Gateway API objects (Gateway, HTTPRoute) to Lattice services and target groups.

The problem it solves

Cross-cluster, cross-VPC service calls usually need a mesh or per-service load balancers.

What it does

  • A Gateway with class amazon-vpc-lattice represents a service network.
  • An HTTPRoute becomes a Lattice service and rules; pods become targets.
  • Works across EKS clusters and with EC2 or Lambda targets in the same service network.
  • Use IAM auth with pod identity for callers.

Manifests

yamlgateway.yaml
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Gateway
metadata:
  name: shop
spec:
  gatewayClassName: amazon-vpc-lattice
  listeners:
    - name: http
      protocol: HTTP
      port: 80
---
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: HTTPRoute
metadata:
  name: orders
spec:
  parentRefs:
    - name: shop
      sectionName: http
  rules:
    - backendRefs:
        - name: orders
          kind: Service
          port: 8080
89.6

Lattice versus PrivateLink, Transit Gateway and meshes

In plain words

These tools overlap but solve different problems.

The problem it solves

Choosing wrongly adds cost or leaves gaps in security and routing.

What it does

  • PrivateLink: one provider service exposed to consumer VPCs through endpoints, layer 4, no routing rules.
  • Transit Gateway: network connectivity between networks (layer 3), needs distinct CIDRs and security groups per service.
  • Lattice: application layer discovery, routing and IAM auth across VPCs and accounts, overlapping IPs allowed.
  • Service mesh (Istio, App Mesh style): in-cluster features such as mTLS, retries and rich telemetry via sidecars; AWS App Mesh is being retired, so check its end-of-support date before using it.
Pick one
OptionVPC Lattice
Choose whenmany services across VPCs and accounts need routing and IAM auth
Avoid whenyou only need raw network reachability
OptionPrivateLink
Choose whenone service shared with consumers who may overlap
Avoid whenyou need path routing
OptionTransit Gateway
Choose whenbroad network connectivity including on-premises
Avoid whenyou want per-service authorisation
Check yourself
Which supports overlapping CIDRs and path routing?

VPC Lattice.

89.7

Observability and limits

In plain words

Lattice emits access logs and metrics for each service, giving visibility into service to service traffic.

The problem it solves

East-west traffic is often a blind spot.

What it does

  • Access logs to CloudWatch Logs, S3 or Firehose per service or network, with request path, caller identity and target latency.
  • Metrics for request count, response codes and latency per service and target group.
  • Check quotas for services per network, associations and rules.
  • Cost scales with requests and data; model it with the current rates before moving high-volume traffic.

Enable logs

hcllattice-logs.tf
resource "aws_vpclattice_access_log_subscription" "orders" {
  resource_identifier = aws_vpclattice_service.orders.arn
  destination_arn     = aws_cloudwatch_log_group.lattice.arn
}
