Section 90 of 93

Amazon Bedrock and SageMaker for platform teams

7 concepts · about 45 minutes

Platform teams are increasingly asked to host AI workloads safely. This section covers what Bedrock and SageMaker provide and what the platform must govern. It is an overview for operators, not a data science course.

Goals
  • Distinguish Bedrock managed foundation models from SageMaker model building and hosting
  • Secure and govern generative AI access with IAM, VPC endpoints, guardrails and logging
  • Plan cost, quotas and operations for AI workloads as a platform team
90.1

Bedrock and SageMaker compared

In plain words

Amazon Bedrock gives API access to foundation models from several providers. Amazon SageMaker is a platform to build, train, tune and host your own models.

The problem it solves

Teams do not know whether to call a managed model API or run their own endpoints.

What it does

  • Bedrock: serverless, pay per token (on-demand) or provisioned throughput; models from several providers; features include Knowledge Bases (RAG), Agents, Guardrails and model evaluation. Check the current model list and regions.
  • SageMaker: notebooks, training jobs, pipelines, model registry, real-time, serverless and batch inference endpoints.
  • Bedrock suits applications that use existing models; SageMaker suits custom models or strict hosting control.
  • Both can be used together, for example SageMaker for a fine-tuned model and Bedrock for a general one.
AI platform
OptionBedrock
Choose whenyou need text, image or embedding models behind an API
Avoid whenyou must control model weights and hosting
OptionSageMaker
Choose whenyou train or fine-tune custom models
Avoid whena managed model API already fits
OptionBoth
Choose whencustom model plus a general assistant
Avoid whena single model serves the use case

Call a model

pythonconverse.py
import boto3

bedrock = boto3.client("bedrock-runtime", region_name="eu-west-1")
response = bedrock.converse(
    modelId="REPLACE_WITH_MODEL_ID",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": [{"text": "Summarise this runbook in three bullets."}]}],
    inferenceConfig={"maxTokens": 300, "temperature": 0.2},
)
print(response["output"]["message"]["content"][0]["text"])
Check yourself
Which service bills per token?

Bedrock on-demand inference.

90.2

Access control for Bedrock

In plain words

Bedrock access is controlled by IAM. Model access must also be enabled, and IAM policies restrict which models each role may invoke.

The problem it solves

Open access lets any workload call any model, which creates cost and data governance risk.

What it does

  • Allow bedrock:InvokeModel and bedrock:Converse on specific model ARNs only.
  • Use SCPs to block Bedrock in Regions or accounts that should not use it.
  • Use VPC interface endpoints (bedrock-runtime) so traffic stays private, with endpoint policies.
  • Model invocation logging to CloudWatch Logs or S3 captures prompts and responses; handle as sensitive data.

Least privilege policy

jsonbedrock-policy.json
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [{
    "Effect": "Allow",
    "Action": ["bedrock:InvokeModel", "bedrock:Converse"],
    "Resource": "arn:aws:bedrock:eu-west-1::foundation-model/REPLACE_WITH_MODEL_ID"
  }]
}
90.3

Guardrails, RAG and agents

In plain words

Guardrails filter inputs and outputs. Knowledge Bases add retrieval from your documents (RAG). Agents let models call tools.

The problem it solves

Raw models can leak sensitive data, produce harmful text or answer without company knowledge.

What it does

  • Guardrails: denied topics, content filters, PII redaction, word filters and contextual grounding checks.
  • Knowledge Bases: ingest documents from S3 to a vector store (OpenSearch Serverless, Aurora pgvector, and others) and retrieve relevant chunks at query time.
  • Agents: orchestrate API calls with action groups defined by OpenAPI schemas; give them narrow IAM roles.
  • Treat model output as untrusted input in downstream systems.

Guardrail

bashCreate guardrail
aws bedrock create-guardrail --name shop-guardrail \
  --blocked-input-messaging "Request blocked" --blocked-outputs-messaging "Response blocked" \
  --sensitive-information-policy-config '{"piiEntitiesConfig":[{"type":"EMAIL","action":"ANONYMIZE"}]}'
Check yourself
Why treat model output as untrusted?

It can be wrong or manipulated, so validate it before using it in other systems.

90.4

SageMaker building blocks

In plain words

SageMaker offers managed notebooks, training jobs, pipelines, a model registry and inference endpoints.

The problem it solves

Data scientists need repeatable environments and a path from experiment to production.

What it does

  • Training jobs run containers on managed instances and write artifacts to S3; Spot training lowers cost with checkpoints.
  • Pipelines define steps as a DAG; the Model Registry versions and approves models.
  • Endpoints: real-time (always on), serverless (scales to zero), asynchronous (queue based) and batch transform.
  • Run in a VPC with private subnets, KMS encryption and network isolation for sensitive data.
  • Studio spaces replace notebook instances for most new work; check the current user experience.

Endpoint config with autoscaling target

hclsagemaker.tf
resource "aws_sagemaker_endpoint_configuration" "model" {
  name = "model-v3"
  production_variants {
    variant_name           = "primary"
    model_name             = aws_sagemaker_model.model.name
    initial_instance_count = 2
    instance_type          = "ml.m5.large"
  }
}

resource "aws_sagemaker_endpoint" "model" {
  name                 = "model"
  endpoint_config_name = aws_sagemaker_endpoint_configuration.model.name
}
90.5

Network and data security

In plain words

Keep training data and endpoints private, encrypted and auditable.

The problem it solves

Data used for training and prompting is often the most sensitive data in the company.

What it does

  • Private subnets and VPC endpoints for S3, ECR, CloudWatch and the SageMaker API.
  • KMS customer managed keys for S3, EBS volumes and endpoints.
  • IAM execution roles scoped to specific buckets and prefixes; separate roles per team.
  • Data classification: do not send regulated data to a model or Region that policy does not allow; check provider data handling terms.
  • Bedrock does not use your prompts to train base models by default; confirm in the current service terms.

Endpoint

hclbedrock-endpoint.tf
resource "aws_vpc_endpoint" "bedrock" {
  vpc_id              = aws_vpc.app.id
  service_name        = "com.amazonaws.eu-west-1.bedrock-runtime"
  vpc_endpoint_type   = "Interface"
  subnet_ids          = aws_subnet.private[*].id
  security_group_ids  = [aws_security_group.endpoints.id]
  private_dns_enabled = true
}
Check yourself
How do workloads reach Bedrock without the internet?

Through an interface VPC endpoint for bedrock-runtime.

90.6

Cost and quota management

In plain words

AI costs scale with tokens or instance hours. Quotas limit throughput.

The problem it solves

A prompt loop or oversized endpoint can burn a monthly budget in days.

What it does

  • Bedrock token cost = (input tokens x input price + output tokens x output price) per request, multiplied by volume. Example: 2,000 input tokens and 500 output tokens at assumed prices of 3 and 15 dollars per million tokens is 2,000 x 3 / 1,000,000 + 500 x 15 / 1,000,000 = 0.006 + 0.0075 = 0.0135 dollars per request; check real prices.
  • Set Budgets and anomaly detection; tag by application, use application inference profiles for cost attribution where available.
  • Quotas: tokens or requests per minute per model and Region; request increases early.
  • SageMaker: stop idle notebooks and endpoints, use serverless or async endpoints for spiky use, Savings Plans for steady use.

Verify arithmetic

pythoncost.py
input_tokens, output_tokens = 2000, 500
in_price, out_price = 3.0, 15.0  # dollars per million tokens, assumed
per_request = input_tokens * in_price / 1e6 + output_tokens * out_price / 1e6
print(per_request, per_request * 100000)
90.7

Operating AI workloads

In plain words

Operate AI services like any production service, with extra attention to evaluation, drift and safety.

The problem it solves

Model quality can degrade silently, and outputs are non-deterministic.

What it does

  • Monitor latency, errors, throttles and token usage in CloudWatch; trace calls with X-Ray or OpenTelemetry.
  • Evaluate quality with fixed test sets before and after changing a model, prompt or retrieval setup.
  • Version prompts and configuration in Git; roll out changes gradually.
  • SageMaker Model Monitor detects data and model drift for hosted models.
  • Plan fallbacks: retry with backoff, a cheaper model or a graceful degraded answer.

Alarm on throttles

hclbedrock-alarm.tf
resource "aws_cloudwatch_metric_alarm" "throttles" {
  alarm_name          = "bedrock-throttles"
  namespace           = "AWS/Bedrock"
  metric_name         = "InvocationThrottles"
  statistic           = "Sum"
  period              = 60
  evaluation_periods  = 3
  threshold           = 10
  comparison_operator = "GreaterThanThreshold"
}
Check yourself
Compute the per-request cost above for 100,000 requests.

0.0135 x 100,000 = 1,350 dollars at the assumed prices.

← PreviousNext →
Section 91 of 93

Which AWS service for which job

7 concepts · about 50 minutes

With hundreds of services, the skill is narrowing quickly to two or three candidates and choosing with evidence. This section gives a method and decision tables.

Goals
  • Choose compute, storage, database, messaging and networking services from requirements
  • Apply a repeatable decision method instead of picking familiar services
  • Record decisions and their trade-offs
91.1

A decision method

In plain words

Ask the same questions in the same order: what is the workload shape, what are the constraints, and what is the cheapest thing that meets them.

The problem it solves

Teams choose by habit or hype, and then redesign when scale, cost or compliance arrives.

What it does

  • Step 1 workload shape: request response, event driven, batch, streaming, stateful.
  • Step 2 constraints: latency, throughput, data residency, compliance, team skills, budget.
  • Step 3 pick the most managed option that fits; move down to lower-level services only for a stated reason.
  • Step 4 record the decision, rejected options and the trigger that would change it.

A decision record

yamladr-0007.yaml
id: ADR-0007
decision: Use ECS on Fargate for the orders API
context: Small team, steady web traffic, no Kubernetes expertise
options:
  - EKS rejected for operational overhead
  - Lambda rejected for steady high concurrency cost
revisit_when: more than 40 services or a need for custom operators
Check yourself
What should a decision record include besides the choice?

Context, rejected options and the trigger to revisit.

91.2

Choosing compute

In plain words

Compute ranges from functions to full servers. Move toward more control only when needed.

The problem it solves

Running everything on EC2 is costly to operate, and running everything on Lambda hits limits.

What it does

  • Lambda: short, event driven, spiky; up to 15 minutes per invocation.
  • ECS on Fargate or App Runner: containers without servers; steady services.
  • EKS: Kubernetes ecosystem and portability.
  • EC2: special hardware, licensing, full OS control, or heavy steady use with commitments.
  • Batch: queued jobs on managed compute.
Compute
OptionLambda
Choose whenevent driven, spiky, short tasks
Avoid whensteady high load or long running
OptionFargate
Choose whencontainers with a small team
Avoid whenGPUs or privileged mode
OptionEKS
Choose whenKubernetes tooling is a requirement
Avoid whenno one can run upgrades
OptionEC2
Choose whenspecial hardware or licences
Avoid whenyou want no patching
Check yourself
Which compute option supports tasks longer than 15 minutes without servers?

Fargate (ECS or Batch), not Lambda.

91.3

Choosing data stores

In plain words

Pick the data store by access pattern first, then scale and consistency.

The problem it solves

A relational database forced into a key lookup role, or the reverse, causes cost and pain.

What it does

  • DynamoDB: key based access at any scale, single-digit millisecond latency.
  • Aurora or RDS: relational, joins, transactions.
  • ElastiCache: caching and sessions.
  • S3: objects and data lakes. EFS or FSx: shared files.
  • OpenSearch: search and log analytics. Redshift: data warehouse.
  • Neptune, Timestream, DocumentDB, MemoryDB: specialised patterns; check current fit.
Data
OptionDynamoDB
Choose whenknown access patterns and huge scale
Avoid whenad hoc queries and joins
OptionAurora
Choose whenrelational integrity and moderate scale
Avoid whenmillions of writes per second on a key
OptionS3 plus Athena
Choose wheninfrequent analytical queries
Avoid whenlow-latency transactions
91.4

Choosing messaging and integration

In plain words

Use queues for work, topics for fan-out, event buses for routing, streams for replay, and workflows for orchestration.

The problem it solves

Using a stream where a queue is enough costs money, and using a queue where replay is needed loses data.

What it does

  • SQS buffer; SNS fan-out; EventBridge routing and SaaS events; Kinesis or MSK ordered replay; Step Functions orchestration; API Gateway or AppSync synchronous APIs.
  • Keep each message small and idempotent; add DLQs everywhere.
Check yourself
Which service orchestrates multi-step workflows with retries and approvals?

Step Functions.

91.5

Choosing networking and edge

In plain words

Pick network services by scope: inside a VPC, between VPCs, to on-premises, and to the internet.

The problem it solves

Peering meshes and public endpoints for private traffic add risk and cost.

What it does

  • Same VPC: security groups, subnets. Service access: VPC endpoints.
  • Between VPCs: peering for two, Transit Gateway for many, Lattice for application services, PrivateLink for one provider service.
  • On-premises: VPN quick start, Direct Connect for steady bandwidth.
  • Internet edge: CloudFront for HTTP, Global Accelerator for TCP or UDP and fixed IPs, Route 53 for DNS, WAF and Shield for protection.
Between VPCs
OptionPeering
Choose whentwo VPCs, simple
Avoid whenmany VPCs
OptionTransit Gateway
Choose whenmany VPCs and on-premises
Avoid whenper-service authorisation
OptionLattice
Choose whenapp-level routing and IAM auth
Avoid whenraw network transit
91.6

Choosing security and governance services

In plain words

Layer prevention, detection and response: SCPs and IAM prevent, Config and GuardDuty detect, Security Hub and automation respond.

The problem it solves

Enabling tools without a model leaves gaps and alert fatigue.

What it does

  • Prevent: SCPs, IAM boundaries, VPC endpoints policies, Control Tower controls.
  • Detect: CloudTrail, Config, GuardDuty, Inspector, Macie.
  • Respond: Security Hub, EventBridge, Systems Manager Automation, Lambda.
  • Protect data: KMS, Secrets Manager, S3 Block Public Access, backups with Vault Lock.

Org policy example

jsondeny-regions.json
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [{
    "Effect": "Deny",
    "NotAction": ["iam:*", "organizations:*", "support:*", "cloudfront:*", "route53:*"],
    "Resource": "*",
    "Condition": {"StringNotEquals": {"aws:RequestedRegion": ["eu-west-1", "eu-central-1"]}}
  }]
}
91.7

Choosing observability and operations

In plain words

Start with the managed tooling, then add third-party tooling where it fills a gap.

The problem it solves

Teams pay for several overlapping monitoring tools while still missing key signals.

What it does

  • CloudWatch metrics, logs, alarms, Synthetics canaries and Application Signals for SLOs.
  • X-Ray or OpenTelemetry for traces.
  • Systems Manager for fleet operations; CloudTrail for API audit; Config for configuration history.
  • Managed Prometheus and Grafana if you run Kubernetes and want the open source stack.

Alarm to SNS

hclsns-alarm.tf
resource "aws_cloudwatch_metric_alarm" "latency" {
  alarm_name          = "api-p99-latency"
  namespace           = "AWS/ApplicationELB"
  metric_name         = "TargetResponseTime"
  extended_statistic  = "p99"
  period              = 60
  evaluation_periods  = 5
  threshold           = 1
  comparison_operator = "GreaterThanThreshold"
  alarm_actions       = [aws_sns_topic.oncall.arn]
}
Check yourself
Which services provide traces on AWS?

X-Ray, or OpenTelemetry through a collector.

Section 92 of 93

Architecture scenarios part one

6 concepts · about 60 minutes

Four worked scenarios applying the decision method. Each lists requirements, a design, a diagram, numbers and trade-offs. Prices are deliberately left symbolic; use the current price pages.

Goals
  • Design a static site, a three-tier web app, an event-driven pipeline and a batch system
  • Justify each service choice and estimate capacity with explicit arithmetic
  • Identify failure modes and cost drivers per scenario
92.1

How to read the scenarios

In plain words

Each scenario starts with requirements, then picks services by the rules from the previous section, then checks failure and cost.

The problem it solves

Memorising architectures does not transfer. Reasoning does.

What it does

  • Requirements: traffic, latency, availability, data, security.
  • Design: smallest set of managed services.
  • Numbers: estimate capacity with arithmetic, not guesses.
  • Failure: what breaks first and how it recovers.
  • Cost drivers: the two or three line items that dominate.

Quick capacity helper

pythoncapacity.py
def concurrency(rps, avg_seconds):
    return rps * avg_seconds

print(concurrency(200, 0.25))
Check yourself
200 requests per second at 250 ms average needs how much concurrency?

200 x 0.25 = 50.

92.2

Scenario 1 Static website

In plain words

A marketing site with global visitors, a few deployments per day and no server logic.

The problem it solves

Servers for static files add patching, scaling and cost with no benefit.

What it does

  • S3 private bucket for files, CloudFront in front with Origin Access Control, ACM certificate in us-east-1, Route 53 alias.
  • WAF only if abuse is a risk. CloudFront Function for redirects and SPA routing.
  • Deploy by syncing to S3 and invalidating only unhashed files.
  • Availability follows S3 and CloudFront; no AZ design needed.
  • Cost drivers: data transfer out and requests. If 1 TB leaves per month, multiply 1,000 GB by the current per-GB rate.

Deploy

bashPublish
aws s3 sync ./dist s3://example-site --delete --cache-control "public,max-age=31536000,immutable" --exclude index.html
aws s3 cp ./dist/index.html s3://example-site/index.html --cache-control "no-cache"
aws cloudfront create-invalidation --distribution-id E1ABCDEF12345 --paths "/index.html"
Check yourself
Why give index.html a different cache header from hashed assets?

It must always revalidate, while hashed assets never change.

92.3

Scenario 2 Three-tier web application

In plain words

A customer-facing web app: presentation, application and database tiers with 99.9 percent availability.

The problem it solves

Single instances and public databases fail and get breached.

What it does

  • Edge: CloudFront and WAF. Entry: ALB in public subnets across 3 AZs.
  • App: ECS on Fargate in private subnets, 3 tasks minimum, target tracking on CPU 60 percent.
  • Data: Aurora PostgreSQL Multi-AZ with a reader, in isolated subnets; ElastiCache for sessions.
  • Secrets in Secrets Manager; one NAT gateway per AZ or VPC endpoints for AWS services.
  • Capacity: 600 requests per second peak at 100 ms average gives 60 concurrent requests. If a task handles 20 concurrent, you need 3 tasks, plus one extra for AZ loss = 4.

Capacity arithmetic

pythontiers.py
import math
rps, seconds, per_task = 600, 0.1, 20
concurrent = rps * seconds
tasks = math.ceil(concurrent / per_task)
print(concurrent, tasks, tasks + 1)
Check yourself
Why add one task beyond the computed count?

To keep capacity if one AZ is lost.

92.4

Scenario 3 Event-driven pipeline

In plain words

Uploaded files trigger validation, enrichment and storage, with bursts of 10,000 files in minutes.

The problem it solves

Synchronous processing times out and loses files under bursts.

What it does

  • S3 event to EventBridge, then SQS queue with a DLQ, then Lambda with reserved concurrency 50.
  • Step Functions Express for multi-step enrichment or Standard if a human review is involved.
  • Results in DynamoDB; failures to the DLQ with an alarm.
  • Visibility timeout at least six times the function timeout; partial batch responses enabled.
  • Throughput: 10,000 files, 2 seconds each, concurrency 50 gives 10,000 x 2 / 50 = 400 seconds, about 6.7 minutes.

Verify

pythonburst.py
files, seconds, concurrency = 10000, 2, 50
total = files * seconds / concurrency
print(total, total / 60)
Check yourself
What protects the database from the burst?

Reserved concurrency on the function plus the queue buffer.

92.5

Scenario 4 Batch processing

In plain words

A nightly job processes 2 TB of data in under 3 hours using many short tasks.

The problem it solves

A fixed fleet sits idle most of the day, and one big server is a single point of failure.

What it does

  • EventBridge Scheduler starts a Step Functions workflow; Distributed Map or AWS Batch fans out tasks on Fargate or EC2 Spot.
  • Input and output in S3; checkpoints so Spot interruptions only repeat small chunks.
  • Capacity: 2 TB in 200 chunks of 10 GB; each chunk takes 30 minutes on one vCPU task. With 40 parallel tasks, 200 / 40 = 5 waves x 30 minutes = 2.5 hours, within the 3 hour limit.
  • Cost drivers: vCPU-hours (200 x 0.5 h = 100 vCPU-hours) times the Spot or on-demand rate.

Arithmetic

pythonbatch.py
chunks, parallel, minutes = 200, 40, 30
waves = chunks / parallel
print(waves, waves * minutes / 60, chunks * minutes / 60)
Check yourself
How many vCPU-hours does the job use?

200 chunks x 0.5 hour = 100 vCPU-hours.

92.6

Failure review and cost drivers

In plain words

After the design, ask what breaks first, how you know, and what each costs.

The problem it solves

Designs that look fine on paper hide single points of failure and surprise bills.

What it does

  • Static site: origin bucket deletion is the main risk, so enable versioning and replication.
  • Three-tier: database failover time and connection storms; use RDS Proxy if connections spike.
  • Pipeline: poison messages and throttling; DLQ and alarms.
  • Batch: Spot interruptions; checkpoints and retries.
  • Largest cost lines usually: data transfer, NAT gateways, always-on databases, and logs.

Alarm on DLQ depth

hcldlq-alarm.tf
resource "aws_cloudwatch_metric_alarm" "dlq" {
  alarm_name          = "orders-dlq-not-empty"
  namespace           = "AWS/SQS"
  metric_name         = "ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible"
  dimensions          = { QueueName = "orders-dlq" }
  statistic           = "Maximum"
  period              = 60
  evaluation_periods  = 1
  threshold           = 1
  comparison_operator = "GreaterThanOrEqualToThreshold"
}
← PreviousNext →
Section 93 of 93

Architecture scenarios part two

6 concepts · about 60 minutes

The second set of four scenarios covers larger and more constrained designs. As before, numbers are worked explicitly and prices are left symbolic.

Goals
  • Design a data lake, multi-Region active-active, SaaS multi-tenant and hybrid architecture
  • Reason about data consistency, tenant isolation and connectivity trade-offs
  • Produce a decision record and a failure review for each design
93.1

Scenario 5 Data lake

In plain words

Collect application logs, database exports and clickstream for analytics by many teams with access control.

The problem it solves

Siloed exports and unmanaged buckets give no governance or shared catalog.

What it does

  • Ingest: Firehose for streams, DMS or exports for databases, S3 for files.
  • Storage zones in S3: raw, cleaned, curated, with Parquet partitioned by date.
  • Catalog and governance: Glue Data Catalog and Lake Formation (LF-tags for PII).
  • Query: Athena for ad hoc, Redshift Serverless for heavy BI.
  • Capacity: 500 GB per day raw; Parquet at about 4 to 1 compression gives roughly 125 GB per day curated, which is 125 x 365 = 45,625 GB, about 45.6 TB per year (measure your real ratio).

Verify

pythonlake.py
raw_gb_day, ratio = 500, 4
curated = raw_gb_day / ratio
print(curated, curated * 365, curated * 365 / 1000)
Check yourself
What gives column level access control on the lake?

Lake Formation grants and LF-tags.

93.2

Scenario 6 Multi-Region active-active

In plain words

A global service must keep running if a whole Region fails and serve users from the nearest Region.

The problem it solves

A single Region is a single failure domain, and cross-Region distance adds latency.

What it does

  • Traffic: Route 53 latency routing with health checks or Global Accelerator.
  • Compute: identical stacks in two Regions, deployed from the same pipeline.
  • Data: DynamoDB global tables (multi-writer, last writer wins) or Aurora Global Database (single writer, fast cross-Region replicas); choose by write pattern.
  • Design for conflicts: use idempotent writes, per-user home Region, or CRDT-like merges.
  • Test with FIS and game days; cost is roughly double plus replication transfer.

Global table

hclglobal-table.tf
resource "aws_dynamodb_table" "sessions" {
  name             = "sessions"
  billing_mode     = "PAY_PER_REQUEST"
  hash_key         = "id"
  stream_enabled   = true
  stream_view_type = "NEW_AND_OLD_IMAGES"
  attribute {
    name = "id"
    type = "S"
  }
  replica {
    region_name = "us-east-1"
  }
}
Check yourself
What is the main data risk with multi-writer replication?

Conflicting concurrent writes to the same item; last writer wins unless you design around it.

93.3

Scenario 7 SaaS multi-tenant

In plain words

A SaaS product serves hundreds of customers from shared infrastructure with strict data isolation and per-tenant billing.

The problem it solves

Per-customer stacks do not scale operationally, while fully shared stacks risk cross-tenant leaks and noisy neighbours.

What it does

  • Models: silo (account or stack per tenant), pool (shared with tenant ID on every row), bridge (mix).
  • Identity: Cognito or an IdP issues tokens with a tenant_id claim; the API uses it for every data access.
  • Data isolation: DynamoDB with tenant ID as partition key prefix and IAM conditions via dynamodb:LeadingKeys, or schema/row-level security in PostgreSQL.
  • Noisy neighbour control: usage plans, per-tenant throttles, and tenant-aware metrics.
  • Cost attribution: tag where possible; otherwise allocate by usage metrics.

Leading keys condition

jsontenant-policy.json
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [{
    "Effect": "Allow",
    "Action": ["dynamodb:GetItem", "dynamodb:PutItem", "dynamodb:Query"],
    "Resource": "arn:aws:dynamodb:eu-west-1:111122223333:table/data",
    "Condition": {"ForAllValues:StringEquals": {"dynamodb:LeadingKeys": ["${aws:PrincipalTag/TenantId}"]}}
  }]
}
Check yourself
What stops a tenant reading another tenant's items in DynamoDB?

An IAM LeadingKeys condition bound to the tenant identity, plus tenant checks in code.

93.4

Scenario 8 Hybrid with on-premises

In plain words

Core databases stay in a data centre for now while new services run in AWS and must call them with low latency.

The problem it solves

Moving everything at once is risky, but split systems need secure and reliable connectivity and shared identity.

What it does

  • Connectivity: two Direct Connect locations with a VPN backup into a Transit Gateway.
  • DNS: Route 53 Resolver inbound and outbound endpoints.
  • Identity: IAM Identity Center federated with the corporate IdP; AD Connector or Managed AD for Windows workloads.
  • Data movement: DMS and DataSync; S3 as landing zone; Storage Gateway for file access.
  • Plan the exit: dependencies mapped, then migrate in waves.
  • Latency: a 60 km fibre path adds about 0.3 ms one way at 5 microseconds per km; measure real round trip times.

Verify the latency arithmetic

pythonlatency.py
km, us_per_km = 60, 5
one_way_ms = km * us_per_km / 1000
print(one_way_ms, one_way_ms * 2)
93.5

Choosing between the eight designs

In plain words

Real systems combine patterns. Use the same questions to select which parts you need.

The problem it solves

Copying a reference architecture whole imports complexity you do not need.

What it does

  • Start with the simplest scenario that meets requirements.
  • Add multi-Region only for a measured business need; Multi-AZ covers most availability goals.
  • Add silo tenancy only for compliance or very large customers.
  • Add Direct Connect when VPN bandwidth or latency is insufficient.
  • Revisit annually, and after every major incident.
Add complexity when
OptionMulti-Region active-active
Choose whenRTO of seconds across a Region failure is required
Avoid whenMulti-AZ already meets the SLO
OptionSilo tenancy
Choose whencontracts or regulation require isolation
Avoid whentenants are small and numerous
OptionDirect Connect
Choose whensteady high bandwidth or strict latency
Avoid whenoccasional small transfers
Check yourself
When is multi-Region justified?

When a measured business need exceeds what Multi-AZ can deliver.

93.6

Failure review and decision records

In plain words

End every design with a failure review and a written decision record.

The problem it solves

Without a record, the reasons behind a design are lost and repeated debates follow.

What it does

  • Failure review table: component, failure, detection, impact, recovery.
  • Decision record: context, options, decision, consequences, revisit trigger.
  • Keep both in the repository next to the infrastructure code.
  • Review after incidents and update.

Failure table as data

yamlfailure-review.yaml
- component: Aurora writer
  failure: AZ outage
  detection: CloudWatch alarm and RDS events
  impact: writes pause for the failover time
  recovery: automatic failover to the reader
- component: Lambda consumer
  failure: poison message
  detection: DLQ depth alarm
  impact: one message delayed
  recovery: fix and redrive
